andersen-little-mermaid-1837:
Hans Christian Andersen published 'The Little Mermaid' in 1837, in his early set of tales told for children. The story, in a classic English rendering from his collected Fairy Tales, is the source of the modern mermaid tale. It is far sadder than the films that borrowed it.

The youngest daughter of the Sea King longs for the world above the waves and for a human soul. She trades her voice to a sea witch for legs, and wins the prince's love but not his hand. Refusing to kill him to save herself, she dissolves into foam, and is lifted toward a new hope. Andersen's tale turns on love, pain, and the hunger for an immortal soul.
arxiv-2510-00137:
Nima Sheikholeslami and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on training search engines that use neural networks. Such retrievers score documents against a query, and good ranking needs high scores for relevant items. The standard training loss, they prove, ignores how well scores separate good from bad items. That flaw leaves scores poorly calibrated for later use, such as retrieval-augmented generation.

The team proposes the MW loss, which directly targets the area under the ROC curve. It pushes each relevant document's score above each irrelevant one's score. The authors prove the loss upper-bounds a natural measure of ranking error. In tests, retrievers trained with MW loss beat contrastive ones on ranking quality and calibration. The gains held both inside and outside the training data's home territory. The paper also urges AUC as a standard diagnostic for retrievers.
arxiv-2510-00237:
Xiaofeng Lin and three colleagues published this 2025 paper challenging a popular claim about fine-tuning language models. The common story says supervised fine-tuning merely memorizes, while reinforcement learning truly generalizes. The authors test that story on two decision-making benchmarks, Sokoban and a card arithmetic game. They find the blame lies largely with how the training data was written.

When training used one fixed instruction template, models clung to its wording and failed on rephrasings. Adding varied prompt wording during training broke that shortcut and restored strong generalization. For harder tasks, chain-of-thought demonstrations gave the model an algorithmic scaffold to transfer. Combining prompt variety with chain-of-thought matched or beat reinforcement learning on their benchmarks. The authors argue the fix is data curation, keeping fine-tuning's simplicity and stability intact.
arxiv-2510-00437:
Xiaokai Chang and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on primal-dual splitting algorithms for hard optimization problems. The Chambolle-Pock algorithm is a workhorse for structured convex problems in imaging and beyond. Its step sizes, though, must stay inside a restrictive range for proof of convergence. The authors extend a convex-combination trick from saddle-point problems to composite monotone inclusions, a broader problem class.

Their new scheme keeps both an extrapolation step and the convex combination step. Rewritten as a fixed-point iteration, it converges under a far more relaxed step-size condition. The authors prove a matching sublinear convergence rate for the method. A concrete example shows the relaxed condition cannot be loosened any further. Benchmarks on image denoising, inpainting, matrix games, and LASSO problems beat leading rivals. Bigger safe steps translate directly into fewer iterations on real problems.
arxiv-2510-00837:
Ott and four co-authors tackle hierarchical classification in this 2025 arXiv paper on contrastive learning. Many real label systems form trees, from biological taxonomy to product catalogues, yet standard classifiers treat classes as a flat list. That throws away the relationships between levels, along with useful training signals. The authors propose two hierarchical contrastive learning methods that identify which features matter at each level of the tree.

One variant clusters embeddings with a Gaussian mixture model, while the other uses attention to select level-specific features, mimicking human processing. Both model class imbalance at higher levels of the hierarchy explicitly. On CIFAR-100 and ModelNet40, the methods reached state-of-the-art results in linear evaluation. They beat earlier hierarchical contrastive methods by about two accuracy points in the authors' comparisons.
arxiv-2510-00937:
Opper and Reich control digital twins whose physical counterparts are only partially observed, in this 2025 arXiv paper on stochastic control. A digital twin mirrors a physical system, but sensors see that system noisily and incompletely, which breaks most optimal control machinery. Control for fully observed diffusions is well understood through Bellman's principle or Pontryagin's maximum principle. The authors merge two newer tools to handle the partial case.

Ensemble Kalman filtering assimilates incoming measurements into the twin's state estimate online. The McKean-Pontryagin approach then derives control laws from coupled mean-field equations for states and co-states. Because filtering and control are computed simultaneously and interactively, no separation principle is needed. Numerical tests on a controlled Lorenz-63 system and an inverted pendulum show the framework working in real time. The authors pitch it at weather prediction, medicine, and engineering twins, with deeper theory left open.
arxiv-2510-01137:
Dadsetan and Rudzicz make private fine-tuning of language models more sample-efficient in this 2025 arXiv paper. Differentially private training adds noise to gradients so individual data points stay protected, but that noise wrecks the gradient matrix's natural low-rank structure. Optimization then slows, and teams burn more data and compute to reach the same quality. The authors treat the noised gradient as a corrupted matrix and repair it after the fact.

Their algorithm uses random matrix theory to denoise the gradient and restore its low-rank shape and signal alignment. Because it is only post-processing, the privacy guarantee of the underlying method stays intact. Applied to fine-tuning RoBERTa on GLUE tasks, the method improved sample efficiency over leading approaches. Training time dropped substantially when near-optimal performance was acceptable, which suits many practical private deployments.
arxiv-2510-01237:
Nandakishor proposes judging a language model's confidence before it writes anything, then routing the question accordingly. Hallucinations are usually fought after generation, which wastes compute and still leaks errors. Three signals combine into one reliability score in this design.

Internal representation alignment, layer-by-layer convergence, and a learned confidence estimator vote together. High confidence earns local generation, middling scores trigger retrieval, and the weakest cases go to bigger models or humans. Tests on knowledge-heavy questions detected hallucinations far better than baseline checks. Costs fell substantially compared with post-hoc correction pipelines. Four pathways sort questions by trust instead of treating all alike. Retrieval support rescues the middle band without overspending. False alarms stayed rare, which keeps the human queue short. Pre-generation checks cost less than post-hoc repairs by design. Reliability becomes a routing decision, made early and cheaply.
arxiv-2510-01337:
Lachapelle asks when actions learned from raw video, without any labels, can be trusted to mean what they should. Latent action policies promise robot skills from unlabeled footage, a huge prize. Without care, though, the learned action codes may scramble the true controls beyond recognition.

The paper spells out what a good latent action representation must satisfy. Statistical benefits and specific failure sources receive formal treatment. An entropy-regularized objective provably identifies the right representation under stated conditions. The analysis also explains the empirical success of discrete action codes in current practice. Behavior cloning's label hunger is the pain point being relieved. Injectivity of the action map is the mathematical heart of the proof. Entropy regularization does quiet but decisive work in the objective. Video-only learning scales where labeled demonstrations cannot. Identifiability turns a heuristic into a guarantee.
arxiv-2510-01537:
Rani and co-authors run a month-long test of whether chatting with an AI teaches people to spot fake news on their own. Sixty-seven participants judged headline and image pairs, discussed their calls with an AI helper, then faced fresh items without help. Belief correction and skill building are different goals, and the study separates them.

Help worked while it lasted, lifting accuracy sharply during assisted sessions. Yet unassisted performance on new items fell markedly by the fourth week. The system corrected beliefs without building lasting judgment, and reliance grew instead. Designers who want real discernment must train the skill itself, not just supply answers. The AI partner explained verdicts, which felt like tutoring during the assisted rounds. Dependency grew quietly because the help never faded or asked learners to try first. Weekly waves let the team watch skill, not just scores.
arxiv-2510-01637:
Xie and co-authors watermark language-model output in a way that reveals exactly where someone later edited the text. Watermarks normally just certify origin, but real outputs get revised, paraphrased, and spoofed after generation. Their framework partitions the vocabulary into disjoint subsets and enforces a combinatorial pattern across them during writing.

A global statistic detects the watermark's presence overall. Lightweight local statistics then flag the neighborhoods where edits disturbed the pattern. Tests across editing scenarios on open models showed strong localization accuracy. Provenance survives revision, and tampering leaves a map of itself behind. Type-I error and detection accuracy grade the new task formally. Deterministic patterns make deviations mechanically visible. Rolling hashes could cut the localization cost further in principle. Human revision and spoofing attacks are both in scope. Edits stop being invisible once the underlying pattern breaks.
arxiv-2510-01737:
MacKay examines whether whole economies can obey a law like the second law of thermodynamics in this 2025 paper. Earlier work with Chater had derived an entropy function for exchange economies from a list of axioms. Under those axioms, a change of state is possible only when total entropy does not fall. MacKay asks whether concrete agent-based models actually meet those axioms.

The models cover crowds of agents who meet in pairs and swap durable goods, including money. Each swap is weighted by the agents' utility for the outcome. MacKay proves that a large class of these models satisfies the axioms in the thermodynamic limit, where the number of agents grows without bound. In that limit the entropy takes a clean form. It equals the logarithm of the partition function of the models' stationary distribution. The result ties economic entropy to money flow, prices, and a notion of economic temperature.
arxiv-2510-01937:
Capobianco, Hartmann, Kunz, and Vas study light rings around spinning black holes in a swirling universe in this 2025 relativity paper. A swirling background rotates the whole spacetime around the hole. The black hole's own spin then interacts with that background swirl. This spin-spin coupling breaks the symmetry between the upper and lower hemispheres.

The team computed photon rings and shadows for these hybrid spacetimes. For suitable spin and swirl values, as many as three distinct light rings can appear. In the nonspinning swirling case the rings usually share features, but here each ring typically has its own radius. The shadow shapes inherit these asymmetries. Conical singularities in the geometry also diverge at a critical combination of the two rotation parameters. Such exotic surroundings could one day leave fingerprints in telescope images of black hole shadows. The work extends exact-solution studies of how environments deform relativistic optics.
arxiv-2510-02437:
Schib and co-authors simulate whole populations of planets born from collapsing disc clumps. Their 2025 astronomy paper presents a synthesis code called DIPSY. Disc instability is a top-down route to giant companions. A heavy gas disc fragments directly into clumps. Earlier population studies leaned on strong simplifications. DIPSY runs an end-to-end global model instead. Starting conditions follow observations and fluid simulations. Host masses span from tiny stars to five suns. The synthesis tracks clump birth, growth, scattering, and ejection across full systems.

Brown dwarf counts from the model match direct imaging surveys. The agreement supports the synthetic population as a test tool. Many clumps form through repeated fragmentation of infalling discs. Dynamical fights among clumps eject large numbers of them. Gas accretion onto clumps also shapes final masses strongly. Future surveys can test the many predictions offered. Formation theories gain a sharper statistical mirror.
arxiv-2510-02537:
Mielke writes teaching notes on two classic ways to measure distance between probability patterns. His 2025 teaching paper explains the Hellinger and Fisher-Rao distances. Hellinger distance compares whole measures, ones that do not sum to one. Restricting it gives Fisher-Rao distances on special families. Bell curve families get treatment there. The notes trace the history back to Hellinger and Kakutani. Relations between the two distances get careful comparison. Their distinct features matter for different uses. A dynamic picture describes curves in Hellinger space through a growth equation. That growth rule replaces the flow rule used in transport theory.

Worked cases cover two classic families of random laws. Product laws and cone shaped spaces also appear. The shortest paths in these spaces receive direct attention. Students gain one doorway into several literatures. Two research fields share these tools. Clear history helps readers place the names correctly.
arxiv-2510-02637:
Mehdizadeh and Hilbert watch language model agents grow social networks and inherit human-like biases. Their 2025 computational social science paper runs a large simulation. Agents powered by four different language models built the networks. The team collected more than a million linking decisions. Agents saw the current network before choosing each connection. Pure popularity ruled the baseline rounds. Agents favored nodes that already had many links. Adding social attributes changed the structure sharply. Age, gender, religion, and political orientation entered the prompts.

Networks then split into like-minded clusters. Political and religious attributes fragmented the groups most. Age and gender shifted structures more gradually. One-way biases appeared in ties between unlike groups. Each model family built noticeably different networks too. Deployed agent societies may polarize by default. Designers of multi-agent systems should audit for this drift.
arxiv-2510-02737:
Corblet, Fox, and Galichon build a model of markets where the same people match again and again. Think of workers and firms who pair up period after period. Each match can change a worker's skills over time. The model extends a classic static matching model from 1971. Prices clear the market in each period. Agents look ahead when they choose a partner.

The team proves that an equilibrium exists for this dynamic market. They show it solves the same problem a social planner would solve. A steady-state version of the equilibrium exists as well. They give two algorithms to compute it. Both algorithms can also be used for estimation. The authors then fit the model to data on Swedish engineers. The fit traces how job-specific skills build up over a career.
arxiv-2510-02837:
Kim and co-authors argue that grading AI agents by their final answer is not enough. Modern agents use tools and take many steps to solve a request. A right answer can still hide wasted steps or made-up facts. A wrong answer can hide sound work that slipped late. The team built TRACE, a framework that grades the whole path an agent takes. It needs no single correct path as a reference.

TRACE keeps an evidence bank as the agent works. Facts gathered in early steps are stored. Later steps are judged against that stored evidence. Scores cover speed, false claims, and how well the agent adapts. The team built a test set full of flawed agent runs with known scores. TRACE graded those runs well, even with small open models. Applying TRACE to live agent runs then revealed habits that answer-only grading had missed.
arxiv-2510-02937:
Tasa-Chaveli and co-authors report a first in interstellar chemistry. They found calcium sulfide gas around a massive young star. The disk is called G351.77-mm1. Calcium sulfide is a refractory compound, one that stays solid except under fierce heat. The ALMA array recorded the disk at fine detail. This find is the first of its kind in the interstellar medium.

One clean spectral line anchored the claim for calcium sulfide. Three more lines, partly blended, backed it up. Two kin species, potassium sulfide and its hydrogen form, showed tentative hints. Their amounts sit about a thousand times below common sulfur gases. Against total sulfur, the gap grows to about five orders of magnitude. These rare species are thus not the missing sulfur store. The result opens a window on the hot hearts of star-forming disks.
arxiv-2510-03037:
Giri and co-authors simulate the largest radio galaxies in the universe. Giant radio galaxies stretch past seven hundred kiloparsecs. Twin jets from a central black hole inflate vast glowing lobes. New telescopes keep finding odd shapes in those lobes. The team ran five three-dimensional relativistic simulations. Jets of low and high power started from varied spots. Each jet fought a different path through its surroundings.

Sky maps at one gigahertz were built from the runs. The shape of the surroundings steered the outcome strongly. Weak jets spread into wide lobes, while strong jets stayed narrow. Wings and lopsided cocoons appeared from that shaping alone. Slowing jets shed thin, magnetized threads inside the cocoon. Those threads lived only a few million years. Bright zones mid-cocoon in strong cases mimicked a restarted source. A sideways fade of brightness can expose a truly fading source instead.
arxiv-2510-03237:
Lima stretches the classic magnetic vortex into wide disks with rings by bending the field theory behind it. Abrikosov-Nielsen-Olesen vortices model flux tubes in superconductors. They are self-dual, flux-quantized, and energetically stable. Lima embeds them in a non-canonical multi-field theory. An O(3) sigma model couples to a gauge field non-minimally. A real scalar field completes the cast of fields.

A hyperbolic extension of the model triggers geometric expansion. Self-dual vortices deform from tight cores into disk-like profiles. Concentric energy rings form around the core during expansion. Spreading the energy lowers its peak concentration notably. Magnetic flux stays quantized despite the deformation. A singularity persists at the vortex origin throughout. The total energy sits below the corresponding magnetic flux. Numerical integration mapped the field profiles in detail.
arxiv-2510-03337:
Lebedev, Kazantsev, and Stasenko present a 2025 arXiv paper on reading emotions from faces when some emotions are rare in the training data. Their data set holds face images sorted into seven emotional states across many ages. Common feelings swamp rare ones, which drags down accuracy for the rare classes. Their network uses memory cells with an attention step that focuses on the most telling parts of each face.

The team trained the model on six emotion classes at a time, leaving one out on purpose. A correction step then tried to restore the missing class without full retraining. Correction worked for every left out class, though the gains varied by emotion. Happy faces, which resemble other classes, were restored best, while sadness and anger proved harder. Scores for small classes rose on test data. The method suits tasks like fraud watch, where the rare case matters most.
arxiv-2510-03637:
Latushkin and Pogan present a 2025 arXiv paper deriving formulas that express solutions of abstract wave equations through the eigenvalues and scattering resonances of the generator. Wave behavior like decay and oscillation is read off from spectral data. Earlier formulas covered self-adjoint operators, but many systems are not self-adjoint. This work builds a resonance scheme by extending resolvents from Banach spaces into Fréchet spaces. Solutions then split into two parts.

The first part is a finite rank contribution computed from eigenvalues and resonances. The second part comes from a partial Laplace inversion whose exponential behavior the authors control. Applications include Schrödinger operators with nonsymmetric complex matrix potentials and linearizations of nonlinear wave equations. Aharonov-Bohm and black box Hamiltonians also fit the scheme. Resonance expansions give analysts a common language for decay across wave problems. Extending them beyond the self-adjoint world removes a restriction.
arxiv-2510-03837:
Fan and Musialski present this 2025 arXiv paper on giving computer-aided design models shape and meaning at once. CAD parts are stored as meshes, and engineers often need each part labeled for editing or analysis. Most reconstruction tools recover only the surface geometry, with no labels attached. The authors add part segmentation to a neural method that rebuilds surfaces from point data.

Their pipeline attaches a small segmentation head to an existing signed distance network called FlatCAD. Training labels come from another tool, PartField, so no hand-made category list is needed. On sampled CAD meshes from the ABC dataset, the labels stayed smooth and matched the true parts closely. Segmentation scores stayed high even when the rebuilt geometry was thin or flawed. Adding the head did not hurt reconstruction quality in paired tests. The approach offers a practical route to labeled CAD models without curated taxonomies.
arxiv-2510-03937:
Tudor wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in probability theory, on deciding whether a random process returns home or wanders off forever. Such processes are Markov chains, where each step depends only on the current state. A chain is recurrent if it surely returns, and transient if it may escape for good. Researchers classify chains using mean drift, the average push at each state.

The paper first surveys the four main drift criteria used for this classification. It then gives a simple new criterion for a borderline case called null recurrence. The main result is a transience criterion for chains whose jumps are uniformly bounded and whose drift fades toward zero. Unlike rival tests, it needs no condition on second-moment drifts. Tudor supplies families of drifts where the new test applies while older ones fail. Sharper criteria help analysts classify chains that model queues, populations, and algorithms.
arxiv-2510-04037:
Salman and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on tracking a moving vehicle's position, speed, and acceleration from distance measurements alone. Radar and sensor networks estimate a target's motion from range signals, and most earlier work stopped at position and velocity. Adding acceleration gives a fuller picture of how a vehicle moves. The authors bring in one extra signal: the derivative of the range rate, which captures how the closing speed itself changes.

Their method works in stages, first fixing position with time-of-arrival techniques. Reformulated least squares formulas then yield velocity in closed form. The range-rate derivative finally produces acceleration, using the earlier position and velocity estimates. Simulations showed better kinematic estimates than existing methods, especially the weighted variant under low noise. The closed-form solutions also ran about ten times faster than the competing method.
arxiv-2510-04337:
Natarajan and Sheffer present this 2025 arXiv paper extending a distinct distances bound from algebraic curves to the far broader class of Pfaffian curves. Given points on two curves, how few distinct distances can they determine? Pach and de Zeeuw had bounded the count for algebraic curves using the proximity technique of Solymosi and Zahl. Pfaffian curves also cover graphs built from exponentials, logarithms, powers, trigonometric functions, and integrals, where algebraic tools fail.

The authors show the same lower bound survives the generalization intact. The number of distinct distances grows at least on the order of the three-quarter power of the two point counts, capped by the quadratic terms. Keeping the exponent through such a wider curve class is the substance of the result. Distinct distance problems sit at the heart of discrete geometry, with relatives in incidence theory and additive combinatorics.
arxiv-2510-04537:
Sharon Mary Tomson, Boris Goncharov, and Rutger van Haasteren wrote this 2025 paper on hearing the mergers of giant black hole pairs. Galaxy mergers should bring supermassive black holes together about once a year across the universe. Pulsar timing arrays can catch the gravitational waves from such events by watching radio pulses. The team built a search method for the signal of a merger. They tested it on simulated array data.

Their signal model covers the inspiral, the merger burst, the ringdown, and the memory shift in spacetime. Test binaries spanned a wide mass range and sat at distances from a few to one hundred megaparsecs. With twenty five pulsars timed for thirteen years at high precision, the signals stood out clearly. The method pinned down masses and distances and located the source on the sky to about a degree. That accuracy could let light based telescopes join the follow up.
arxiv-2510-04737:
Yusuf Amidu, Khaled Elbassioni, and Adriana Gabor wrote this 2025 paper on allocating resources when requests come and go. Cloud slots, beds, and bandwidth are claimed by requests that arrive over time. Each request states how long it stays, what it needs, and what it pays. The operator must accept or reject, without knowing future arrivals. The authors build algorithms on the primal dual method, a classic online strategy.

Their guarantee grows with the log of two spread measures in the data. One spread covers how value density varies, and the other covers how durations vary. They prove results for two variants. One variant adds a load balancing duty across resources, and the other lets a request consume several resources at once. The same framework absorbs the duties without losing its guarantee. Threshold methods reached similar bounds with more case work. A method for many variants eases both theory and practice.
arxiv-2510-05037:
Belén Costanza and nine co-authors hunt for fingerprints of warm dark matter in this 2025 arXiv paper. Warm dark matter particles move faster than cold ones, which smooths small structures. The team uses 1,024 computer simulations of galaxy formation from the DREAMS project. Each simulation assumes a different particle mass.

A neural model reads summary statistics for fourteen galaxy properties in each run. Population averages recovered the true particle mass with high accuracy, reaching an R-squared near 0.94 in their tests. Subhalo gas mass carried the strongest signal of any single property. A fancier graph network on individual halos added little beyond the global statistics. Simple formulas from symbolic regression captured much of the same relation.
arxiv-2510-05137:
Maojia Song, Renhang Liu, and five co-authors design a harder exam for web-searching AI in this 2025 arXiv paper. Deep search questions need several hops of evidence gathering. Most benchmarks leak the reasoning path inside the question itself. A single pass-rate score also hides why a system failed.

Their benchmark, WebDetective, asks hint-free multi-hop questions inside a controlled Wikipedia sandbox. Every model action stays traceable there. Separate metrics score search sufficiency, knowledge use, and refusal behavior. Testing 25 leading models exposed systematic weaknesses everywhere. Models often gathered enough evidence yet failed to use it well. They also almost never refused when evidence was lacking. A companion workflow with verification loops improved both search and synthesis.
arxiv-2510-05237:
Maximilian Bachmaier, Gia Dvali, and Juan Sebastián Valbuena-Bermúdez re-derive a classic quantum effect with classical-looking tools in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Witten effect says a magnetic monopole in a theta-vacuum gains an electric charge. That charge is proportional to the theta angle. The authors reformulate theta-vacua using a massless Chern-Simons 3-form field.

Inside that framework, the monopole's induced charge emerges from effective classical equations of motion. The derivation doubles as evidence that instantons keep a nonzero vacuum susceptibility even under Higgs constraints. Numerical relaxation confirms the monopole indeed acquires the predicted charge. The team also finds the monopole polarizes in a constant electric field. Its oppositely charged constituent bosons separate slightly inside the core.
arxiv-2510-05637:
Iannello and colleagues compute with living neurons instead of simulated ones. Reservoir computing projects inputs through a fixed, high-dimensional system before simple readout training. Usually that system is an artificial recurrent network. Their 2025 system uses a culture of real neurons on an electrode array.

Electrodes deliver encoded input images as electrical stimulation to the culture. Other electrodes record the evoked activity across many sites. Those responses form a biological feature space for classification. A simple linear classifier trained on them sorted digits from a custom dataset. An artificial reservoir trained on the same task provides the comparison. Living neurons bring rich nonlinear dynamics at remarkable energy efficiency. The biological reservoir supported classification effectively in their tests. The work also probes how real neural circuits process information. Low-power adaptive settings are where such substrates look most attractive.
arxiv-2510-05837:
Chen and colleagues fix exploration collapse in reinforcement learning for language models. Verifiable-reward training over-rewards dominant answer modes until entropy collapses. Sampling the same modes then reinforces them further, trapping the policy. Their 2025 EEPO framework breaks that loop with a sample-then-forget rollout.

The model first generates half of its trajectories normally. A lightweight unlearning step then temporarily suppresses those sampled responses. The second rollout stage must therefore explore different output regions. Across five reasoning benchmarks, EEPO beats the standard GRPO baseline. Relative gains average about one quarter on one model family. Another model improves by roughly one third on average. Training efficiency stays comparable to the baseline throughout. Out-of-distribution performance suffers most when entropy collapses unchecked. Strategic exploration replaces indiscriminate randomness in the rollout design.
arxiv-2510-06137:
Maity and three co-authors explain trapped excitons in moiré materials in a 2025 condensed matter study. Stacked two-dimensional crystals let researchers engineer excitons for future optoelectronics. Cheap continuum models often disagree with first-principles calculations, as seen for intralayer excitons in tungsten disulfide and diselenide bilayers.

The team built an atomistic framework around the Bethe–Salpeter equation with localized Wannier functions as its basis. Including dielectric screening from hexagonal boron nitride encapsulation proved essential for matching every observed feature. Their analysis reveals a competition between Wannier and charge-transfer characters. Atomic relaxation shifts band gaps at different stacking regions, and the environment tunes the electron–hole interaction. The lowest bright exciton is Wannier-like in the mixed bilayer but charge-transfer-like in twisted diselenide wrapped in boron nitride. Removing that wrapping flips it back to Wannier-like. Atomistic modeling thus becomes a practical design tool for excitonic devices.
arxiv-2510-06337:
Tuziemski and four co-authors re-examine quantum advantage claims under honest end-to-end runtime accounting in a 2025 quantum physics paper. On classical hardware, runtime is roughly computation plus a small constant. On quantum machines, overhead cannot be separated from computation, so excluding it biases comparisons.

The authors define grounded runtimes for digital and analogue quantum computers. They also set out how to choose strong classical baselines. Three celebrated case studies then fail the stricter test. An annealing result used annealing time as a proxy for total runtime. A Simon's problem experiment ran about a hundred times slower than a tuned classical baseline at tested sizes. A hybrid algorithm's claimed advantage vanished under fuller benchmarking. Their conclusion is blunt: no runtime-based quantum advantage has yet been demonstrated under grounded metrics. Credible claims need careful time accounting and matched classical competitors.
arxiv-2510-06637:
Prakhar Srivastava, Farrin Sofian, Francesco Immorlano, and Stephan Mandt work on forecasting chaotic systems from sparse measurements. Their 2025 paper uses data assimilation, which blends model forecasts with fresh observations. They build on autoregressive diffusion models, a newer generative approach to prediction. Guiding those models with data had been little studied.

Their framework adds a small controller network to a pretrained model. The controller is trained offline by previewing future model rollouts. It learns small corrections that expect data still to come. At run time, the update becomes a single forward pass with on-the-fly fixes. That avoids the expensive extra computations older methods need. Tests covered two classic chaotic equations and six data regimes. The method beat four leading baselines on stability, accuracy, and physical realism. The results suggest learned controllers can make diffusion forecasts both cheaper and steadier.
arxiv-2510-06837:
Abhishek Setty charts a route for solving differential equations on quantum computers. His 2025 paper works within the quantum linear systems framework. The method combines block encoding with a tool called quantum singular value transformation. Differential equations sit at the heart of fluid dynamics and heat modeling.

Setty demonstrates the pathway on a three-band linear system first. He then extends it to two fluid problems, the heat equation and the nonlinear Burgers equation. For the heat equation, his scaling analysis tracks how finer grids change the problem's difficulty. Circuit depth emerges as the bottleneck for the method. The nonlinear problem is tamed by a Carleman linearization, which turns it into linear form. That linearized system can be block encoded and solved in the same framework. The paper is candid about limits. Better estimates of the smallest singular value and shallower circuits are still needed before problems become practical.
arxiv-2510-06937:
He Huang and six co-authors design relay strategies for the vehicle networks of future 6G systems. Their 2025 paper tackles real-time communication among fast-moving vehicles. Cars must exchange safety and traffic data with minimal delay. The vision mixes satellite, airborne, and ground links into one space-air-ground system.

The authors first prove that channel capacity has an upper bound for any fixed number of relays. More relays do not automatically mean more capacity, which surprises intuition. They then propose a cooperative algorithm with a low-complexity rule for choosing relays. Simulations compare their scheme against existing vehicle-to-everything solutions. Their algorithm raised device-to-device channel capacity noticeably in the tests. Reported gains ran from roughly zero point eight to two point five kilobits per second. Knowing the capacity ceiling helps engineers pick sensible relay counts. That keeps ultra-massive vehicle networks fast without wasteful overbuilding.
arxiv-2510-07037:
Rajvee Sheth leads a team surveying how language technology handles people who mix languages mid-sentence. Their 2025 paper reviews code-switching research in the era of large language models. Code-switching is everyday speech for much of the world. Yet most models stumble on mixed-language input, and training data for it is scarce.

The survey is the first map of code-switch-aware research. It spans five areas, twelve task types, and more than eighty languages. Thirty datasets get cataloged and compared. The authors trace the shift from rule-based systems to multilingual pretraining and instruction tuning. Fluency in generation and speech has improved in the model era. Factual consistency and low-resource language pairs still lag badly. Semantic accuracy can drop by up to fifteen percent on switched input. The paper closes with a roadmap stressing inclusive datasets and evaluation. A resource collection accompanies the survey.
arxiv-2510-07237:
Cheng, Miller, and co-authors extend a classic number puzzle into many dimensions. Their 2025 paper generalizes Zeckendorf's theorem. That theorem says every whole number can be written uniquely as a sum of non-adjacent Fibonacci numbers. Earlier work stretched the result to multi-dimensional settings for the Fibonacci rule alone. This team handles a large family of growth rules at once. The rules are defined by a fixed vector of weights that shrinks in a regular way.

Under those conditions, every integer vector has exactly one valid representation of the required form. The proof uses carrying and borrowing steps that reshape any sum into the legal pattern. The result unifies many scattered representation systems under one theorem. It also raises new questions about decompositions governed by arbitrary gap rules. Such unique coding systems interest number theorists and numeral system designers.
arxiv-2510-07437:
Parulekar and Jyothi introduce LASER, a rubric that grades speech recognition with a language model instead of a word counter. Their 2025 paper attacks a fairness flaw in word error rate. That standard metric punishes spelling variants, number formats, and transliteration choices that change nothing in meaning. LASER's prompt teaches the grader detailed error types with Hindi examples, marking which differences deserve no penalty. A top model running the rubric agreed with human judges at a very high correlation level in Hindi tests.

The Hindi-taught rubric transferred surprisingly well to related languages like Marathi and to unrelated ones like Malayalam. A smaller model fine-tuned on word-pair examples learned to predict penalty types with accuracy near ninety percent. That opens a cheaper path to deployment than calling a giant grader for every transcript.
arxiv-2510-07937:
Elbar and Santambrogio wrote this 2025 paper on two interacting populations that spread through space. Species crowd each other and drift toward preferred regions. Cross-diffusion equations capture that motion, with each population responding to the total density. The authors work on a one-dimensional ring to dodge boundary effects. Their diffusion is of fast type, which degenerates in tricky ways. Each population feels its own external potential.

For rough starting data with bounded entropy and a mixing condition, they prove global weak solutions exist. The result extends a recent theorem that covered only ordinary linear diffusion. Handling the fast-diffusion range required new estimates across the full exponent interval. Such existence theorems are the license that applied modelers need before trusting simulations. Cell migration and tumor growth models use exactly this kind of system. The proof techniques may also serve related degenerate equations in population dynamics.
arxiv-2510-08137:
Petropoulos and Antonakopoulos wrote this 2025 engineering paper describing a configurable FPGA accelerator for the matrix multiplications behind neural network inference. The design combines systolic arrays with high-bandwidth memory and on-chip UltraRAM. Two processing unit variants share the same interfaces but differ in computing power. A heuristic schedule moves weights between units to keep the arrays fed.

The authors report notable throughput and energy efficiency gains over prior work on ResNet models. Because the interfaces stay fixed, the architecture ports across models and future FPGA generations. They also sketch an extension emulating analog in-memory computing devices. Adding device noise models would turn the accelerator into a testbed for next-generation analog chips. One reconfigurable design thus serves both today's inference workloads and tomorrow's hardware research.
arxiv-2510-08237:
M. Krtička and A. Couture examine in a 2025 arXiv paper how much a key neutron capture value can wobble for atomic nuclei. The value, called MACS, averages how likely a nucleus is to capture a neutron at star-like heat. Standard codes compute it from average traits and ignore swings in single resonances. Real values can stray far from the average, the authors note.

They simulated many resonance sequences, adding each known source of random variation. They checked how neutrons with different orbital motion add to the total spread. From this work they derived simple formulas that estimate the spread from one spacing value and the star's heat. Real nuclei matched the formulas well in their checks. For nuclei with wide spacing, the expected spread passed twenty-five percent at low heat, so code values need caution there.
arxiv-2510-08737:
Justin Lin and Julia Fukuyama, writing for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, cluster patients by why a model classified them as it did, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Black-box models predict well but cannot explain themselves, a serious flaw in high-stakes medicine. SHAP analysis assigns each feature a value quantifying its contribution to each single prediction. The authors cluster samples by these explanation values instead of raw data.

Samples grouped this way share not just a prediction but the reasons behind it, mapping distinct pathways to the same outcome. A simulated experiment demonstrates the method's mechanics in a controlled setting. A case study then applies it to Alzheimer's disease data from the ADNI database. The authors also generalize the waterfall plot, a standard SHAP visualization, to multi-class problems. They argue explanation-based clustering reveals structure invisible in the raw data.
arxiv-2510-08937:
Serbetci, Chu, and Molisch revisit cognitive radio, the idea of borrowing idle airwaves, for modern 5G-style networks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A secondary system may transmit only when it will not harm the spectrum's primary owner. Much older research assumed simple setups that today's networks outgrew. The authors instead study infrastructure systems where base stations aim multiple beams, and where the exact positions of the primary receivers are not fully known.

They write a detailed protocol that decides, beam direction by beam direction, whether a secondary transmission risks interfering with primary users at their possible locations. The rules are stated as probabilities rather than certainties. They then compute three quantities: the chance of catastrophic interference, the chance of a missed chance to transmit, and the achievable data rate. Each is traced against both systems' power levels and the sensing window, giving planners a realistic ledger of gains.
arxiv-2510-09537:
Arthur Bizzi and nine co-authors, among them Tiago Novello, present FLOWING in a 2025 arXiv paper, a method for morphing images and shapes. Morphing blends one object into another over time, needing a warping that aligns features and a smooth interpolation between them. Neural networks that represent shapes implicitly are flexible and differentiable, but extracting clean morphs from them usually needs costly regularisation and unstable training.

FLOWING instead builds the warping as a differential vector flow, a field of small motions integrated over time. Encoding flow properties directly into the network design guarantees continuity, invertibility, and coherence through time by construction. The approach yields accurate, structure-preserving morphs of two-dimensional images and three-dimensional shapes alike. Across face and image morphing and Gaussian splatting morphing, the method reached state-of-the-art quality with faster convergence than rivals. Code and pretrained models are publicly available.
arxiv-2510-09637:
Thibault Leduque, Maxime Kaczmarek, Hervé Michallet, Eric Barthélemy, and Nicolas Mordant watch water waves change character in a 2025 arXiv paper. They run experiments on two-dimensional random waves in a large tank, measuring the surface shape across space and time with stereoscopic profilometry. At fixed water depth, tuning the peak frequency of the wave maker changes how dispersive the waves are, meaning how strongly speed depends on wavelength.

In shallow water the waves are weakly dispersive and solitons, solitary waves that hold their shape, can propagate. Random forcing then produces soliton gases, dense crowds of these pulses. In deep water the waves disperse and wideband spectra develop weak turbulence instead. Changing frequency and amplitude crosses a clear threshold between the soliton and soliton-free states. The soliton gas reshapes the wave spectrum and the distribution of surface heights, and reflections from the tank walls also leave strong marks.
arxiv-2510-09737:
Paride Crisafulli and five co-authors build large comorbidity networks from Finnish health records in a 2025 arXiv paper. Comorbidity networks link diseases that occur together in the same patients, and their structure can reveal how illnesses cluster across a population. The data come from electronic health records of the Wellbeing Services County of Southwest Finland, coded with the finest level of the international disease classification.

The authors group patients into cohorts by age interval and sex and construct a network for each. Links are kept only when statistically validated, and the networks are then partitioned into communities of diseases. Communities are dominated by a few disease categories, and similar communities recur across cohorts. All communities organise into a hierarchical tree, letting the authors cluster them by shared disease classes. A dismantling analysis further identifies which disease categories hold each network together most strongly.
arxiv-2510-10337:
Zhu and co-authors survey the rise of the robochemist in this 2025 arXiv review paper on laboratory automation. Chemistry has long relied on manual, slow bench work. Some automation exists, but robotics and AI are now joining into autonomous systems that design, run, and analyze experiments.

The authors call this new paradigm the robochemist. They review how far such systems have come and what they can already do, from robotic synthesis platforms to AI that plans reactions. Autonomous labs promise faster discovery and safer handling of dangerous steps. The review maps the field at its cusp, where the pieces exist but integrated, self-driving chemistry is only beginning to prove itself.
arxiv-2510-10737:
Zhiyuan Chen settles a finite generation question for a class of valuations in algebraic geometry, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Valuations measure how functions vanish along geometric objects. Quasi-monomial ones are a tractable family built from simple coordinates. In K-stability theory, a hard problem is showing that the graded algebra attached to such a valuation is finitely generated, meaning a finite set of elements produces all the others.

Finite generation was known for such valuations on models of a special Fano type, in both global and local settings. Chen generalizes those results with a different argument, studying the extended Rees algebra of the valuation. As consequences, his results cover fibrations of Fano type with singularities worse than the previously handled class, plus graded algebras from the multi section ring of arbitrary divisors.
arxiv-2510-11237:
Finding sparse solutions to large linear inverse problems, where measurements are noisy and the system is ill-posed, is computationally demanding. Malena Sabaté Landman and Yuji Nakatsukasa propose faster solvers for this task in a 2025 arXiv numerical analysis paper. The target is regularization with an lp penalty, which favors sparse answers, handled through iteratively reweighted schemes that solve a sequence of quadratic approximations.

Flexible Krylov methods can solve each problem in the sequence efficiently, but guaranteeing convergence makes each iteration more complex than traditional approaches. The authors add randomization in the style of sketch-and-solve methods, sketching the problem down to a smaller size while keeping the flexibility of the Krylov subspaces. For memory-limited cases that need inner-outer schemes, they propose a sketch-to-precondition method that speeds up each subproblem. A variety of numerical examples demonstrate the performance of the resulting algorithms.
arxiv-2510-11537:
Tagging every token in a Vietnamese sentence, for tasks like named entity recognition, is harder than in English because annotated resources are scarce and the language's structure is rich. Ba-Quang Nguyen proposes a hybrid architecture for the job in this 2025 arXiv natural language processing paper. His model, TextGraphFuseGAT, bolts a graph attention network onto PhoBERT, the pretrained Vietnamese transformer encoder, adding explicit relational links between tokens.

The model builds a fully connected graph over the token embeddings PhoBERT produces, applies a graph attention layer to capture inter-token dependencies, then a self-attention layer before classification. Nguyen evaluated it on three benchmarks: COVID-19 named entity recognition, speech disfluency detection, and VietMed-NER, a difficult medical spoken-language dataset with eighteen entity types. The method beat strong baselines, including transformer-only models and BiLSTM-CNN-CRF pipelines, supporting the hybrid design.
arxiv-2510-11837:
Dominik Schwarz proposes a new security architecture for large language model applications. The threat is form-first attacks such as prompt injection and jailbreaking, where hostile instructions hide inside ordinary user input. Current defenses mostly filter outputs after the fact, which Schwarz calls brittle. The root problem, in his 2025 arXiv paper, is that models cannot reliably tell trusted instructions from untrusted data.

His design, Countermind, moves enforcement before and during inference instead. A fortified perimeter validates and transforms every input, using a semantic boundary logic and a text crypter that shrinks the plain-text attack surface. Inside, a parameter-space restriction mechanism steers which internal meaning clusters the model may use. A self-regulating core adapts defenses through an observe-decide-act loop fed by an audit log. Further layers sandbox non-text input and guard context. The paper is a design proposal with an evaluation plan, not finished results.
arxiv-2510-11937:
Arjun Devraj and six co-authors fix a hidden flaw in how cloud giants steer internet traffic. Providers have split up their traffic engineering, dividing the network among controllers working alone so one failure hurts only its slice. The team's 2025 arXiv paper finds the slices can drift apart. Left alone, controllers settle on clashing allocations that overload some links by thirty percent beyond capacity.

Their system, Symphony, attacks the divergence head-on. Adding a quadratic penalty term to each controller's objective makes its allocations sturdy against demand wobbles. Controllers then naturally converge to compatible choices without any coordination. A randomized slicing algorithm spreads critical traffic sources across slices, shrinking the damage any failure can cause. On real cloud wide-area networks, Symphony cut divergence-induced congestion fourteenfold. It reduced the blast radius of failures by seventy-nine percent compared with current practice, keeping the split's safety without its chaos.
arxiv-2510-13037:
Xie, Zhou, Liang, Favaro, and Sesia extend conformal prediction to open-set, imbalanced classification in this 2025 arXiv paper. Conformal methods wrap a classifier's output in a prediction set with guaranteed coverage, but they assume a finite, known label list and split data randomly. With rare classes and possibly unseen labels at test time, coverage can fail or sets can grow uselessly conservative.

The authors build a new family of conformal p-values that test whether a point belongs to a never-seen class. They prove their optimality and uncover a connection to the classical Good-Turing estimator for the chance of encountering a new species. They also design selective sample splitting that partitions training and calibration data by label frequency, with re-weighting that preserves finite-sample guarantees. Simulations and real data showed valid coverage even with infinitely many possible labels, plus more informative predictions under extreme imbalance.
arxiv-2510-13337:
Nekrasov and co-authors extend relativistic reflection modeling for black hole X-ray spectra in this 2025 arXiv paper. X-rays from a corona reflect off the accretion disk, imprinting broadened spectral features shaped by the black hole and the corona's geometry. The lamp post model treats the corona as a point on the rotation axis, which fits data but cannot measure the corona's radial size.

The authors implement a radially extended, ring-like corona inside the relxill model, letting fits vary the source position in two dimensions. Simulated profiles show how the extension changes spectra. Applying it to XMM-Newton and NuSTAR observations of the Seyfert galaxy ESO 033-G002, the model fit well. It placed the source within three gravitational radii of the black hole, while its angular position stayed poorly constrained. A compact corona near the innermost stable orbit explains the data as well as a point source.
arxiv-2510-13737:
Thiele and Teyssier compare three subgrid recipes for how cosmic rays diffuse through a simulated galaxy. Their 2025 arXiv paper post-processes a magnetized, star-forming galactic disk computed with the RAMSES code. Most galaxy simulations just fix one diffusion constant everywhere. Real interstellar gas varies so much that the true value swings by orders of magnitude.

Each recipe builds the diffusion coefficient from local turbulence and plasma conditions instead. All three draw only on subgrid turbulent energy plus standard fluid variables. The resulting coefficients depend sharply on how the local magnetic field tilts. Values span roughly five orders of magnitude across the disk. Midplane cosmic ray energy densities range from about one to one hundred electron-volts per cubic centimetre. Simple estimates then show the galaxy's gamma ray glow hinges on gas density and turbulent confinement. The spread warns modellers that one constant hides real physics.
arxiv-2510-13937:
Iye Szin Ang and co-authors work on automatic rock classification, a problem with stakes for recycling, mining, and industrial sorting, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Identifying minerals from Raman spectroscopy, which reads how materials scatter laser light, is largely solved. Deciding the rock type is harder, because the same minerals form different rocks depending on their proportions and how the rock formed.

The team combines geological knowledge with deep learning and compares five machine learning methods. A one-dimensional convolutional network, which scans spectra for patterns, classified minerals with accuracy above ninety-eight percent, and an uncertainty-aware variant scored nearly as high. On whole rock samples, results varied by rock type: limestone was classified best, while rocks built from similar mineral mixtures were confused more often. The authors frame their system as a step toward better material characterization and sorting technology.
arxiv-2510-14137:
Faezeh Dehghan Tarzjani and Bhaskar Krishnamachari teach a neural network to predict wireless network throughput, a quantity that exact math can compute only at exponential cost, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is heterogeneous multi-hop networks running the p-persistent CSMA random-access protocol, where each device transmits with its own probability and interferes with neighbors near and far.

Simple models that assume one shared interference domain underestimate throughput badly in sparse layouts. A standard graph convolutional network errs heavily, because its symmetric averaging mixes a node's own interference with cascading higher-order effects. Their Decoupled Graph Convolutional Network processes a node's own transmission probability separately from neighbor interference, and replaces plain averaging with learnable attention, yielding interpretable per-neighbor weights. The result is prediction error near three percent, far better than strong baselines, plus gradient-based network optimization that lands within one percent of the optima.
arxiv-2510-14737:
Park, Wang, and Yu study, in a 2025 arXiv paper, image classification where the right label depends on how closely you can look. Hierarchical systems predict names at several levels of a taxonomy, from broad to specific. They usually assume every training image carries a complete, fine-grained label. Real annotation is messier: a distant bird gets labeled bird, a close-up gets bald eagle, depending on image quality and the annotator's skill.

The authors introduce ImageNet-F, a benchmark rebuilt from ImageNet with three levels modeled on human categorization: basic, subordinate, and fine-grained. Using a vision-language model as a stand-in for ambiguity, they generate realistic mixed-granularity labels. Their free-grain learning methods add semantic guidance, through pseudo-attributes from vision-language models, and visual guidance, through semi-supervised learning. Together with strong baselines, these methods substantially improved performance under mixed supervision.
arxiv-2510-14937:
Zhu and co-authors test, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether machine learning can screen for mental illness from real clinical conversations. Depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder are leading causes of disability. Yet primary care providers misidentify depression or anxiety in over sixty percent of cases, and stigma and scarce resources delay diagnosis further. The team worked with a rare dataset: five hundred fifty-three semi-structured interviews, each paired with a confirmed diagnosis.

They benchmarked several model families, including zero-shot prompting of GPT-4.1 Mini and Meta's LLaMA, and fine-tuned RoBERTa models using low-rank adaptation. Across all three conditions, the models exceeded eighty percent accuracy. Performance was strongest for PTSD, reaching eighty-nine percent accuracy and ninety-eight percent recall, meaning nearly every true case was caught. A subtler finding: shorter, focused context segments improved recall, suggesting concentrated narrative cues, not whole transcripts, sharpen detection.
arxiv-2510-15137:
John Ellis and four colleagues revisit one of the leading models of the early universe in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Starobinsky model describes inflation, a burst of rapid expansion just after the Big Bang, and matches sky data well. The team asks how quantum corrections, called radiative corrections, change its predictions once the inflaton field also couples to ordinary matter.

The inflaton's own self-interactions turned out to matter little, since they enter only at higher order during inflation. Couplings to light matter particles mattered far more, shifting two key numbers that telescopes measure in the cosmic microwave background. Using Planck satellite data, the team capped the coupling to light fermions and, with it, the temperature at which the universe reheated after inflation. Newer ground-based data from the ACT survey pointed instead to a narrow allowed range for that same coupling.
arxiv-2510-15237:
Yee Lam Elim Thompson, writing from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, measures whether an AI triage tool actually sped up radiology reports in a working hospital. This 2025 paper studies software that flags suspected pulmonary embolism, a dangerous lung blood clot, on chest CT scans and pushes those cases up the reading queue. The setting is a single large academic medical center.

The study covered more than eleven thousand scans taken before and after the tool arrived. For clot-positive scans during work hours, the average time from scan to first report fell by about twenty-two minutes after the tool arrived, a statistically solid gain. Off hours, the saving was under three minutes and not significant. A workflow model fed with hundreds of thousands of system records predicted similar savings, and Thompson argues that workflow details decide whether such tools pay off.
arxiv-2510-15337:
Yeichan Kim, Ilmun Kim, and Seyoung Park study when borrowing data from related tasks helps a model that fits its training data exactly. Their 2025 arXiv paper sits where transfer learning meets benign overfitting, the surprising fact that hugely overparameterized models can generalize well. The test case is the minimum-norm interpolator for high-dimensional linear regression, which fits every training point yet often predicts well.

Their two-step transfer version first learns from a source dataset, then adjusts on the target data. The authors derive finite-sample risk bounds and pin down when the transfer version beats learning from the target alone. Some regimes are free lunches, where shifted source data helps at almost no cost. A data-driven procedure flags which sources are informative, and an ensemble combines several helpful transfer models. Experiments confirmed the advantage and matched the theory's predictions.
arxiv-2511-00137:
Soichiro Suzuki studies identities and inequalities for an integral transform built from squares of Bessel functions. That transform is central to optimal constants in smoothing estimates for the free Schrodinger formula, following work by Walther. A second expression through the Fourier transform was found by Bez and co-authors for special parameter values.

New identities connect and extend those images for the transform and its linked constants. Harmonic analysis readers get sharper tools for smoothing estimates, which measure how answers of dispersive equations gain regularity. Bessel-squared transforms encode radial pattern, so exact identities translate into optimal constants for physical estimates.
arxiv-2511-00437:
Andrej Arbuzov, Uliana Voznaya, and Aliaksandr Sadouski examine a technical choice in precision particle physics calculations: the factorization scale. In electron-positron annihilation processes like the QED Drell-Yan-like reactions they study, corrections from initial state radiation depend on that scale choice. A poor choice can distort predictions, while a well-tuned one keeps approximations honest.

The authors analyze different prescriptions for setting the scale, working at leading and next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy, where the largest radiation effects are summed in order. They then compare each prescription against known complete one-loop and two-loop results. The comparisons single out the scale choices that track the exact answers best, giving calculators a firmer basis for future precision work.
arxiv-2511-00537:
Peter Atandoh, Jie Zou, Weikang Guo, Jiwei Wei, and Zheng Wang improve sentiment analysis, the task of reading emotion in text. Pretrained language models capture rich context, yet they falter on subtle emotional cues, new domains, and lopsided class mixes. The authors blame weak semantic grounding, poor transfer across language patterns, and bias toward dominant sentiment classes in ordinary setups.

Their framework answers with three parts. Contextual instruction injects domain-aware guidance to settle ambiguous sentiment. Semantic enhancement augmentation paraphrases training text while keeping sentiment fixed, hardening robustness. A multi-refined feature extractor pairs a multi-scale encoder with an affect-aware context encoder. Across IMDb, Yelp, Twitter, and Amazon benchmarks, the system beat strong baselines consistently, with the largest relative gain on the noisy Twitter data.
arxiv-2511-00637:
Emmeran Johnson, Alberto Rumi, Ciara Pike-Burke, and Patrick Rebeschini study adversarial shortest path problems where costs are sparse. A learner repeatedly routes through a network while an adversary sets costs, and feedback is full information. Known bounds for mirror descent with negative-entropy regularization grow with the log of the whole state-action space, even when only a few pairs ever cost anything. The authors show that worst-case bound is optimal, yet blind to sparsity.

Negative entropy provably fails to adapt: its regret still scales with the log of the state count on sparse problems. A family of power-norm regularizers adapts instead, scaling with the log of the number of costly pairs, and a matching lower bound proves that optimal. With unknown transitions, though, sparsity stops helping: minimax regret grows polynomially with the full space regardless.
arxiv-2511-00737:
Jaewoo Park, Chenghao Quan, and Jongeun Lee make privacy-preserving inference fast by flipping where the encryption sits. Homomorphic encryption lets computation run on sealed data, but its cost has confined it to simple tasks, and coupling it with hyperdimensional computing still left batch inference slow with heavy transmission overhead. Their EP-HDC instead encrypts the model itself and runs inference on the client.

Client-side encryption slashes the overhead of sealing and shipping data, and the design scales across many clients while protecting both user data and model parameters. Design space exploration covers quantization, architecture, and encryption settings. On face and emotion datasets with the BFV encryption scheme, throughput and latency for batch inference improved by orders of magnitude over previous privacy-preserving methods, with accuracy loss under one percent.
arxiv-2511-00937:
Bogdan Radovic, Vesna Gotovac Dogas, and Katerina Helisova solve a classification problem for random sets: given shapes produced by a random process, decide which model made each one. Their likeness measure between two realizations comes from estimates, built on data, of a distance built on geometric features.

The features used are the boundary curvature of connected components and their perimeter to area ratios. Both unsupervised and supervised sorting methods are applied on top of that measure. A simulation study with known random set models checks that the method works. The team then applies it to a real task, classifying histological images of breast tissue, separating mastopathy samples from mammary cancer samples.
arxiv-2511-01037:
Mihailo Stojnic analyzes the asymmetric binary perceptron, a simple neural network model used as a storage memory, through the lens of fully lifted random duality theory. The model is believed to show a statistical computational gap: below one density of stored patterns, suitable weights exist, but finding them efficiently may only be possible below a lower density.

Stojnic applies a parametric form of the duality theory and tracks how its key sequence behaves across lifting levels. The behavior changes character after the second level, which he connects to the gap between the two thresholds. Numerical values at the second level give a critical density estimate, and by the fifth level the estimate settles lower, which he reads as satisfactory convergence toward the satisfiability threshold.
arxiv-2511-01237:
Vishakha Lall and Yisi Liu use human gaze to guide object detection in first person video. Where a person looks is a rich signal about what matters in a scene, yet standard detectors weigh every region of the frame equally.

Their framework, Eyes on Target, feeds gaze derived features into the attention mechanism of a vision transformer. That biases it toward regions the viewer attended, with depth awareness built in. Experiments and ablation studies show consistent gains in detection accuracy over gaze blind baselines. The gains appear on a custom egocentric simulator data set. They also appear on public benchmarks drawn from the Ego4D and Ego-CH-Gaze collections. They also add a metric for the importance of gaze aware attention heads, showing how gaze cues reshape the transformer's attention.
arxiv-2511-01437:
Elian Neppel and colleagues describe the software behind MoonBots, a modular space robot system whose parts are spread across computers, networks, and even different celestial bodies. Physical modularity in robotics is familiar; their claim is that software, communication, and orchestration need the same careful modular treatment.

The design combines component based design, a data oriented message model built on ROS2 and Zenoh, and a rollout orchestrator that manages complex multi module builds. At its center sits their open source Motion Stack, proven over months of field work with self assembling robots, inter robot teamwork, and remote operation. The designs support dynamic reconfiguration and decentralized control while cutting linking and maintenance overhead, and the authors propose the patterns for robotic systems at large.
arxiv-2511-01637:
Abjijit Banerjee, Sujoy Majumder, and Debabrata Pramanik work on a uniqueness question in value distribution theory. If a meromorphic function and one of its derivatives agree on a set of values, must they be related? Their setting lifts the question to several complex variables.

They study a power of a meromorphic function on complex m-dimensional space. The power shares a value with its k-th order directional derivative. The derivative is taken along a chosen direction, rather than a single axis. The results extend earlier uniqueness theorems from one variable to the higher-dimensional case. A series of examples accompanies the theorems, showing that in certain respects the conclusions cannot be improved, so the results are best possible.
arxiv-2511-01737:
Obaidullah Zaland and four colleagues test whether fairness is worth its price when phones and edge devices train a shared model. Federated learning lets devices collaborate without surrendering their data. But edge environments are volatile. Resources flicker and client hardware varies wildly. So picking which clients train each round shapes both accuracy and equity.

The team benchmarks fairness-aware client selection methods, RBFF and RBCSF, against random and greedy selection on CIFAR10, FashionMNIST, and EMNIST, measuring fairness, model performance, and time. More equitable selection gave clients a slightly fairer chance to participate, but slowed global training in volatile conditions. The study maps the fairness-performance and fairness-speed trade-offs and points out where current fair selection strategies still fall short.
arxiv-2511-01837:
Isabela Suaza-Sierra, Hernan Moreno, Luis De la Fuente, and Thomas Neeson predict reservoir water temperatures across ten reservoirs. The reservoirs sit in the Red River Basin of the southern United States. The team then insists on understanding the predictions. Temperature governs water management, ecosystem health, and climate resilience, but a black-box forecast alone teaches nothing about the physics.

From more than 10,000 depth-resolved temperature profiles, ensemble and neural models reached high skill, with the best root-mean-square error near 1.2 degrees Celsius. SHAP analysis ranked the drivers: air temperature, depth, wind, and lake volume, in consistent patterns across reservoirs. Kolmogorov-Arnold networks then distilled the behavior into ten progressively richer equations. They are mostly linear and rational in form. Their accuracy rose with complexity, but gained little beyond five predictors. That is a clean simplicity-versus-accuracy trade-off.
arxiv-2511-02037:
Carlos Garcia Diaz, Q. Daniel Wang, and fourteen co-authors study a distant galaxy whose light is bent and magnified by a nearer group of galaxies. Their subject is PJ1053+60, a hyperluminous infrared galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young. The team works with X-ray data from the XMM-Newton telescope and new infrared spectroscopy.

The X-ray glow turns out to be hard to explain. Part comes from a known active galactic nucleus nearby on the sky, and part from massive X-ray binaries in the galaxy itself. That part is about fifty times brighter than local galaxies would predict. The authors conclude that another active nucleus, hidden in the brightest galaxy of the lensing group, is likely adding the extra light.
arxiv-2511-02437:
K. M. D. Chan, D. T. Crommelin, and M. R. H. Mandjes build one mathematical frame for two spreading processes that are usually modelled apart: infections and rumours. In reality the two coevolve, since what people hear shapes how disease moves. Their framework is a general class of interaction-driven fluid-limit models written as coupled ordinary differential equations. It contains classics such as the SIR epidemic model and the Daley-Kendall rumour model as special cases.

For the whole class, the authors classify long-run behaviour under explicit conditions on a dependency graph recording which compartments drain into which. When the conditions hold, vanishing states are expected to decay exponentially, as a stated conjecture proposes; when they fail, decay can slow to an algebraic crawl. Worked examples, including a rumour-dependent epidemic model, show how a small change to the dependency graph can flip the long-run behaviour entirely.
arxiv-2511-03137:
Shipeng Cen and Ying Tan enlist a multimodal language model to help design a better optimizer. Their base is the fireworks algorithm, a search method inspired by exploding fireworks, which struggles on tangled, high-dimensional, black-box problems. Their 2025 framework adds a concept they call the Critical Part, extending the algorithm to harder tasks and letting the model read the search process in several modes at once.

They test the approach on two hard cases: the traveling salesman problem and an electronic design automation problem. Optimizers produced under the framework matched or beat state-of-the-art results on many instances of both. The authors present the work as evidence that language models can do more than write code: they can guide the design of the algorithms themselves.
arxiv-2511-03237:
Souvik Rana and co-authors offer MUTANT, a recipe for building tokenizers that serve many languages at once. Tokenizers split text into pieces before a language model reads it, and poor splits raise cost and hurt quality. The task is hardest where scripts differ widely and words carry rich endings, as across India.

MUTANT pays close care to word lists, training mix, and language-aware pre-splitting. Its India-focused version keeps pieces that respect word structure and scores best among rivals tested. Across English, code, and twenty-two Indian languages, it cut average piece counts sharply versus strong baselines. Faster reading followed, with quality on tests held steady. Detailed side tests show which design choices carried the gains.
arxiv-2511-03337:
Riccardo Tripodi presents audio2chart, a system that turns raw song audio into playable Guitar Hero style charts. Chart writing by hand is slow, skilled work. The system treats chart making as sequence prediction, emitting note tokens step by step in time with the music.

A baseline that ignores audio already predicts charts surprisingly well, which shows how patterned chart styles are. Adding true audio listening lifts accuracy across the board, proving the sound itself carries useful cues. Code for training and use is public, and pretrained models are shared for others to build on. The work opens automatic charting to wider study and to players who want charts for songs that lack them.
arxiv-2511-03637:
Yili Wang, Wenbin Zhao, Che Ming Ko, Feng-Kun Guo, and Ju-Jun Xie test whether a puzzling particle is a bound pair of kaons by watching how it flows in proton-lead collisions. The particle, f0(980), might be a kaon-antikaon molecule or a compact quark state. A coalescence model fed by a hybrid simulation supplies the kaon maps needed to form it.

Predicted output and sideways flow match measurements from two LHC detectors well, backing the molecular picture. Its flow breaks the simple constituent-count scaling that the deuteron obeys under the same settings, though. That breakdown is itself a clue, showing molecular binding leaves marks beyond total counts. Heavy-ion flow thus becomes a structure probe for exotic hadrons.
arxiv-2511-20137:
Chita builds a solar flare detector from radio parts instead of satellites. His 2025 paper describes a VLF monitoring system. Very low frequency radio runs from three to thirty kilohertz. Such waves bounce off the ionosphere's lower layers. Solar flares disturb those layers almost at once.

Distant transmitters supply the signals being watched. Their stations sit thousands of kilometers away. A magnetic loop antenna receives the faint reflections. A low-noise amplifier and converter digitize them. A spectrum analyzer displays the incoming patterns. Data came from a remote, interference-quiet site. Collection ran over several days of observation. Flare-driven ionosphere changes shift the received signal visibly. The setup costs far less than satellite instruments. Independent researchers can assemble it themselves. The D region, sixty to ninety kilometers up, does the reflecting. Magnetic storm warnings could ride on such systems. Accessibility is the design's central virtue.
arxiv-2511-20437:
Bergonzoni, Riso, and Pupillo entangle atoms sitting tens of micrometers apart. Their 2025 paper proposes fast two-qubit gates for neutral atom computers. Today's best gates rely on the Rydberg blockade effect. Blockade works only when atoms sit a few micrometers apart. Wider links usually require physically shuttling atoms around. Shuttling takes hundreds of microseconds, far slower than gates.

Their scheme uses resonant dipole-dipole spin exchange instead. A single smooth laser pulse excites, exchanges, and de-excites the atoms. Optimal control shapes that pulse for speed and fidelity. Atoms separated by more than twenty micrometers can now interact. That stretches the entangling range by roughly an order of magnitude. Gate speeds rival the fastest blockade gates at short range. Fidelities reach levels fit for error correction. Long-range links suit sparse parity-check codes especially well. Quantum information could cross registers without moving atoms.
arxiv-2511-20537:
Staiger and a large team measure atomic nuclei by the light of stripped atoms. Their 2025 paper uses extreme ultraviolet light from highly charged ions.
