Lutetium and ytterbium ions sat in Tokyo's electron-beam ion trap. Their line energies shift slightly with nuclear size. Those tiny shifts encode charge radius gaps directly.

Two charge states of each element were measured and cross-checked. State-of-the-art theory supplied the matching predictions. A new scheme tracks how nuclear shape and surface softness add doubt. Both charge states gave the same radius gap, cross-checking the method. Optical isotope shifts and muonic atom data joined a combined fit. Lutetium-175's radius came out at 5.291 femtometers, below ytterbium-174's. That ordering restores the expected odd-even pattern along the chain. The error shrank threefold versus the 1979 scattering value. A long-standing flaw in rare-earth radius tables is resolved.
arxiv-2511-20737:
Daeheon Jeong and colleagues introduce in 2025 CANVAS, the first benchmark for whether vision-language models can do interface design by actually operating design software. Designers refine screens step by step in tools like Figma, and new models can invoke such tools directly, but existing benchmarks only grade generated code, not tool use. In CANVAS the model works through tool calls, such as creating a rectangle as a button background, inside design software.

The benchmark holds 598 tasks drawn from 3,327 human-made mobile interfaces across 30 function categories, from onboarding to messaging. One task type is replication, rebuilding a whole screen from a reference image. The other is modification, changing one part of an existing screen. Models are scored on structural, compositional, and semantic similarity plus component-level attributes. Leading models issued more strategic tool calls and produced better designs, and the authors catalogue the common error patterns the rest fell into.
arxiv-2511-21637:
Vijay Vazirani unifies an auction used by central banks with a classic market model, in 2025. Klemperer's Arctic Auction allocates liquidity to banks pledging collateral of varying quality, a mechanism the Bank of England and the IMF have used in practice. Linear Fisher markets, where buyers spend fixed budgets on divisible goods, are the theoretical bedrock of market equilibrium computation.

Vazirani shows that an Arctic Auction equilibrium is exactly the solution of a Rational Convex Program, a family of optimization problems with rational data he introduced earlier. That bridge exposes deep structural parallels between auction design and convex optimization. Building on the primal–dual techniques developed for the linear Fisher market, he then derives the first polynomial-time algorithm for Arctic Auction equilibria. A mechanism long valued in financial crises thus gains firm algorithmic foundations.
arxiv-2511-21837:
Bode and Hsueh work in knot theory, the mathematics of loops and tangles in three-dimensional space. A fibered link is the binding of an open book, whose pages sweep around it; a braided open book is a special structured version. Montesinos and Morton had asked some years ago whether every canonically fibered link, one built in the standard layered way, is the binding of a braided open book.

The authors answer yes. Their main new technical tool is the mutual arc presentation. A way of describing two links together with arcs drawn on shared pages, which they consider of independent interest in its own right. They prove that any fibered link admitting such a presentation is the binding of a braided open book. Using connected sum and cabling, they also produce braided open book bindings that are not canonically fibered.
arxiv-2511-22237:
Song, Luo, and Wan, computer vision researchers, protect images from AI forgery by making them invisible to AI. As generative editing makes tampering effortless, detectors trained on yesterday's fakes keep missing tomorrow's. Their proactive trick uses the Segment Anything Model backwards. They add carefully crafted adversarial perturbations that blind SAM to the protected image's content, turning it into a blank canvas from the model's perspective. Edit the image afterward, and the forged region suddenly becomes visible to the model, betraying the tampering.

Naive attacks cannot fully blind a model as perceptive as SAM, especially along edges and textures. So a frequency-aware optimization strategy deepens the blindness and sharpens the localization of later edits. Experiments show effective tamper localization without training on forged examples. The authors frame the shift from post-hoc forensic analysis to proactive protection as the scalable route to image authentication.
arxiv-2511-22337:
Singh, Watanabe, Moser, and Dengel, researchers at RPTU Kaiserslautern and the German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, let experimenters label data by showing hand signs while the data is being recorded. Tools like Label Studio make people annotate afterwards, which is slow with large datasets and unreliable for labels like emotions, where subjects must recall what they felt. HandyLabel instead recognizes gestures in real time and maps them to labels through a customizable web interface, so annotation happens in the moment, when memory is fresh.

Comparing gesture models on the open HaGRID dataset, with and without skeleton-based preprocessing, ResNet50 fed skeleton images performed best, reaching an F1 score of 0.923 on the benchmark. A user study with 46 participants validated the workflow: 88.9 percent of them preferred HandyLabel over traditional post-hoc annotation tools.
arxiv-2511-22637:
Bradd, Higson, and Yuncken open a two-part project re-proving a representation theory cornerstone with geometry. Harish-Chandra's principle says every tempered irreducible representation of a real reductive group is either square-integrable modulo the centre or sits inside one parabolically induced from such a representation. The missing tool is a groupoid attached to the Satake compactification, the closure of the group's symmetric space inside all its subgroups.

This first paper constructs that groupoid three ways and shows they coincide. It is defined first as a topological groupoid, a special case of Omar Mohsen's construction. It is then re-derived from Lie theory, borrowing from Toshio Oshima. It is finally identified with the b-groupoid of the compactification as a manifold with corners. The sequel will use this groupoid and its operator algebra for a proof of the principle, an account of how the tempered dual is assembled.
arxiv-2511-22737:
Jan and colleagues propose an agentic AI framework helping disabled and neurodivergent people eat healthily and keep daily routines. Over a billion people live with disability. Existing wellness tools rarely adapt to their cognitive, sensory, and mobility needs. The design is a three-layer multi-agent system coordinated by a hybrid reasoning engine through a shared blackboard and event bus.

Four specialised agents do the work: a meal planner, an adaptive reminder agent, a food guidance agent for shopping and cooking, and a monitoring agent tracking intake and physiology. Health records, wearables, and smart kitchen devices feed in through a policy-controlled layer guarding privacy and consent, while explainable AI modules state why decisions were made and clinician dashboards aid supervision. Evaluation on synthetic data showed better nutritional adherence, reminder responsiveness, and user satisfaction with fewer caregiver interventions, though real clinical validation is still ahead.
arxiv-2511-22837:
Xie and Li prove a mirror symmetry equivalence for six-dimensional spaces built by gluing cotangent bundles of lens spaces along circles. Such plumbings generalise Smith and Wemyss's double bubble plumbings. Their wrapped Fukaya categories, encoding the symplectic geometry, are predicted to match derived categories of coherent sheaves on crepant resolutions of corresponding compound A_n singularities.

The proof verifies a Lekili-Segal conjecture for these affine A_n plumbings, establishing the equivalence after completion. Localising yields an equivalence between the full plumbing's wrapped Fukaya category and the crepant resolution's relative singularity category. That generalises the Smith-Wemyss result and partially answers their realisation question. As a consequence, when the singularity is isolated, they obtain a faithful representation of the pure braid group on n plus one strands in the plumbing's graded symplectic mapping class group.
arxiv-2511-23237:
Sönnerborn characterizes which quantum states evolve as fast as physics allows, saturating the Margolus-Levitin quantum speed limit. The bound tying a system's minimum evolution time to its average energy above the ground state. The classic result covered pure states and perfectly distinguishable endpoints, but which mixed states, the realistic noisy case, can hit the generalized bound at arbitrary fidelity was unknown.

Using a purification-based proof, he shows saturation happens precisely when three structural criteria hold together, the state lives only on the ground level plus one excited level. Every weighted eigenvector is a fixed superposition of one ground and one excited eigenvector, and those eigenvectors evolve in mutually orthogonal two-dimensional subspaces. The criteria impose a strict rank bound, so no full-rank faithful state can ever saturate. And for qubits he derives a tight purity-resolved version of the bound that recovers the pure-state limit.
arxiv-2511-23337:
Polesello evaluates how sensitively the proposed FCC-ee collider could hunt a dark photon. A hypothetical heavy cousin of the photon that mixes weakly with ordinary light and could connect to dark matter. The study targets dark photons produced alongside a photon and decaying into a muon pair. Scanning masses from 0.4 to 360 giga-electronvolts with a parametrized simulation of the planned IDEA detector across all four FCC-ee running energies.

Both prompt decays and long-lived ones, where the dark photon travels before decaying, are analyzed. And the 95 percent confidence sensitivity on the mixing strength is computed run by run and combined. The Z-pole sample, 205 inverse attobarns, gives the best reach for masses between 10 and 85 giga-electronvolts in their results. While the long-lived search leans hard on precise vertexing of two nearly parallel muon tracks, a demanding benchmark for the future detector's design.
arxiv-2512-00337:
Number theory asks which algebraic number fields admit a Euclidean algorithm for their ideal classes. Sunil Kumar Pasupulati studies Euclidean ideal classes in real biquadratic fields in 2025, from a genus-theoretic perspective. Earlier work by Lenstra reached such results only by assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

Under that hypothesis, a field with unit rank at least one has a Euclidean ideal exactly when its class group is cyclic. Later work aims to remove the assumption in special families. Pasupulati obtains unconditional existence results via genus theory, progress toward proofs that need no unproven conjectures. Biquadratic fields, built from two square roots, are a family small enough to settle completely.
arxiv-2512-00637:
Amr Ahmadain and Ming Yang wrote a 2025 physics paper on strings moving on a cone. In string theory, a moving string sweeps out a surface called a worldsheet. They study a model of closed bosonic strings in a flat, two-dimensional cone, written in polar coordinates.

The authors compute a key quantity, the cylinder partition function, for that setup. To do the math, they first place the worldsheet on a rectangular lattice, a grid of points. Then they take the limit as the grid spacing shrinks to zero. Work like this links string motion near a sharp tip to black hole entropy, the count of a black hole's hidden states.
arxiv-2512-00737:
G Channagowdra and a large team of physicists report a new magnetic effect in a 2025 paper. They study altermagnets, a recently named class of magnets. An altermagnet has no net magnetic moment, yet it breaks a deep symmetry that mixes space reversal and time reversal.

Most altermagnets have two magnetic sites with opposite spins, linked by a rotation inside the unit cell. Using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, the team reads each sublattice on its own through circular dichroism. They report a doubled form they call bi-altermagnetism. The finding sharpens how scientists can detect and sort these unusual magnets.
arxiv-2512-00837:
Yukang Lin and seven coauthors present WaterSearch in a 2025 paper on watermarking AI text. Watermarks hide a detectable signal inside text written by large language models. That signal helps prove where text came from, which supports accountability and trust.

Most methods steer token choices as text is generated, then detect the signal with a statistical test. Lin and coauthors take a search-based route that also weighs text quality. Their quality-aware framework looks for watermarked outputs that still read well. Balancing detection strength against readability is key if watermarks are to be used on real products.
arxiv-2512-01437:
Suhyeon Lee and Hyeongyeong Kim study a selfish mining push on Monero in 2025. Selfish mining hides found blocks to gain an edge. The Qubic pool said it ran such a push on the Monero coin network. Claims of that scale need hard proof.

The pair rebuilt Qubic-linked blocks from node and pool data. They found ten spans that fit selfish mining acts. In those spans, Qubic's share of mining power rose to a mid range. It never hit full control of the chain. Their work shows both the real reach and the clear limits of the push.
arxiv-2512-01537:
Eliya Nachmani and Tal Shuster build a new audio codec for speech and sound. Neural codecs now rebuild sound with high quality. Most squeeze sound with stacked vector codes. Those codes limit the shape of the latent space. Correlations between traits are then hard to keep.

Their codec, q2d2, uses two-dimensional quantization instead. That form keeps richer geometry in the latent space. Richer form should yield better sound at the same bit rate. Better codecs cut bandwidth for calls, streams, and stored voice data. Two-dimensional codes also ease streaming, since partial sound can be rebuilt early while later bits are still on their way.
arxiv-2512-01937:
On an energy level of a mechanical system, motion is governed by a geometric structure called an odd-symplectic form. Samanyu Sanjay's 2025 paper studies the special Zoll case, where the motion is as regular as possible: every path closes into a circle, up to a uniform change of time scale.

The question is whether Zoll forms are locally the best possible in a precise sense, systolic optimality measured in a smooth, second-order way. Systoles compare the shortest closed motion against the total volume, a classic theme in geometry. Settling the local question clarifies how rigid these perfectly periodic systems are among their neighbors.
arxiv-2512-02037:
Pairs trading bets that two assets that usually move together will return to their shared pattern after drifting apart. Marek Adamczyk's 2025 study applies deep learning to this classic statistical arbitrage strategy on the Polish equities market, with a twist on how the pair is built.

Instead of a second, highly correlated asset, Adamczyk substitutes a replication of the first asset built from so-called risk factors, chosen to mimic it as accurately as possible. Trading the gap between an asset and its synthetic twin is the strategy's engine. The study tests whether modern learning methods sharpen a well-worn idea on a smaller European market.
arxiv-2512-02137:
If the early universe changed phase, bubbles of the new state would have nucleated, grown, and collided, shaking spacetime itself. Katarina Trailović's 2025 paper studies the gravitational waves from such bubble collisions, with attention to their polarization, a property detectors may one day measure.

New physics beyond the Standard Model could drive a first-order transition in the universe's first instants, long before any light existed to observe it. Gravitational waves from the collisions would carry the news across cosmic time to future observatories. Knowing their polarization in advance helps instrument designers and analysts recognize the signal when it comes.
arxiv-2512-02237:
Young stars grow by pulling in gas from the disks around them, and the rate of that infall shapes how disks evolve and planets form. Sean Brittain and three co-authors trace in 2025 how accretion rates change as intermediate-mass stars age from T Tauri youth toward Herbig maturity.

They compare the younger intermediate-mass T Tauri stars with the older Herbig stars they become, using median accretion rates as the yardstick. How quickly accretion fades sets the clock for planet formation, since planets must assemble before the gas is gone. The evolutionary picture helps observers read a young star's age and future from its present appetite.
arxiv-2512-02737:
Tristan Amadei and co-authors locate drones from their camera view alone, without paired training data. In places where satellite navigation is denied, image based localization keeps unmanned aircraft on course. Standard methods match drone images to geo referenced satellite views.

Training those methods needs large paired drone and satellite datasets, which are costly and often unavailable. The team's self supervised approach learns from reference imagery alone. Cheaper training could bring reliable visual navigation to more regions and missions, from rescue work to inspection flights. Less gear on the ground means more flights can be run by small teams with small funds and short lead times.
arxiv-2512-03137:
Some quantum materials hide particles that carry no charge. Penghao Zhu, Archisman Panigrahi, Leonid Levitov, and Nandini Trivedi look for a way to spot them in this 2025 work. The materials are quantum spin liquids, and the hidden particles are called spinons.

Spinons do not respond to normal electric or magnetic probes, so clear signs are rare. The authors propose using strain, a gentle stretch or squeeze, as a probe. A clear strain response could reveal spinons at work. That would give labs a new tool for a long-standing puzzle in condensed matter physics. A strain probe would suit labs that can stretch samples while watching for spinon signs.
arxiv-2512-03237:
A 3D scan shows shape, but not what things are made of. Nafiseh Izadyar and Teseo Schneider tackle that gap in this 2025 work. Material traits decide how objects look, yet most shape data sets ignore them.

The authors use large language models in two stages to infer materials from point clouds. The clouds come with rough segment labels. Knowing material from shape alone could help robots grasp objects safely. It could also improve virtual scenes, where surfaces must react to light in a realistic way. Coarse segments are enough to start, which suits scans made by fast capture tools.
arxiv-2512-03337:
Who gets to write the encyclopedia is changing again. Aliakbar Mehdizadeh and Martin Hilbert study Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, in this 2025 work. A quarter century ago, Wikipedia's crowd model replaced the old expert-driven standard.

The authors ask whether AI and human encyclopedias rest on the same grounds of authority. They call the shift epistemic substitution, a swap in what counts as trusted knowledge. Their study matters as readers turn to AI text for facts. It helps frame debates on trust, authorship, and truth online. Authority shifts matter because readers rarely check who, or what, wrote an encyclopedia entry.
arxiv-2512-03737:
Searching a healthcare platform is a high-stakes task, where a poor match can point a patient toward the wrong care. Chuyue Wang and colleagues at Meituan and Tsinghua University present AR-Med in a 2025 preprint, a system already running on an online medical delivery platform. Ordinary search methods often miss the meaning of complicated, detailed medical queries.

AR-Med uses a large language model whose reasoning is grounded in verified medical knowledge fetched at query time, reducing made-up answers. To keep the service fast and affordable, the team distils big teacher models into compact student models. They also built LocalQSMed, a benchmark labelled by several experts, to keep offline scores honest against online behaviour. In experiments the system reached accuracy above ninety-three percent, a large jump over the platform's previous system, with matching gains in user satisfaction.
arxiv-2512-03937:
Polarisation in social networks is often measured by scores that also flare up on random networks, confusing structure with chance. Giulia Preti, Matteo Riondato, Aristides Gionis, and Gianmarco De Francisci Morales build a cleaner yardstick in a 2025 preprint on social and information networks. Their measure, DSP, is based on diffusion and has a statistical null model built into its definition.

Unlike the popular Random Walk Controversy score, DSP drops the idea of special influencer nodes: every node can start a random walk. The authors list properties a good polarisation measure should have and test them on reference networks with known shapes. DSP sits near zero for cliques and random graphs, and scores genuinely split networks as expected. Applied to United States Congress data, it shows polarisation climbing in recent years, an interpretable diagnostic for societal fragmentation.
arxiv-2512-04137:
Da Xu presents a conditional proof of the Spacetime Penrose Inequality, a deep bound linking a spacetime's total mass to the area of its trapped surfaces. Penrose proposed that mass must be at least the square root of the trapped area over sixteen pi, a claim tied to cosmic censorship. Xu's 2025 arXiv paper proves the bound for asymptotically flat data obeying the dominant energy condition, for a marginally outer trapped surface chosen to maximize area.

The proof leans on a favorable jump condition that Xu shows is guaranteed by the structure of the optimization itself. Extending the result to the outermost such surface still needs one hypothesis: that the area maximizer is the outermost surface, a point tied to weak cosmic censorship. Xu flags the gap openly, noting merger counterexamples where the general claim would fail without it. Honest conditional progress maps exactly where this famous inequality stands.
arxiv-2512-04337:
Jasper Edwards, Guifré Molera Calvés, John Morgan, and M. Cheung report a rare catch: a solar storm's front edge crossing the radio beams of two Mars craft at once. The craft, Mars Express and Tianwen-1, were sending signals toward Earth when a coronal mass ejection swept through them. A radio dish in South Australia picked up both signals. Their 2025 arXiv paper reads the storm's imprint in that data.

Signs of the storm showed up in signal strength, in pitch noise, and in phase leftovers for both craft. The phase patterns matched closely even though the two signals had quite distinct pitch trends. Time lags between the craft ran from a few seconds to about fourteen, set by whether the wiggles sat on the up or down leg of the path. Such paired readings give a rare ground truth for how storm fronts move and thicken near the Sun.
arxiv-2512-04737:
Luigi Brugnano, Gianmarco Gurioli, and Felice Iavernaro extend a family of numerical methods for fractional differential equations to problems that mix several fractional orders at once. Fractional equations, whose derivatives take non-integer order, model materials and processes with memory. The Fractional HBVM methods, a Runge-Kutta style class, already solved same-order systems well, with public Matlab code that beat rivals. Multi-order systems, common in real work, were left unhandled. Their 2025 arXiv paper closes that gap.

The extension keeps the core design of the first methods while letting each equation carry its own order. Full construction details go with the theory. A new Matlab code handles the case of two distinct orders, with tests showing the approach holds its accuracy and speed. Engineers modeling springy materials, batteries, and living tissue often face mixed orders, so a ready solver widens what can be worked out with care.
arxiv-2512-04837:
Jikang Cheng, Renye Yan, Zhiyuan Yan, and co-authors run a sanity check on deepfake detectors trained across many domains at once. The field chases generalizable detectors, yet real-world fakes vary enormously. Training on large multi-domain data looks like the practical fix. Their 2025 arXiv paper shows a trap inside that fix: differences between domains can swamp the subtle gap between real and fake faces.

Within each domain, detectors rank real and fake well, scoring high on ranking measures. But when the domain is unknown, single-image verdicts fail far more often. The team defines a fresh evaluation setup that exposes this gap between ranking skill and true accuracy. Their results argue that headline scores flatter today's detectors. Honest, domain-blind tests matter before such tools guard elections, courts, or news feeds.
arxiv-2512-05237:
Elizabeth Champion and six co-authors simulate a classic many-body model on a single superconducting qudit — a quantum device with nine usable levels instead of the usual two. Most quantum simulations run on qubits, yet many systems map more naturally onto multi-level units. The model, named for Lipkin, Meshkov, and Glick, is a benchmark for collective quantum behaviour and phase transitions.

By moving into a rotated frame, the team realizes the model's twisting interaction and any field using several simultaneous drives on the one device. With universal control and readout, they study five fingerprints of quantum criticality: dynamical phase transitions, the closing energy gap, Kibble-Zurek-style dynamics, order-parameter statistics, and excited-state transitions. Each protocol extracts its property without knowledge of the system's states, so the recipes extend to harder models. The results promote high-dimensional transmon qudits as a platform for many-body physics.
arxiv-2512-05337:
Minh Vu, Andrey Lokhov, and Marc Vuffray show that symmetric linear dynamical systems can be learned from remarkably few observations. The problem is system identification: watch a noisy linear process evolve — seeing all of it, or only part — and recover the matrix that drives it. Their estimator, built on the method of moments, recovers a symmetric driving matrix with small error in every entry from a single trajectory whose length grows only logarithmically with the system's dimension.

The result holds whether the matrix is sparse or dense, and the estimator needs no problem-specific regularization to behave. Logarithmic sample needs are striking because the matrix has quadratically many entries; symmetry and moment structure do the heavy lifting. For applications like structure discovery — finding which components of a network actually interact — an estimator that is accurate, assumption-light, and frugal with data is exactly what has been missing.
arxiv-2512-05537:
Namu Park and eight co-authors test whether language models can flag the incidental findings in radiology reports that truly need follow-up. Incidentalomas — unexpected lesions spotted while looking for something else — are easy to lose in a report, and current automated systems classify whole documents rather than single lesions. The team put together hundreds of annotated reports with over a thousand verified lesion findings. They compared supervised transformer encoders against generative language models at lesion level.

An inference strategy, feeding lesion-tagged text with anatomy-aware prompts, grounds the models' reasoning. The best anatomy-informed configuration beat every supervised baseline and matched the agreement level of annotators; a majority-vote ensemble of top systems did better still. Error analysis shows the anatomy-aware models reason about context, distinguishing actionable findings from benign ones. The authors offer the approach as an interpretable route to surveillance of incidental findings in workflows.
arxiv-2512-05637:
Denis Grebenkov and Yilin Ye study particles that wander by diffusion and multiply only when they touch a special boundary. Such boundary catalytic branching shows up across physics, chemistry, and biology. Left alone, the population can grow without bound. The question is whether the layout of the space can be used to hold it in check, by adding regions that absorb particles.

The pair sets up a spectral problem of Steklov type and reads the answer from its leading value. That value draws a sharp line between runaway growth and extinction in a bounded domain. It also gives the exact absorption rate that balances birth on the boundary against losses, yielding a steady population. Above a certain catalytic rate, no balance exists and growth cannot be stopped. The framework offers a practical way to design spaces that tame such growth.
arxiv-2512-05737:
Armand Leclerc, Guillaume Laibe, Elliot Lynch, and Nicolas Perez study how pressure bumps and dips shape the ringing of astrophysical discs. Such discs of gas and dust surround young stars, and they are not smooth: pressure rises and falls with radius. The team uses wave topology, a framework that sorts waves by travel bands. They derive a local rule that folds pressure gradients into wave behavior.

They highlight a previously unrecognized frequency mixing the disc's epicyclic sway with sound. They also give an exact test for when a mode branch can cross between the inertial and pressure bands. Pressure extremes act as waveguides for these modes. A mode trapped at a bump can vibrate at any frequency, so it can answer any forcing. A mode at a gap keeps one fixed frequency instead. Such signatures could one day serve as disc seismology, revealing hidden structure from preferred tones.
arxiv-2512-06137:
Alan Chen, Tejas Kotwal, and Govind Menon analyze what entropy does to the training of the simplest deep network: layers of linear maps, no nonlinearities, whose product is a single matrix. This study applies a recent entropy formula as a regularizer. They characterize equilibria and gradient flow for energies depending on singular values.

The landscape turns out strikingly clean. The only equilibria are minimizers, forming one orthogonal orbit. The singular values do not repel. The flow collapses to one dimension, giving explicit relaxation rates. Entropy is concave in the Euclidean view, not in the network's own geometry. Exact results calibrate intuition for real networks.
arxiv-2512-06937:
S G Dani and Ojas Sahasrabudhe revisit a classic theorem about continued fractions, the nested divisions that build numbers step by step. For ordinary real numbers, Lagrange showed long ago that a number built from a square root has an expansion that eventually repeats in a cycle. Extending that tidy pattern to complex numbers has proved tricky, and the literature holds several partial versions.

The authors widen the idea in two ways. First, they allow a more general kind of continued fraction, not just the kind produced by rounding to the nearest whole number. Second, they restate the question using quadratic and Hermitian forms and the sequences of matrices tied to them. Their main result reads as a matrix version of Lagrange's theorem in that broader setting. The same approach also extends a recent result by Hines about complex numbers that resist close approximation, the badly approximable ones.
arxiv-2512-07037:
Josep M Rocafort and co-authors warn that image super-resolution has learned to please the eye at the expense of the truth. Modern models rebuild sharp, lovely detail from small images, but their generative power can hallucinate: changing what a picture actually shows while looking better than ever. People spot such high-level changes easily, yet the standard quality scores used in the field barely notice them.

The team builds the first data set annotated with fidelity scores for several super-resolution models, and uses it to grade how leading systems preserve content. They then test how existing quality metrics line up with human fidelity judgments, finding foundation models better suited to the job. Finally, they fine-tune super-resolution models using the fidelity feedback itself. Both faithfulness to the original scene and perceptual quality improved, suggesting fidelity can guide training as well as judging.
arxiv-2512-07237:
Cheng Zhang and co-authors give video generators a faithful way to understand the camera that supposedly shot their footage. Controlled video generation lives or dies on camera geometry, yet older encodings pretend every camera is a simple pinhole, ignoring the varied lenses and distortions of real devices. Their Relative Ray Encoding describes each pixel's viewing ray directly, carrying the full package: the camera's six-degree-of-freedom pose, its internal settings, and its lens distortion, in one consistent representation.

Two angles, pitch and roll, turn out to carry the secret of fixing the starting orientation absolutely. Together the pieces form a unified encoding that plugs into a pre-trained video diffusion transformer through a small attention adapter, adding under one percent of trainable parameters. Camera control and picture quality both reached state-of-the-art levels.
arxiv-2512-07637:
Hao Yang and ten co-authors wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on how small galaxies point. Satellite galaxies orbit inside a larger halo, and their long axes are not random. The authors ask what those pointing patterns reveal about tides and friction.

They use TNG50, a detailed simulation of cosmic structure formation. Two alignments come under the lens in their analysis. Radial alignment measures how major axes aim toward the galactic center. Orbital alignment measures how they line up with the direction of motion. Radial alignment proves much the stronger of the two signals. Both run stronger for dark subhalos than for visible satellites. Inward and outward movers show opposite orbital behavior, for linked reasons. Tidal stripping, orbital decay, and the radial pattern together explain the split. A mock observer test holds a warning for real telescopes. The alignment seen for Milky Way satellites turns out to be a projection effect.
arxiv-2512-07737:
Andrew Senior and twenty-four co-authors wrote this 2025 quantum computing paper. Fault-tolerant quantum machines need error rates far below what physical qubits offer. Quantum error correction bridges that gap, if its decoder is fast, accurate, and scalable.

No decoder had yet met all three demands at once for key codes. The team introduces AlphaQubit 2, a neural network decoder. It reaches near-optimal logical error rates for surface codes and color codes. Realistic noise at large scale is the setting for those results. For the color code, it runs orders of magnitude faster than rival accurate decoders. On commercial accelerators, it decodes in real time, well under a cycle's budget. The surface code is handled to record distances with better accuracy than leading rivals. The color code is decoded in real time for the first time at such scale.
arxiv-2512-07837:
Selime Beyza Özçevik and Abdullah Dertli wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on number sequences and spinors. Number sequences serve mathematics, physics, medicine, and engineering alike. The authors view them through the broad frame of Horadam numbers, a family that generalizes many famous sequences.

Their focus narrows to the special cases tied to Cartan numbers. On those structures they define spinor transformations, importing a tool from geometry and physics. New types of spinors arise from that definition. The paper then analyzes the key properties of the new objects. Two active research areas, sequences and spinors, are bridged by the construction.
arxiv-2512-08037:
Justin F Niedermeyer, Nathan K Lysne, Katherine C McCormick, and a large team of atomic physicists posted an experimental study on arXiv in December 2025. Their platform is an array of trapped ions, each held in its own microtrap site. Unlike ions in one shared trap, whose motions are always coupled, these ions can have their motional modes coupled or decoupled on demand.

The team shows that a single quantum of motion, one phonon, can be shared coherently among two or three ions. By slowly tuning the ions around a closed loop in their control space, they make the phonon wavefunction pick up a topological Berry phase. They detect that phase through interference, and study how it breaks down when the tuning runs too fast. The work shows how precise control of ion motion in two dimensional arrays can open new many body physics.
arxiv-2512-08537:
Zhen Zou, Xiaoxiao Ma, Jie Huang, Zichao Yu, and Feng Zhao, computer vision researchers in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Hybrid generators that pair autoregressive modeling with diffusion make striking images, but they are slow: one part generates step by step, and the other denoises step by step. Their framework, Fast ARDiff, speeds up both halves together inside one system.

On the autoregressive side, an entropy informed guessing strategy keeps the draft model bold enough to match the target model, cutting rejected guesses. On the diffusion side, a dynamic scheduler lets the autoregressive part lead, and a joint distillation scheme trains the diffuser to work in very few steps. During use, shallow entropy signals filter out weak drafts before they waste computation. Across models, the framework multiplied speed several times over with no quality loss on standard tests, a general recipe for practical hybrid generators.
arxiv-2512-08637:
Cagatay Ayhan and coauthors present a new way to study recordings from groups of neurons in the brain. Modern tools can record spike trains from many cells at once, but it is hard to pull clear signals from such data. Single cells may respond weakly, even when the full group carries useful information about a stimulus.

Their method uses topological data analysis, with a distance between spike trains and persistent homology to capture shape across scales. Tests use mouse insular cortex data recorded during water stimuli at different warm temperatures. The group level patterns separate the stimuli well, even when single neurons do not. Two stability results support the method, showing the patterns hold up under small changes and noise.
arxiv-2512-08937:
Harsh Kumar and coauthors compare advice from large language models with advice from online human communities for everyday well being questions. Advice seeking is a core human behavior. The internet reshaped it first through forums and then through language models. Whether model advice matches the wisdom of a crowd was unclear.

Two studies with expert raters compared top voted forum advice against model generated advice on the same questions. Models ranked significantly higher overall, and also on effectiveness, warmth, and willingness to seek advice again. One recent model beat a newer one on all measures except sycophancy, suggesting benchmark gains do not always improve advice giving. A second study shows human advice can be lightly polished, without obvious signs, until it competes with model comments. The authors draw design lessons for systems that blend model, crowd, and expert input.
arxiv-2512-09037:
Vighnesh Naik and Markus Heyl study why coherent quantum dynamics can persist for a long time in two dimensional magnets with long range interactions. Such systems are hard to predict. The authors join large scale neural quantum state simulations with an effective theory to explain the behavior.

On a two dimensional transverse field Ising model with power law interactions, they observe long lived oscillations after a sudden quench from a ferromagnetic starting state. The explanation is the formation of bound states of magnons, the basic excitations of the magnet. Effective attractive interactions between magnons, generated by the long range couplings, bind them together and slow relaxation. The authors argue the effect is generic for two dimensional long range magnets. It should be directly observable on current quantum simulation platforms,.
arxiv-2512-09137:
Nickholas Gutierrez, Rodrigo Araiza Bravo, and Susanne Yelin compare three quantum architectures. Spin squeezing is a strong resource for quantum metrology. Interacting qubit platforms offer several ways to create squeezing and later reverse it during a sensing run. All models use the same sequence: coherent spin preparation, one axis twisting, field encoding by a weak rotation, time reversal, and collective readout.

A single quantum perceptron reaches the same optimal sensitivity as a quantum reservoir computer, but squeezes faster. Stacking perceptrons into a layered network amplifies that speed up, cutting optimal squeezing time while keeping sensitivity at the Heisenberg limit. Using layers sequentially, so each squeezes the other in turn, makes the two responses add constructively and boosts sensitivity further. With more layers, the gain grows while total squeezing time falls. Network structure itself becomes a metrology resource.
arxiv-2512-09337:
Kentaro Kawato develops better estimators for causal mediation analysis, the study of how a treatment's effect flows through a middle variable, the mediator. Standard estimators, based on influence functions or inverse probability weighting, both divide by estimated propensity scores. That makes them unstable and prone to covariate imbalance in finite samples, exactly when researchers need them most.

Kawato instead builds weights directly, with an algorithm that penalizes how spread out the weights are while forcing rough balance in covariates and the mediator. He proves convergence rates for those weights and shows the resulting direct and indirect effect estimators are asymptotically normal and reach the semiparametric efficiency bound, the best possible precision. In simulations, his estimator beat the standard ones and a regression-based estimator, especially when models were misspecified. He applies the method to a study of how media framing shapes attitudes toward immigration.
arxiv-2512-09737:
Alexander M. Imre leads a team presenting a faster version of tensor LEED, a surface method for determining the arrangement of atoms at a surface. Quantitative low-energy electron diffraction compares measured diffraction intensities against computations for a proposed structure, and they are sensitive to structural changes. Finding the best-fit structure needs many evaluations, which is expensive even with the tensor-LEED shortcut.

The authors reformulate the optimization using a tree-based data structure, a parameter tree, which avoids extra function calls. In their code, they are computed on the fly rather than looked up from grids, removing a limitation of algorithms and opening the door to optimization methods. Built in Python with the JAX library, the code supplies gradients of the agreement factor used to judge fits and can run on graphics processors. Together these changes cut computing time by more than an order of magnitude.
arxiv-2512-09937:
Huidong Hu and colleagues watch two giant eruptions on the Sun change direction as they rise. Coronal mass ejections often start by moving sideways, not straight out, before turning to radial motion. That turn shapes their space weather impact, yet it is poorly understood. Using multi wavelength observations, the team followed two large eruptions from one active region. Both first moved non-radially beneath a system of overlying loops aligned with the eruption's magnetic flux rope.

As they rose, the eruptions bulged sideways on their upper flanks. That lateral deformation swung their direction by roughly twenty-five degrees from the eruption site. The part that had been the upper flank then became the leading edge. The overlying loops never strapped over the rope, but their magnetic tension still gripped its legs and limited radial expansion. The authors call this the first study of lateral deformation during this transition.
arxiv-2512-10337:
Shuo Li and a large team of astronomers rebuilt the catalog of M-type stars from the tenth data release of LAMOST, a major Chinese sky survey. M stars are the most common kind of star in our galaxy, so a clean catalog matters for many studies. Their 2025 work began by purifying the existing list rather than starting over.

The team removed spectra that were not really M stars, fixed wrong dwarf and giant labels, and updated many radial velocities, leaving a cleaner catalog of more than eight hundred thousand spectra. They then predicted temperature, surface gravity, and chemical makeup for each star using a neural network ensemble trained on values from another survey. Their errors came out clearly smaller than in earlier work, for both dwarf and giant stars.
arxiv-2512-10737:
Helen Paffard and Diogo Pacheco study how politics moved into football fandom online. After the Brexit referendum, in 2016 and 2017, campaigners of many stripes worked UK football fan communities on Twitter. These are spaces with fierce collective identities and tribal loyalties. Such loyalties make members easy to rally and hard to convert.

Mixing social network analysis with content analysis, the authors trace how political talk became embedded in match talk. Parties, media outlets, activist groups, and anonymous influencers all appear, mobilising support and provoking reactions. Case studies cover hashtag hijacking, where fan tags were flooded with campaign material, embedded activism inside fan groups, and political megaphones who amplified messages through fan followings. The paper draws out the general mechanisms by which campaigns exploit supposedly non-political spaces, and points toward a broader framework.
arxiv-2512-10837:
Giulio Belletti gives a clean test for when a sequence is q-holonomic. The name marks a q-deformed form of holonomic: the sequence obeys a recurrence whose coefficients are polynomials. His theorem says a sequence passes the test exactly when an elimination condition holds for every subset of its variables. The same test holds for ordinary holonomic sequences. It ties the two theories together.

Two payoffs follow. Several closure facts come with it. Facts only conjectured for q-holonomic sequences now follow at once. More strikingly, Jones-style sequences built from links in any closed three-manifold are q-holonomic. That in turn implies the Reshetikhin-Turaev invariants of those manifolds are q-holonomic in their colours. A test about sequences thus yields a structural result in quantum topology. The paper runs eleven pages.
arxiv-2512-10937:
Matt Wilson connects three fields that rarely share a vocabulary. Agents that act under partial information, the causal structures studied in physics foundations, and logic in computer science. His bridge is a correspondence between classes of agent-state policies for deterministic partially observable decision problems and one-input process functions, the classical deterministic shadow of higher-order quantum operations.

From that correspondence he builds a category of types with a star-autonomous structure, where one-step policy evaluation and multi-agent observation constraints are interpreted by cuts and monoidal products. Observation-independent decentralised problems emerge as the natural home for multi-input process functions, the objects used to model indefinite causality. The payoff is a strict separation result. On some such problem, policies exploiting an indefinite causal structure earn strictly higher finite-horizon rewards than any policy confined to a fixed causal order, a proved advantage for causality itself.
arxiv-2512-11037:
Yuan Zhou and colleagues study active solids that live on curved surfaces, from cell membranes to tissues and engineered materials. Such materials draw energy from within and push back in non reciprocal ways, so cause and response are not symmetric. Most theory for them assumes flat sheets, leaving curvature effects largely unexplored.

Combining a general theory written for curved spaces with computer simulations, the team finds that curvature patterns where activity concentrates. It also opens gaps in the vibration spectrum, shifts special points where modes merge, and creates unusual defect modes. These results lay groundwork for flow and deformation models of living matter on curved surfaces. The work also matters for designing active metamaterials with tailored responses.
arxiv-2512-11237:
Yuxuan Han and colleagues recover the true surface colour of a face, called albedo, from an ordinary smartphone video shot in uncontrolled lighting. Clean albedo capture normally needs studio lighting rigs, which are costly and impractical. In the wild, shadows and coloured light bake themselves into naive estimates, ruining the separation between skin colour and illumination.

Their WildCap method first uses a learned model to relight the footage into more constrained conditions, then applies physics based inverse rendering. A new texel grid lighting model explains leftover artefacts, such as baked shadows, as clean albedo seen under local lighting rather than as skin colour. During optimisation the method samples a diffusion prior for plausible albedo while fitting the lights, resolving ambiguities between the two. Results beat prior methods in the same setting and narrow the gap with studio capture substantially.
arxiv-2512-11437:
Akash Ghosh and colleagues present CLINIC, a benchmark for judging whether language models can be trusted in healthcare across many languages. Medical language models promise better workflows and decisions, yet most are trained in a few high resource languages and are rarely tested for trustworthiness elsewhere. That gap endangers deployments in the linguistically diverse settings where health systems actually operate.

CLINIC evaluates models on five dimensions of trust: truthfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and privacy, broken into eighteen tasks. Coverage spans fifteen languages from every major continent and topics from diseases and prevention to tests, treatments, surgery, and medication. The extensive evaluation found models struggling with factual correctness, showing bias across demographic and language groups, and leaking under privacy and adversarial pressure. The authors offer the benchmark as a foundation for safer global medical AI.
arxiv-2512-11537:
Stefan Hägele and colleagues fuse two views of radar signals to classify objects hidden behind obstacles. Millimetre wave radar senses where cameras fail, in bad weather or under occlusion, and its signals are naturally complex valued, carrying both strength and phase. Progress is slowed by how few labelled radar datasets exist.

RadarFuseNet runs two complex valued convolutional extractors, one on the raw in phase and quadrature signal and one on its frequency transform. A bidirectional cross attention mechanism, weighted by phase information, lets each domain enrich the other before classification. On the authors' own dataset of occluded objects, collected at two radar frequencies, the network beat every comparison and ablation model. The authors present the design as among the first complex valued dual domain fusion frameworks for radar classification.
arxiv-2512-11737:
Charles M Elliott and Achilleas Mavrakis analyze schemes for fluid flow on moving surfaces. Think of oil films, cell membranes, or soap sheets that flow while the sheet itself moves with a set normal speed. The flow obeys the Navier-Stokes equations written on the evolving surface.

The team builds two fully time stepped finite element schemes. A Lagrange multiplier enforces the set normal speed, and Taylor-Hood elements handle velocity and pressure. They prove stability and best possible error rates for velocity and pressure, with care about which geometric data each scheme needs. New projection tools handle the moving time steps. Simulations confirm the theory, and a penalty method is compared.
arxiv-2512-11837:
Mahmut S Gokmen and co-authors introduce Vision Foundry, a no code platform that lets medical researchers train foundation vision models. Self supervised learning can exploit vast unlabeled medical image sets, but the setup work shuts out most clinical teams. Vision Foundry hides that machinery behind a HIPAA compliant service.

It wraps the DINO-MX framework with tricks like magnification aware teaching and light fine tuning. Trials span brain tissue segmentation, lung cellularity scoring, and coronary calcium scoring. Models from the platform beat generic baselines on accuracy and held up across imaging protocols with little labeling. The point is to move expert effort from wrestling servers to asking clinical questions.
arxiv-2512-13237:
Arnab Sharma studies how to train dense retrieval models when training labels are noisy. Retrieval models score which documents answer a query, and they feed question answering systems. Sparse annotation and labeling errors make that training data unreliable.

His label weakening approach replaces a single forced label for each query-document pair with a set of plausible labels. The set draws on both the recorded supervision and the model's own confidence. He tested two retrieval models and one re-ranking model on four ranking data sets, with noise added by a semantic-aware method. Label weakening beat ten state-of-the-art loss functions designed for noisy labels.
arxiv-2512-13437:
Alexander Guterman and Andrey Yurkov open a two-part study of linear maps that preserve the Cullis determinant. This determinant generalizes the ordinary one to rectangular matrices of size n by k, where the matrix is taller than wide. Preserver problems ask which linear changes leave a given quantity untouched.

This first part solves the case where k is at least four, n is at least k plus two, and n plus k is even. All preserving maps are nonsingular and take the form of two-sided matrix multiplication. The square case was solved by Frobenius long ago, and the nearly square case by the same authors in earlier work.
arxiv-2512-14337:
Tony Cai, Abhinav Chakraborty, and Lasse Vuursteen study the cost of adaptation under differential privacy in a 2025 paper. Adaptive methods perform near optimally across many function classes without knowing the smoothness in advance. In non private statistics that adaptivity is often free.

The setting is density estimation under federated differential privacy, which covers both central and local privacy models. For global estimation, the authors prove an unavoidable adaptation cost under privacy, unlike the free non private case. For pointwise estimation, privacy adds another logarithmic factor on top of the known penalty. They propose an adaptive estimator with a new noise mechanism that improves on prior adaptive private methods. New lower bound tools capture the limits of private adaptive inference.
arxiv-2512-14437:
Jingeon An Lacroix and Kiichi Tashiro study a parabolic free boundary version of the Allen Cahn equation in a 2025 paper. The Allen Cahn equation can be viewed as a diffuse form of mean curvature flow, where an interface moves by its own curvature.

In their version, the equation holds where the solution stays between minus one and one, with a gradient condition on the free boundary. They prove an interior parabolic estimate for the interface that is uniform in the small parameter and in time, under a bounded curvature assumption. They also show the normal velocity and mean curvature of level surfaces differ by at most order epsilon. So the interface evolves by almost mean curvature flow.
arxiv-2512-14537:
Miriam Gutiérrez-Fernández and five co-authors generate synthetic heart signals to feed data-hungry medical AI. Doctors map atrial fibrillation, a common irregular heartbeat, from sensors on the skin, but paired recordings of skin and heart-surface signals are rare. The team trained variational autoencoders, generative models that learn a signal's pattern, to invent new electrograms.

One model specialized in normal rhythm and reproduced simulated signals most faithfully. A second, conditioned on rhythm type, could produce either normal or fibrillation signals with somewhat lower quality on the normal ones. Adding a moderate amount of synthetic data improved a downstream reconstruction task, a first proof that the approach helps.
arxiv-2512-14737:
Guanlin Jing and Huayi Qi tackle a privacy problem in the growing Internet of Agents, where software agents talk to each other and someone must later check what was said. Billing, compliance, and accountability all need audit trails, yet reading the messages would expose private content. Their 2025 system, zk-MCP, is built on the Model Context Protocol.

The system pairs zero knowledge proofs with normal MCP exchanges, so a message can be checked for format and type without revealing its contents. Agents can audit each other in both directions, one side reviewing content quality while the other checks usage counts. The authors built the full system with Circom proofs and report that checking stays fast, with negligible added delay.
arxiv-2512-14837:
Raghuveer Garani and three coauthors ask whether neutron stars could expose dark matter that slips into extra dimensions. In their setup, fermionic dark matter can move through added space dimensions, while normal matter stays in the usual three. Dark matter that drifts into a neutron star would settle and build up inside it.

Extra dimensions soften how the gathered dark matter resists gravity, so even a modest amount can collapse into a black hole. Such holes live longer than normal ones and can eat the whole star, leaving a black hole of about the Sun's mass. For likely interaction sizes, dark matter heavier than about 10 TeV may already be ruled out if more than two extra dimensions of femtometer size exist. That bound is far sharper than in the plain three dimension case.
arxiv-2512-14937:
Abhijeet Parida and eight coauthors improve brain tumor scans not by building bigger AI models, but by cleaning up their output. Gliomas are the most common malignant brain tumors in adults and among the most lethal, with typical survival under 15 months. Precise maps of the tumor on MRI scans guide surgery and radiation, yet big pretrained models often mislabel tissue.

The errors include false positives, swapped labels, and breaks between slices. The team's adaptive post processing fixes these flaws in maps from models trained for other tumor types. In BraTS 2025 challenge tasks, the ranking score rose by 14.9 percent for the sub-Saharan Africa task and 0.9 percent for adult glioma. The authors argue the field should shift effort from ever larger models to careful, cheap cleanup steps that clinics can actually run.
arxiv-2512-15337:
Pietro Metuh and six coauthors build a quantum light source that lives entirely on one chip, from layered materials only a few atoms thick. Scalable photonic quantum technology needs sources, waveguides, and detectors integrated together. Their platform uses strain engineered bilayer WSe2 emitters, which sit on multimode WS2 waveguides fitted with grating couplers.

The emitters shine bright, highly polarized light that couples into the waveguides well. Under discrete state excitation, they emit single photons of high purity into the waveguide. Purity measures came out at g2(0) values of 0.003 from one port and 0.076 from cross correlated ports, both near the ideal of zero. The out coupled rate at the first lens reached about 357 kilohertz, implying a waveguide coupled rate of at least 1.68 megahertz. The work opens a path to scalable quantum photonics from van der Waals materials.
arxiv-2512-15537:
Menghua Deng and co authors find anomalous dynamical scaling at topological quantum critical points in a 2025 paper. When a quantum system is driven across a critical point, defect formation usually follows Kibble Zurek scaling. At critical points that are also topological, edge modes may change that story.

Studying driven dynamics of bulk and boundary order parameters in quantum spin chains, the team finds bulk behavior follows standard scaling. Boundary dynamics at topological criticality, though, obey a modified scaling law beyond the Kibble Zurek frame. Tests in free fermion models show the same anomaly in defect production. The findings tie the effect to the interplay of topology and driven dynamics.
arxiv-2512-16037:
Ayush Jain, Rahul Kulkarni, and Siyi Lin survey a fast-growing topic in a short 2025 paper on arXiv. Banks, insurers, and security firms now use machine learning on huge data sets to catch fraud. These systems often act like black boxes, which raises concerns about trust, fairness, and legal compliance.

The authors review big data tools, fraud models such as anomaly detectors and graph methods, and ways to explain model choices. Named explanation tools include LIME, SHAP, counterfactual examples, and attention maps, each weighed for use at scale. They flag open problems in speed, real-time use, and explaining graph and time-based models. The paper closes with a framework that pairs scalable data systems with context-aware explanations and human feedback.
arxiv-2512-16137:
S Fujiyama, K Ueda, and Y Otsuka report heat transport calculations in a 2025 arXiv physics paper. Their material is a molecular quantum spin liquid, a crystal whose magnetic moments never settle into order, even when cold. They computed how sound-like vibrations, called phonons, move through the lattice from first principles.

The phonons crawl at an average speed of only about 700 meters per second, and some modes sit below 10 inverse centimeters in energy. That confines the classic low-temperature heat law to below 2 kelvin. As the lattice approaches peak magnetic frustration, it stiffens rather than softens, ruling out softness as the cause of the spin liquid state. Comparing with experiments, the missing heat flow follows a power law matching two-dimensional magnetic excitations with a Dirac-like spectrum.
arxiv-2512-16337:
Nikoloz Kurtskhalia, Nikolai Maltsev, and Zaza N Osmanov study particles near tiny black holes in a short 2025 paper posted to arXiv. An electron trapped on a magnetic field line near a primordial black hole, one with less mass than a star, gets flung around as the field rotates. Earlier work in flat spacetime defined a light cylinder, the surface where rotation speed would reach light speed.

Adding real gravity through the Schwarzschild metric changes that surface beyond recognition: the modified light cylinder no longer looks like a cylinder at all. The authors compute its new shape, then find the maximum energies electrons can reach given three cooling effects. Inverse Compton scattering, curvature radiation, and synchrotron radiation each cap the acceleration. The results refine estimates of how such small black holes might shine.
arxiv-2512-16537:
Hui Liu and Ligong Bian boost a cosmic origin story in a 2025 arXiv paper. The universe holds more matter than antimatter, and one proposed birthplace for that imbalance is the first-order electroweak phase transition, when bubbles of the new vacuum phase expanded through the early cosmos. CP violation near the bubble walls seeds a chiral imbalance, but usually too feebly.

A primordial magnetic field changes the arithmetic. Through the chiral magnetic effect, the field can amplify the chiral chemical potential that the CP violation creates near the walls. The authors show the resulting baryon asymmetry grows by several orders of magnitude. That lift would let fermion-sector CP violation explain the observed imbalance even where electron dipole moment limits had seemed to forbid it. The mechanism ties magnetogenesis and baryogenesis closer together.
arxiv-2512-16637:
Shuang-Hong Li, Wei-Yang Lai, and Hong-Ying Jin compute the masses of excited light mesons, particles made of a quark and an antiquark, using QCD sum rules. Their sums are pushed to next-to-leading order for sharper results.

To reach excited states, they build several probe currents that include covariant derivatives. The sums run up to dimension-8 condensates, with both loop and quark-condensate fixes. Using Gaussian sum rules, they obtain several spin-2 nonets whose masses match lab data well. Laplace sums add spin-0 and spin-1 states that also fit. One spin-2 current is shown to couple to two distinct states, proof the method can split close levels.
arxiv-2512-16737:
Sayan Dutta and coauthors build coarse-grained models for small organic molecules used in screens and solar cells. Coarse-graining lumps atoms into beads to speed up simulations, but standard models are tuned in bulk and fail at thin film surfaces.

Their fix lets the forces between beads depend on local density, so surface zones are treated unlike bulk zones. Tests on free-standing films show the new models match full atom runs on bulk density, pair structure, and molecule tilt at the surface. The match matters for predicting how molecules line up at interfaces, where device performance is often set.
arxiv-2512-16837:
Arturo de Giorgi and coauthors work out how lab searches change when nature holds not one axion but a whole spectrum of them. Axions and kin are light particles posited by many extensions of the Standard Model, and most hunts assume a single species.

The team derives general formulas for axion-photon mixing with many axions at once. They then trace the effects for light-shining-through-a-wall tests, helioscopes, and haloscopes. Many axions can boost a signal through coherence and interference, or suppress it. By varying test settings across searches, teams can spot the fingerprint of several axions and learn their traits, instead of misreading them as one.
arxiv-2512-16937:
Meir Shimon argues that puzzles about Boltzmann Brains, lone minds formed by chance in an eternal universe, come from the frame used to describe expansion. In the standard cosmic frame, ordinary observers like us look vastly outnumbered by such freak minds, a result that undercuts trust in our own reasoning.

Shimon recasts the same universe in the comoving frame, where space is globally static and masses grow over time. In that telling, ordinary observers hugely outnumber both Boltzmann Brains and quantum freak observers. He takes that as proof the comoving frame is the cognitively stable choice, the one where our place in the cosmos makes sense.
arxiv-2512-17037:
Tobias Rüttenauer, Kasimir Dederichs, and David Kretschmer compare immigrant residential segregation across 717 urban areas in 30 European countries, the broadest such map to date. Segregation shapes access to jobs and schools, yet cross-country evidence at fine scale was missing.

Using harmonized 1 by 1 kilometer census grids from 2021 and 2022, they compute spatially weighted dissimilarity indices for every area. A specification curve over 16,164 regression models hunts for robust links. Segregation runs higher in Western and Northern Europe than in most of the East and South, driven largely by gaps between diverse urban cores and uniform suburbs. Local demography, economy, and housing link strongly; national policy links do not.
arxiv-2512-17137:
Puyang Wang and coauthors present SDUM, a Scalable Deep Unrolled Model meant to rebuild MRI scans under any protocol with one system. Clinical MRI varies by body target, contrast, sampling pattern, and speedup, yet most learned rebuilders serve one protocol only.

SDUM joins a Restormer reconstructor, a learned coil sensitivity estimator, sampling-aware data consistency, and conditioning on cascade step and protocol data, trained with progressive cascade growth. Quality scales as the log of parameters up to 18 cascades. One model trained on mixed data topped all four CMRxRecon2025 tracks with no task tuning, and beat prior winners on CMRxRecon2024 and fastMRI brain tests.
arxiv-2512-18237:
Shahram Najam Syed, Yitian Hu, and Yuchao Yao at Carnegie Mellon University rebuild large scenes in 3D from a single moving camera. Solving depth, camera pose, and radiance separately breaks down at scale. Ambiguous depth creates ghost geometry, pose drift corrupts alignment, and one global neural radiance field cannot hold hundreds of meters of content. Their 2025 framework learns all three jointly, so each part corrects the others.

A vision transformer depth network, trained with metric scale supervision, gives consistent depths across wide views. A feature space bundle adjustment layer refines poses from learned descriptors instead of brittle keypoints, suppressing drift. Local radiance fields are added and frozen on the fly as view overlap drops, covering city block scale on one GPU. On the Tanks and Temples benchmark, trajectory error falls to between 0.001 and 0.021 meters across eight sequences. That is up to 18 times lower than BARF, with no calibration needed.
arxiv-2512-18637:
Suhani Verma and nineteen coauthors present a 2025 method for the motion of radiating point charges. The work combines the covariant Lorentz-Dirac treatment with Landau-Lifshitz order reduction, which removes the runaway and preacceleration flaws of the raw theory. A post-Newtonian Hamiltonian step completes the setup, and energy balance is verified in relativistic single-particle cases.

For many-body systems the team pairs the Darwin Hamiltonian with the leading 1.5 post-Newtonian radiation-reaction term. Simulations of charge-neutral binaries, with equal or unequal masses, show orbits decaying and rounding out, with steady Hamiltonian decrease matching dipole losses. The method mirrors gravitational radiation reaction while staying workable for studies of energy-losing and possibly chaotic motion.
arxiv-2512-18837:
Yuanchao Xu and five co-authors generate data by following a distribution's own dynamics, read through Koopman operator theory. Generative modeling usually needs the target's potential function, which is rarely known. Their method, KSWGD, posted to arXiv in December 2025, learns the Langevin generator straight from recorded paths, since the Koopman operator exposes the distribution's spectral structure without knowing it.

Paired with Wasserstein gradient descent, the scheme holds an almost constant dissipation rate, which yields linear convergence and dodges the vanishing gradient stall of kernel particle methods. A Feynman-Kac reading clarifies the probability behind it. On curved manifolds, multi-well systems, and high-dimensional stochastic equations, KSWGD beats baselines on both speed and sample quality. The work gives operator theory a concrete seat inside modern generative modeling.
arxiv-2512-18937:
Joost Jorritsma, Pascal Maillard, and Peter Mörters chart the exact moment a growing random network gels into one connected piece. In their models, vertices arrive one by one and link to earlier vertices with probabilities set by arrival times, covering uniform growth and preferential attachment. Percolation theory asks when a giant component appears. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, describes the critical window around that threshold in fine detail.

Whenever the threshold is positive, the window's width shrinks like one over the square of log n, with a second phase transition at its upper edge. Inside the window, the largest component holds about the square root of n over log n vertices, and susceptibility stays finite throughout. The proofs couple component explorations to branching random walks trapped in an interval, a technique giving sharp control over a notoriously slippery regime.
arxiv-2512-19237:
Poonam Sharma and Suman Banerjee reframe social marketing profit around motifs, the small recurring patterns inside a network. Classic profit maximization picks seed users whose spread earns the most. Here, profit sits in motifs, and it pays out only once enough members of a motif have been reached.

The authors prove their motif-oriented problem is NP-hard, so exact answers are out of reach at scale. Their method builds on reverse reachable sets in three stages: estimating influence, choosing seeds, and scoring motif profit. Tests on a real social network dataset, plus time and space analysis, show the approach is workable. Marketers can thus target group patterns, not just people.
arxiv-2512-19437:
R. Ammendola and a large PTOLEMY team report first results on an ultra-precise high-voltage system. PTOLEMY aims, in the long run, to catch the cosmic neutrino background by electron capture on tritium bound to graphene. Even its small prototypes chase the neutrino mass, and that demands extreme energy sharpness at the beta-spectrum endpoint.

Electrode voltage must hold steady to a few parts per million and be watched in real time. The chain they built stacks commercial precision voltage references, read by precision multimeters and a field mill. Worst-case precision already reaches a fraction of a part per million per kilovolt board, presently limited by field mill noise.
arxiv-2512-19637:
Carolina Gonçalves and three co-authors turn a quantum effect into a microscope. Their tool is Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. Two photons that meet at a beam splitter tend to leave together. That leaves a dip in paired counts, and the dip shifts with tiny changes. The team aims the effect at clear samples that twist light's polarization. Past quantum microscopes of this kind failed on samples more than a few micrometers thick.

The fix is a photon-pair source with a long coherence length, over a millimeter. That stretches the dip, so normal thickness changes barely register. Shifts in the dip then track the twist in polarization. The team built a stats model and a best-fit method for the local twist angle. Scanned images match classic polarized-light images, while the setup runs at its sharpest setting.
arxiv-2512-19737:
Clément Elliker, Jesse Read, Sonia Vanier, and Albert Bifet recast train-delay forecasting as a simulation problem. Instead of regressing future delays directly, they learn the step-by-step dynamics of how delays propagate, then roll those dynamics forward with Monte Carlo sampling so uncertainty comes along for the ride. Their algorithm, Drift-Corrected Imitation Learning, extends the well-known DAgger method with distance-based drift correction.

The correction fights covariate shift during rollouts without needing an external expert oracle or adversarial training. Evaluation uses a real-world Infrabel dataset covering more than three million Belgian train movements, focusing on forecasts up to thirty minutes ahead. DCIL beat traditional regression models and behavioral cloning on the same data, which the authors credit to respecting the sequential, uncertain nature of delay spread.
arxiv-2512-20337:
Alexandre Landry solves the field equations of a modified gravity theory for an expanding universe filled with an electromagnetic source. The theory is F(T) gravity in its teleparallel Robertson-Walker form, where torsion rather than curvature drives gravity. He treats all three spatial curvature cases, negative, flat, and positive.

For the flat case, Landry finds new solutions of that theory valid for any scale factor form. For the curved cases, he obtains exact solutions plus far-future rough forms covering slow, linear, fast expansion, and expansion without limit. Each solution is written as an analytic function tied to an equation of state for the field. The catalogue is meant for future work on the cosmos, including models of the early-universe plasma.
arxiv-2512-20437:
Paul J Christiansen and co-authors tune a toy climate model with quantum kernels. Lorenz-96 is a small system that mimics atmospheric chaos, making it a standard surrogate for testing calibration methods. Their pipeline automates history matching, replacing classic Gaussian process emulators with quantum versions.

Three quantum kernel designs, distinguished by their feature-map circuits, undergo thorough hyperparameter optimization. A dimensionality argument suggests quantum kernels should be more expressive than classic ones. Statevector simulations confirm two of the three beating the canonical classic kernel at the tuning task. The authors then chart the route to real hardware through shot-based evaluation and randomized measurements. Low qubit counts and shallow circuits make the method friendly to today's noisy devices.
arxiv-2512-20537:
Josh Green, Joshua Snow, and Jingbo B Wang prepare quantum states by unmaking them. Loading a desired state into a quantum computer is a bottleneck for many methods. Their Schmidt Spectrum Optimization method targets states described as matrix product states and works backwards: disentangle first, then reverse.

Classic tensor-network optimization computes layers of two-qubit gates that progressively strip entanglement from the target. Reversing the finished sequence yields a preparation circuit for the original state. Benchmarks cover random matrix product states and approximations to ground states of local Hamiltonians. Against earlier variational and disentangling-based methods, the new method improves results substantially. The authors present it as a scalable approach for a step every quantum method needs.
arxiv-2512-20637:
Tabidah Usmani, Sara Zahid, and Amna Javaid hunt elephant flows, the rare huge transfers that dominate network traffic, across networks that behave differently. Detectors trained in one environment usually degrade in another, a failure called domain shift. Their unified approach adds application-aware and security features to the usual size-based signals.

Evaluation spans campus traffic and two public security data sets, UNSW-NB15 and CIC-IDS2018. Performance swings widely by domain, which is precisely the authors' warning about single-domain validation. Adaptive thresholding and careful feature engineering steady the model, and cross-validation reaches a near-perfect F1 overall. Feature importance confirms size rules the task, with total bytes on top, while the added features sharpen accuracy and interpretability.
arxiv-2512-20737:
Dimitrios Antonopoulos and Dimitrios Mitsotakis explain a puzzling pattern in wave simulations. Finite element methods split a region into small pieces and approximate solutions on each piece. For certain energy-saving schemes, odd-degree polynomial pieces give the best accuracy, while even-degree pieces do worse. Nobody had pinned down why the parity mattered.

The pair show the effect is built into the spaces themselves. A standard projection of derivatives has a special super-approximation property only for odd degrees. They then apply the finding to the regularized long wave equation. Their scheme conserves mass and energy, approximates impulse closely, and comes with error bounds proved in advance.
arxiv-2512-21137:
Murdoch Gabbay proposes writing down what a distributed algorithm means before writing how it runs. Protocols are usually stated as state machines, step-by-step rules that bury the key guarantees. Gabbay instead states them as axioms, in a three-valued modal logic over semitopologies. The axioms fix the traits a correct run must have, while the code beneath can vary. Worked cases cover a simple voting protocol, Bracha's broadcast, and crusader agreement. Two come as full axiom systems.

The payoff is a spec more precise than prose yet more abstract than code. It suits reasoning about correctness, resilience, and failure.
