colebrooke-miscellaneous-essays-vol1-183:
H. T. Colebrooke opened Indian studies to Britain, and his Miscellaneous Essays of 1837 gather the founding papers of the field. Volume I ranges widely over the Vedas, Sanskrit grammar, Hindu law, and astronomy in turn. Colebrooke learned Sanskrit while serving in India and wrote with an accuracy that set the field's standard for a century.

Each essay settled some question scholars had only guessed at before: the age of texts, the shape of law, the reach of Indian astronomy. Together they form the charter collection of British Indology, the shelf where the subject begins. Later researchers built on Colebrooke's groundwork in nearly every branch of the subject he touched.
colebrooke-miscellaneous-essays-vol2-183:
Volume II of Colebrooke's Miscellaneous Essays, also dated 1837, completes the pair with more of his pioneering studies of India. Indian philosophy, mathematics, and literature take the stage in these later papers, each handled at first hand. Colebrooke writes as the first European scholar to master many of these sources in the original tongues.

His essays on Hindu algebra and on the philosophies of India carried whole fields into English for the first time. Read with the first volume, the set shows one scholar mapping a civilization's learning almost alone, essay by essay. The two volumes together remain the foundation shelf of British Indology today.
das-guldne-vliess-oder-das-allerhochste-: Das güldne Vliess, 1737. The golden fleece. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
das-guldne-vliesz-oder-das-allerhochste-: Das güldne Vliess, 1737. Another edition. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc10158837:
The Gene Ontology Consortium reports the 2023 state of its knowledgebase in this paper. Gene Ontology is a shared system for describing what genes and their products do, used by labs across the world. Its terms cover gene jobs in all forms of life, from bacteria to humans, and even in viruses.

The paper describes the current data, tools, and annotation work behind the resource. It notes how the terms are kept accurate as biology advances. For many working scientists, this update is the reference that explains the vocabulary their own databases speak.
europmc-pmc10304137:
Barsouk and co-authors review head and neck squamous cell carcinoma in a 2023 paper, covering its spread, risk factors, and prevention. This cancer group arises in the mouth, throat, voice box, and nearby sites. Together these cancers rank among the most common worldwide, with hundreds of thousands of new cases each year.

The review explains the main risks, led by tobacco, alcohol, and HPV infection. It covers signs, staging, and the standard treatments. It stresses prevention and early detection, where the largest gains in survival are still to be won.
europmc-pmc10338337:
Jiang led a team in 2023 that trained a language model on hospital notes. Doctors write free-text notes on each patient in the health record. Older risk tools need neat, coded data, which is slow to build and hard to deploy. The team named its model NYUTron and taught it on raw clinical text.

NYUTron then took on five forecast tasks with strong scores. The tasks were return to hospital in 30 days, death in hospital, illness load, length of stay, and claim denial. Scores ran from 78.7% to 94.9% on a standard scale. The model beat older tools by 5 to 15 points. The team also ran it live in a trial at their own health system.
europmc-pmc10468537:
Bied, Ho, Ginhoux, and Blériot reviewed macrophages in tumours in 2023, tracing them across place and time. Macrophages are immune cells that keep tissues in balance. Inside tumours they pile up and tend to aid growth, in both the first tumour and its spreads. They are the most common immune cell in that zone.

Their sheer variety has slowed study for years. Bied lists the known subtypes and the job of each at each stage of cancer. Some subtypes ready a distant site before cancer cells arrive, paving a niche for spread. Others then feed the new tumour once it lands. Gaps in this map still block drugs that target these cells.
europmc-pmc10910037:
Guo and colleagues review a master switch for swelling and immunity that is also a drug target in this 2024 paper. NF-kappaB is a protein complex that turns genes on when cells face stress or infection. Found nearly 40 years ago, it was first tied to inflammation, meaning the body's swelling defence response. Its reach has since proved far wider.

The review explains how the switch is built, fired, and kept in check. It maps how the switch talks to other signal paths, among them PI3K/AKT, MAPK, JAK-STAT, Wnt, and Notch. Roles in cancer growth and in the tissue around tumours get close attention. The authors then survey drugs that block the switch at varied points, from blockers of its activators to gene-based tools. They close with open questions for turning this knowledge into care.
europmc-pmc11153137:
Xu and a large team built an AI foundation model for pathology slides in this 2024 paper. A single tissue slide image can hold tens of thousands of small tiles, which makes whole-slide learning hard. Earlier models sampled only a few tiles and lost the slide-level context. A foundation model is a large AI system trained once and then adapted to many tasks.

Their model, Prov-GigaPath, was pretrained on 1.3 billion tiles from 171,189 slides, the authors report. The slides came from over 30,000 patients across 31 tissue types in one US health network. A new architecture borrowed a long-context method to handle gigapixel slides. On a benchmark of 26 tasks, the model took top scores on 25. It beat the second-best method clearly on 18 tasks.
europmc-pmc11814237:
Chen and colleagues wrote a 2025 review on lactate and cancer. Lactate is a chemical that cells make when they break down sugar. Long seen as waste, it now looks like an active signal. A related process called lactylation can switch genes on or off.

Inside tumors, lactate shapes how cancer cells grow and hide from immune cells. It also helps tumors build blood vessels and resist drugs. Chen focuses on two control points: an enzyme that makes lactate and transporters that move it. Blocking them may improve future cancer care.
europmc-pmc1198037:
Pardo and colleagues studied a scarring lung disease and one protein in 2005. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens lungs over time. Scar tissue builds up and breathing worsens. No clear cause or cure was known.

Gene screens flagged a protein called osteopontin as highly raised. It sat in lung lining cells of patients. Wash fluid from patient lungs also held more of it. Added protein made lung cells move and multiply faster. Pardo links osteopontin to the scarring drive itself. Blocking its anchors slowed those cell responses. It appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2005.
europmc-pmc1367837:
Missmer and co-authors studied corn toxin exposure and birth defects on the Texas-Mexico border in 2006. Neural tube defects doubled there among Mexican-American women in 1990 to 1991. The surge matched a crop year tied to fumonisin in animals. Fumonisin is a mold toxin that often contaminates corn.

Exposure was estimated from a blood marker ratio and diet recall. Moderate tortilla intake, 301 to 400 in the first trimester, raised odds. The odds ratio was 2.4 versus low intake, with adjustment. Higher intake bands showed no added risk in these data. Missmer gives the first population test of the fumonisin hypothesis.
europmc-pmc1483837:
Even asthma patients on daily preventive drugs often fare poorly. Partridge and co-authors asked 3,415 adults in eleven countries about their asthma in 2006, for the INSPIRE study. All were prescribed regular inhaled steroids, drugs that calm airway swelling.

Three quarters still used rescue inhalers daily. Half had uncontrolled asthma by a standard questionnaire. Even well-controlled patients averaged six flare-ups a year. A flare took about five days from first signs to peak. Most patients answered a flare by puffing more rescue drug, not more steroid. Partridge calls that habit a missed chance to head off attacks.
europmc-pmc1557737:
A 21-gene test aims to forecast which breast cancers will return. Habel and co-authors checked it in 2006 in a community hospital population, beyond the trial setting where it was built. They studied women with node-negative cancer who had died of the disease, matched with survivors.

The test's Recurrence Score tracked the risk of breast cancer death. That held for women treated with the hormone drug tamoxifen and for those not treated. Ten-year death risk in treated women ran 2.8 percent in the low score group. It rose to 10.7 percent in the middle group and 15.5 percent in the high group. Habel supports the test's use in daily care.
europmc-pmc1559637:
Getting care is not just about clinics being open. Dixon-Woods and co-authors reviewed studies in 2006 on how vulnerable groups in the UK reach health care. Simple counts of visits, they argue, miss the real story.

They offer a concept called candidacy. It describes how a person's claim to care is judged, by themselves and by services, in an ongoing negotiation. Social context, resources, and service design all sway the outcome. Services define what counts as a proper case, while people define what counts as a proper need. Dixon-Woods urges attention to how weakness in that negotiation leaves some people out.
europmc-pmc1570337:
Counting links alone misjudges how picky a species is about partners. Blüthgen and co-authors built better measures in 2006 for plant-pollinator webs. Old indices ignored how often visits happen and grew with web size.

Their two indices use visit frequencies and the math of information. One, d prime, scores the pickiness of a single species. The other, H2 prime, scores the whole network. Applied to two pollinator webs, the indices exposed contrasts older tools missed, like a link between pollinator pickiness and abundance. Tests showed the network index stays steady despite web size or sampling effort.
europmc-pmc1636037:
A T cell signal tied to neutrophils shows up in asthmatic airways. Bullens and co-authors measured IL-17 messages in sputum in 2006, from 39 asthma patients and 15 healthy people. IL-17 comes from a T cell lineage distinct from the allergy-linked type.

Sputum IL-17 and IL-8 messages ran significantly higher in asthma. IL-17 tracked T cell presence, and both signals tracked neutrophil counts in the airways. High levels persisted in moderate-to-severe patients despite inhaled steroids. Bullens links the Th17 lineage, through IL-17, to the neutrophil influx seen in severe asthma flares.
europmc-pmc1868037:
Bisht, Maitra and co-authors packaged curcumin into nanoparticles in 2007 to make the turmeric compound usable against cancer. Curcumin, the yellow pigment of turmeric root, kills many cancer cell types in the lab and slows tumors in animals. It barely dissolves in water, though, so almost none reaches the blood after swallowing.

Their formulation, nicknamed nanocurcumin, wraps curcumin in micelles built from three linked polymers. Light scattering and electron microscopy showed a tight size spread around 50 nanometers, a millionth of a millimeter scale. Unlike free curcumin, the packaged form disperses readily in water. In cell tests it matched the free compound's therapeutic strength. The work offers a route to deliver water-shunning drugs through the body without losing their punch.
europmc-pmc1925137:
Chambers, Goodell and co-authors showed in 2007 that blood-forming stem cells wear out with age even as their numbers grow. These cells, taken from mice aged 2 to 21 months, replenish all blood cell types for life. Age-related stem cell decay may shorten lifespan by failing tissues that need constant renewal.

Purified old stem cells performed worse in function tests despite being more numerous. Activity scans across more than 14,000 genes found about 1,500 switched up with age and 1,600 switched down. Stress, inflammation, and protein-clumping genes dominated the up group. Genome protection and chromatin remodeling genes fell in the down group. Whole chromosome regions lost coordinated control, and overall activity rose loosely. Mice carrying a mutant p53 aged early as organisms, yet their stem cells uncoupled from that pace.
europmc-pmc2008837:
Drasar and Irving compared cancer rates across countries in 1973 to test environmental links. Breast and colon cancers were common in rich countries and rare in poorer ones. The team correlated rates for breast, colon and stomach cancer with diet measures. They also used indicators of standard of living. Their question was which shared factors tracked the disease patterns.

Breast and colon cancer were both highly correlated with fat intake. They were also highly correlated with animal protein intake. Stomach cancer behaved differently in the comparisons. The pattern supported a dietary and environmental influence, rather than geography alone. Earlier work from the same laboratory had pointed to gut bacteria as one possible link between diet and colon cancer.
europmc-pmc2117937: A medical paper on the histological changes produced by ricin and abrin intoxications. The poisons' effects on tissue. This article preserves that toxicology research. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2124637: A medical paper on experimental anaemias in the rabbit. The bloodless bunnies. This article preserves that hematology research. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125337: A medical paper on the numerical laws governing the rate of excretion of urea and chlorides in man. The urine math. This article preserves that physiology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128137: A medical paper on the treatment of anoxemia in pneumonia in an oxygen chamber. The oxygen cure. This article preserves that therapeutics. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2130937: A medical paper on skin infection of rabbits with hemolytic streptococci from a patient. The rabbit skin. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2137937:
Hinney and co-workers ran a genome-wide association study in 2007 for extreme obesity starting early in life. Obesity is strongly inherited, yet the genes behind it were poorly known. The team scanned 440,794 single-letter DNA variants in 487 extremely obese young Germans and 442 lean controls. They then checked the strongest hits in 644 independent families with obese children.

Six variants in one gene, FTO, showed the strongest link to obesity. The top variant carried an odds ratio of 2.76, and its corrected significance passed the strict threshold. That odds value pointed to a real effect rather than chance variation in this sample. Both tested FTO variants were confirmed in the family study. Nine other promising variants failed to confirm. Only the FTO signals counted as true positives.
europmc-pmc2265037:
Högberg and a large team compared body fluids in 2008 as measures of phthalate exposure in new mothers. Phthalates, plastic softeners, may harm development around birth. Choosing the right sample type matters for judging exposure. Forty-two Swedish first-time mothers gave breast milk, blood and urine two to three weeks after delivery. Collection used special pumps and treated glassware to avoid contaminating samples with phthalates from equipment.

In milk and blood, phthalate compounds sat near the detection limit when found at all. In urine, most breakdown products were detectable at levels comparable to general populations in the United States and Germany. Urine levels did not correlate with milk or blood levels for any single compound. The authors conclude urine is far more informative for monitoring. Milk levels also cannot estimate an infant's intake from breastfeeding.
europmc-pmc2409737:
Forrest and colleagues pitted a blood score against doctor-rated fitness in lung cancer in 2004. The patients, 109 in total, had inoperable non-small-cell lung cancer and were getting platinum-based chemotherapy. The blood score, the Glasgow Prognostic Score, combines an inflammation marker with a nutrition protein.

Doctors also rated each patient's fitness on the standard ECOG scale, which grades how active a patient remains. When both measures entered the same survival model, only the blood score predicted survival on its own. Its hazard ratio was 1.88, with a significance value of 0.002 in the analysis, while fitness and white cell count dropped out. The authors argued that an objective lab score beats a subjective fitness grade for these patients. That matters when deciding who is strong enough for harsh treatment.
europmc-pmc2531137:
Thun and a large group of collaborators pooled data in 2008 on lung cancer in people who never smoked. Such cancers are puzzling, and claims about sex and race differences needed checking on firmer numbers. The team combined 13 cohort studies, covering over 630,000 people for incidence and 1.8 million for deaths, plus registry data from ten countries where few women smoked.

Men died of lung cancer at higher rates than women in every age and racial group, though new-case rates were similar once age was standardised. Asians living in Korea and Japan, and African Americans, died at higher rates than people of European descent. Rates among American women barely changed from the 1930s to today, arguing against claims that risk is rising. Rates in East Asian women were high and varied widely.
europmc-pmc2600337:
The WHO/OIE/FAO H5N1 Evolution Working Group proposed in 2008 a single naming system for the highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu virus. The virus had appeared in more than 60 countries and kept diversifying, but laboratories used different names for the same emerging lineages, confusing comparisons. Convened in Toronto in 2007 with backing from the three agencies, the group set out to fix the chaos.

They analysed 859 nearly complete haemagglutinin gene sequences, the gene that has stayed in the lineage since its 1996 ancestor in Guangdong. Family trees from three methods supported grouping the circulating viruses into clades. These branches are designated by a hierarchical numbering system, not by place names. The scheme removes stigmatising geographic labels, and the authors urge its adoption worldwide and its extension to other influenza lineages.
europmc-pmc2603037:
Ho and Gruswitz presented a program called HOLLOW in 2008 for cleanly visualising the inside surfaces of protein channels. Channels and cavities matter for understanding how molecules travel through proteins, but standard viewers bury the inner surface under the outer one. Researchers had to clip views or hand-pick residues, and both tricks left stray surface fragments behind.

HOLLOW instead fills the interior volume of a protein with dummy atoms, casting the empty space like a mould. The surface of that cast closely matches the channel's true inner surface and can be displayed alone, free of superfluous pieces. The authors demonstrate it on channel proteins such as the ammonia channel. The program is written in Python and released freely for other researchers to use.
europmc-pmc2633437:
Cunningham and colleagues reported in 2009 on what happens when a body-wide infection strikes a brain that is already failing. They used mice with early prion disease, a fatal illness that slowly kills nerve cells. In these mice, brain immune cells called microglia sit primed, ready to react, yet stay fairly quiet.

The team injected a bacterial toxin fragment that mimics infection into the mice. Diseased mice, unlike healthy ones, produced far more brain inflammation signals, such as interleukin-1 beta. They burrowed and moved much less, grew cold, and showed new problems with thinking. A later, larger dose hurt coordination and muscle strength only in the diseased group. After those mice recovered, the same problems returned earlier than expected, so a single infection had sped the disease itself.
europmc-pmc2661137:
Moraes and colleagues reported in 2009 that a fatty diet can kill nerve cells in the part of the brain that controls hunger. In rodents, rich diets dull the brain's response to leptin and insulin, two hormones that curb appetite. The dulling involves local inflammation, and inflammation can switch on cell death programs, so the team looked for dying cells.

Rats on the fatty diet showed clear signs of neuron death in two hunger centers, the arcuate nucleus and the lateral hypothalamus. Surviving neurons also held fewer connections. The harm tracked the diet's makeup, not just its calories: animals fed the same calories of lean food were spared. A sensor called TLR4 played a double role. It helped start the inflammation, yet its presence also limited further cell death. The findings suggest obesity may partly reflect lost brain cells, not only weak signals.
europmc-pmc2680737:
Saisho and colleagues measured in 2007 the size of the human pancreas across the whole lifespan, from birth to age 100. The pancreas makes insulin, and its size might matter for diabetes, but basic reference data were lacking. The team measured organ volume on scans from 135 children and 1,886 adults without pancreas disease, and checked fat content in 47 organs after death.

The organ grows steadily through childhood, levels off between ages 20 and 60 at about 72 cubic centimeters, then shrinks in old age. Obesity enlarged every part: total volume rose by about a third, and fat volume by about two thirds. Fat inside the pancreas also climbed with age. Surprisingly, people with type-2 diabetes carried no more pancreas fat than others of the same age and weight. Fatty pancreas, the data say, follows age and body size, not diabetes itself.
europmc-pmc2687937:
Stamatovic, Keep, and Andjelkovic reviewed in 2008 how the blood-brain barrier, the sealed lining of brain blood vessels, gets pried open in disease. The barrier's tightness comes from junction complexes that glue neighboring lining cells together, blocking leaks between cells. Almost no traffic crosses by bubbles through the cells either, so the brain stays chemically sheltered.

In many brain disorders this seal fails. Inflammation, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and epilepsy can all loosen the junctions. Blood cells then slip into brain tissue, and fluid follows, swelling the brain. At the same time, the cells' bubble transport wakes up and ferries large molecules across. The review maps the routes of opening and the signal pathways that control them. Knowing the locks, the authors argue, is the start of learning to close the barrier again, or to open it briefly for drugs.
europmc-pmc2688237:
Sokka and colleagues, with the QUEST-RA Group, compared in 2009 how rheumatoid arthritis plays out in women and men across 25 countries. Their registry held 6,004 patients seen in ordinary clinics, not trials. Whether the disease, an immune attack on the joints, runs worse in one sex had long been disputed.

On every standard activity measure, women scored worse than men. They reported more swollen and tender joints, more pain and fatigue, and stiffer daily function. Their composite activity scores ran clearly higher. Yet the gaps were small to middling, and for swollen joint counts the sex difference was the smallest of all. That pattern raises a caution: measures heavy on patient report may rate women's disease as worse than the joint damage itself warrants. Treatment use, including steroids and biologic drugs, was broadly similar between the sexes.
europmc-pmc2689237:
Johnson, Greaves, and Repta reported in 2009 on a primer they wrote to help health researchers handle sex and gender properly. The two words are often confused or ignored, though biology and social roles both shape illness, behavior, and treatment response. Sloppy use weakens studies and hides inequalities that better design could expose.

Their primer defines sex as the biological side and gender as the social side. It then shows how such an analysis can be woven into research at each stage, from question to reporting. They offer three workable approaches at different depths, so teams can start where they stand. The authors also describe spreading the primer to funders, journals, and research groups, and the pushback and confusion they met. Their closing plea is simple: keep asking, in every study, whether sex and gender could matter.
europmc-pmc2696037:
Johannes and a large team tested in 2009 whether chemical marks on DNA, inherited without any change to the DNA letters themselves, can shape visible traits. Such epigenetic marks can pass from parent to offspring, but separating their effects from ordinary gene differences had blocked the field. The team bred plant lines from two parents with nearly identical DNA but contrasting mark patterns.

The resulting lines differed in flowering time and height, and about 30 percent of that variation was heritable, passed down faithfully. The mark differences themselves stayed stable for at least eight generations without any selection. That stability means mark variants, called epialleles, can in principle be hunted with the same mapping tools used for genes. Population genetics, the authors argue, must stop treating DNA letters as the only inheritance in town.
europmc-pmc2779337:
Hall and Garthwaite asked in 2009 what concentration of nitric oxide, a gas signal used across the body, tissues actually experience in life. A decade earlier, about one micromolar looked plausible from electrode readings and receptor potency guesses. Since then, direct electrode measurements in cells and tissues had produced an irreconcilable spread of values, leaving experiments hard to calibrate.

They weigh four alternative lines of evidence. These include quantitative study of the enzyme nitric oxide activates. They include computer models built from the amount and activity of nitric oxide synthase in cells. New biosensors watched single cells release the gas. The target enzyme itself served as a built-in sensor in challenged tissue. All converge far lower than once thought: from about one hundred picomolar up to roughly five nanomolar. Real signaling, they argue, works at these trace levels.
europmc-pmc2782137:
Tsuda, Sato, Stoddard, Glazebrook, and Katagiri mapped in 2009 the network behind robust plant immunity. They used Arabidopsis mutants that knock out hormone signaling sectors. Some mutants lost one sector, others lost all together. Plants fight biotrophic pathogens, which feed on living tissue, with two recognition modes. Three hormone sectors shape the response. Single mutants barely dented either immunity mode.

A quadruple mutant missing all the sectors lost almost all immunity of both kinds, and suffered badly against a necrotrophic fungus too. They fit measurements from every mutant combination to a model. Each hormone sector, they found, can help against both pathogen types. That runs contrary to the usual split. The two immunity modes share one network but use it differently. Sectors amplify each other in the pattern-triggered mode. In the effector-triggered mode they back each other up. That backup explains its robustness.
europmc-pmc2784037:
Rajilić-Stojanović and co-authors built in 2009 the Human Intestinal Tract Chip, a phylogenetic microarray for profiling the microbes of the human gut. The gut hosts thousands of microbial types that aid digestion and health, but counting them well was hard. They designed over forty-eight hundred probes from two variable regions of the ribosomal RNA gene, covering eleven hundred forty distinct microbial types drawn from over sixteen thousand gut sequences.

The chip proved highly reproducible, with repeat readings matching almost perfectly. It measured mixtures faithfully down to types forming a tenth of one percent of the community. Tracking stool samples from ten adults, five young and five elderly, showed each person's gut community was individual and fairly stable over time. Its stable core, shared across people, consisted of members of three great bacterial groups: Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Firmicutes.
europmc-pmc3039637:
Smith, Devane, Begley, and Clarke set out in 2011 how to review whole sets of systematic reviews, using maternity care as their working example. Single reviews already gather many trials, yet decision makers now face stacks of overlapping reviews of uneven quality on the same topics. A review of reviews lets readers compare their findings side by side.

The paper walks through finding reviews, judging their quality, and presenting results so the strength of each conclusion is clear. Quality checks cover how widely each review searched, how studies were chosen, and whether bias and disagreement between studies were handled. The authors flag common pitfalls at each step and offer practical fixes. Their aim is to help clinicians and policy makers trust, or discount, summaries built on summaries.
europmc-pmc3041737:
Bacon and Aphramor argued in 2011 that health care should stop making weight loss its main goal for heavier patients. Standard advice tells people classed as overweight or obese to diet and exercise, which reliably sheds weight for a short time. Most people regain it, and the authors say the weight focus itself can cause harm, from shame and eating disorders to endless loss and regain cycles.

They present an alternative called Health at Every Size, which targets health habits and outcomes directly, without a weight goal. Trials of that approach improved blood pressure, blood fats, eating and activity habits, and self esteem, the authors report. In their reading, it matched or beat dieting programs on health gains without the downsides. The paper makes the ethical case for shifting care toward weight neutral goals.
europmc-pmc3052437:
Szanto and colleagues uncovered in 2010 a teamwork trick that lets two immune cell switches control far more genes together than either could alone. One switch, called PPARγ in short, is turned on by fats and calms inflammation in macrophages and dendritic cells. The other responds to a calming signal molecule. Inflammatory signals suppressed the fat switch, while the calming signal boosted it.

The boost worked because the two switches meet on the control regions of shared target genes and help each other grip the DNA. With both present, more genes responded and each responded more strongly. The partnership differed between cell types, helping explain why the same signal does different things in different immune cells. The authors present this as a general way that inflammation signals tune fat sensing switches. It may matter for diseases where both systems are involved, such as artery disease and diabetes.
europmc-pmc3154137:
Chris Cotsapas and colleagues tested how widely genetic risk is shared across autoimmune diseases in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Genome studies had flagged many risk variants for diseases such as Crohn disease, lupus, and type one diabetes, with some variants appearing in two diseases. The team built a new statistic to catch variants tied to several diseases at once, without requiring all of them.

Applied to just over a hundred known risk variants across seven diseases, the method found nearly half linked to multiple diseases, each in its own subset. Proteins coded near variants sharing the same disease subsets also interact with each other, hinting at shared disease machinery. Borrowing strength across diseases, the authors argue, can reveal mechanisms no single-disease study would show.
europmc-pmc3160337:
Silvia Cermelli and colleagues tested tiny RNA molecules in blood as markers of liver disease severity in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Four such molecules are often disturbed in liver scarring and liver cancer. The team first watched their release from infected liver cells in the lab, then measured them in patients with chronic hepatitis C or fatty liver disease.

Three of the molecules ran high in patient blood, and two of them climbed in step with scarring stage and inflammation in both diseases and in a repeat patient group. Their levels also tracked standard liver enzyme measures, while virus amount in hepatitis C showed no link. The authors propose the pair as gentle blood tests for staging liver disease without biopsy.
europmc-pmc3241537:
J. L. Villano and colleagues analyzed three decades of United States registry data on primary central nervous system lymphoma, in this 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. This rare lymphoma arises in the brain and related sites without disease elsewhere. Using the national SEER datasets for 1980 to 2008, they tracked incidence and survival by age, sex, and race.

Overall the disease stayed rare, affecting well under one person in a hundred thousand each year, and struck men more than women. Incidence dipped in the late nineteen-nineties, then rose slightly, with the sharpest climb in people over seventy-five. Among younger patients, incidence ran higher in Black than in white Americans, while the pattern reversed at older ages. Five-year survival favored white patients in the younger group, driven by white women. The authors stress that survival remains poor overall.
europmc-pmc3316137:
Küllenberg, Taylor, Schneider, and Massing reviewed the health effects of eating phospholipids, a class of fats found in every cell membrane. Claims for their benefits date back to the early nineteen hundreds, spanning heart disease, inflammation, and cancer. Phospholipids carry fatty acids into the membranes of body cells, and changing that membrane mix can change how the cell behaves.

The review surveys phospholipids from soy, egg yolk, milk, and sea sources, since the attached fatty acids decide much of the effect. Across studies, eating them seemed to help in several diseases with few serious side effects, and they sometimes softened the side effects of drugs. The authors caution that most evidence comes from cell and animal work, with only limited proof in people, and call for stronger human trials.
europmc-pmc340937:
Papagno and a large team reported in 2004 that HIV wears out killer T cells by pushing them toward old age before their time. The team studied virus-specific CD8 cells from patients and modeled first encounters in the lab.

Acute infection massively activated CD8 cells, far beyond those aimed at HIV itself. That activation drove cells into later, worn stages of development. Patients whose disease advanced carried more of these highly aged cells, which copy themselves poorly. The authors argue that relentless stimulation spends the immune system's reserves, a mechanism that may explain how activation turns into deficiency.

franklin-commission-animal-magnetism-183:
Benjamin Franklin and fellow commissioners test Mesmer's claims in their famous report of 1784, here in an 1837 printing. Bailly and Lavoisier join Franklin in blindfold trials at Paris. Imagination, not magnetic fluid, proves to work the seeming cures when patients cannot tell real passes from sham ones.

Controlled tests turn here, perhaps for the first time, on a medical craze. The verdict has stood ever since in the judgment of science. Mesmer's empire of fashion cracked under one careful, polite inquiry. The report remains a model of how to test a wonder: fair in form, firm in method, and deadly in its calm conclusions.
frus-1861-d137:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 July 1861. The dispatch is document 137 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The printed order puts Dayton's 5 July report after Seward's of the 6th. Dates, not file order, give the true sequence here. Dayton wrote from a Paris still calm about the war, unaware of the clash that would come in Virginia within the month. True sequence matters in this file, since the mails often crossed in transit. True sequence, once restored, lets the Paris story read as it was lived.
frus-1861-d237:
Seward heard from James Shepherd Pike on 12 June 1861, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 237 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the opening months of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d37:
Thomas Corwin, the American minister to Mexico, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 May 1861. The dispatch is document 37 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Corwin reported from a capital torn by its own recent civil war. Mexico's debts to Britain, France, and Spain raised fears of European troops near Texas. His May letter gave Washington a close view of a weak neighbor at a risky hour. European fleets would in fact land in Mexico within the year, which gives his fears a sharp point. His fears were not idle, as the landings in Mexico soon proved to all.
frus-1862-d137:
A dispatch dated 4 September 1862 carried word from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 137 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d237:
Document 237 is the second Seward letter to William Stuart dated 11 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to the British legation's acting head on the same day.

The habit of splitting business across same-day letters makes the printed file look repetitive, yet each sheet had its own purpose. For a reader now, the pairs are a gift. They show the exact order and shape of work in the week before Antietam. Every office in Washington knew a decisive battle was near. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d337:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 21 October 1862 in a letter printed as Document 337 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote as the European question of the fall neared its answer: Britain was backing away from joint action. His reports in late October traced the French reaction to that retreat. For the Union, the news was the year's best from abroad, and the Paris file records the moment it became clear. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d37:
By the date of 25 March 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 37 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d437:
On 11 September 1862 Gabriel García Tassara wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from Washington. His note is Document 437 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Tassara wrote six days before Antietam, in the tensest week of the autumn. Whatever its formal subject, a Spanish note that week landed on a desk waiting for battle news from Maryland. Spain's attitude mattered to the Union because of Cuba and because Madrid's voice counted in Europe. The note belongs to the small set of Washington exchanges through which Seward kept Spain informed and correct. Above all, he kept it neutral while the war hung in the balance.
frus-1862-d537:
Roest van Limburg addressed this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 July 1862. It is Document 537 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

A month had passed since the June cluster. The Dutch minister's July note took up the standing business between the two governments. It did so in a harder season. Union armies had fallen back in Virginia, and foreign legations in Washington were revising their estimates. The Netherlands, a commercial power, cared most that the war's rules at sea stay predictable. Van Limburg's note is part of the quieter middle file of the Dutch correspondence, where routine and principle were usually mixed in the same page.
frus-1862-d637:
Townsend Harris sent this dispatch from Japan to the Secretary of State on 7 June 1861. It stands as Document 637 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

In June 1861 Japan still knew nothing reliable of the American war. Harris's business was entirely Japanese. It covered the treaty ports, the exchange of officials, and the safety of the small foreign community. His letters home traveled for months and arrived as history. For the reader, the Japanese file is the volume's most exotic strand. It records America's first embassy in Edo. That embassy ran on its own clock while the republic fought at home. The dispatch sustains that parallel story into the war's first summer.
frus-1863p1-d137:
This dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 28 March 1863, sits among same-date sheets from both men. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 137 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, set among a cluster of same-date sheets from both men.

Adams wrote on the last day of a crowded month at the legation. His March mail had tracked the ship question to its hottest point yet. This dispatch is the London half of the 28 March cross in the file. It shows the envoy's steady craft: facts first, heat last, in a city where the South's friends made plenty of both.
frus-1863p1-d237:
The State Department's mail for London dated 15 July 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 237 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d337:
A formal note dated 12 December 1862 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 337 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d37:
Judah P. Benjamin, the Confederate secretary of state, sent this letter to John Slidell on 17 October 1862. Slidell was the South's envoy in Paris. The letter is document 37 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Slidell's brief was the hardest the South gave any man: bring France, and with it Europe, to back the new republic. Benjamin's letters fed him the arguments and the news from home. This one came a month after Antietam, as the South's hopes of foreign aid began to thin. It stands in the Union's printed record as a piece of the foe's own file, kept for all to read.
frus-1863p1-d437:
The date 2 April 1863 heads a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d537:
A 27 May 1863 dispatch from F. W. Seward, the assistant secretary reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d637:
Document 637 in the volume is a letter of 9 October 1863 from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The value of the London file is its view from inside Britain: cabinet moods, press talk, and opinion's turn after Gettysburg and Vicksburg.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d137: Roosevelt wrote to General Dwight Eisenhower, commanding Allied forces in North Africa, on November 17, 1943. The letter is Document 137 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The president was then in Eisenhower's theater, on his way to Cairo, and the theater commander stood close to the journey's route. The record names the two men and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d237:
Joint Staff Planners drafted a proposed agenda, marked Enclosure C, for President Roosevelt's first meeting with Marshal Stalin at Tehran. Prepared aboard the Iowa between 15 and 19 November 1943, the secret paper went straight to the President and was not approved by the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Only two items are listed for the Americans to raise. One is Soviet help in strategic bombing, including the use of Soviet bases by American forces. The other is zones of military responsibility if Germany collapsed completely under the Rankin C plan. Three more items are held in reserve, to be answered only if Stalin raised them: Turkey and Sweden, the Italian fleet and shipping, and Soviet entry into the war against Japan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d337:
James Byrnes, director of war mobilization, telegraphed President Roosevelt from Washington on 27 November 1943 with a fresh landing craft idea. It builds on the production argument running through the Cairo conference papers, where landing craft supply set the limits for every planned operation.

Shipbuilder Francis Gibbs advises Byrnes that, if authorized at once, forty to fifty extra ships could probably be delivered in the time allowed. They would be nearly identical with the infantry landing craft but make twelve knots. They would be converted from army cargo vessels under contract in Gulf yards. Their service would be in MacArthur's theater, with first deliveries inside sixty days. Even if unfit for every landing craft duty, they could free true landing ships from non-combat work. Byrnes asks Roosevelt to wire back authority to proceed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d37: Churchill answered Roosevelt on October 5, 1943, a day after the president's letters to London and Moscow. His message is Document 37 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The autumn exchanges between the two men were near daily as the Moscow foreign ministers' meeting neared. The catalog record gives the date and the names and nothing further. The text itself, in the Foreign Relations series, carries whatever business the day required.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d437: Historians at the State Department drafted the editorial note listed as Document 437. Notes of this kind sit between the wartime papers in the Cairo-Tehran volume. They explain background that the papers themselves assume. They also identify officials and point readers toward related records. The conferences behind the volume met in late 1943. Allied leaders used them to align strategy for 1944. The note helps a modern reader follow that crowded record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d537:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant wrote directly to President Roosevelt from London on January 3, 1944, bypassing the State Department channel he also used. Winant's standing with both governments made his direct line to the President a working part of the alliance. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The volume's later pages follow the conferences' business into 1944, and this message belongs to that follow-through. Winant reported on Britain as it turned from summit decisions to the invasion year. For readers, a direct ambassador-to-president report shows how much Roosevelt governed through personal channels laid over the formal diplomatic machine.
frus-1944-quebec-d137:
Civil affairs in the Balkans is the subject of this State Department briefing paper prepared for Quebec in September 1944. American planning covered only Greece, Yugoslavia, and Albania, the countries expected to be liberated territory. A combined Anglo-American military headquarters would run relief, but American participation was tiny: sixty-three officers against several thousand British personnel.

The paper's sharpest point concerns UNRRA, the relief agency. Washington wanted it given maximum responsibility and insisted relief be distributed without discrimination by race, creed, or politics. Supplies must not become a political weapon in Yugoslavia's civil strife, the authors warn. They also wanted the Russians fully informed, to allay suspicion and set a useful precedent.
frus-1944-quebec-d237:
Hull sent Roosevelt a department study on September 11, 1944, about British chiefs of staff proposals for Italy's overseas territories. The Joint Chiefs saw no direct objection from narrow national security, since American postwar military interests were not affected. From the broader view, though, they held America should not support the proposals before learning Russian views.

Hull added that the proposals had never been considered by the British War Cabinet and did not represent British government policy. The enclosed experts' memorandum preferred giving all Eritrea to Ethiopia, under obligations to the future international organization: ports and airfields open to United Nations forces in an emergency, and technical personnel employed. That would satisfy Ethiopia's claim and give her an outlet at Massawa.
frus-1944-quebec-d37:
Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on August 30, 1944. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It sits in the last run of letters before the September conference.

By August 30, the German retreat in France had become a rout. The leaders' business was turning toward the war's end. At issue were Germany's treatment and aid to Britain. The Pacific war also demanded attention. Roosevelt's letter belongs to that pivot from campaign to conference. For readers, it shows the President in writing. He set out his positions days before hosting Churchill in Canada.
frus-1945-50-intel-d137:
Souers, the director of central intelligence, sent a memorandum to the National Intelligence Authority on 2 February 1946. The new director reported upward to the board that owned his group, days after its creation. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Early reports from a first director set the pattern of an office: what it tells its masters, and how often. Souers wrote as the group stood up its staff and took its first tasks. Readers can place this paper beside the January directive that created both board and group. The directive promised a servant. This memorandum shows the servant's first accounting. It began the reporting habit that bound the central system to the secretaries above it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d237:
The Assistant General Counsel, Central Intelligence Agency (Pforzheimer) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 6 January 1949. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 237, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Three men — Dulles, Jackson, and Correa — were touring the CIA's work for the Council and taking notes for a report.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d337:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Committee on 27 January 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 337 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d37:
Appleby of the Budget Bureau wrote to Attorney General Clark on 31 October 1945. A budget official writing to the head of the Justice Department marks a question that crosses money and law. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The FBI's foreign intelligence work raised exactly such questions: it cost money, and its legal footing in peacetime was open to doubt. Appleby's letter brought the bureau's scrutiny to the Justice Department's door. Readers can see the net widening here. The intelligence fight was no longer only about who spied where; it was about authority and appropriations, the two things that make agencies real. This letter is an early sign of that harder phase.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d137:
American control of Bremen is the sticking point in this top secret cable of 5 January 1945. Secretary of State Stettinius writes to Ambassador Winant in London about the ports that would feed the American zone in Germany. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Formal action had been stalled to avoid a sharp clash. On 4 January a formula was worked out in Washington. War Department officials and Joint Chiefs men sat with Lord Halifax and General Macready. The British said they would recommend it to London. Under the formula, the Bremen and Bremerhaven enclave sits under complete American control, military government included. It would still be run, on paper, as a subdistrict of the larger British area around it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d237:
London was thinking of putting Iran on the Big Three agenda, Winant reported on 9 January 1945. His one-paragraph cable from London, number 296, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It came out of a general talk on Iranian matters at the Foreign Office that day.

The official who handles Iranian affairs directly, Winant writes, said serious thought is being given to one step. At the next Big Three meeting, the general question of Iran should be raised. The focus would be Soviet pressure in connection with the recent incidents over oil concessions. The short cable shows the Iran quarrel moving from embassy channels toward the leaders' table at Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d337:
Two records of the same Yalta plenary survive, and this one, kept by H. Freeman Matthews, covers February 5, 1945, on Germany. Roosevelt opened by saying the leaders should talk of the broad aims of peace, not Dakar or China. Zones of occupation came first, since matters there were coming to a head.

He showed a map and linked it to his Quebec talks with Churchill. Then he corrected himself: the map in fact came from the zones protocol drawn up by the European Advisory Commission. Matthews catches a small human slip that the smoother Bohlen record leaves out. Reading both versions shows how minutes differ.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d37: The president turned back to the Moscow channel on 31 December 1944, writing to Ambassador Harriman that day. The message is document 37 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. Instructions sent to Harriman at year's end helped him prepare the Soviet side of the coming summit, where his local knowledge would matter throughout the Yalta meetings.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d437:
Hiss's notes of February 10, 1945, catch Molotov haggling over one phrase in the Polish formula. Stettinius said the Americans would withdraw the final sentence Molotov disliked. The President would stay free to speak to the American people about reports from his ambassador. Molotov proposed a small amendment to the previous day's text.

His condition: the United States and Britain would establish diplomatic relations with the new government as soon as possible, as the Soviet Union had done. Eden objected that this would be a new government. Molotov answered that their situations differed, since Moscow had already recognized the present one. The shorthand preserves the last inch of the Poland bargain.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d137:
Acting Secretary Grew settled a timing question with London in a telegram to Ambassador Winant on July 12, 1945. The message is document 137 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Lord Halifax had asked, for Churchill and Eden, on which day the President and Secretary Byrnes would arrive at Terminal.

The British leaders wanted to time their own departure so as to arrive the same day. Grew answers that the present schedule allows the President and the Secretary to reach Terminal about 3 p.m. local time on Sunday, July 15. He notes that Halifax has been informed. The synchronized arrivals were partly courtesy and partly tactics: neither Western leader wanted the other to have a head start with Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d237:
Acting Secretary Grew gave Rome its green light in a letter to Ambassador Tarchiani dated July 7, 1945. The letter is document 237 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Tarchiani had told him the day before that the Italian government had decided to declare war on Japan.

The news will be greeted with approval by the American people, Grew writes. The timing of the announcement is for Italy to decide. The British, French, and Soviet governments have already been informed of American approval and have raised no objection. The American government naturally hopes the announcement will come at an early date. The letter closed the diplomatic round that let a former enemy state join the war's last campaign as a gesture of good faith.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d337:
McCloy answered Clayton on June 21, 1945, with a first, informal reaction on paying for German civilian supplies. The hard point, he wrote, was justifying Army funds once the armies sat in separate zones. Army money spent on supplies would aid civilians in liberated countries, not American troops. That was hard to defend in Congress.

Yet McCloy conceded the other side of the case. An American commander, as a Control Council member, acted as an agent of his government. Government policy included using German resources for the freed areas. He promised the War Department would study the matter and reply formally.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d37: No objection to the Berlin area: Truman's extract to Churchill of May 28, 1945, is a single sentence of substance. Stalin had informed him through Hopkins that he would like the three-party meeting held in the Berlin area. Truman would reply that he had no objection to the Berlin area. The first two paragraphs of the message, omitted from this printing, appear elsewhere in the volume. The extract's brevity is its meaning: the place of the next summit was settled almost as an aside, while Hopkins was still in Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d437:
British draft instructions on Czechoslovakia are shared with Washington in a British Embassy paper dated June 28, 1945. It paraphrases a Foreign Office telegram of June 22. The Foreign Office's next telegram would contain the text of instructions it proposed to send Mr. Nichols, its ambassador in Prague. Before despatching them, London was anxious to know the State Department's views.

The Embassy is told to discuss the draft with the Department and send comments as soon as possible. The matter, London notes, concerns the Americans more closely in its immediate aspect. American troops occupied a large part of Czechoslovakia, and the American zone in Germany marched for many miles along the Czech frontier.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d537:
Phase II commitments to Britain are recalled in a briefing book paper on lend-lease after Germany's defeat. At Quebec in September 1944, President Roosevelt agreed to Prime Minister Churchill's proposal. Britain should go on receiving lend-lease aid after Germany's defeat. The basis would let her shift some work from war goods to civilian output.

A memorandum of November 25, 1944, reported the Phase II program to Roosevelt. Its authors were the American committee of Morgenthau, Stettinius, and Crowley. The program set 2.7 billion dollars for war goods and 2.8 billion for other goods, for the British Commonwealth. Such a program, they stated, would let Britain and America free manpower for reconversion. It would ease living standards, and partly revive exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d637:
An extract from Grew's memo of his June 25, 1945 talk with Ambassador Bonnet forms document 637 here. Printed in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam, it covers the same talk as document 616. The extract kept here gives the first sore point in full: the Levant.

Bonnet said France felt it had won little satisfaction on a string of issues. On Syria, he charged, the United States was backing the British position. Grew cut in to correct him. U.S. policy, Grew said, rested in no respect on Britain's stand. It followed Washington's own view of the matter, which the ambassador knew very well. The sharp little exchange shows how raw Franco-U.S. feeling ran that summer. It also shows Grew refusing to let France frame the Levant clash as an Anglo-U.S. plot.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1037:
Ambassador John Winant cabled the Secretary of State from London on July 24, 1945. The European Advisory Commission had met the night before to finish two outstanding documents. One snag was a matter of translation in the additional requirements agreement for Germany.

Soviet delegate Saksin said his government approved a title ending certain additional requirements to Germany. The English text reads requirements to be imposed on Germany. The gap arose when the Soviet team first cabled the title home, unaware the English and French texts carried the stronger phrase. Saksin would seek fresh instructions. Winant suggests Mosely might see Gusev at Potsdam to speed those instructions along.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1137:
A second memorandum from Poland's deputy premier Mikolajczyk bears the same date, 24 July 1945. Two formal papers in one day show how hard he pressed his country's case while the summit sat. He could not wait for a better moment; the decisions were being made that week.

Poland's western border and its future vote were the stakes. Mikolajczyk spoke for the part of the Polish government that had not come from Moscow's camp. His papers asked the Western powers to hold to their pledges. This one is the middle piece of the day's trio, and the urgency in it is plain.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1237:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 16 July 1945. Grew held the department in Washington while Byrnes traveled to the summit. His message of the day before the opening kept the chief abroad in touch with the home office.

Such eve-of-summit cables carried last news, pending files, and the state of affairs at home. The department's two halves had to act as one through the talks. This note is an early link in that daily circuit. It shows the machine starting its Potsdam rhythm: Washington reporting, the team abroad reading, both sides writing back.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1337:
Ambassador Wallace Murray in Iran cabled the acting secretary of state again on 30 July 1945, his third message from Tehran in four days. By then the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill, and Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945 was nearing its close. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A third cable in a short run tells readers the Tehran post saw no pause in its work as July ended. Murray's messages form a small run within the volume, and each one adds a piece to the picture Washington held of Iran. They reward readers who want to see diplomacy as daily reporting rather than as treaties alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-137:
On July 30, 1945, Bohlen again kept the minutes of a Potsdam meeting. The conference was in its last three days. Charles Bohlen's Russian fluency made his records central to the American file. This set was printed in the second Potsdam volume with his other minutes.

Late-stage minutes carry the feel of a race to finish. Points once debated at length now get short, sharp treatment. Bohlen's account preserves that pressure on the page. Readers can trace the final shaping of agreed lines. The record shows both the substance of the talks and the strain of their closing days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-37:
A rapporteur's report, in translation, records Molotov's account of the foreign ministers' meeting of July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The report is frank about how little the morning had settled.

On German economic principles, the authorized commission had not finished its work. The question was not in fact discussed, and the commission was told to finish by July 21. The Polish question met the same fate for the same reason, with the same deadline set. On the peace settlement, the drafting commission had also failed to produce a text. Its members were busy in other commissions, Molotov explains. The ministers therefore resolved to meet at 3:45 that afternoon themselves. At that sitting an amendment to paragraph 3 was adopted, and the report quotes its new opening words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d737:
Charles Yost of the Central Secretariat wrote this memorandum on August 9, 1945, a week after Potsdam closed. Document 737 belongs to the conference's aftermath. The secretariat had managed the flood of texts for three delegations. Its work did not end when the leaders left. Yost's memo entered the second Potsdam volume.

Aftermath papers settle the record while memories stay fresh. They chase missing copies and fix the order of texts. Readers gain a clerk's-eye view of a summit's remains. The document shows history being filed, literally, by the men who ran the paper. That filing is why the conference can still be studied in such depth.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d837:
The British delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 19, 1945, as document 837. It dates from the conference's third day. British drafts in the first week stated London's aims while Churchill still led the team. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

An early British text shows the alliance's second voice in full confidence. Readers can compare it with the drafts London tabled after the election changed its team. The document marks how much of Britain's line survived that change. It also shows the conference's three-way drafting race at its start: each side writing, each side reading the others overnight.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d937:
American staff wrote this undated paper on valuing removable equipment in the Ruhr, filed with the July 25, 1945 papers. Much talk at Potsdam turned on what Ruhr gear was worth, and what share might go to the Soviet Union. The paper argues that the whole valuation fight is a dead end.

Value shifts with method: cost minus wear, replacement cost, or worth as a going concern. Turning marks into dollars adds a second dispute. The only realistic answer, the paper says, is a percentage of equipment, not a price. A share means the same thing to both sides, whatever values each side computes.
frus-1964-68v06-d37: A third 1964-1968 FRUS editorial note from the 1968 Vietnam volume. The context. This note provides that background. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
gao-gaoreports-b-295737: USA Fabrics doubled its April 2005 protest — two dockets, one textile fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Paired filings get one careful answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-297137: Testek took its October 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297537: MMI-Federal Marketing Service took its February 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299037: Margni took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Short names get the same full hearing as the long ones.
gao-gaoreports-b-299237: Hawkeye Glove Manufacturing took its March 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Even glove contracts get the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299737: HealthStar VA took its June 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest and rules. Veteran-care contracts get the same fair-bid law as any federal deal.
gao-gaoreports-b-307137: The Energy Department's uranium deal got a fiscal ruling in this July 2006 GAO call, which tests the 2004 agreement with the enrichment corporation. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the atomic bargain was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-308037: The Legal Services Corporation's lease got a fiscal ruling in this September 2006 GAO call, which tests the deal with its friends group. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the cozy lease was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-311137: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by National Conference Services, Inc. and Direct Marketing Productions, Inc. d/b/a Technology Forums, Inc. The April 25, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-537: Trade agreement enforcement workload was growing in 2005, and GAO's report says further improvements were needed to handle the load. The findings demand the capacity. The report warns that the trade deals deserved policing. The improvements had to come. The trade deals deserved policing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-637: Tax-cheating civilian contractors faced few consequences in 2005, and GAO's report says thousands abused the system with little penalty. The findings sound the alarm. The report warns that the cheats deserved consequences. The abuse had to be stopped. The cheats deserved consequences.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-737: Iraq's private security providers needed better use in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were required to improve the contractors' role. The findings demand the oversight. The report warns that the hired guns deserved managing. The use had to be improved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-137: The IRS's 2005 financial statements got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report examines the books for fiscal years 2005 and 2004. The findings grade the accounting. The report shows the tax collector's own money was checked. The statements had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-237: Power market shake-ups still had snags in 2005, and GAO's report says the key hurdles stood. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the power buyers deserved honest rates. The power markets deserved honest reckoning. The hurdles had to fall.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-337: Asian soybean rust threatened U.S. crops in 2006, and GAO's report says USDA needed to build on 2005 experience to minimize the damage. The findings prescribe the preparation. The report warns that the bean fields needed defending. The experience had to be used.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-437: Egypt's military aid needed measuring in 2006, and GAO's report says State and the Pentagon had to assess how the financing achieved U.S. goals. The findings demand the evaluation. The report warns that the billions to Cairo needed justification. The program had to be assessed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-537: The transformational satellite program needed more homework in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon needed more knowledge before its new approach. The findings demand the research. The report warns that the orbital network should not be built on hope. The knowledge had to come first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-737: Embassy staffing reforms were slowly taking hold in 2006, and GAO's report says rightsizing approaches needed more coordination. The findings press for action. The report warns that the diplomatic posts should fit their missions. The rightsizing had to be coordinated. The posts should fit their missions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-137: Training minority health workers got a fair process in 2007, and GAO's report says the grant awards included independent review. The findings credit the procedure. The report shows the pipeline for diverse caregivers was being built honestly. The process protected the purpose.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-237: Chasing offshore tax cheats took too long in 2007 — GAO's report says the evasion cases needed more time than the rules allowed. The findings demand patience for complexity. The report's point: the hidden-money trail cannot be rushed without losing the money.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-37: America's recycling bins were half-empty in 2007, and GAO's report says more effort could lift municipal recycling rates. The findings press for action. The report argues that the trash of today was the resource of tomorrow. The bins deserved better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-737: Data breaches were a dime a dozen by 2007 — but GAO's report says hard proof of the resulting identity theft stayed thin. The findings split the scare from the evidence. The report's nuance matters: frequent breaches, murky fallout, and a policy debate running on anecdote.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-837: Federal networks stayed leaky in 2007 despite the progress memos — GAO's report says the cyber weak spots would not die. The findings list the persistent holes across the agencies. The report's weary refrain: reported progress is not the same as fixed problems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-37: GAO published its findings on legal Services Corporation: Improved Internal Controls Needed in Grants Management and Oversight in 2007. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-437: The Government Accountability Office dug into national Flood Insurance Program: Financial Challenges Underscore Need for Improved Oversight of Mitigation Programs and Key Contracts in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-837: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at securing, Stabilizing, and Rebuilding Iraq: Progress Report: Some Gains Made, Updated Strategy Needed. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
hawthorne-twice-told-tales-1837:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published Twice-Told Tales in 1837, the story collection that made his name in America. The book is a founding text of the American short story as a serious art. Hawthorne had burned or buried early tales, and friends urged these into print at last.

Tales like The Minister's Black Veil and Wakefield probe hidden sin and quiet obsession in New England. Sketches of streets, inns, and old customs sit beside the darker moral fables in this volume. A hooded minister, a man who leaves home for twenty years, and gray champions fill its pages. The tone is gentle on the surface and unsettled below, Hawthorne's mark from the very start. Poe praised the tales' unity of effect, a standard the short story still chases.
irish-constitution-1937:
