Ireland adopted a new constitution in 1937, approved by the voters in a referendum that July. Éamon de Valera, head of the government, shaped the text himself. Bunreacht na hÉireann, its Irish name, replaced the Free State charter of 1922. It cut the last cords binding Dublin to the Crown, while stopping short of the word republic.

The charter names the state Ireland, claims the whole island as the national territory, and gives the president a direct election. It promises strong rights for citizens and the family, with a Catholic coloring that marked its age. Courts gained the power to strike down laws that broke it, a lasting change. The document that finished the work of Irish independence still rules the republic today, amended many times but sound in its frame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-samuel-call:
Samuel Löw, known also as Samuel Kollin or Kelin, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Talmudist born at Kolin, Bohemia, about 1720, he was the son of Nathan ha-Levi. For nearly sixty years he presided over a yeshivah at Boskowitz, Moravia. He died there on May 20, 1806.

The entry centers on his writings, above all Mahazit ha-Shekel, a large subcommentary on the Magen Abraham section of the Shulhan Aruk. That work was printed at Vienna in 1807 and 1808 and reprinted several times. Two shorter works on ritual law appeared later at Lemberg. The article also notes his son Wolf Boskowitz, who preached at his funeral. As a period reference, it preserves the publishing history of a commentary that later scholars kept reprinting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maccabees-books:
Books of the Maccabees, four works bearing one name, are surveyed in a long Jewish Encyclopedia article of 1906. Four scholars share the writing. The entry states at once that only the First Book counts as a reliable historical source. The others are treated with more caution.

The article gives the first book a close reading. It covers forty years, from Antiochus's rise in 175 to Simon's death in 135 years before Christ. Sections treat the revolt's start, the wars of Judas, and the rule of Jonathan and Simon. The style is praised as simple, terse, and modeled on the Old Testament histories. The entry argues the book was written in Hebrew, though only the Greek survives. Origen and Jerome are cited for the lost original. For readers, the piece sorts four confusing books by value and date.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malter-henry-10:
Henry Malter, an American rabbi and scholar, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Zabno, Galicia, on March 23, 1867, he studied at Berlin and Heidelberg, taking his doctorate in 1894. He also trained for the rabbinate at Berlin's Hochschule. In 1899 he served as librarian of Berlin's Jewish community library.

The article follows his move to America. In 1900 he became professor of medieval philosophy and Arabic at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati. Two years later he also took the pulpit of that city's Sheerith Israel congregation. His publications joined Hebrew bibliography to Arabic philosophy. He produced a Hebrew edition of Steinschneider's Jewish Literature with fresh notes. He also edited a treatise of the Arab thinker al-Gazzali, printed at Frankfort in 1896. The entry catches a Galician scholar remaking himself as an American professor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mecia-matthew-d:
Mecia de Viladestes, a Jewish mapmaker of Majorca at the opening of the fifteenth century, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Richard Gottheil. His surviving work is a chart dated 1413, once kept in the convent of Val de Cristo near Segorbe and in the encyclopedia's day held by the Bibliothèque Nationale at Paris. The map gives special prominence to the African coastal voyages of Jacme Ferrer, another Majorcan.

The entry places Mecia in the Judaeo-Catalan school of chart-makers and names his model: the chart rests on the work of Jaffuda Cresques, probable maker of the atlas of Charles V. It also records a permit of January 20, 1401, found in the Majorcan archives, allowing "the convert Macia" to land in Sicily, probably this same man. Six sheets of the chart were reproduced at Paris in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-b-micha:
Menahem ben Michael was a Karaite philosopher and poet of Babylon. Kaufmann Kohler and A. Biram profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A contemporary of Saadia, he corresponded on philosophy with the Rabbanite thinker David al-Mukammas, whom he had met in Babylon. Later, poor and displaced, he wrote from Alexandria. He wrote to the Karaite community of Cairo, begging aid. Even after moving to Cairo he kept up the correspondence from a distance. He was too conscious of his poverty to approach so prominent a man directly.

In one letter, answering a reproach, he affirmed his belief both in the creation of the world and in the heavenly bodies. What survives is slight: verse rules for ritual slaughter, three poems in the Karaite prayer-book, and citations as a grammarian by later Karaite authors. The entry closes by warning against confusing him with another Menahem of Saadia's circle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-millaud-arthur-:
Albert Millaud, born in Paris in 1836, was a French journalist and playwright, the son of the press magnate Moïse Millaud. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He published a book of poems at eighteen to considerable success, an early sign of the wit that made his name.

In 1869 Millaud joined the Figaro and created the light feuilleton style the paper kept ever after, writing under the names Baron Grimm and La Bruyère. For the stage he turned out a string of sarcastic successes, many built around the actress Madame Judic, from Madame l'Archiduc in 1874 to Mam'zelle Nitouche in 1883. His own papers, the Revue de Poche and Gazette de Hollande, both failed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moscato-judah-a:
Judah Aryeh Moscato, called Leone in Italian, was a rabbi, poet, and philosopher of sixteenth-century Italy. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Osimo near Ancona, he moved to Mantua after the Jews were expelled from the Papal States in 1554. There he studied with leading scholars and became chief rabbi in 1587.

Moscato was a child of the Renaissance, at home in the classical languages and in philosophy. His fifty-two sermons, printed as Nefuzot Yehudah in 1588, opened a new epoch in Jewish preaching. They follow the rules of rhetoric yet treat their subjects in a natural way. His Kol Yehudah, printed after his death, was the first commentary on the Cuzari of Judah ha-Levi. It has been printed with that work ever since.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-pavia-:
Moses of Pavia, surnamed Gaon, was an Italian scholar placed by his entry in the eleventh century. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Kaufmann identified him with a teacher who left Pavia about the year 900 after a quarrel. The record is tangled, and the entry says so plainly.

Whatever his dates, the medieval schools cite him as a gaon in their treatises on terefot, the laws of animal defects. Rieti's poem Mikdash Me'at reports that he died a martyr's death, apparently in 1096. In the printed Tosafot he is usually confused with Moses of Pontoise. The entry preserves a name the tradition honored but could not pin down.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-musarnikes-lit-:
Musarnikes, the Moralists, was the nickname for the followers of Rabbi Israel Lipkin of Salant in Russia. Joseph Jacobs and Peter Wiernik wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on the movement. Lipkin held that Talmud study alone left the feelings untrained. About 1842 he founded a society at Wilna for studying books on religious morals.

The movement spread to Kovno and beyond, and its opponents feared a split like the Hasidic one. His pupils carried it into yeshivot at Kelm, Slobodka, and Lubtch, with funds gathered for married students of musar. Under later leaders the moral study sometimes hardened into harsh self-scrutiny and seclusion. A riot at Slobodka in 1897 first brought the Musarnikes to the outside world's notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nassau-adolf-ri:
Adolf Ritter von Nassau was an Austrian journalist in Vienna. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Pohrlitz, Moravia, on Dec. 25, 1834. He was educated at Vienna. His first post was as stenographer to the Austrian Parliament.

Nassau then joined the Presse as its parliamentary reporter. When the Neue Freie Presse was founded, he joined its staff. In 1871 he bought the Presse itself. He ran it as chief editor and owner for six years. The Länderbank bought the paper in 1877, and he retired. He lived quietly in Vienna after leaving public life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nemirov-11437:
Nemirov was a town of Podolia famed for learning and loss. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Before 1648 it drew Jews as a center of study. Its rabbis, like Lipmann Heller, held high repute. Then came the Cossack uprising of that year.

Refugees swelled the town's Jews past six thousand souls. Three hundred Cossacks came under false Polish flags. Greek townsmen urged the Jews to open the gates. The Cossacks rushed in and massacred six thousand Jews. Most chose death over forced baptism that day. A requiem for them is still read in Podolia. Under Turkish rule a tax tyrant there was executed. In 1896 the town counted 2,874 Jews in all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nyons-11637:
Nyons is a town in Dauphiné, an old part of France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish group lived there before the year 1300. A Latin text from 1322 speaks of old Jews there. It also speaks of new Jews who had just come.

The new Jews had fled the Comtat-Venaissin when cast out. Two of them won sway with the dauphin Humbert the Second. The town was also home to Isaac ben Mordecai. Men called him Maestro Petit, or the small master. He wrote the Azharot, a poem in verse form. It lists the six hundred and thirteen laws of Moses. His notes on the Talmud won wide respect too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-simon:
Simon ben David Oppenheim was an Austrian writer and judge. Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Kromau, in Moravia, in 1753. He died at Pest, where he served as dayyan, in 1851. A dayyan is a judge in a Jewish court.

Simon read at Prague in the late years of his youth. The entry brands him a man who stole others' work. His first book, from 1789, took from Baruch Lindau. Lindau's text book on land and nature came out in 1788. Simon's book on right conduct took from an older work too. That older work was by Jehiel ben Jekuthiel Anaw. Ezekiel Landau spoke harsh words on Simon's pride. He blamed his grand titles on his first book's front page.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pasuk-11937:
Pasuḳ is a Hebrew word that means a verse of the Bible. Crawford Howell Toy and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word comes from an Aramaic root meaning to cut off. A verse is a small cut of text, and the name fits that sense.

Verse division is old, and a form of it appears in the Septuagint. The divisions used now came from the Masorites. Their work fixed the Hebrew text for later ages. In later Jewish German usage the word widened. It came to mean any Bible book except the Pentateuch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perl-joseph-120:
Joseph Perl was a Galician patron of Jewish learning. He was born at Tarnopol in 1774 and died there in 1839. Isidore Singer and N. Slouschz wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Wealth let him spend his life on reform. Two emperors honored him with decorations.

Perl founded the first modern Jewish school in Poland. In 1815 he built a Reform synagogue beside it. Both works came from his own purse. He fought Hasidic mysticism with satire instead. His Megalleh Temirin posed as a Hasidic text. The parody fooled even Hasidim for years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polemics-and-po:
Polemics means attacks on Judaism and the Jewish replies to them. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote a long article on that fight of books. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The writers begin with the ancient pagan world. Pagans by and large left other faiths alone. Toward Judaism, though, they showed open anger.

The first anti-Jewish writings came from Egypt, the article says. A priest named Manetho made up tales about the Jews in Egypt. He claimed that sick outcasts left Egypt under a priest named Moses. Later writers took up these tales and made them worse. Jewish writers answered with works in defense of their faith. The article traces that long fight of books across the ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pulitzer-joseph:
Joseph Pulitzer was an American editor and journalist of great fame. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Budapest in Hungary in 1847. He was taught in private, not in public schools. In 1863 he left his home town for America.

Pulitzer reached the States in time for the Civil War. He joined the Federal army as a cavalry private. He fought until the close of the war. Work in New York failed him after his discharge. He went west to St. Louis to seek his fortune. There he joined the Westliche Post as a reporter. He rose to lead that German paper in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahamim-nissim-: Nissim Rahamim was a Turkish rabbinical writer who lived at Smyrna. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Smyrna in 1828. His Hebrew work Har ha-Mor came out at Salonica in 1835. It holds sermons and essays on Maimonides. That is nearly all the entry reports about him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riccio-paulo-la:
Paulo Riccio was a Jewish convert to Christianity from Germany. Kaufmann Kohler and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked in the first half of the sixteenth century. He taught philosophy at the University of Pavia.

The article says he later served as physician to Emperor Maximilian I. He leaned toward astrology and the Cabala. He debated Johann Eck on life among the stars. Erasmus thought very highly of him, they note. Riccio tried to convince Jews of the Gospels' truth. His best known work translates part of Gikatilla's cabalistic book. Emperor Maximilian ordered him to translate the Talmud into Latin. Only three tractates of that work survive. They are the earliest Latin Mishnah renderings known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenbach-ottom:
Ottomar Ernst Felix Rosenbach was a German physician born at Krappitz, Silesia, on January 4, 1851. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree in 1874, after service as a war volunteer.

Rosenbach worked at Jena and at the Allerheiligen Hospital in Breslau, where he led the medical department. In 1896 he left his professorship and moved to Berlin to practise. His books treat the vagus nerve, heart disease, seasickness, and the limits of therapy. One late work, Arzt Contra Bacteriologe, reached English readers in a 1904 translation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rules-of-r-ishm:
The Thirteen Rules of Rabbi Ishmael are rules for drawing laws out of the Torah. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Rabbi Ishmael b. Elisha compiled them for the elucidation of the Torah.

Strictly, the thirteen are expansions of Hillel's older seven rules. They stand in the Baraita of Rabbi Ishmael, the introduction to the Sifra. The first two match Hillel's: reasoning from lesser to greater, and analogy. The rest refine how general statements and particular cases limit each other. Several handle a detail set apart from its general rule on purpose.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomon-william:
William Salomon was an American financier born at Mobile, Alabama, on October 9, 1852. Joseph Jacobs and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a great-grandson of Haym Salomon, of Revolutionary fame.

Salomon entered Speyer and Company in New York in 1867, aged fifteen. He worked for its Frankfort house and its London branch as well. By 1882 he was a member of the New York firm itself. He left in 1899 and founded William Salomon and Company in 1902. In railroad finance he helped reorganize the Baltimore and Ohio line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-nath: Schulim Ochser wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel ben Nathan, a writer of prayers who lived in the fourteenth century. Almost nothing else about him is known. Even his birthplace and home are unrecorded. He wrote three prayers that survive in manuscript. In those manuscripts he is sometimes called by the name Rabanu. The entry rests on Zunz's history of Jewish liturgical poetry, which lists him on a single page.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-savoy-13237:
Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Savoy. The old duchy joined the kingdom of Sardinia in 1720. France took it in 1860. When Philip Augustus expelled the Jews from France in 1182, many fled to Savoy. More came after the second expulsion in 1306. Amadeus the Fifth granted Savoy's Jews many privileges.

Savoy stands out in the horror of the Black Death. In 1348 accusers claimed the plague poison was made at Chambéry. Jews were massacred in town after town. At Montmélian the mob stormed the prison and killed the prisoners. Eleven survivors were later burned alive in a barn. A document preserves the victims' names from Aiguebelle. Yet Jewish life soon resumed. The dukes themselves often borrowed from Jewish lenders. One duchess pawned her jewels to two Jews in 1366.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwalbe-gustav:
Gustav Schwalbe, a German anatomist and anthropologist, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman, published in 1906. Schwalbe was born at Quedlinburg on August 1, 1844. He studied at Berlin, Zurich, and Bonn. He took his medical degree in 1866. He then climbed the academic ladder quickly.

Schwalbe taught at Halle, Freiburg, and Leipsic in turn. He became professor of anatomy at Jena in 1873. Königsberg followed in 1881, and Strasburg in 1883. He edits journals on anatomy and on anthropology. His textbooks cover neurology and the organs of sense. His studies treat the thickness of nerve fibers. Later works take up Pithecanthropus, the Neanderthal skull, and the prehistory of man. Pagel's lexicon supplies the outline of his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seraphim-13437:
Seraphim are a class of heavenly beings named only once in the Old Testament. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. Isaiah saw them standing before God's throne in a famous vision. Each had six wings, two covering the face, two the feet, and two for flight.

They call to one another, Holy, holy, holy, without pause. Their voices shake the thresholds of the Temple. One seraph touches Isaiah's lips with a live coal from the altar. That touch cleans the prophet from sin. Readers learn how little the Bible says about these beings, and how much later readers built on that brief, vivid scene.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shekinah-lit-th:
Shekinah, literally the dwelling, names God's majestic presence among human beings. Kaufmann Kohler and Ludwig Blau wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the term. Rabbis used it instead of naming God directly in some verses. That avoided crude pictures of God in bodily form.

The word grows out of verses about God dwelling in Israel. He dwells in the Tabernacle, in Jerusalem, and on Mount Zion. His glory rested on Mount Sinai in Exodus as well. Like Memra and Glory, Shekinah softens biblical language about God. The entry traces how Jewish thought kept God near his people. At the same time it kept Him above human shape and limit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simmons-laurenc:
Laurence Mark Simmons was an English rabbi born in London in 1852. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the City of London School. In 1873 he went to the Rabbinical Seminary at Breslau. He held degrees from London and from Victoria University, Manchester.

In 1877 he became minister to the Manchester Congregation of British Jews. He served at the Park Place Synagogue there. Simmons wrote often for the Jewish Quarterly Review and other journals. He also reprinted Maimun ben Joseph's Iggeret ha-Shemad in 1893. He died at Manchester on April 5, 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sola-de-13837:
De Sola was a Sephardic family with roots in Toledo and Navarre. Joseph Jacobs and Clarence I de Sola wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Family tradition traces its members to the eighth and ninth centuries. One member, Baruch ben Ishac ibn Daud, raised its standing in Navarre. The family later flourished in Cordova and Seville.

Persecution drove the family to Tudela in 1146. It took the surname De Sola in the late twelfth century. The name came from an estate in northern Spain, it is said. Fresh persecution drove the family to Granada in time. The edict of 1492 then banished it from Spain. Its branches scattered to Portugal, Holland, and beyond.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-south-carolina-:
South Carolina was one of the thirteen original states of America. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Most Jewish events in the state center on Charleston. Its first charter, drawn by John Locke in 1669, gave liberty of conscience. Jews, heathens, and dissenters were all named in that grant.

Yet Jews seem not to have come until 1695. A Jew named Simon Valentine held land there by 1698. By 1703 protest arose against Jewish strangers voting in elections. Many early settlers came from London or the English colonies. In 1755 Joseph Salvador bought 100,000 acres near Fort Ninety-six. He paid 2,000 pounds for that vast tract of land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-samuel-14:
Samuel Stern was a Hungarian physician born at Halas on September 16, 1839. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at the universities of Prague and Vienna. For a time he worked as assistant physician at Vienna's communal hospital. His career stayed in that city.

In 1863 Stern became a lecturer at the University of Vienna. By 1870 he was assistant professor of clinical propedeutics there. That field teaches students how to examine patients before diagnosis. His 1868 book studied functions of the nervous system. A later work argued for the teaching clinic as a research institute. In 1877 he published a guide to diagnosing chest diseases. The short entry records a teacher of clinical method.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sussmann-shabbe:
Shabbethai ben Eliezer Sussmann was a scholar of the eighteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. His life is known mainly through his books. His chief work bears the title Me'ir Natib. It appeared at Altona between 1793 and 1802.

Me'ir Natib is a general index in three volumes. It covers the tosafot glosses on the entire Talmud. Such an index saved scholars long searches through dense pages. In its introduction Sussmann names four other works he wrote. Their titles include Ner Tamid and Katit la-Ma'or. None of those four books was ever published. The brief entry preserves a reference tool and its lost companions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhuma-b-skola:
Tanhuma ben Skolastikai was a Palestinian teacher of the Law. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. His exact period is not known to scholars. One guess makes him a son of Joshua ben Hananiah. The Palestinian Talmud mentions him only once.

That single mention preserves a prayer he read. It asks God to destroy the evil desire within hearts. The prayer calls that desire the yeast in the dough. It confesses that humans lack strength to resist alone. Frankel held that this Tanhuma is Tanhuma ben Abba himself. Bacher's work on the Palestinian amoraim supports the question. The entry shows how one prayer carries a sage's whole record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terquem-olry-14:
Olry Terquem was a French mathematician born at Metz in 1782. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Terquem entered the Ecole Polytechnique in Paris in 1801. He taught higher mathematics at Mayence and Grenoble. From 1815 he served as librarian in Paris.

With Gerono he founded a mathematics journal in 1842. He also edited a bulletin on the history of mathematics. Napoleon III made him an officer of the Legion of Honor. Terquem wrote handbooks and an unfinished history of artillery. He also pled for reform within Judaism. His pamphlets even urged a Sunday Sabbath. France's chief rabbi led his funeral.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-transmigration-:
Transmigration of souls, the passage of a soul through many bodies, is examined here. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Pythagoras taught that the freed mind takes new bodily form. It may return as human or as animal. Purified at last, it rejoins its eternal source.

The doctrine was foreign to Judaism until the eighth century. Muslim mystics then influenced Karaites and other dissenters. Saadia first mentions the belief in Jewish writing. He protested against it with some contempt. Believers argued from animal traits in human character. A gentle man, they said, holds a lamb's soul. They also cited verses from Deuteronomy and Psalms. Saadia refuted both lines of argument.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tuchmann-jules-:
Jules Tuchmann was a French folklorist born in Paris in 1830. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Privately educated, he died in Paris in 1901. He spent his whole life tracing the supernatural in folk belief. His findings filled the journal Melusine for years.

His great series was called La Fascination, the evil eye. It ran through all ten volumes of Melusine. Though named for one subject, it covers far more ground. Witches, witchcraft, and folk medicine all enter its pages. The article calls it perhaps folklore's most thorough single study. Few branches of the field received such deep treatment. His work still anchors study of the evil eye.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vambery-arminiu:
Arminius Vámbéry was a Hungarian traveler and scholar of the East. He was born near Presburg on March 19, 1832. Isidore Singer and Louis H. Gray wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Poor as a boy, Vámbéry still reached gymnasium and university study. Turkey's language and culture drew him most.

In 1854 Vámbéry went to Constantinople as a tutor. He later served a Turkish pasha as secretary. In 1861 he crossed Central Asia disguised as a dervish. He traveled under the name Rashid Effendi. His road ran through Persia to Khiva, Bokhara, and Samarkand. No European had made such a trip before, and his account made him famous.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiller-lazare-:
Lazare Jean Weiller was a French manufacturer and author. He was born at Schlettstadt, Alsace, on July 20, 1858. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Paris and at Oxford. He devoted himself to electric metallurgy. His copper alloys made long distance telephones possible.

In 1883 France made Weiller a knight of the Legion of Honor. He advised the state on railways and colonial affairs. In 1902 he traveled to the United States on a mission. His book on America ran through fifty editions. His treatise on electric lines became a classic. He also took a bold part in the Dreyfus case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winawer-simon-1:
Simon Winawer was a Russian chess master. Isidore Singer and A. Porter wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Warsaw in 1839. In 1867 he watched chess games at a Paris café. On impulse he entered a tournament held there. To everyone's surprise he took second prize.

Winawer then devoted himself to the game in earnest. At Paris in 1878 he again took second prize. At Vienna in 1882 he shared first with Steinitz. At Nuremberg in 1883 he won first prize outright. His form declined after those peak years. Dresden and Budapest gave him only sixth place. Monte Carlo in 1901 left him prizeless.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wysber-ludwig-1:
Ludwig Wysber (born 1817) was a Hungarian news writer with a dark past. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He began life as a street peddler in Pesth. He then sang in the chorus of the German stage there.

Small posts on local papers came next in his rise. In the March days of 1848 he won leave to print a paper. His paper, Der Patriot, spoke for the Kossuth party. It won wide sway in that fight for a free land. From 1850 to 1870 his name turns grim in the tale. Counts of theft from traders and priests fill the years. He used false names and fled arrest more than once. One book of Hungarian life scenes bears his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zemah-ben-kafna: Zemah ben Kafnai was gaon of Pumbedita from 936 to 938. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held that post when Saadia was put back at Sura. Saadia had been cast out and then restored to his chair. No facts of the life of Zemah are known at all. No works of his hand are named in the entry. The note rests on a writ of Sherira and two pasts.
matthews-bible-1537:
John Rogers, writing under the name Thomas Matthew, put together Matthew's Bible in 1537. It was the first Bible printed in England under a royal licence. Rogers stitched it from the best English work of his day: William Tyndale's New Testament and first five books of the Old Testament, plus Myles Coverdale's version of the rest.

The result is a bridge between Tyndale, who was executed for his translating, and the Great Bible that followed two years later. Much of its wording passed into every later English Bible. Readers get the complete Old and New Testaments in the forceful early Tudor English that defined the tradition.
openalex-w2033809437:
Ana Maria Sanchez-Cuervo, Mitchell Aide, Matthew Clark and Andres Etter mapped land cover change in Colombia. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. Colombia is rich in species and habitats. Yet it lacked a consistent map of land change. Such maps help target conservation work.

The team used satellite images to map land cover each year. They covered the decade from 2001 to 2010. Detailed images from Google Earth trained and checked the maps. Most municipalities gained woody vegetation over the decade. Gains clearly outweighed losses at the national scale. Regrowth was strongest in moist mountain forests. The Llanos region lost the most woody cover. The authors call the Andean recovery a conservation chance.
openalex-w2101607137:
Linhai Wang, Sheng Yu, Chaobo Tong and colleagues sequenced the sesame genome. Their paper appeared in Genome Biology in 2014. Sesame is prized for its rich, high-quality oil. It grows widely in warm regions worldwide. Its molecular biology had barely been studied before.

The team assembled a high-quality genome from scratch. It holds roughly twenty-seven thousand genes. An ancient whole-genome doubling event stood out. Gene comparisons revealed how oil production is supported. Some fat-building gene families had expanded. Fat-breakdown genes had shrunk by contrast. Genes active in seed oil pathways differed between varieties. The genome gives breeders a map for improving oil yield.
openalex-w2104040437:
Maria Van Kerkhove, Katelijn Vandemaele, Vivek Shinde and colleagues pooled world data on severe flu outcomes. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2011. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic raised urgent policy questions. Leaders needed to know who faced the highest risk. Targeted protection depends on such knowledge.

Countries shared case data with the World Health Organization. The team combined records across many nations. They compared mild cases with severe and fatal ones. Chronic conditions, pregnancy and age were examined closely. Patterns of risk emerged across very different settings. Some factors raised risk in nearly every country. The analysis guided vaccine and treatment priorities. It also improved planning for future pandemics.
openalex-w2106948237:
Philipp Kapranov, Georges St Laurent, Tal Raz and colleagues measured how much human cell RNA remains unexplained. Their paper appeared in BMC Biology in 2010. Most RNA made by human genes does not code for proteins. How much of it is unknown mattered for genome science. Some dismissed such RNA as mere noise.

The team measured RNA from the cell nucleus. They excluded the well-known ribosomal RNA fraction. Most remaining RNA mass was un-annotated, they found. It matched no known gene or function. They call this share the genome's dark matter. Its size argues against dismissing it as noise. Regulation roles may hide in that mass. The paper sharpened debate on genome function.
openalex-w2109936637:
Katrin Kuhls, Mohammad Zahangir Alam, Elisa Cupolillo and colleagues typed a leishmaniasis parasite across the Americas. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2011. The parasite causes visceral disease from the southern United States to Argentina. Its American origin was debated. It may have arrived in recent times from the Old World.

The team used fine DNA markers to type the samples. American groups showed little diversity between them. That low variety points to a recent shared origin. Checks against Old World samples backed the import idea. European settlement likely brought the parasite across the sea. Infected dogs may have carried it on ships. Knowing its past helps track its current spread.
openalex-w2137236837:
V. Khachatryan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration published this study in the Journal of High Energy Physics in 2010. They measured how pairs of charged particles line up in angle after proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Such patterns reveal how particles are produced and whether dense collision systems act as a group.

Data came from collisions at three energy levels recorded by the CMS detector. Short-range pair patterns were described with a simple cluster model. In busy events with many particles, a striking new structure appeared at middle momenta. Pairs stayed linked across a long stretch in one angle while pointing the same way in the other. Nothing like it had been seen in proton collisions before.
openalex-w2139967537:
V. Khachatryan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration published this study in Physical Review D in 2015. They tested the spin and parity of the newly found Higgs boson, basic traits that confirm what kind of particle it is. They also probed how it interacts with other force-carrying particles, hunting for odd couplings.

The team used the full first run of CMS data from proton collisions at two energy levels. They studied several Higgs decay paths, including decays to lepton pairs and photon pairs. A wide range of spin-two models was ruled out with high confidence. Mixed-parity spin-one options were also excluded, and limits were set on eleven anomalous coupling terms.
openalex-w2160639837:
Iván Rosas, Thomas Richards, Kazuhisa Konishi, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2008. They hunted for blood proteins that can flag idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive lung scarring disease. A simple blood test could spare patients risky biopsies and help track how the disease advances.

The team measured forty-nine proteins in plasma from patients and healthy controls. A five-protein signature separated the groups with very high accuracy, catching nearly every patient. Two signature proteins, MMP1 and MMP7, also ran high in patients' lung tissue and lung wash fluid. They stayed normal in two other lung diseases and helped tell this fibrosis apart from a look-alike condition, hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
openalex-w2261604737:
Rodrigo Meucci, Anaclaudia Fassa, and Neice Faria published this systematic review in Revista de Saúde Pública in 2015. They estimated how common chronic low back pain is worldwide, broken down by age and sex. Their search covered three major medical databases for population studies that measured the condition directly.

Twenty-eight studies made the final set, though about a third scored poorly, mostly for low response rates. Reported prevalence ran from about four in a hundred young adults to roughly twenty in a hundred in some adult ranges. Studies of adults overall clustered between about four and twenty percent. Among older Brazilians, one in four people reported chronic low back pain, the highest figure found.
openalex-w3000706737:
Palaniappan Seedevi, Abirami Ganesan, Meivelu Moovendhan, and colleagues published this study in Scientific Reports in 2020. It tests two sugar-chain extracts from the seaweed-like alga G. lithophila as treatments for diabetes. The tests used rats made diabetic with a drug called streptozotocin.

Both the crude extract and a version enriched in the sugar rhamnose were fed to the diabetic rats. Treated rats gained body weight and pancreatic insulin, while their blood sugar fell, compared with untreated diabetic rats. Harmful blood fats dropped and the protective fat fraction rose. Protective enzymes in the liver, kidneys, and pancreas also rose, while a marker of cell damage fell.
openalex-w3011642937:
Lorenzo Galluzzi, Ilio Vitale, Sarah Warren, and colleagues wrote these consensus guidelines in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer in 2020. They define immunogenic cell death, a form of cell death that can wake up the immune system. The topic matters for cancer treatments that aim to turn dying tumor cells into a vaccine-like signal.

Dying cells spark lasting immunity only when they show enough telltale features to alert immune cells. The authors give an updated working definition of this death type. They list the cell and tissue factors that decide whether the response takes hold. They also survey the lab and animal tests now used to detect it, and set guidelines for judging claims in future studies.
openalex-w3012798837:
Bo Xu, Bernardo Gutiérrez, Sumiko Mekaru, and colleagues published this data paper in Scientific Data in 2020. It presents a live, case-level dataset from the COVID-19 outbreak. Cases of the new coronavirus were first reported in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 and then spread worldwide.

To aid tracking and analysis, the team collected and cleaned records of individual cases. Their sources were health reports at national, provincial, and city levels, plus further online reports. Each record is placed on the map, and extra details are included where reports gave them. The open dataset let researchers follow the epidemic's spread in near real time during its first months.
openalex-w3095607637:
Alexander Wezel, Barbara Herren, Rachel Bezner Kerr, and colleagues wrote this review in Agronomy for Sustainable Development in 2020. It sets out the principles and elements of agroecology and what they imply for remaking food systems. Experts broadly agree the current global food system fails on nutrition and degrades land and wildlife.

Agroecology appears in three forms at once: a science, a set of farm practices, and a social movement. The authors review its concepts and history across all three forms. They connect that history to a recent shared list of ten elements meant to guide transitions. The review gives farmers, researchers, and policymakers a common language for moving farms toward sustainability without losing sight of hunger and rural poverty.
openalex-w3125505637:
Mireya Vilar-Compte, Soraya Burrola-Méndez, Annel Lozano-Marrufo, and colleagues published this systematic review in the International Journal for Equity in Health in 2021. It examines how urban poverty limits access to a healthy diet around the world. Cities usually offer better food access than the countryside, but not to their poorest residents.

Following standard review methods, the team gathered studies in English and Spanish from 2000 to 2019. Eligible work dealt with food access or with outcomes such as anemia, overweight, and missing micronutrients among the urban poor. The poor face outsized barriers to healthy food and a higher risk of malnutrition in both its forms. The review weighs how strongly poverty itself drives those outcomes.
openalex-w3164401237:
Amy Nivette, Renee Zahnow, and colleagues ask what stay-at-home orders did to city crime around the world. Their study appeared in Nature Human Behaviour in 2021. When COVID-19 spread, governments ordered people to stay home, changing daily routines almost overnight. Whether crime rose or fell under those orders was unclear.

The team gathered daily crime counts from twenty-seven cities in twenty-three countries across four continents. They used interrupted time series methods, which compare crime before and after the orders began. Looking across many cities at once shows whether patterns seen in one place held elsewhere. That breadth helps separate local quirks from effects shared worldwide.
openalex-w3164981937:
Diana Buitrago, Mireia Labrador, Juan Pablo Arcon, and colleagues study how DNA methylation reshapes the folding of the genome. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications in 2021. Methylation adds a small chemical tag to DNA. The team added this tag to yeast cells, which normally lack it, to isolate its direct effects.

Methylation shifted the small protein spools, called nucleosomes, that DNA wraps around. It also changed how chromosome regions touch each other, tightening areas near centromeres and reducing contacts between chromosomes. Together, these physical changes altered gene activity. The work shows methylation can steer genes by reshaping structure, not only by blocking proteins.
openalex-w3173594637:
Sebastian Bahamonde, Konstantinos Dialektopoulos, Celia Escamilla-Rivera, and colleagues review teleparallel gravity in Reports on Progress in Physics in 2023. Teleparallel gravity is Einstein's other way of describing gravity, built on twisting space rather than curving it. Interest in it has grown fast in recent decades.

The review first builds the theory as a gauge theory, the same style used for other forces in physics. It then shows a version that matches general relativity exactly, before sorting the many modified versions proposed since. Later sections cover stars, black holes, and cosmology. The result is a single map of a sprawling field, open questions included.
openalex-w3183695837:
André Devaux, Jean-Pierre Goffart, Peter Kromann, and colleagues examine the future of the potato in Potato Research in 2021. Feeding a growing world well, without wrecking the environment, is the challenge ahead. The potato already grows widely and matters most in poorer countries hit by hunger. The authors ask what role it can play in fairer food systems.

Food security, they note, rests on supply, access, healthy use, and stability over time. The paper reviews the potato's place in world food supply, then weighs how research could help. Rural systems in low-income countries need higher yields above all. Industrial systems need tighter control of water, land, and chemicals. Matching both paths is the paper's central task.
openalex-w7164301637:
Jerrold Levy, of Duke University, led a 2026 laboratory study with Juntendo University colleagues on how bacterial endotoxin injures white blood cells in sepsis. Sepsis involves runaway inflammation in which dying cells spill contents, called DAMPs, that fuel further damage. The team exposed rat white blood cells to endotoxin in a dish and looked for signs of ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death.

Endotoxin caused marked injury: membranes ruptured, cell interiors collapsed, and contents spilled out. Iron accumulated inside the cells and in their mitochondria and lysosomes, a ferroptosis-linked pattern. Damaged DNA escaped the cells, and two overlapping styles of inflammatory cell death appeared side by side. The authors link this mix to the clotting-inflammation spiral that damages organs in sepsis.
openalex-w7204253337:
Carlos Everton Costa Leal de Sousa and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva published a Portuguese-language documentary analysis in Brazil in 2026 on accessibility inside Brazil's National Digital Education Policy. The policy, created by a 2023 law, governs how digital education reaches public schools, including students with disabilities. The authors read the law together with five later decrees, opinions, and resolutions, tracking where accessibility is mentioned, how binding it is, and whether it connects to execution mechanisms.

Accessibility appears recognizably in the policy's principles, above all in the school digital education axis, the authors find. But it thins out near implementation: it is absent from the connectivity strategy, monitoring goals, teacher training plans, and the operational definition guiding the curriculum. The gap between rule and school practice, they conclude, is written into the policy's own design.
openalex-w7208752437:
Iasmyn Santana Rodrigues and Karla Goncalves Macedo write on neuromarketing, the field that joins marketing with neuroscience to study how the brain responds to products and brands. Their focus is nostalgia as a brand strategy aimed at Generation Z, the young consumers now entering the market in force. The study is exploratory and bibliographic, built on leading theoretical work in the field rather than new experiments.

Brands compete hard for attention, and the authors examine how sensory cues and fond memories can shape buying choices below the level of conscious reasoning. Nostalgia is a strong lever: remembered feelings attach to products and can tilt decisions that shoppers believe are purely rational. For companies, the lesson is to understand the hidden motives of customers; for readers, the study doubles as a guide to noticing when their own memories are being marketed to.
openalex-w7212426437:
Isadora Stroka Fernandes and Luciana Osorio Cavalli count ward stays for sore throat and tonsil flare-ups in Brazil from 2010 to 2024. They set the whole land next to Parana state, one of its parts. The work is a chart read from a state bank of ward costs and stays. Both ills are lung-way germs that strike the young most. Yet each year they send a fair stream of kids to beds.

More than one hundred sixty thousand stays filled the span. Just over half were kids under ten. Stays peaked in the cold and fall months, a clean sign of the season's pull. Then 2020 broke the line: stays fell by more than half as the COVID-19 years began. Stays in Parana ran a bit shorter than the land's mean. The tale helps health chiefs staff for the cold surge, and read how a shock can thin a ward fast.
openalex-w7212746137:
Roberto de Paula Pinto leads a team that maps soils in Brazil's Cerrado by screen, in place of long treks on foot. Soil maps guide farms, builds, and green care. The old way to make them joins desk work, field digs, and lab tests. It is slow, dear, and hard to keep fresh. The team used space shots, height maps, and plant cover data for land near the Agua Limpa farm.

On screen, they sorted the land by slope, rock base, and plant skin. That sort let them draw soil lines with far less leg work. They then checked the new map next to an old half-fine map of the same ground. The test tells how far a screen map can be trusted. For a land as wide as the Cerrado, fast maps that hold up are worth much to farms and green plans alike.
openalex-w7213237637:
Solange Maria de Souza Moura leads six peers in a study of how we draw and share what we know. Their class, in a Bahia grad scheme on the spread of lore, took signs and marks of the day as its theme. To sum the term's path, the group turned to cordel: the cheap rhyme books sold at fairs in Brazil's dry north-east. Verse was the tool that held the term's thought.

Their stance cuts at the grain of the day. Life run by code, watch, and mart bends how we know and share. The group holds that rule, right, and thought are one cloth, not three. A fair share of marks and lore needs all three in view. The cordel close makes the point in form: folk verse can carry high thought, and the path of lore need not wear a suit.
openalex-w7213319037:
Luis Fernando Oliveira Duarte and Emerson Gervasio de Almeida sort the cash rule of Brazil's state-run colleges. A hard cap on state cash, set in 2016, squeezes these schools year by year. The pair read past work from 2017 to 2025; seventeen studies made the set. They sorted the ills, the acts, and the trends.

The ills start at the top: plans and spend drift apart, and clout, not need, steers much of the cash. Waste in the back rooms adds its share. The acts that fight back span plain sight on the books and cost calls made by math ahead of time. They span hunts for cash past the state, shared votes on spend, and fresh signs to grade the rule. One catch stands out: what works at one school may flop at the next. Each house must fit the fix to its own walls.
openalex-w7213535437:
Talma Cristeles Chagas Oliveira and co-authors examine criminal protection for child victims of sexual violence in Brazil. Their 2026 article uses library and research. It joins punishment of the offender with protection of the victim's procedural rights, under the doctrine of full protection.

Despite a wide legal framework, effective response is weakened in practice, the authors find. Proof is hard to gather, especially in sexual crimes inside families. Institutional revictimization remains a risk, and protection networks work poorly together. Special testimony rules for children are discussed as one safeguard. National public security data support the picture of a system whose laws outrun its daily coordination.
openalex-w7213864437:
Laurindo Hilário Canganjo leads a large team proposing mediation for conflicts inside a school in Bailundo, Angola. Their 2026 case study concerns a named secondary school in Huambo province. The research is qualitative, applied, and action-based, using library and historical methods.

Schools in the municipality lack strategies to settle differences without sanctions or court routes, the authors say. That gap feeds high failure, forced transfers, and absence. Mediation is offered as a way to improve relations among teachers, pupils, and school leadership. The team aims to lower internal conflict across Angolan education, with this school as the worked example for a different, restorative approach.
openalex-w7213883937:
Nathanael Lucas Freitas de Sousa and co-authors review strength training for older people with sarcopenia. That age-linked condition cuts strength, muscle mass, and physical performance. Their 2026 narrative review covers PubMed and SciELO work from 2021 to 2025, keeping twelve articles.

Assessment tools in the literature include screening questionnaires, hand grip measurement, body scans, walking speed, and timed movement tests. Strength training brought nerve and muscle adaptations, more strength, and preserved lean mass, the review finds. Balance, gait, and physical performance also improved. Regular, progressive, individually fitted training can cut functional limits, the authors conclude, helping older people keep autonomy and independence.
openalex-w7214401137:
Innaê Cerqueira Ferreira Gonçalves Nascimento led a 2026 article connecting collaborative learning with the sociocultural theory of Lev Vygotsky. Vygotsky held that human development grows out of social life, shaped by culture and language. Learning, on that view, is social from the start, and students grow by working with teachers and peers who can stretch them a little beyond what they manage alone.

The authors trace that idea from mental development to teacher training and finally to school assessment. They pair Vygotsky with Theodor Adorno's warning about barbarism inside education to argue for assessment that mediates and converses rather than merely sorting students. Such assessment, they say, should respect students' real living conditions, especially in socially vulnerable settings like those they note in Tocantins, Brazil.
openalex-w7215035837:
Elena Bessa Magaldi Alves led a 2026 article that reads Brazil's decriminalization of marijuana possession for personal use through the political philosophy of Thomas Hobbes. The Supreme Federal Court's ruling is read beside Hobbes's ideas on security and the limits of state power, and beside critical penal studies. The method is a close reading of literature, documents, and the leading case.

Prohibition, the authors find, though said to protect social order, widens criminal justice discretion, adds to penal selectivity, and restricts autonomy, intimacy, and dignity out of proportion. In Hobbesian terms, security supports state power only while it is aimed at keeping individuals safe; it does not justify total suppression of liberty. The court's decision, they conclude, is a real restraint on punitive power, joining social order with fundamental rights and with individual guarantees as a condition of legitimate state action.
plos-pbio-0020137:
Hunter B. Fraser, Aaron E. Hirsh, Guri Giaever, and co-workers studied noise in gene activity in PLOS Biology in 2004. Noise here means random wobble in how much protein a gene makes from cell to cell. Too much wobble can harm a cell, so genes may have evolved ways to keep it low.

The authors show that key genes, the ones a cell can least afford to get wrong, tend to run with less noise. Cells seem to spend more control effort where errors cost most. That is an elegant piece of design logic in gene regulation. It also matters for medicine and bioengineering, where steady output from a gene can be as vital as the output level itself.
plos-pbio-0020237:
David G. Ransom, Nathan Bahary, Knut Niss, and a large team identified a zebrafish gene in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mutant fish called moonshine fail to make blood properly. The team found the broken gene codes for TIF1γ, a protein that helps control which genes are read.

Blood formation needs tight gene control as stem cells mature into red and white cells. TIF1γ proves essential for that program in the fish embryo. Zebrafish with this fault give researchers a living model of blood failure. The work also links a general gene-control protein to one clear job, a connection that helps make sense of similar proteins in humans.
plos-pone-0000037:
Tamayo Uechi, Yukari Nakajima, Akihiro Nakao, and co-authors knocked down ribosomal protein genes in zebrafish to see what development requires of them. Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, and each one is built from many proteins. Zebrafish embryos grow in the open, which makes them ideal for watching development go right or wrong.

Silencing one ribosomal protein gene after another produced developmental defects in the growing fish. That result says these factory parts are not interchangeable spares; each is needed for the embryo to form correctly. The work speaks to human ribosomopathies, diseases where faulty ribosomal proteins cause birth defects, and it shows why a small fish can model them.
plos-pone-0000137:
Gabriel D. Puccini, Albert Compte, and Miguel Maravall published this neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It concerns the barrel cortex, the part of a rodent's brain that processes touch from its whiskers. Neurons there prefer stimuli moving in certain directions, and the authors ask how that preference changes with the stimulus.

Direction selectivity is not a fixed property; it depends on what the whisker feels. The authors map that dependence in detail. The findings matter for understanding how the brain builds a stable sense of touch from signals that keep changing, a core problem in sensory neuroscience.
plos-pone-0000237:
Julie S. Nielsen, Marcia L. Graves, Shierley Chelliah, and colleagues published this cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Podocalyxin is a protein related to CD34, found on the surface of certain cells. The authors show it is a potent inducer of microvillus formation, driving cells to grow the tiny finger-like projections called microvilli.

Microvilli expand a cell's surface for absorbing and sensing. A single protein that can spark their growth is a strong lever over cell shape. The finding matters for understanding how epithelial surfaces, from gut to kidney, build their texture, and how that texture goes wrong in disease.
plos-pone-0000337:
Naoki Nariai, Eric D. Kolaczyk, and Simon Kasif published this computational biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Predicting what a protein does from its sequence is a central problem in genomics. The authors present a probabilistic method that predicts protein function by combining heterogeneous genome-wide data. Each kind of evidence tells part of the story.

Single data sources mislead often; combining them probabilistically weighs each by reliability. The method is aimed at the thousands of proteins whose jobs remain unknown. Better function prediction speeds every field that starts from a genome sequence, from medicine to agriculture.
plos-pone-0000437:
Sabrina Absalon and colleagues studied how a single-celled parasite places its internal skeleton, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Trypanosoma brucei, which causes sleeping sickness, has a basal body, the anchor from which its whip-like flagellum grows. The team showed basal body positioning is controlled by flagellum formation itself.

Cell architecture in this parasite is precise: the flagellum's position shapes the whole cell and its swimming. If building the flagellum also positions its anchor, the two processes must be tightly linked. Understanding such construction rules matters because the parasite's form is bound up with its life cycle in the tsetse fly and the human bloodstream.
plos-pone-0000537:
M. Thomas P. Gilbert and colleagues compared ways to pull DNA out of stored tissue samples, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Hospitals keep tissue fixed and set in wax blocks. Those blocks hold DNA that doctors and researchers want to read more and more. The team asked which lab methods for getting nucleic acids out of such blocks are in fact useful.

Fixing harms DNA, so methods differ a lot in what they can recover. A fair side-by-side test saves each lab from running the same contest again. The question had weight in 2007. Gene testing was then moving into stored samples, from old hospital blocks to museum specimens.
plos-pone-0000637:
Florin Popescu, Siamac Fazli, Yakob Badower and colleagues tested a leaner setup for brain-computer interfaces in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their system classifies imagined movement from a single trial using just six dry EEG electrodes. EEG records brain waves from the scalp. It can detect mental states without surgery. But the gear has been bulky, and the signals hard to read.

Dry electrodes skip the gels and caps that make standard EEG cumbersome. If six of them still classify motor imagination well, interfaces become far easier to wear and use. The study matters for assistive technology, where people who cannot move may one day steer devices by thought alone.
plos-pone-0000737:
Ramón Díaz-Uriarte and Oscar M. Rueda presented ADaCGH, a software tool for a heavy cancer-data task, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Copy number alterations, stretches of DNA gained or lost, are associated with complex diseases including cancer. A common technique to detect them is array-based comparative genomic hybridization, or aCGH. Platforms were spreading, and the need to identify reliable signals was growing.

ADaCGH runs as a web-based application and as an R package, the standard statistics environment. Its key feature is parallelization, splitting the computation across processors to handle large arrays. Faster, accessible analysis helps smaller labs use aCGH without owning serious computing power.
plos-pone-0000837:
Fumitaka Kugimiya, Hiroshi Kawaguchi, Shinsuke Ohba and colleagues traced bone formation to one kinase and one master gene, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Despite much accumulated knowledge of the signals regulating bone formation, the molecular network was not clarified enough to reach clinical application. Their experiments show that mice with only one working copy of the GSK-3 beta gene displayed increased bone mass.

The title states the mechanism: GSK-3 beta controls osteogenesis, bone building, through regulating Runx2 activity. Runx2 is the master transcription factor for bone-forming cells. A kinase that sets the brake on Runx2 is a candidate target for osteoporosis drugs, where more bone is the goal.
plos-pone-0000937:
Dominik Heyers, Martina Manns, Harald Luksch and colleagues traced a vision route tied to the magnetic compass of migrant birds, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The bird compass seems to need light. Eye cells with cryptochrome proteins and a forebrain area called Cluster N both fire up when songbirds orient by the magnetic field at night.

The team used neuronal tracing to link those structures into one pathway. A mapped route turns a strange sense into anatomy that can be studied. It supports the idea that birds may quite literally see the magnetic field. Few senses have been pinned to a circuit this clearly.
plos-pone-0001037:
Tatjana Seizova-Cajic, Janette Smith and Janet Taylor studied movement illusions caused by long vibration of the body sensors, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Proprioception is the sense of where the body is and how it moves. Its channels adapt to steady stimulation, but that adaptation was poorly described.

The team used vibration, a classic proprioceptive stimulus, over long periods. They report reversals and aftereffects: the felt movement can flip or linger after the stimulus stops. Such illusions expose the rules the brain uses to read body signals. Understanding them matters for balance, rehabilitation and any device that speaks to the body through touch.
plos-pone-0001137:
Oleic acid, a common fat, can push blood vessel wall cells to multiply and move, steps that feed artery disease. Yan Zhang and colleagues tested a counterweight in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They studied PGC-1alpha, a regulator of cell energy use, in rat vascular smooth muscle cells.

The authors report that PGC-1alpha inhibits the growth and migration that oleic acid triggers in these cells. The exact chain of events behind oleic acid's effect was unclear when they began. Their result links a metabolic regulator to the behavior of vessel wall cells, a connection that matters for understanding how fatty acids affect arteries.
plos-pone-0001237:
Pten is a tumor suppressor gene, a brake on cell growth whose loss feeds many cancers. Tsai-Ling Lu and colleagues studied mice engineered to lose Pten in adult tissues, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Earlier work had removed the gene in single tissues to model particular tumors.

A temporally controlled loss of Pten across all adult tissues let the authors compare tumor spectrum, latency, and incidence across organs in one system. Which tissues form tumors, how fast, and how often reveals how widely the brake matters. The mouse work informs the many human cancers where Pten is lost.
plos-pone-0001337:
Cells with double the normal chromosome number are called tetraploid cells. They are a way station on the road to cancer, and they resist radiotherapy and chemotherapy unusually well. Ilio Vitale and colleagues designed a strategy to kill them preferentially, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Tetraploidy is both an adaptation to stress and an intermediate step between normal chromosome counts and the chaos of advanced tumors.

The authors report that inhibition of Chk1, a checkpoint kinase, kills tetraploid tumor cells through a p53-dependent pathway. A drug that selectively removes the most resistant cells would be valuable. Their strategy exploits a weakness created by the extra chromosomes themselves.
plos-pone-0001437:
Virginie van Wassenhove, Dean Buonomano, and Shinsuke Shimojo wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how time can feel warped. Judging how long a thing lasts is key for sight, thought, and action. Felt length often strays from clock length, bent by many traits of the event. The team tested warps within and across the senses.

They asked which traits of a flash or a tone most bend felt time. Their tests span sight and sound to find shared rules. The results help pin down where in the brain time is built. They also shed plain light on why brief events can feel long, and long ones brief.
plos-pone-0001537:
Masaaki Kotera and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on searching chemistry by part, not by name. Biochemists often speak of compounds by the parts they hold. Models of cell chemistry need that link between names and parts too. The team built a way to search compounds by their groups and sub parts.

Their tool ties free text names to exact chemical parts in a shared base. That tie lets labs ask which pathways hold a given part. Such part based hunts can flag drug leads and toxic risks. The work aids the field that maps all small molecules in cells.
plos-pone-0001637:
Shigeyuki Kawa, Kei Kitahara, Hideaki Hamano, and their co-authors reported a new kind of antibody interaction in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The paper centers on rheumatoid factor, an antibody that binds the tail end of other antibodies. Doctors have known about it for more than sixty years. It shows up in several autoimmune diseases, where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues.

The team's work links this antibody behavior to autoimmune pancreatitis, an uncommon form of pancreas inflammation. The full text gives the binding tests, the patient samples they used, and the new interaction they describe between two immunoglobulins. Findings of this sort can sharpen diagnosis, since antibody patterns in the blood are often the first clue that an autoimmune disease is present.
plos-pone-0001737:
Gilles Crevel, Dorothy Bennett, and Sue Cotterill studied a human protein linked to cancer changes in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is TTC4, which carries TPR motifs, repeat units that mediate protein contacts. Its gene sits in a region linked to breast cancer, and melanoma cell lines had shown point mutations in the protein.

The authors report that TTC4 interacts with CDC6, a protein that licenses DNA copying, and may act as a co-chaperone helping the Hsp90 folding machine. The full text gives the interaction tests and the alterations seen in transformed cells. A protein touching both DNA copying control and a cancer-linked region is a natural suspect in how normal cells turn malignant.
plos-pone-0001837:
Zheen Zhao, Warren D. Taylor, Martin Styner, and their co-authors measured hippocampus shape in late-life depression in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Major depression in the elderly is associated with brain structural changes and vascular lesions, and changes in the limbic system have been noted. Studies of hippocampal volume in depression had shown variable results, possibly because volume alone is too crude.

The team analyzed hippocampus shape, a finer measure, in older adults with and without depression. The full text gives the shape maps and where patients differed. Shape analysis can localize change to specific subregions of the memory center, sharpening both diagnosis research and theories of how depression injures the aging brain.
plos-pone-0001937:
Fengping Wang and co-authors read the full genome of a deep-sea bacterium in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The bacterium, Shewanella piezotolerans WP3, came from deep-sea sediment. It bears two rare traits at once: it thrives under great pressure, and it likes the cold. It also draws energy by reducing iron.

The team sequenced its whole genome and studied gene function to learn how it copes with the deep sea. Kin of this group live in many settings, so WP3 is a window on adaptation at the extremes. Genes that grant pressure and cold tolerance could also be of use in industry.
plos-pone-0002037:
Yutaka Kondo and co-authors showed that cutting a gene-tagging enzyme destabilizes cancer cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Tags on histones, the spools that wind DNA, govern how open each gene is to use. Cancer cells show wide faults in those tag patterns. The enzyme in view, G9a, adds methyl tags to a specific spot, lysine 9 of histone H3.

When the team downregulated G9a in cancer cells, the centrosomes, the hubs that organize cell division, were disrupted. Chromosomes then grew unstable. A tag enzyme tied to division order is a drug target worth noting.
plos-pone-0002137:
Rajani Srikakulam, Li Liu, and Donald Winkelmann studied how muscle proteins get folded into shape, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Myosin is the motor protein that drives muscle contraction, and it needs help to fold and assemble correctly. General helper proteins called chaperones do much of this work, joined by a specialist helper named UNC45.

Vertebrates carry two UNC45 genes, and one form, Unc45b, is found in striated muscle such as heart and skeletal muscle. The team examined how Unc45b works with the chaperone Hsp90 and how the pair handles the unfolded myosin motor piece. The study adds detail to how muscle builds its own moving parts.
plos-pone-0002237:
Joshua Hunter, Ramesh Gujjar, Cullen Pang, and co-authors compared two enzymes of the tuberculosis bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mycobacterium tuberculosis kills about 2 million people a year, so new drug targets are badly needed. Thymidylate synthase enzymes, which help build DNA, are proven drug targets in other species.

The TB genome encodes two such enzymes, ThyA and ThyX, an unusual pairing. The team measured how each one works and which compounds it binds. Knowing how the two differ shows which one a drug must hit, and what shape that drug should take. Groundwork like this precedes any new medicine for a stubborn disease.
plos-pone-0002337:
Varsha Agarwal, Reddy Kommaddi, Khader Valli, and co-authors measured drug-breaking enzymes in the human brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cytochrome P450 enzymes process most medicines. They can inactivate a drug so it can be excreted, or convert it into an active metabolite that does the real work. The liver does most of this, but the brain has its own set.

The team found high levels of one enzyme, CYP3A43, in human brain. They showed it metabolizes alprazolam, a common anti-anxiety drug, into its active metabolite. Local drug processing in the brain may explain why the same dose affects people so differently.
plos-pone-0002437:
Bouchez and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Valérie Bouchez, Valérie Caro, Erwan Levillain, among others. Its subject is genomic Content of Bordetella pertussis Clinical Isolates Circulating in Areas of Intensive Children Vaccination. The objective of the study was to analyse the evolution of Bordetella pertussis population.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002537:
Juste and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Ramon A. Juste, Natalia Elguezabal, Joseba M. Garrido, among others. Its subject is on the Prevalence of M. avium Subspecies paratuberculosis DNA in the Blood. The rest of the title points to Healthy Individuals and Patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Mycobacteria, such as M.

tuberculosis infect billions of humans. However, because of appropriate immune responses and antibiotic therapy, overt mycobacterial diseases occur far less frequently. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002637:
In 2008, Yu-Chih Chen and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about oct-4 expression maintained cancer Stem-Like properties in lung Cancer-Derived CD133-Positive cells. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Yu-Chih Chen, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. CD133 (prominin-1), a 5-transmembrane glycoprotein, has recently been considered to be an important marker that represents the subset population of cancer stem-like cells. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002737:
Yihong Yao and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of type i interferon: potential therapeutic target for psoriasis?. The catalog record names Yihong Yao first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Psoriasis is an immune-mediated disease characterized by aberrant epidermal differentiation, surface scale formation, and marked cutaneous inflammation. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002837:
In 2008, Natalia Ospina-Álvarez and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Temperature-Dependent sex determination in fish revisited: prevalence, a single sex ratio response pattern, and possible effects of climate change. Authorship is credited in the record to Natalia Ospina-Álvarez and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. In gonochoristic vertebrates, sex determination mechanisms can be classified as genotypic (GSD) or temperature-dependent (TSD). The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002937:
Clemens Cohen, Maja Lindenmeyer, Felix Eichinger and co-authors improved gene profiling of diabetic kidney disease in 2008. Diabetic nephropathy is a slow metabolic disease that turns into scarring kidney damage over years. Profiling its gene activity is tricky because changes are subtle and can be missed.

Their method analyzes microarray data one probe at a time rather than in averaged sets. That finer approach promised clearer detection of the processes at work. Published in PLOS ONE, it offers kidney researchers a sharper tool for a disease that creeps forward in small steps. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003037:
Georgette Suidan, Jeremiah McDole, Yi Chen and co-authors showed CD8 T cells altering blood-brain barrier proteins in 2008. Barrier disruption marks immune brain disorders as varied as viral hemorrhagic fevers, cerebral malaria, and acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalitis. Models had proposed that immune cells promote vessel permeability in these diseases.

The team reports CD8 T cells induce changes in tight junction proteins, the seals between vessel cells. Published in PLOS ONE, that gives a direct mechanism for barrier opening. It identifies the seal proteins as points where protective treatment might act. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003137:
Praveen Sethupathy, Hoa Giang, Joshua B. Plotkin and colleagues scan the human genome for signs of natural selection in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Many researchers think that variants in the non-coding part of the genome explain much of the trait variation among humans, and between humans and other primates. If so, those regions may be changing fast under selection.

The authors carry out a genome-wide analysis focused on human cis-elements, the control sites near genes. Readers see where the data point to recent selection outside protein-coding DNA. The work helps frame how control DNA, not just genes themselves, may shape human traits.
plos-pone-0003237:
Levi Yafetto, Loran Carroll, Yunluan Cui and colleagues measure the fastest spore launches in fungi in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A variety of spore discharge processes have evolved among the fungi. Those with the longest ranges are powered by hydrostatic pressure and include squirt guns that are most common in the Ascomycota and Zygomycota. In these fungi, fluid-filled stalks support single spores before launch.

Readers get high-speed measurements of discharge mechanisms the eye cannot follow. Fungal launches rank among the fastest movements in nature, the title claims. Understanding them serves both basic biology and possible bio-inspired design of micro launch systems.
plos-pone-0003337: Ki-Hong Jung and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 refining lists of rice genes that respond to light. The work used rice oligonucleotide arrays and checked gene redundancy, where near-duplicate genes can blur the lists. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record names no genes and states no findings.
plos-pone-0003437:
Matthew D. Hall, Luc F. Bussière, and Robert Brooks studied mating gifts in crickets in this 2008 paper. In this ground cricket, males give females a food gift during mating. Such gifts cost the male resources he could use elsewhere. The team varied diet quality and wing form in their tests.

Wing form matters because some crickets trade flight gear for reproduction. Males and females shifted their investment as diet changed. Poor food rewired the balance between offspring and survival. The study shows how resources steer mating effort in both sexes.
plos-pone-0003537:
Maria Arantzazu Sanchez-Fernandez and co-authors decoded a call between bone cells in this 2008 paper. Bone is rebuilt by osteoblasts and dissolved by osteoclasts. The two cell types must work in tight coordination. How builders are summoned to a site was unclear.

Osteoclasts were shown to control osteoblast movement, called chemotaxis. They send a signal, PDGF-BB, to the PDGF receptor beta on builders. That call directs where rebuilding cells travel. The finding reveals how the skeleton coordinates its constant remodeling. Bone loss with age traces back to this same builder and destroyer balance.
plos-pone-0003637:
Luc Letenneur, Karine Pérès, Hervé Fleury, and colleagues published this cohort study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Herpes simplex virus, the cause of cold sores, can hide in the body for life. Because the virus reaches the nervous system, it has been proposed as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease.

The authors followed a population sample and checked who carried antibodies to the virus. They then compared Alzheimer's rates between those with and without signs of past infection. Work of this kind tests whether a common, lifelong virus could be one piece of the cause of dementia.
plos-pone-0003737:
