Sarah Sundelacruz, Michael Levin, and David L. Kaplan published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Guiding stem cell behavior is central to regenerative medicine. Ion flows across cell membranes are powerful signals in the body, yet their role in stem cells was poorly understood.

The team showed that membrane potential, the voltage across the cell surface, helps control stem cell fate. Mesenchymal stem cells shifted between fat-forming and bone-forming paths as their voltage changed. The result adds bioelectricity to the toolkit for steering stem cells toward wanted tissues.
plos-pone-0003837:
Haiwei Luo, Jian Shi, William Arndt, and colleagues published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Prochlorococcus is a group of tiny marine cyanobacteria that carry out much of the ocean's photosynthesis. Some of their species relationships had stayed unresolved by standard sequence comparisons. Gene order offered another character.

Using the arrangement of orthologous genes as a phylogenetic signal, the team rebuilt the genus's family tree. The gene-order approach settled relationships that sequence data alone had left fuzzy. It also shows a general tool for sorting out close relatives in other microbe groups.
plos-pone-0003937:
Michael Humbert, Robert A. Rasmussen, Helena Ong, and co-authors tried a focused vaccine idea against HIV-1 in 2008. Vaccines usually work by raising antibodies that block a virus. HIV-1 keeps escaping those antibodies through many tricks. The team asked whether guiding the response to one weak spot could help.

They call that guiding approach immunofocusing in their PLOS ONE article. They used copies of the virus envelope as the training material. The aim was antibodies that block many HIV-1 branches, not just one. Such breadth is the central hurdle for any HIV vaccine. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004037:
Yong-Jun Liu, Christopher J. Papasian, Jian-Feng Liu, and co-authors questioned a rule in genome studies in 2008. Genome-wide association studies hunt DNA links to common diseases. Replication in a second sample is treated as the gold standard. Enthusiasm for such studies had produced many published claims.

Their PLOS ONE article asks whether replication deserves that status. Failed replication can reflect study design, not a false first result. The authors weigh costs and limits of the replication demand. The debate shapes how genetic findings enter medicine. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004137:
Antonio Alcina and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It centres on IL2RA, the gene for part of the receptor that binds interleukin-2, a key immune signal. That receptor helps run immune responses and keeps the immune system from attacking the body itself.

The team re-tested and fine-mapped three gene variants in the IL2RA region that earlier work had linked to multiple sclerosis and type 1 diabetes. They found the links are uneven: the variants do not tie to both diseases in the same way. The result sharpens the map of a gene region where immunity and autoimmunity meet.
plos-pone-0004237:
Mihai Netea and colleagues published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lipoproteins are the blood's fat carriers. They improve outcomes in severe Gram-negative infections by soaking up LPS, the toxin on those bacteria's surfaces. Mice lacking the LDL receptor carry sevenfold higher LDL levels.

The team used invasive Salmonella typhimurium infection to test this defence role. They report that lipoproteins are a key part of host defence against this invader. The finding recasts cholesterol carriers as part of the immune system. Salmonella typhimurium is a close relative of the typhoid germ.
plos-pone-0004337:
Dylan Thompson and colleagues published this exercise science study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Physical activity is prescribed for health, and many different recommendations exist for gauging whether a person is active enough. The team asked whether twelve commonly used physical activity recommendations classify people in the same way.

Their subjects were middle-aged men, a group often told to move more. They report confusion and conflict in assessing the men's physical activity status: the same men count as active by some rules and inactive by others. When the yardsticks disagree, public health advice loses its force.
plos-pone-0004437:
Fungi may owe part of their chemical skill to genes stolen from bacteria long ago, argue Imke Schmitt and H Thorsten Lumbsch in PLOS ONE in 2009. The chemicals at issue are polyketides, natural products with many uses in medicine. Learning how fungi gained the machinery to make them could speed the search for new drugs.

Genes sometimes jump between unrelated species, a process called horizontal gene transfer. The authors present evidence that an ancient jump of this kind, from bacteria into fungi, boosted what fungi can build. That would mean fungal chemistry is partly a borrowed toolkit, refined over vast time. The idea reshapes how scientists trace the family history of drug-making genes, and where they look for new ones.
plos-pone-0004537:
Two ways of switching on the same growth pathway start mammary tumors from different cells, report Brigitte Teissedre, Alicia Pinderhughes, Angela Incassati, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The pathway is the canonical Wnt and beta-catenin system, which regulates stem and progenitor cells. When it is disturbed, it drives many human cancers, including a share of breast cancers.

The team compared mice carrying MMTV-Wnt1 with mice carrying a shortened, always-on beta-catenin. Both turn the pathway on, but in distinct progenitor cells, and they activate a second pathway, Hedgehog, to different degrees inside the tumors. Those differences matter because a tumor's cell of origin shapes how it behaves and what drugs it answers to.
plos-pone-0004637:
Growing older changes how toxic the mutant huntingtin protein is, show Elsa Diguet, Fanny Petit, Carole Escartin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Huntington's disease is caused by an abnormal expansion of a repeated tract in the protein huntingtin. Aging likely plays a role in neurodegenerative disorders generally. In Huntington's, its role was unclear.

For a given tract length, the probability of disease onset rises with age in a known pattern. The team asked whether normal aging itself modulates the neurotoxicity of mutant huntingtin in model systems. If aging brain tissue becomes more vulnerable, then the disease is a product of the mutation plus time, not the mutation alone. That distinction shapes when preventive treatments would need to start.
plos-pone-0004737:
Kiyotaka Takishita and colleagues proposed how a key energy gene reached the plastids of many algae, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many algae carry plastids taken from red algae long ago. These groups include dinoflagellates, some parasites, and brown algae kin, plus other major sea and fresh water lines.

All share a plastid targeted form of an enzyme used in sugar breakdown. The team set out a claim for how the gene for it evolved. Tracing gene moves helps explain how photosynthesis spread. It also clarifies the family tree of algae that drive ocean food webs. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004837:
Zhi-Qiang Du and colleagues performed association and haplotype analyses of candidate genes for scrotal hernia in pigs, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Scrotal hernia in pigs is a complex trait likely affected by genetic and environmental factors. A large scale association analysis of positional, and Functional candidate genes was conducted in four genomic regions previously linked to hernia susceptibility on Sus scrofa chromosomes in commercial breeding lines.

Specific variants and haplotypes tracked with risk. Breeders could select against hernia genetically. That reduces animal suffering and economic loss. Pig genetics also models human hernia. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004937:
Myostatin is a growth factor made in muscle and fat. It acts as a brake on muscle growth. Mice born without it grow dramatically larger muscles. They also carry less fat and resist obesity. Tingqing Guo and colleagues asked which tissue explains those benefits. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009.

The team blocked myostatin in muscle alone or fat alone. Blocking it in muscle cut fat mass and improved insulin sensitivity. Blocking it in fat did neither. The muscle, not the fat, holds the lever. That distinction matters for future therapies. Any drug copying these effects should aim at muscle.
plos-pone-0005037:
Synesthetes experience merged senses, like seeing colors in letters. Case reports suggested they enjoy better visual search and memory. Nicolas Rothen and Beat Meier argued those claims need group studies. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They tested thirteen grapheme-color synesthetes as a group. Matched controls took the same tasks.

The group showed no general advantage. Visual search was not broadly better. Episodic memory was not broadly better either. Single cases had fueled the hype. Group data cool it with real numbers. The finding does not deny individual gifts. It shows synesthesia itself is no general cognitive boost. That distinction matters for how the condition is studied and portrayed.
plos-pone-0005137:
HPV infection causes cervical cancer. Most infections clear on their own, though. Something else must push a few toward invasive cancer. Shana Wingo and colleagues found a candidate in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied mutations in the gene LKB1. Such mutations are called somatic when they arise in body cells.

LKB1 mutations promoted cervical cancer progression. They supply the second hit that infection alone lacks. The finding names a genetic accomplice in a viral cancer. It may help predict which infections turn deadly. Most will not, and reassurance matters too. The work refines risk for millions of HPV-positive women. It also suggests a pathway that treatment might target.
plos-pone-0005237:
An enzyme called COMT helps tune brain chemicals tied to thinking, heart function, and pain. Common forms of its gene run at different speeds. Nackley and colleagues mapped the slow forms of the human COMT gene in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Three common haplotypes, sets of variants inherited together, differ in enzyme activity. The study enriched the set of marker variants that flag the low-activity forms. Better markers make it easier to sort people by COMT type in studies of cognition, mood, and pain sensitivity. Pain, mood, and thought all shift with this one enzyme, so a good marker set helps many fields at once, not just one.
plos-pone-0005337:
Cancers that look alike under the microscope can carry very different molecular faults and follow different courses. Finding the molecules that truly matter in each case is the hard part. Pinese and colleagues presented a tool for that job, called Messina, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Messina analyzes molecular data to identify biologically relevant molecules in disease. It aims to separate driver signals from the noise of thousands of measurements. A sharper sieve helps researchers pick drug targets and markers that reflect real disease biology. Tools of this kind earn their keep when they cut a list of ten thousand hits to a short list a lab can test in weeks. Not years, with the staff it has.
plos-pone-0005437:
Anna Pei and colleagues checked a basic fact about bacterial genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Genes for ribosomal RNA sit at the heart of how cells build proteins. Workers had long assumed that all copies of these genes inside one genome are much the same.

Using whole genome data, the team compared the copies of one such gene within single prokaryotic genomes. They found more variety between copies than the old view allowed. That variety matters because these genes are often used to name species and build family trees, and hidden differences can skew those results.
plos-pone-0005537:
Natalya Chechko and co-authors scanned the brains of people recovered from panic disorder, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The brain basis of panic is only partly understood. Patients react strongly to vague fear cues, much like animals in learned fear tests, which points to deep brain alarm circuits.

The team used scans while patients viewed emotional faces and scenes. Even in recovery, front brain control of emotion looked unstable, while deep alarm areas stayed overactive. That pattern may explain why panic can return after a person feels well. It also suggests that drug or therapy plans should keep supporting brain control circuits after symptoms fade.
plos-pone-0005637:
Astrid Rohrbeck, Volker Müller, and Jürgen Borlak characterised early lung changes at the gene level in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Lung cancer develops in stages, starting with dysplasia, a disturbed growth that sits at the edge of cancer. The genetics of that early stage were unknown.

Using laser tools, the team cut out dysplastic cells driven by a cancer gene, c-Raf-1, and read their gene activity. They compared the profile with normal tissue. Early gene signatures could one day flag lungs on the path to cancer. Dysplasia can be watched rather than treated at once, so knowing its gene profile could guide that choice.
plos-pone-0005737:
Luca Ticini and co-authors scanned the brains of stroke patients with pusher syndrome in 2009. These patients feel upright when they are in fact tilted far to one side. They push against support, sure they are about to fall the other way.

The team used perfusion imaging, which maps blood flow, to find the brain areas tied to the fault. Knowing which regions misjudge vertical guides rehab for these patients. It also teaches how the healthy brain builds its sense of upright. That sense is so basic that its breakdown shows the machinery plainly.
plos-pone-0005837:
Tim Wolfs and co-authors showed in 2009 that womb infection stalls gut development in fetal sheep. Chorioamnionitis, infection of the membranes around the fetus, is the biggest source of prenatal inflammation and early birth. Babies born after it often face gut and immune problems.

Exposing fetal sheep to endotoxin, a bacterial wall component, disturbed intestinal development before birth. That finding shifts some blame for newborn gut disease to prenatal events. It suggests protecting the fetus during womb infection could prevent later harm. Sheep, with long pregnancies, model the human timeline well here.
plos-pone-0005937:
Sick children in poor regions often meet a health worker before any doctor. A program called IMCI trains those workers to judge common childhood illness in a set way. In 2009, Christiane Horwood, Kerry Vermaak, Nigel Rollins and colleagues judged how well trained workers in South Africa carried out those checks.

South Africa took up the program in 1997 to cut deaths and illness in children under five. An audit like this one shows where training holds up and where it fades in daily practice. The findings can guide retraining and support, so that a child's chances rest less on luck and more on a sound first assessment.
plos-pone-0006037:
Rare family forms of kidney cancer have taught doctors much of what they know about the common kind. Christopher Ricketts, Maurice Zeegers, Jan Lubinski and colleagues drew on that lesson in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tests inherited variants in six genes, among them CDH1, MMP1 and VEGF, in familial and in sporadic renal cell carcinoma.

The von Hippel Lindau gene showed how a family cancer gene can explain sporadic tumors too. Testing a panel of six suspects at once asks whether other genes follow the same pattern. Results of this kind sort real risk variants from near misses and give families with kidney cancer firmer answers about their own risk.
plos-pone-0006137:
A bacterial pump that throws drugs out of the cell has a surprising taste for salt. Saroj Velamakanni, Calvin Lau, Daniel Gutmann and colleagues studied LmrA in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers this multidrug ABC transporter from Lactococcus lactis, a bacterium used in cheese making. The pump can expel a wide range of chemotherapy agents and toxins, despite having no known natural cargo.

LmrA can stand in for its human counterpart ABCB1, a pump that drives drug resistance in tumors. A pump at home with salt as well as drugs suggests its true job may involve cell balance, not defense alone. The dual taste makes the bacterial pump a richer model for the human one.
plos-pone-0006237:
A mosquito finds people largely by smell, and carrier proteins start that sense. Julien Pelletier and Walter Leal catalogued odorant-binding proteins in the southern house mosquito in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. These proteins ferry odour molecules to receptors, the first step in insect smell.

The team analysed the whole gene family and where its members are switched on. The family's size and variety help explain the mosquito's sharp sense of smell. Each carrier is a possible target for repellents or traps. Better smell blockers could cut biting and the diseases mosquitoes spread.
plos-pone-0006337:
A fatal virus of carp-family fish had never been reported in China, despite outbreaks elsewhere. Nian Zhi Zhang and colleagues analysed spring viraemia of carp virus at the molecular level in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Between 1998 and 2002, outbreaks were reported in ornamental and wild fish in Europe and beyond.

Genetic analysis shows how the Chinese viral material relates to known strains. A fatal aquatic disease that might spread in East Asia is the authors' warning. Fish farms and wild stocks across the region are at stake. Molecular tracking is the first defence against its spread.
plos-pone-0006437:
Kyriaki Nomikou and co-authors traced the family history of bluetongue virus in PLOS ONE in 2009. The virus infects livestock and is the type species of the Orbivirus group. Its genome has ten segments of double-stranded RNA, each coding for one viral protein. The team worked with virus samples from the eastern Mediterranean region.

They analyzed the full-length VP3 genes of these isolates and built evolutionary trees from them. Trees like these show how strains relate and how the virus spreads between places. Earlier studies had compared parts of the virus; full genes give a sharper view. The results aid tracking of a costly farm animal disease.
plos-pone-0006537:
Francesco De Francesco and co-authors grew a special set of fat-derived stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human adult adipose tissue is an abundant source of mesenchymal stem cells. It is also easily accessible and yields a considerable amount of stem cells. The team isolated cells marked CD34 positive and CD90 positive from that tissue.

Their title reports these cells can grow as sphere clusters. They produce high levels of VEGF, a vessel growth factor, and form structures in culture. Sphere growth is a sign of stem-like behavior. Such cells could interest regenerative medicine, especially where new blood vessels are needed.
plos-pone-0006637:
Saul Hazledine and co-authors studied calcium waves in roots that host helpful bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Legume plants form a partnership with nitrogen-fixing bacteria called rhizobia. The bacteria live in nodules, small organs on the roots built for them. Signals from the bacteria, called nodulation factors, set off calcium oscillations, waves of calcium in root cells, that start the partnership.

The team used nonlinear time series analysis on those waves. Their title reports signs of deterministic chaos in the signal. A complex code like this may carry more detail than a plain rhythm. Cracking the code could show how plants know their true partners from strangers.
plos-pone-0006737:
Ubydul Haque and colleagues measured malaria across endemic districts of Bangladesh in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria rose steadily after DDT was banned there in 1971. The disease remains a major health problem in thirteen districts. Those districts lie in the south-east and north-east. A national control program, backed by global funding, fights it.

The study estimated how common malaria is in those districts. Prevalence numbers show where the burden is heaviest. They also show whether control efforts are gaining ground. District-level data let programs target bed nets and treatment better. The work gives Bangladesh a firmer baseline for tracking malaria over time.
plos-pone-0006837:
Charlotte L. Ridgway and colleagues linked baby motor milestones to teenage sports in PLOS ONE in 2009. Motor proficiency is positively associated with physical activity levels. The authors asked whether infant development timing predicts later participation. Their data came from the Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966. That cohort has been followed since birth.

They compared the timing of infant motor development with sports at age fourteen. Earlier motor development predicted later sports participation. The prospective design rules out simple reverse explanations. Early movement skills may seed a lasting active lifestyle. The result argues for supporting motor development in infancy.
plos-pone-0006937:
Srikesh Arunajadai took a statistical approach to a hepatitis C enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme is the NS3 helicase, which unwinds double-stranded RNA. How helicases pull RNA strands apart is a basic question in molecular biology. Hepatitis C then infected nearly three in every hundred people worldwide.

Arunajadai built his analysis on single molecule mechanical experiments. Such experiments watch one helicase work in real time. A statistical treatment can extract the step pattern hidden in those traces. Understanding this unwinding step matters beyond basic science. The viral helicase is a possible target for drugs against hepatitis C.
plos-pone-0007037:
Peter Sinnaeve, Mark Donahue, Peter Grass, and colleagues read disease from blood gene patterns in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inflammation drives atherosclerotic coronary artery disease. Whether gene activity in whole blood tracks that disease was unclear. The team sampled peripheral blood from patients with different disease extent.

They compared blood gene expression patterns against how severe the coronary disease was. The patterns correlated with the extent of disease. A blood test reflecting artery disease would be valuable. It could flag risk without invasive imaging, and it might track whether treatment is working.
plos-pone-0007137:
Claas Wodarczyk, Isaline Rowe, Marco Chiaravalli, and colleagues built a new mouse model of a kidney disease gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. Polycystin-1 is the protein faulty in most cases of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. It sits in many cell compartments, including junctions. The team removed it from two brain-lining tissues, the ependyma and choroid plexus.

The mice developed dysfunctional cilia and hydrocephalus, a buildup of brain fluid. That outcome ties this kidney gene to brain fluid flow. It also gives researchers a model for the disease's less studied effects beyond the kidney.
plos-pone-0007237:
Marie-Hélène Perrard, Emeric Chassaing, Guillaume Montillet, and colleagues studied sperm cell division in rats in 2009. In lab cultures, a growth factor called beta nerve growth factor regulates the second meiotic division. It can block secondary spermatocytes at metaphase and lower sperm precursor formation.

Mature eggs also arrest at metaphase in vertebrates, held by cytostatic factor proteins. The authors ask whether those proteins appear in male meiotic cells. They also test how the growth factor changes Mos protein levels in late spermatocytes. Their work compares male and female division control.
plos-pone-0007337:
Frank Leypoldt, Chi-Un Choe, Mathias Gelderblom, and colleagues tested a protective enzyme idea in stroke-prone mice in 2009. Methylated arginines interfere with nitric oxide formation, causing endothelial dysfunction in blood vessels. One such compound, ADMA, predicts cardiovascular events and death in humans, making its removal seem therapeutically attractive.

An enzyme called DDAH-1 breaks down ADMA. The authors study transgenic mice with extra DDAH-1. They report these mice are not protected from ischemic stroke. That negative result matters: lowering a risk marker does not always prevent the event. It redirects stroke prevention research toward other mechanisms.
plos-pone-0007437:
Sam Mathew, Stephen Kerridge, and Maria Leptin published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the genes that start building a fruit fly embryo. Gastrulation is the stage when a simple ball of cells folds into layered tissue. In flies, forming the ventral furrow is the first big fold. Earlier screens had found four genome regions needed for it, with genes identified for three.

The authors zeroed in on the remaining region. It is a small stretch of the genome holding several loci required for gastrulation. Pinning down these genes completes more of the map of early development. Each identified gene gives researchers a handle for testing how the furrow forms. The work closes a gap left open by the earlier genetic screens.
plos-pone-0007537:
Jeremy Marshall and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on reproduction in crickets. After mating, something in the male's ejaculate changes the female. The effect happens before fertilization, a postmating, prezygotic response. The molecule carrying that message was unknown. The team set out to identify the ejaculate protein responsible, using gene silencing to test candidates.

They found the protein and confirmed its role by RNA interference knockdown. Silencing its gene removed the effect on the female. Nailing down one molecule behind a mating message is rare in this field. Ejaculate proteins evolve fast and shape who fathers offspring. A confirmed case gives evolutionary biologists solid ground. It also shows how much communication is packed into a single transfer between the sexes.
plos-pone-0007637:
Renata Mazzucchelli and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on finding the cells that make interleukin-7. IL-7 is required for lymphocyte development and for keeping mature lymphocytes alive. Yet the actual sites of its production had never been clearly identified. The team built a reporter mouse: a glowing protein is made wherever the Il7 gene is switched on. The marker was inserted into the gene's own locus using a large DNA construct.

With the reporter, IL-7 producing cells could finally be seen and located. Knowing the factories tells immunologists where lymphocytes get their essential signal. It also clarifies organs long suspected but never confirmed as sources. A visible map turns a diffuse cytokine into an addressable system. The study is a tool-making paper whose images guide later work. Many questions about lymphocyte survival start with where IL-7 is made.
plos-pone-0007737:
Masayuki Ikeda and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks for the machinery that keeps sleep in its normal order. Mammals cycle through non-REM sleep, REM sleep and waking in a stable sequence. What enforces that order was unknown.

A sudden jump from waking into REM sleep is a mark of narcolepsy. The team studied mice lacking an enzyme called phospholipase C-beta4. In those mice, the normal sleep sequence broke down. Body temperature rhythms also faltered. The enzyme is thus essential for orderly sleep, a clue for sleep medicine.
plos-pone-0007837:
Bibekanand Mallick and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses tiny RNAs to explain how SARS damages the lungs. SARS is caused by a coronavirus and killed a large share of its victims. A typical feature is lung fibrosis, scarring that ends in lung failure.

The authors ran a microRNome analysis on bronchoalveolar stem cells. Those cells help repair the airways. Infection rewires their microRNA patterns, which in turn shifts gene control. The analysis unravels part of the molecular basis of SARS in these cells. It may guide care for lung scarring in related diseases.
plos-pone-0007937:
Meghann Mabon, Barbara Scott, and C. Michael Crowder studied low oxygen and lifespan in worms for PLOS ONE in 2009. Both traits run through the DAF-2 pathway, which responds to insulin-like signals. A plain guess would be that one shared route controls both outcomes.

The worm tests pulled the two outcomes apart. The path from DAF-2 to a long life is not the same path that sets how well a worm bears low oxygen. Each effect uses its own branch steps. That split matters for stroke and heart research, where the hope is to gain oxygen tolerance without unwanted side effects.
plos-pone-0008037:
Anna Hellquist and colleagues nominated a new gene in the hunt for what drives lupus, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lupus is an autoimmune disease in which the body attacks its own tissues, and many genes each add a bit of risk. Earlier scans had flagged one stretch of chromosome 14 in Finnish families.

Fine mapping of that stretch pointed to the gene MAMDC1. The gene is not yet a proven cause, but it is now a named suspect with a clear address. Each suspect gives drug and test makers a fresh place to dig.
plos-pone-0008137:
Yi-men Araya-Ajoy and colleagues linked song pitch in antbirds to the singer's gene variety in PLOS ONE in 2009. Animals in contests need honest signs of quality, signs too costly to fake. In songbirds, hard notes can serve as such signs.

Male ocellated antbirds that sang the highest notes in vocal duels also carried the richest gene variety. High notes are hard to sustain, so they make a truthful badge. A varied genome is a real edge for offspring. The link shows how a sound can report a fact no rival can see directly.
plos-pone-0008237:
Jacqueline M. Cohen and colleagues reviewed research on milk supply and breast cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. Insufficient milk supply means a mother cannot fully feed her infant from her breast. Animal studies had suggested a link between that problem and breast cancer. Whether human studies reported the same link was unknown. The authors ran a systematic review to find out.

They gathered epidemiological studies of human populations on the question. A systematic review weighs all available evidence rather than single reports. Their summary tells doctors and mothers what the record actually shows. It also shows where better studies are still needed.
plos-pone-0008337:
Robert J. H. Payne and Claire Suzanne Grierson built a theoretical model of plant cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rho GTPases are switches that organize cell polarity and growth. In plants, the ROP family fills that role. Several molecules affecting ROP signalling are known. How ROP activity becomes localized in space remained unclear.

Their model explains ROP localisation driven by auxin in Arabidopsis root hair cells. Root hairs grow at a single tip, making them a clean test case. A working model predicts where the switch will concentrate. It guides experiments on how plant cells choose a growth direction.
plos-pone-0008437:
Juliette Desfrancois and co-authors describe a rare T cell type in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper on melanoma, a skin cancer. The cells bear both CD4 and CD8 marks. Most T cells bear just one of those marks. Such double cells had been seen in health and in disease. But no one knew well what they do.

The team find more of these cells in people with melanoma. They test if the cells react to tumor tissue. Their results mark the cells as a tumor-reactive group. That could matter for immune care of cancer. It gives doctors a new cell type to track and study.
plos-pone-0008537:
Kristen Whalen and co-authors study detox enzymes in reef animals in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Marine consumers differ profoundly in tolerance for chemically rich foods. Seaweeds and other prey defend themselves with prostaglandins and like compounds. Few studies have examined the biochemical adaptations behind diet choice. The team focus on glutathione transferases, enzymes that neutralize toxic compounds. They work with consumers that feed on the reef.

They test how these enzymes handle dietary prostaglandins. Stronger detox capacity tracks with tolerance of defended foods. That link helps explain why some consumers eat prey others avoid. The work connects enzyme chemistry to ecology on the reef.
plos-pone-0008637:
Vanessa Jahnke and co-authors test mitochondria in muscle tumor cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondria sense signals linked to variations in energy demand. They regulate nuclear gene expression through retrograde signaling. That pathway is presumed to regulate myoblast proliferation and differentiation. Rhabdomyosarcoma cells are cancer cells of muscle origin. Their growth may involve altered retrograde signals. The team look for evidence of mitochondrial respiratory deficiency in those cells.

They find evidence that respiration is indeed deficient in the tumor cells. Faulty mitochondria may drive the altered gene program of rhabdomyosarcoma. Restoring respiratory function could in principle slow those cells. The work links energy failure to a childhood muscle cancer.
plos-pone-0008737:
Elizabeth LeClair and Jacek Topczewski introduced a fish whisker as a window on tissue repair. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Barbels are feelers that many fishes carry near the mouth. Zebrafish grow a pair of maxillary barbels about a month after hatching. The feelers are thin and nearly clear. Living tissue can be watched through them under a microscope.

The authors described how the barbel grows and how it regrows after damage. Nerves, vessels, and skin all rebuild in view. A small, clear, regrowing appendage gives repair biology a handy living model.
plos-pone-0008837:
Mingyu Liu, Brandon Rakowski, and Edward Gershburg untangled a fight between two herpes virus proteins. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. ICP0 helps herpes simplex virus stay active and copy itself. Without it, the virus tends to fall silent inside cells. Another viral protein, ICP4, can silence the ICP0 gene itself. That silencing would push the virus toward hiding.

ICP0 fought back against ICP4-driven silencing of its own gene. The tug-of-war helps set the balance between active and quiet infection. Latency decides herpes outbreaks and recurrences. Understanding the switch may suggest ways to lock the virus down.
plos-pone-0008937:
Timothy Abuya and colleagues rated programmes that train private drug sellers in Kenya, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In much of Kenya, families buy fever medicine from small private shops. These sellers are often the first help a sick child gets. Training them to handle malaria properly could save lives, if the training works.

The study compared two programmes that had run at moderate scale. It judged them on several sides of success, not just sales or knowledge alone. Shop workers' advice, drug quality, and what customers actually received all counted. The findings help health planners decide which seller programmes deserve wider backing.
plos-pone-0009037:
Juha Rouvinen and co-authors caught allergy proteins in the act of pairing up, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Type I allergy starts when an allergen links two IgE antibodies on a mast cell. That cross-linking triggers the cell to dump its inflammatory chemicals. An allergen made of two identical halves needs only one antibody type to bridge.

The team showed several allergens form such pairs only briefly. These fleeting dimers still boost the allergen's power. A momentary pairing can make cross-linking much easier. Allergy researchers may need to reckon with pairs that standard tests barely see.
plos-pone-0009137:
Gaynor Miller and co-authors used chemical mutagenesis to surface a new weakness in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. ENU mutagenesis sprinkles random mutations through the DNA of mice. Screening the offspring of treated mice reveals what each broken gene does. Fibrillins are strands inside the microfibrils that brace connective tissue.

Mice lacking fibrillin 2 showed a brand-new trait: reduced limb strength. Fibrillin faults already cause Marfan syndrome and a related joint disease in people. Weak limbs add a muscle-side clue to those human conditions. The screen shows how random mutation still finds what targeted studies miss.
plos-pone-0009237:
Irina Bogdarina and co-authors published this rat study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hard times during pregnancy can program a baby for high blood pressure later in life. Earlier rat work tied that programming to the renin-angiotensin system, a hormone circuit controlling blood pressure. Stress hormones called glucocorticoids were suspects in setting the program.

The team studied one gene in that circuit, the AT1b angiotensin receptor gene. They measured chemical marks on the gene, called methylation, and how strongly it was used. Glucocorticoid exposure changed both the marks and the gene's activity. That gives a concrete route by which early stress could raise lifelong blood pressure risk.
plos-pone-0009337:
Nilesh Dharajiya and co-authors published this asthma study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Allergic asthma fills airways with eosinophils, extra mucus, and allergy antibodies. A receptor called Fc gamma RIIb acts as a brake on antibody-driven reactions. It had already emerged as a brake on anaphylaxis and hay fever.

The team tested its role in a mouse model of allergic asthma. The brake receptor inhibited the lung inflammation in that model. Strengthening a natural brake could become a treatment angle that differs from blocking attack signals. The study adds asthma to the list of allergic diseases this receptor helps restrain.
plos-pone-0009437:
Gregory Fournier, Justin Neumann, and Peter Gogarten took up the deep past of the cell in PLOS ONE in 2010. All cells build proteins with a tiny machine called the ribosome. Parts of that machine have stayed much the same across all life. The authors reasoned that those old parts keep traces of how the genetic code first grew.

They read biases in the building blocks used at the most unchanged spots. From those traces they inferred the order in which parts of the ribosome were added long ago. The work offers a way to reconstruct steps from before the last common ancestor of life. It links the code we have now to its earliest form.
plos-pone-0009537:
Jonathon Burman, Jason Hamlin, and Peter McPherson studied a protein that shapes an organelle in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Golgi apparatus sorts and ships proteins inside the cell. Its stacked shape must be kept for that work to run well. The protein Scyl1 belongs to a family of kinase like proteins that lack the usual enzyme activity. It binds tightly to a coat protein of the shipping system.

When Scyl1 was reduced, the Golgi's form broke down. When it was restored, form returned. So this quiet protein helps hold the shipping department together. The finding adds a new part to the machinery that keeps cell compartments in order.
plos-pone-0009637:
Chad Creighton and co-authors searched for new microRNAs in women's reproductive tissues in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that fine tune gene activity after a gene is read. Over seven hundred human microRNAs were known at the time. Many are altered in disease. The team used next generation sequencing, which reads millions of RNA pieces at once, on tissue from the female reproductive tract.

Deep sequencing turned up microRNAs not in the catalogs. Each new one is a possible regulator of fertility, pregnancy, or disease in those tissues. The work expands the parts list for a system where gene timing matters greatly. It gives later studies fresh candidates to test.
plos-pone-0009737:
Aprille Seidel and co-authors published a virology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study looks at defensins, small germ-fighting peptides made by plants and animals. The team tested one defensin from each of the three families against HIV-1, the virus that causes AIDS.

The ring-shaped defensin RTD-1 blocked the virus at entry, the team found. The straight-chain forms HNP-1 and HBD-2 blocked the virus later, even when added twelve hours after infection. All three lowered a cell receptor called CXCR4. The authors also warn that two defensins block a lab marker enzyme, which may cloud older results.
plos-pone-0009837:
Skin renews itself in layers, and oil glands keep it supple. John House and colleagues studied two proteins that adult mouse skin cannot do without. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sebocytes are the cells that make skin oil, called sebum.

The proteins are C/EBP-alpha and C/EBP-beta, regulators that switch genes on and off. Both were required for sebocyte differentiation, the maturing of oil-gland cells. They were also needed for stratified squamous differentiation, the layering of skin cells. Without them, skin's renewal program breaks down. Adult skin must replace itself for a lifetime.
plos-pone-0009937:
When embryonic stem cells grow into body tissues, their master genes must switch off for good. Rodoniki Athanasiadou and colleagues watched one such shutdown in fine detail. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Methylation is a chemical mark that usually silences genes.

The gene is Oct-4, a core keeper of stem cell identity. De novo DNA methylation laid fresh silencing marks across its regulatory region. The targeting spread throughout the region as the cells differentiated. Locking Oct-4 down is one way growing cells commit to a fate. Oct-4 must stay off once a cell picks a path.
plos-pone-0010037:
Pedro Cermeño and co-workers studied ocean plankton in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The other authors were Colomban de Vargas and Fátima Abrantes. Their puzzle was why marine diatom communities changed so slowly. Over the past 1.5 million years, ice ages came and went, yet these communities stayed fairly stable.

The team looked at where phytoplankton live and what keeps their communities steady. Diatoms and other tiny drifting plants form the base of most ocean food webs. Understanding their stability helps predict how oceans may respond to the rapid warming now under way.
plos-pone-0010137:
The authors were Gang Wu, Lisha Zhu, Jennifer Dent, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper built a molecular map for rheumatoid arthritis. Computational biology was playing a growing role in clinical research. Translational medicine, which links lab science tightly to patient care, needs such maps to connect genes, proteins, and disease.

Their map gathers known molecular interactions tied to rheumatoid arthritis into one network. A single map lets researchers spot central players and possible drug targets more easily. It also gives data scientists a base for models that predict treatment response.
plos-pone-0010237:
Gregory Block, Gabriel DiMattia, and Darwin Prockop studied stress signals between cells in 2010. When epithelial cells face stress, a calcium wave spreads from cell to cell. In some cell types, that wave depends on ATP released by injured cells. Their PLOS ONE work used human epithelial cancer cells to trace the wave's control.

They found a protein, stanniocalcin-1, regulates those calcium waves. It acts by prompting bystander cells to release more ATP themselves. The result shows how a local injury signal can recruit neighbors into a coordinated response. The study appeared in 2010.
plos-pone-0010337:
Erick T Tatro and colleagues analyze gene control in the HIV-infected human brain in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. HIV disturbs the brain through inflammation and support cell activation. Tiny RNAs called microRNAs fine-tune gene output, but their role in brain HIV infection was little known.

Profiling frontal cortex tissue from uninfected, HIV, and HIV with depression groups, the team found distinct microRNA changes. More microRNAs fell in the depression group, and changed ones clustered on certain chromosomes. A new analysis method linked changed microRNAs to their target genes. Certain microRNAs, the authors argue, act as key nodes in brain gene networks during HIV infection, possibly tied to mood and thinking disorders.
plos-pone-0010437:
Alison Jones and Ray Berkelmans asked what corals pay for tolerating heat, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reef corals house algae that feed them from sunlight. As oceans warm, corals may swap in algae types that handle heat better. That swap sounds like a rescue, but it may carry costs. The team grew a reef coral with heat-tolerant versus heat-sensitive algae and compared growth.

A coral that survives heat but grows slowly still faces trouble. Slow growth means slower reef building and slower recovery after storms. The study weighs survival today against building tomorrow. Such trade-offs decide which reefs persist under warming. Managers need them measured, not assumed, before betting on tolerant algae as a fix.
plos-pone-0010537:
Jonathan Rios and colleagues linked gene variants in horses to susceptibility to West Nile brain disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. West Nile virus arrived in the United States in 1999 and spread nationwide. It has killed birds, people, and farm animals since. Mouse work had flagged a gene family, OAS, in the innate defense against the virus. The team tested the horse version, OAS1, for links to encephalitis.

Variants in OAS1 tracked with which horses developed brain disease. Genetic risk markers could help owners vaccinate or protect high-risk horses first. They also confirm that innate immunity genes decide outcomes across species. Horses suffer visibly from this virus and are good sentinels for human risk. This study adds a genetic layer to that sentinel role.
plos-pone-0010637:
Megan Olsen and colleagues built a computer model of tumor cell death, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most cancer models count single events like mutations or cell divisions. Their model instead treats each cell as a member of a tissue community with rules of belonging.

In the simulations, tumor cells that broke community rules died selectively. Healthy neighbors following the rules survived. The authors call this idea cellular citizenship. The model is abstract, but it suggests a fresh treatment angle: restore normal community signals, and cancer cells may remove themselves. Testing whether real tumors obey the model comes next.
plos-pone-0010737:
Andreas Rogalewski and colleagues paired a guidance protein with training after stroke in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. After cerebral ischemia, a blocked brain artery, surviving tissue can relearn lost skills. A gene screen had flagged Semaphorin 6A as active during the recovery phase. Semaphorins usually steer growing nerve fibers.

Raising Semaphorin 6A alone helped modestly. Pairing it with motor training produced much better recovery of movement. The protein seemed to prepare the tissue, and practice did the teaching. Stroke rehabilitation already leans on training; adding a molecular helper at the right phase could make those hours count for more.
plos-pone-0010837:
Eli Puterman, Jue Lin, Elizabeth Blackburn and co-authors published this health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long-term stress is linked to faster cell aging, often tracked through telomeres, the protective ends of chromosomes. Yet not everyone under stress shows short telomeres, and the authors asked whether regular exercise shields the body from that wear.

They studied healthy post-menopausal women, measuring telomere length in blood and recording stress levels plus daily vigorous activity over several days. Women were grouped as sedentary or active based on national activity guidance. Among sedentary women, higher stress went with shorter telomeres, while active women showed no such pattern. Puterman and colleagues argue that exercise can buffer stress at the cell level, a finding that ties daily habits to the biology of aging.
plos-pone-0010937:
Jordi Duch, Joshua Waitzman and Luís Nunes Amaral published this sports analytics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Team activities share a credit problem: everyone agrees some players star, but measuring each person's contribution fairly is hard. The authors used soccer as a test bed, analyzing play from the European Cup 2008 tournament.

They built a network method that follows how the ball moves between players and how those passing patterns create scoring chances. From that flow they derived numbers for each player's contribution and for the team's overall performance. Duch and colleagues show that a player's value can be read from the structure of play, not just goals and assists. Their framework is meant to travel beyond soccer, to any team work where credit is disputed.
plos-pone-0011037:
Peter Sokolowski, Francis Saison, Warwick Giles and co-authors published this pregnancy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tension in the uterine wall is thought to help trigger labor, but it had never been charted across a whole pregnancy. The authors followed hundreds of women at an Australian hospital from their first antenatal visit to delivery.

Serial ultrasounds measured the womb's wall thickness and dimensions, and combining them with published pressure data let the team compute wall tension trajectories for each woman. They compared singleton pregnancies ending in preterm or term labor with twin pregnancies, where the wall is stretched further. Sokolowski and colleagues give obstetrics a physical curve to set against the mystery of labor timing. If tension thresholds exist, measuring them could one day flag preterm risk early.
plos-pone-0011137:
Amon, Law, Fitzgibbon and colleagues searched for ovarian cancer markers in PLOS ONE in 2010. This cancer is often found late, when cure is hard. The team compared proteins in blood and in belly fluid from women with and without the disease.

Some proteins rose in the blood of women with ovarian cancer, marking them as candidates for early tests. A blood test that flags the disease sooner could save many lives. The candidates still need checks in larger groups before clinic use. Still, pairing two fluid sources gave the search a stronger starting list.
plos-pone-0011237:
Young, Adetifa, Ota and colleagues tracked TB immune cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. During active tuberculosis, some T cells can attack the germ on several fronts at once. The team measured those versatile cells in patients during illness and again after treatment ended.

Versatile responses expanded during disease and shrank back once treatment succeeded. That pattern makes these cells a sign of current disease activity. Vaccine designers hope to build responses like these in advance. Tracking them gives trials a yardstick for judging whether a vaccine creates the right kind of immunity.
plos-pone-0011337:
Kirill Sergueev and colleagues described in 2010 a faster way to detect the plague germ, Yersinia pestis. Plague still occurs in parts of the world, and it can kill quickly, so a fast and sure test matters for treatment and for public safety. Older tests based on viruses that attack the germ were sure but often slow.

Their method lets those germ-attacking viruses multiply in a sample, then tracks the growth with a sensitive DNA test in real time. More virus growth means the plague germ was present, and the signal appears much sooner than in older assays. A rapid test that stays specific helps clinics confirm cases early. It also gives health officials a stronger tool if plague ever appears as a deliberate threat.
plos-pone-0011437:
Amanda Maestre and co-authors examined in 2010 how a blood-group gene shapes immunity to the malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. The parasite invades red blood cells through the Duffy receptor, and people who lack that receptor resist this route of infection. Most people carry one of several forms of the receptor, and forms differ across world regions.

The team found that a person's Duffy genotype influences the antibody response they build after vivax infection. Two people with the same exposure can therefore end with different levels of immune protection, set partly by their genes. Vaccines against vivax malaria must work across those genetic differences, or they will protect some populations better than others. The study links a classic blood-group story to a practical problem in vaccine design.
plos-pone-0011537:
Anne Berry and co-authors tested in 2010 whether training the senses can sharpen memory in older adults. Working memory, holding a phone number or a plan in mind, erodes with age and limits independence. Perceptual training, practicing fine sensory distinctions such as telling similar tones or textures apart, exercises basic brain processing that memory may draw on.

The study asks whether gains from that low-level practice spill over into working memory, a transfer that brain training often promises and rarely proves. Testing transfer honestly matters, because older adults spend real money and hope on training programs. If perception practice does lift memory, it offers a gentle, drug-free support for aging minds. If it does not, the paper still serves readers by marking the boundary of what such training can do.
plos-pone-0011637:
Eric Nilsson and co-authors mapped gene networks that build the ovary's earliest follicles, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Primordial follicles hold a female's lifetime supply of eggs, held paused in development from before birth. How this founding pool forms is central to understanding fertility and its loss.

Using a systems approach, the team tracked gene activity as follicles develop and charted the regulatory networks involved. Their network analysis highlights control genes that coordinate the process. The map gives fertility researchers concrete candidates for explaining early ovarian failure and for protecting the egg supply.
plos-pone-0011737:
Daniel Kellett and co-authors studied how the cerebellum stores learned responses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cerebellum is best known for balance and smooth movement, but some kinds of learning depend on it too, such as the trained eyeblink response in rabbits. Briefly switching off parts of its circuit had begun to split the roles of its outer cortex and its deep nuclei.

The team looked at how memories settle in the cerebellar cortex over time. Their work tests whether the cortex itself holds the lasting trace or hands it on. The answer adds a memory-filing role to the little brain's known work in movement.
plos-pone-0011837:
Wen Chih Chiang and co-authors described in 2010 an effort to deliver proteins straight to podocytes, the cells that form the kidney's main filter. Podocytes wrap around tiny blood vessels in the kidney and keep needed protein from leaking into urine. Their position exposes them to blood and urine alike, which makes them reachable in principle but hard to target in practice.

The team set up delivery systems designed to carry protein cargo to these filter cells. Reaching podocytes directly matters because damage to them drives many kidney diseases, yet general drugs wash over the whole body. A working delivery route would let future treatments act at the filter itself, where the injury actually happens.
plos-pone-0011937:
Sarah Read and co-workers tested in 2010 whether an arthritis drug could calm the immune overdrive seen in HIV infection. Even when HIV is controlled, constant immune activation helps drive the disease. Leflunomide, a drug that tempers immune cell growth, was a candidate for lowering that activation.

In a randomized study of HIV-1 infected participants, the team measured how the drug affected T cell cycling and activation. Slowing the churn of T cells could, in principle, reduce the damage activation causes over years. The trial gives an early read on whether repurposing an existing immune drug is a safe and sensible path in HIV care.
plos-pone-0012037:
Aurelia Santoro and colleagues brought in 2010 fresh proof that a small branch on the family tree of our cell power plants bears on the risk of Alzheimer's disease. The disease is the most common cause of dementia in old age. Since the power plants, the mitochondria, make the cell's energy and were thought to falter in this disease, changes in their own DNA are a clear place to look.

The branch in point is a subgroup called H5, passed down the mother's line from child to child. People who carry it were found more prone to the late form of the disease, the kind that starts in old age. A sign passed down the mother's side fits the known trend for risk to track the mother's health. It also makes the case that weak energy supply is part of the disease, not just a side show.
plos-pone-0012137:
Saravanan Thangamani, Stephen Higgs, Sarah Ziegler, and co-authors compared two ways of catching chikungunya virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. In nature this virus arrives by mosquito bite, along with mosquito saliva that tampers with the skin's defenses. Lab studies usually inject virus with a needle instead, which skips that whole first act of a real infection.

The team's work shows the immune response differs when the virus comes by mosquito rather than needle. Early events at the bite site shape how the illness unfolds, so the delivery route is part of the disease itself. That lesson affects how vaccines and treatments for mosquito-borne viruses should be tested before anyone trusts the results.
plos-pone-0012237:
Suzanne Kalb, Consuelo Garcia-Rodriguez, Jianlong Lou, and co-authors built a catcher's mitt for botulinum toxins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. These toxins are among the most potent poisons known; the sickness they cause can paralyze breathing and demand weeks of intensive care. There are several types, and the best treatment, an antitoxin matched to the type, works only when given early, so fast typing is critical.

One engineered antibody they made grabs all four major types at once, feeding them into a mass-spectrometer test that tells them apart. A single capture step for every type shortens the race to the right antitoxin. In a food poisoning outbreak or an attack, those saved hours are the point.
plos-pone-0012337:
Brendan Flynn, Amit Bhole, Nima Saeidi, and co-authors showed that stretch protects collagen from being eaten away, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Collagen is the body's main structural protein, filling bone, tendon, skin, and cornea, and enzymes that cut it allow tissues to be remodeled or, in disease, destroyed. The team had earlier proposed that the fibrils resist cutting better when under load.

Testing rebuilt collagen fibrils under mechanical strain, they found the strain indeed stabilizes them against a mammalian collagen-cutting enzyme. That coupling of force and chemistry explains how tendons can bear load for decades while remodeling slowly. It also suggests diseased tissues may lose collagen partly because their mechanics changed first.
plos-pone-0012437:
Henrique Santos, Juliano Cury, Flavia Carmo and colleagues read DNA from mangrove mud to detect oil pollution, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Tiny eukaryotes — single-celled life with a nucleus — respond quickly to contamination, making them good pollution alarms. Naming them by microscope is slow and often fails, so the team used the 18S gene as a DNA barcode instead.

Certain microbe DNA patterns lined up with oil in the sediment, marking them as indicators of contamination. Mangroves shelter coasts and nurseries for fish, yet sit near ports and oil work. A DNA test for hidden oil gives managers an early warning before damage shows in trees and wildlife.
plos-pone-0012537:
Toru Hosoi, Shota Yokoyama, Suguru Matsuo and colleagues removed an immune adaptor protein in mice and watched metabolism, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. MyD88 relays signals from many innate immune sensors, and immune pathways are increasingly tied to obesity-linked diabetes. Removing a relay this central might have protected the mice — or, as it turned out, done the opposite.

Mice lacking MyD88 faced a higher risk of diabetes in the study's setting. The result warns that gut and immune sensing also serve healthy metabolism, not only defense. Blanket suppression of innate immunity could backfire in metabolic disease, a caution for drug design.
plos-pone-0012637:
Nalam, Ahmed, Devi and co-authors compared the genetics of disease-causing Leptospira bacteria from around the world. Leptospirosis spreads from animals to people, often through water, and can be severe. Outbreak teams struggle because telling one strain from another has been unreliable.

Their 2010 study used a large global collection to map how strains relate to each other. Clear family links let health workers trace an outbreak to its source and follow its spread. Better strain naming also helps labs in different countries share results that actually match, and it sharpens vaccine and test design.
plos-pone-0012737:
Spade, Griffitt, Liu and co-authors reported that male queen conch near shore lose their fertility each breeding season. Offshore conch in the Florida Keys breed well, while nearshore animals do not. Their 2010 study examined testes of conch from both settings across the reproductive season.

Nearshore males showed testis regression just when breeding should peak. That local failure helps explain why nearshore conch numbers stay low despite fishing rules. The cause may lie in nearshore water conditions, a lead for reef and fishery managers.  Conch are a valued food and export across the Caribbean region.
plos-pone-0012837:
Fuller, Ross, Szewczyk and co-authors challenged the idea that bone itself must switch on the cells that eat bone. Osteoclasts resorb bone, and some signal from bone was thought to trigger that behaviour. Lab work had shown that blocking a certain receptor on these cells stops resorption, hinting at the trigger.

Their 2010 study found osteoclasts can be activated without bone present at all. That shifts the search for the trigger toward the cells and signals around bone. The result matters for diseases of bone loss, including osteoporosis.  The cells were grown and tested away from bone surfaces.
plos-pone-0331937:
Wenlong Jin and colleagues describe a way to build three-dimensional models of underground rock that leans on expert judgement, not just raw data. Purely data-driven models can miss twisted structures. So the team fed borehole records and survey profiles from a tantalum and niobium mining district in Jiangxi, China, into modelling software. Meanwhile, geologists added rules drawn from their own knowledge of the area.

The rebuilt model placed the richest ore where a sodium-rich granite meets the rocks above and below it, matching what miners see. Guided by those contact zones, the team picked out two promising deep targets for future drilling. They argue that mixing expert rules with data gives models that are both faster to build and closer to the real ground.
plos-pone-0333337:
Peter Okello Oyoo, Simon Okwera, Daniel Micheal Okello, and Basil Mugonola measured how efficiently 191 smallholder dairy households in northern Uganda turn inputs into profit. They compared three ways of keeping cattle: confined zero-grazing, tethering, and open herding. Their 2026 survey analysis fitted a profit frontier model. The model separates bad luck from genuine inefficiency and asks what drives each.

The drivers differed sharply by system. Herd size lifted profits under zero-grazing, while feed costs crushed them. Land helped tethered herds yet hurt herding systems. Education, improved breeds, and closeness to markets cut inefficiency almost everywhere. The model blamed over nine tenths of profit variation on inefficiency rather than chance. Management, not luck, is the main lever.
plos-pone-0340237:
Clara Punzi and four colleagues profile Italy's platform workers in this 2026 study. Gig work through apps is often pictured as a young person's stopgap. The authors test that picture with official survey data from 2018 and 2021. Machine learning models sorted out which traits predict platform work. Explainable AI tools then showed how the models reached their answers.

Platform work in Italy turned out layered and uneven. It mirrors the country's older labour market fractures and regional gaps. Financial vulnerability clustered not among the youngest workers, but among older, established ones. Many had hit job instability, underemployment, or shrinking income from regular work. Platform jobs carried the insecurity typical of non-standard employment. The findings argue against one-size-fits-all gig policy, since the workforce is really several workforces sharing an app.
plos-pone-0342637:
Mary Jewell and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study comparing two ways of finding COVID-19 clusters in Utah: traditional case interviews and genetic sequencing of virus samples. Sequencing can reveal which cases are truly linked, but health departments lacked guidance on using it during a live response. The team compared the populations each method reached and tested ways of grouping cases by their genetic similarity.

Sequencing coverage was uneven, with several non-White patient groups less likely to be sequenced at all. Genetic clusters often disagreed with interview-based ones, and many large interview clusters turned out to mix several separate virus introductions. The authors conclude that genomic data sharpens cluster definitions considerably, provided sampling is broad and cases in suspected clusters are sequenced first.
plos-pone-0344537:
Zahra Sheikhi Darani and Monireh Hosseini propose a new layer for recommendation engines in this 2026 PLOS ONE computing paper. Recommenders in social apps usually balance relevance against a fixed idea of novelty, but what feels new depends on what a person's friends have been seeing and doing.

Their framework scores each item's novelty for each user from social community behavior, and learns how much novelty that user personally likes, resolving the tug-of-war with relevance individually. Bolted onto existing engines as a post-processing step, it lifted diversity, coverage, and novelty on two real datasets, Epinions and LastFM, without sacrificing relevance. The design suits any platform where friends shape taste.
plos-pone-0344737:
Rumford and colleagues, in a 2026 study, watch the eye of a baby zebrafish rebuild itself after light-sensing cells are destroyed. Zebrafish regrow retinal cells that mammals cannot, and immune cells called microglia were suspected of guiding that repair. The team compared normal larvae with mutants bred to lack microglia, after wiping out their cone cells.

Repair proceeded surprisingly well without microglia. Support cells still woke up, multiplied, and produced new cones at much the usual pace, and inflammation-linked genes changed only modestly. A wrinkle appeared, though: a stand-in population of immune cells showed up in the mutants after damage. It rose and fell on a similar schedule, but was much scarcer and carried different surface marks. Because something filled the vacant role, the authors say they cannot cleanly credit or clear microglia. The stand-ins themselves are now a question worth chasing.
plos-pone-0345137:
Hasan Yalim Akin, Gule Cinar, and co-authors asked whether two ancient layers of the immune system interact to decide who gets sick with COVID-19. One layer is a family of natural killer cell receptors, and the other is a set of antiviral genes inherited from Neanderthals. Their 2026 study genotyped one hundred seventy-five unvaccinated patients, spanning no symptoms to severe disease, across several immune genes.

Missing both a protective receptor pattern and the Neanderthal gene variants together predicted symptoms and severe disease far better than either alone, with overall classification accuracy in the high seventies. Age, male sex, and two other gene variants added risk, while one blood group and one gene form protected. The authors present the synergy as a first, needing confirmation in larger and more diverse groups.
plos-pone-0346837:
Gornsawun and colleagues checked a bedside test for an enzyme lack in newborns along the Thai-Myanmar border in a 2026 study. Babies lacking the enzyme can develop dangerous yellowing of the skin and brain harm. Seventy-five babies, grouped by routine cord blood results, were followed with blood tests through their first four months.

The study compared cord blood with later heel-prick samples to see if both give the same answer. It also tracked how enzyme activity changes as babies grow, which affects cutoff choices. Reliable bedside testing matters in remote clinics without full labs, where early warning prevents severe jaundice.
plos-pone-0346937:
Runa Sawayama and Hajime Nobuhara asked if a drone's look can change how folk fly it. They used a phone-like screen trick to drape new looks on the same drone. A large group flew the drone with and sans the trick. The team logged each flight and asked for views in forms.

The looks did not change how much the group worked the sticks. But views of the drone swung a lot. Folk judged its age, its beast-like feel, and its sex in new ways. They even sized up its bulk and heft in fresh ways. The team says looks could help drones win a warm place in daily life.
plos-pone-0347537:
Zhao Wen and colleagues simulated what happens when individual fibres are pulled out of concrete, a small event that decides how well fibre-reinforced concrete resists cracking. Builders commonly mix in basalt or polypropylene fibres, but testing every combination in the lab is slow. Their 2026 study built a computer model combining a phase-field description of damage with a model of the glue-like bond between fibre and cement.

The predicted pull-out forces matched published experiments well. Deeper embedding and thicker fibres raised the peak load for both fibre types, and stronger bonding or a stronger cement matrix improved reinforcement further. The validated model lets engineers screen fibre choices virtually before pouring real concrete.
plos-pone-0347737:
Shijie Zhang and co-workers work on calming vibration in the drivetrain of a large wind turbine. Shaking in gears and shafts wears parts out and cuts efficiency. Their 2026 study models the linked mechanical and electrical system of a big turbine and designs a control scheme on the generator side that narrows the gap between mechanical and electrical torque.

The control also trims unwanted ripples in generator current and magnetic pull. In the model, sideways shaking in key gear parts fell, and tracking of shaft speed grew sharper. Smoother running means less wear and steadier power from each gust. The approach offers turbine makers a software route to longer-lasting machines.
plos-pone-0348137:
Jaeyoung Huh and colleagues teach an artificial intelligence system to upgrade liver ultrasound images from old machines, in this 2026 PLOS ONE imaging paper. Ultrasound is the first test for liver disease worldwide, but aging scanners produce murky pictures that can hide tumors and mislead diagnosis.

Their network learned without paired examples, using images from a twelve-year-old device as input and from a four-year-old device as the quality target, translating between the two styles. Two experienced reviewers judged the enhanced images better. If the gains hold in clinic, hospitals could stretch the useful life of older scanners, a real concern where new equipment budgets are thin.
plos-pone-0348437:
Björn Högberg and Cristian Bortes asked if stress in class spreads from teen to teen. They used data on Swedish teens, first at age thirteen, then at age sixteen. Then they ran the sums in a huge range of ways. The count of model runs topped nine thousand. Each run changed a choice such as the test type or the stress gauge.

Most runs found a spread, but a weak one. The size of the spread swung a lot, and at times it flipped sign. Few runs cleared the bar for trust. The team says stress in school comes more from the school itself than from friends. Fix the real loads first, they urge.
plos-pone-0348537:
RETRACTION: The PLOS One Editors have withdrawn a study of new fluorine-rich drugs. The study claimed these drugs could fight tumours that grow with little oxygen. After it came out, readers flagged faults in its data files. Some chart traces looked far too much alike for drugs said to be distinct. The stated tests also did not match the work.

The editors then checked the raw files the authors sent. Key claims in the text were not backed by those files. Bars on key charts did not match the raw data either. One author replied but took no stand on the choice. With the results in doubt, the journal pulled the study in full.
plos-pone-0348737: Wagner and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on brown trout swimming downstream. The fish faced water that speeds up and flows at high rates. The team paid close attention to how the trout moved, not just where they ended up. The findings matter for fish passage design at dams and weirs, where fast water can block or harm migrating fish.
plos-pone-0349237:
Yaojun Zhang, Changqiang Shen, and Ying Xiong improved a computer vision model for spotting rice diseases in 2026. Finding and locating disease early protects harvests, yet field images are cluttered, lesions are small, and heavy models run slowly.

Their model swaps in a light backbone that reads fine detail cheaply, uses an upsampling step that keeps detail, and adds flexible convolution in the neck. Against the base model it gained a little accuracy, ran notably faster, and cut computing cost and size greatly. A lighter, quicker detector is what drones and farm phones can realistically carry.
plos-pone-0349437:
Narayani Paudel Ghimire and colleagues piloted Forum Play, a form of participatory theatre, to promote respectful maternity care in urban Nepal in 2026. Mistreatment during facility births is widely reported there, and training rarely lets staff rehearse kinder behaviour.

Doctors and nurses in two large hospitals took part, with one group acting out scenes of oppression drawn from their own work and stepping in to change them. Surveys before and after compared their reported views and behaviour with a control group. Theatre based practice offers a low cost way to shift ward culture, and this pilot tests whether it moves real attitudes.
plos-pone-0349937:
Xiaobo Xu and seven colleagues dissect a grain toxin's dangers entirely on the computer. Their 2026 case study is zearalenone, an estrogen-like contaminant made by Fusarium fungi in cereals. It threatens food safety worldwide. The team combined network toxicology with molecular docking and dynamics simulations. Instead of dosing animals, they predicted which human proteins the toxin grips. Kidney damage was the hypothesised harm under the microscope.

Five core targets emerged, including well-known signalling and cancer-related proteins. The affected routes touch immune injury, inflammation, cell death, and genetic mutation. Docking and simulation both showed the toxin binding its targets snugly. Pathways famous in cancer biology appeared among the hits. The authors present the pipeline itself as a deliverable. Fast, animal-free toxicity screening could triage the thousands of food contaminants regulators face, reserving slow laboratory proof for the likeliest threats.
plos-pone-0350337:
Margaret Fletcher and co-authors follow in 2026 children with attention and hyperactivity disorder in a large United States development study, asking what shapes how they fare over five years. Children reported on family conflict, kind behaviour, and school life, while records tracked medicine use and social conditions. Growth modelling sorted children into paths such as resilient, declining, or slowly improving.

Medicine patterns linked only weakly to which path a child followed, though one non stimulant type tied to poorer outcomes. Social and structural factors mattered far more, above all ethnic discrimination, plus sex, insurance, and parents' work and partnership. Support should address context, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0350637:
Jung-Bin Park and co-authors built a deep learning tool in 2026 to warn of brain complications after surgery for Moyamoya disease in children. The rare condition narrows brain arteries, and surgery to improve blood flow can still be followed by strokes or bleeds.

The team turned blood pressure waves recorded during surgery into images and trained several image networks on them, testing on a later group of patients kept aside. Heat maps showed which wave features drove each call. A warning drawn from signals already collected could help teams watch the riskiest children more closely after surgery.
plos-pone-0350737:
Sudip Saha and colleagues designed a defense for the computer systems that watch networks for intruders. Such detectors use deep learning, but attackers can fool them with tiny, carefully crafted changes to data. Their 2026 study tested a hybrid design that mixes normal training with attack training and adds guidance drawn from what the model gets wrong.

Tested on data covering spying probes, shellcode, and worms, the system stayed accurate on clean traffic and held up far better under two common attack methods than standard neural networks. It beat the comparison models by a clear margin and also made fewer overconfident mistakes. The work matters for hospitals, banks, and factories, where a fooled detector can open the door to real damage.
plos-pone-0350837:
Lana Zuriegat and colleagues reviewed two hundred and thirty four patients with diabetic foot infections at a large hospital in Jordan. Foot infections drive long stays and amputations in diabetes. Culture results, drug resistance, first drug choices, and stay length were charted. Therapy counted as right only when a drug given in the first two days covered every germ found at the right dose and route.

Staph germs caused half of infections, and two thirds of germs resisted multiple drugs. First therapy was right in under half of cases. Yet only infection severity, not resistance or wrong first therapy, clearly predicted longer stays in adjusted models. Severity triage and faster culture guided switches matter most, the data suggest.
plos-pone-0351137:
Sepsis, the body's overwhelming response to infection, fills intensive care units in Tanzania, and Atala Jongo and colleagues tracked adults with the condition at a national referral hospital. Their 2026 PLOS One study followed patients over six months in 2023, screening everyone admitted to the unit.

About two hundred fifty patients were screened, with sepsis defined by organ failure scores within the first day. The team recorded how common sepsis was, how many patients died, and which traits predicted death. Referral hospitals receive the sickest patients from wide regions, so their numbers show the burden at its heaviest and where resources matter most.
plos-pone-0351337:
Valuable uranium sits in sandstone along the southern Junggar Basin in China. Qing Wang and colleagues studied drill cores from the Louzhuangzi area. They wanted to learn why the metal gathered there. Their work combined field mapping with microscope studies. Chemical probes examined the rock in fine detail. The paper appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Ancient rivers built the rock formation in two layers. Winding rivers laid down the upper layer. Braided rivers built the lower layer. The lower sands let fluids pass easily. Uranium-rich ore sits mostly in that lower layer. Moving fluids later changed the rock and dropped their uranium load. Explorers can now aim drill holes more wisely.
plos-pone-0351437:
