Viet-Linh Nguyen and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study of parasites in free-roaming cats caught through a trap-neuter-return program in New York City. Samples from eighty-seven cats, collected in spring and summer 2023, were tested for gut parasites, blood parasites, and exposure to Toxoplasma. Urban cats can carry organisms that also infect people, yet city-level data were scarce.

More than half the cats carried at least one parasite, most commonly the roundworm Toxocara, found in over half. Young male cats were the heaviest shedders of roundworm eggs, marking them as key drivers of contamination in shared spaces. About one in eleven cats showed antibodies to Toxoplasma. The authors recommend folding disease surveillance into neutering programs to watch risks for both cats and people.
plos-pone-0351537:
Yuemei Li authored this 2026 PLOS One modeling paper on how rock slowly deforms under load when it is also hot, a problem for deep underground engineering. Older creep models often ignore how heat damage builds over time and describe the final, accelerating stage of deformation poorly. Li combines damage mechanics with fractional calculus to build a model in which heat and stress damage grow together over time.

Checked against laboratory creep tests run at four temperatures from room level up to one hundred degrees Celsius, the model's curves matched the measured behavior closely through all three creep stages. It also captured the turning point into accelerated creep better than the classic model it improves on. The author offers it as theoretical support for judging the long-term stability of hot, deep rock projects.
plos-pone-0351637:
Yuta Nakaniida and colleagues asked whether the softness of the eye's front window relates to blood flow at the back of the eye. They measured one hundred healthy eyes with an air-puff device that films the cornea bending, and with a laser method that estimates flow in the optic nerve head. Eye length, corneal thickness, and pressure were recorded too, since each can sway the readings.

Eyes whose corneas bent more under the puff tended to have slower measured flow in the nerve head tissue. The link survived in the team's best statistical model, which also included sex. Cornea and nerve head are far apart in the eye, so a shared trait, perhaps the stiffness of connective tissue throughout the eye, may drive both. If so, a quick cornea test could hint at circulation deeper in the eye.
plos-pone-0351837:
Eline Kroeze and four colleagues trace what care costs in the six months around a stay in Dutch short-term residential care, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. This care is meant to return older patients home independent, yet fewer than half manage it. National claims for more than sixteen thousand patients admitted in 2022 were sorted into cost paths, with a palliative group set aside in advance.

One latent group of about a fifth of patients consumed nearly two fifths of all spending, driven by hospital returns and nursing home admission. Dementia and several diagnoses raised the odds of belonging, but prediction overall was weak. The authors conclude the variation lives in how care is organised, not who the patients are.
plos-pone-0351937:
Diogo Mochcovitch and colleagues present a case study of a training workshop that spread through Quebec primary care largely on its own. The workshop, called STAT-C, teaches family doctors and nurses how to handle sick leave tied to common mental health problems. The team followed its spread for a year after it was showcased at an innovation meeting.

They gathered documents, sat in on monthly meetings, and interviewed the workshop's creators, clinicians, decision makers, and end users. The workshop met most of the checklist points used to judge whether an idea is ready to grow. Interview accounts covered why sites picked it up and what helped or blocked its spread. Cases like this show how good ideas can travel without a central push.
plos-pone-0352137:
Cassandra Barber and four co-authors address a quiet problem in cattle research in this 2026 PLOS ONE article. Lab tests that measure gene activity need steady reference genes for comparison, yet the usual choices may shift between tissues or animals. The team hunted for better candidates in the breathing and immune tissues of cattle.

Starting from dozens of public gene datasets from healthy cattle, they ranked genes by how little their activity varied. Five candidates emerged, and lab tests on tissue from calves infected with a respiratory virus confirmed one gene as steady in most tissues checked. Reliable reference genes make later studies of cattle lung disease far more trustworthy.
plos-pone-0352237:
Yun Song and three colleagues trace how shocks ripple between farm, energy, and money markets under Chinese policy uncertainty. Their 2026 study connects four series: agricultural futures, crude oil, the US dollar, and an index of China's economic policy uncertainty. Average spillovers can hide the real action. The authors therefore use a quantile method that watches calm periods and extremes separately. Crises, in this design, get their own measurement rather than blurring into the mean.

The extremes dominated. Return spillovers at the tails ran far higher than at typical levels. Bad times plainly wire the markets tighter together. Specific crises visibly amplified the transmission. Policy uncertainty itself behaved as part of the system, not background noise. For traders and regulators, the lesson is to watch the tails. Diversification that looks safe in normal months can evaporate exactly when a policy shock hits all three markets at once.
plos-pone-0352337:
Giuliana Nardacchione, Pierluigi Zoccolotti, and Chiara Valeria Marinelli published this 2026 study testing a popular theory of dyslexia. The procedural hypothesis blames weak rule-learning memory. Thirty-two young adults with dyslexia and sixty controls learned an artificial grammar, and the task was split apart to see which kind of learning each person used.

Adults with dyslexia learned the grammar rules and statistical patterns about as well as controls, using stored examples too, though forming those examples was harder. Nardacchione finds little support for the procedural theory and highlights strengths dyslexic adults use to compensate.
plos-pone-0352437:
Marta Majewska and seven colleagues profile the blood chemistry of COVID-19 at four depths of severity. Their 2026 study drew plasma from twenty patients and five healthy controls. Patients were classed by lung involvement and the breathing support they needed. A broad, untargeted scan detected over five hundred metabolites per sample. The team then asked how the chemical picture morphs as the disease deepens, rather than comparing sick and healthy in one lump.

Severity rewired metabolism step by step. The chemical distance from healthy grew steadily across the groups. Early and moderate disease centred on disturbed fatty acid handling. The severest group shifted toward pyrimidine metabolism, the chemistry of building DNA letters. That fits frantic virus replication and immune cell multiplication. One amino acid pathway stayed disturbed across nearly all stages. Fine-grained staging like this could eventually match treatments to the metabolic phase a patient is actually in.
plos-pone-0352937:
Liangliang Jiang and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One remote-sensing study of how Central Asia's vegetation withstands and recovers from drought, season by season. Western Central Asia suffers frequent spring droughts, while the Aral Sea basin gets fewer but harsher summer and autumn droughts. The team measured two qualities: resistance during drought and resilience afterward, across croplands, grasslands, forests, and sparse vegetation.

Croplands in northern Kazakhstan tended to bend but bounce back, while sparse lands downstream of the Aral Sea resisted yet recovered poorly. Rainfall and dryness of the air together drove over half of the variation in resilience. Spring vegetation was both toughest and quickest to recover, and spring also accounted for the largest share of vegetation loss. Long summer droughts hit grasslands hardest. The authors say seasonal detail like this sharpens drought planning.
plos-pone-0353137: Fan, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on safe ways to test tax-risk software. Real tax records are private, so Fan built a simulation that makes fake but realistic data. Rules check that the fake data obey set limits, and the setup can be rerun the same way each time. Shared test data of this kind let tax offices and researchers compare detection tools fairly.
plos-pone-0353237:
Yulin Li and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of a simple blood ratio in critically ill bowel disease patients. The ratio compares hemoglobin with the spread of red cell sizes. It tracks inflammation in the body. The data covered an unusual subgroup. These were intensive care patients with bowel disease who all died within thirty days. The question was whether the ratio related to sepsis during the stay.

Patients who developed sepsis had lower ratios on arrival. Each step up in the ratio came with notably lower odds of sepsis. The pattern was steady and straight-line. The authors are candid about the limits. This hand-picked subgroup cannot speak for patients in general. They frame the result as a hypothesis about end-stage bowel disease. Future studies in broader groups should test it.
plos-pone-0353837:
Zeyu Zhang and three colleagues develop a questionnaire for gauging how ready trainee teachers in China are for artificial intelligence, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Five hundred and twenty-eight pre-service teachers answered the draft survey, which the team split into halves to discover and then confirm its structure. The finished tool has fourteen items across three themes: how well teachers understand AI, how risky they judge it, and how confident they feel academically.

Statistical checks showed the three-part structure fit well and each theme measured consistently. Trainees who had already used AI scored higher on literacy and confidence, but slightly lower on caution. Teacher educators now have a tested yardstick for a fast-moving part of training.
plos-pone-0354037:
Henry Mensah and three colleagues soak cowpea seeds in a mutation-causing chemical to breed better varieties, in this 2026 PLOS ONE experiment. Cowpea is a staple protein crop in West Africa, and creating fresh genetic variety is the first step in improving it. Seeds of one cultivar were treated at three strengths of the chemical, grown out, and scored for flowering, pod, seed, and yield traits.

Counter to expectations, germination and survival rose with the chemical dose. The lowest dose gave the best average yield, and two standout plants produced roughly double the control's harvest. Those two mutants advance to the next generation of trials, where their advantage must prove stable and heritable.
plos-pone-0354137:
Krokovsky and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, ask what happens when two mosquito-borne viruses infect the same cells. Zika, West Nile, and Mayaro viruses now overlap in parts of the world, thanks to trade, travel, and a warming climate. A mosquito or a person could carry two at once, or catch one after another.

The team infected monkey kidney cells with Zika plus West Nile, or Zika plus Mayaro, either together or one after the other. When the viruses arrived together, Zika's output fell, a pattern called interference. When Zika arrived first, it held its ground. When Zika arrived second, it was shut out. The partner viruses, by contrast, grew just as well whether Zika was present or not. Six days after infection, the team measured viral RNA and cell damage. The authors frame these dish results as a first step toward understanding double infections in real hosts.
plos-pone-0354237:
Yevusiak and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial called REST, about stopping the weight-loss drug semaglutide. The drug helps many people with obesity lose a large amount of weight and improves heart and metabolic health. Yet most people regain weight after stopping suddenly, and the health gains fade.

The trial will enroll people who have already lost at least a tenth of their body weight on the drug and whose weight has leveled off. Half will taper the dose slowly over sixteen weeks before stopping, and half will stop at once. The main measure is how much weight each group regains. Blood pressure across a full day and levels of a hunger hormone will also be tracked. The team expects that a slow taper will soften regain. Their design speaks to a common real-world problem: how to come off a drug many patients cannot take forever.
plos-pone-0354337:
Wei and colleagues, in a 2026 study, model how blue honeysuckle branches shake when a harvest machine vibrates them. Mechanical shaking can knock ripe berries loose, but the trunk and roots soak up much of the energy, weakening the force at the fruit. The team simplified a forked branch into a Y shape and wrote the equations of its motion.

Their math shows that when the branch sits at a small angle to the shaking direction, a certain shaking speed can trigger parametric resonance. That is a runaway wobble that could shake fruit free or, if uncontrolled, harm the branch. The unstable zone depends on shaking strength, speed, and branch size. Computer models of the branch and real shaking tests on branches matched the theory well. The authors offer the model as a design basis for honeysuckle harvesters that shake hard enough to pick, but not to damage.
plos-pone-0354737:
Jiafeng Zhang and co-authors compare in 2026 two Chinese made tests that count HIV virus in blood against a leading imported reference test. Counting the virus guides treatment and diagnosis, but cost and speed limit use in poorer settings. Plasma samples from several hundred infected people were run through all three tests.

Both local tests found slightly more positives than the reference and agreed with it closely on counts across virus subtypes. Small average biases stayed within a narrow range. The authors say the local tests meet needed standards while costing less and returning results faster, helping close a monitoring gap where resources are tight.
plos-pone-0354837:
Qi Liu, Yang Liu, and Yumei Zhang present a 2026 trial plan for people who lose language after a stroke. The plan tests magnetic stimulation aimed at the right side of the cerebellum, a rear brain area now linked to speech. Participants in the subacute stage would receive either real or sham stimulation alongside speech therapy.

Follow-up stretches to one year, with a standard aphasia battery as the main measure. Brain scans and a test of nonverbal thinking add detail on how any change happens. Because recruitment was still under way, the document sets out methods and hopes rather than results, and it records any side effects tied to stimulation.
plos-pone-0354937:
Abdelmuhsen Abusneina and Soad Elwirfli published a cautionary analysis in 2026 about cancer gene signatures built around the loss of a gene called PTEN. Researchers often read a tumor's pattern of gene activity as a signature of some process, here glutaminolysis, the cell's use of the amino acid glutamine. The authors show that when PTEN is deleted, neighboring genes are often deleted along with it, as passengers.

Those passenger deletions can distort the signature, making it look as if glutamine use changed when the true cause sits nearby in the genome. Their case argues for location aware signature design: checking what else a deletion drags with it. The lesson reaches beyond one gene, to any study that reads meaning into cancer's copy number changes.
plos-pone-0355437:
Xiaomin Lin and Xudong Huang examine in 2026 whether a simple index built from blood sugar and blood fat relates to early kidney damage in a very large Chinese sample. The damage sign is a raised level of a protein in urine. Tens of thousands of adults from eight centres were included, with many health factors accounted for in the models.

Higher index values linked steadily to higher odds of the urine sign, in a straight line pattern. The link held for people with and without diabetes, but was stronger where diabetes was present. Because the data are a single snapshot, the authors say follow up studies must show whether the index comes before damage.
plos-pone-0355737:
Giulia Tomasetig and seven colleagues scan the brains of professional artists as they judge their own paintings, in this 2026 study. Twenty artists rated artworks by themselves and by others inside an MRI scanner, and in a second task they mentally relived the moment they had conceived each of their pieces. The design tests whether the physical act of making art stays embedded in how its maker later experiences it.

Judging their own work, compared with others', engaged brain regions tied to action and to the emotional feel of movement. Reliving creation recruited a network involved in motor thinking. Artists who showed stronger activity in a movement-planning region during that reliving also judged their works more favorably. The authors read this as support for an embodied view: for painters, the gestures of creation remain part of the finished artwork's experience.
plos-pone-0355937:
Jianfan Zhou and colleagues test whether two simple blood-based scores can flag adults at risk of poor mental health. One score mixes blood sugar and fat measures, and the other compares two blood cell types tied to inflammation. Several hundred adults at a hospital in Shandong, China, completed a standard symptom checklist and gave fasting blood samples for both scores.

Higher values on either score tracked with higher symptom totals across most areas, including low mood, anxiety, and body complaints. Adults high on both scores fared worst. Among several machine learning models, a regularized regression sorted risk best, though modestly. Zhou and colleagues suggest routine blood scores could help flag patients who deserve a closer mental health check.
plos-pone-0356237:
Suzanne Ablard and seven colleagues evaluate community hubs designed to keep urgent-care patients out of hospital in England, in this 2026 qualitative study. The hubs help paramedics and other clinicians route people with pressing but non-emergency needs into nearby community services instead of an ambulance trip. The team interviewed twenty-one staff working in, or referring into, hubs at three locations and analyzed the conversations thematically.

Staff said the hubs genuinely improved integrated working, giving clinicians rapid access to community support for patients. But three brakes limited their impact. Fuzzy eligibility rules created a tension between easy access and consistent decisions. Ambulance services engaged unevenly. And hiring and keeping staff with the right skill mix proved hard. The authors conclude the model can simplify access and prevent needless hospital trips if referral processes, ambulance buy-in, and workforce planning are fixed.
plos-pone-0356837:
Jiyan Zhang and co-authors build a math method for picking the most useful features from data when no labels exist to guide the choice. Feature picking cuts noise and cost in machine learning, but common tools can flatten the hidden shape of a dataset. Their method uses a curvature-aware penalty to keep complex shapes intact, a compression step to drop repeated features, and a filter that resists stray outliers.

Across nine standard test datasets, the method chose feature sets that performed better than rival approaches, and the team proves their solving routine settles properly. Zhang and colleagues aim the tool at tasks such as image and gene analysis. Those datasets are wide, messy, and unlabeled. Keeping true structure matters more than raw size.
plos-pone-0357037:
Qi Zhang and colleagues used advanced eye imaging to document what near-sightedness does inside the eyes of rats, in a model where lenses placed before the eyes drive them to grow myopic. Their 2026 study scanned the animals after eight weeks with a technique that measures both tissue thickness and blood flow without contact, comparing them against normally sighted controls.

The myopic eyes were longer, as expected, but also showed thinner choroid and retinal layers and reduced blood flow in the inner retina, differences clear at most measurement points. Those three changes mirror what doctors fear in severe human myopia, where stretched, underfed tissue can tear or degenerate. The imaging markers give researchers a way to track candidate treatments in animals over time.
plos-pone-0357737:
Mina Hwang and Yeji Hwang published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on depression in people with cognitive impairment, asking whether who provides their daily care matters. Using a national sample of older adults, they analyzed just over five hundred people needing help with everyday activities. Care networks were sorted by who helped: spouses, children, extended family, friends and neighbors, paid carers, or public services.

Five network types emerged, the largest centered on children and the smallest on friends and neighbors. Compared with child-centered care, people whose networks centered on public services, and those with mixed networks, scored higher on depression, even after adjustments. Pairwise tests showed the same two types also exceeded spouse-centered and friend-centered networks. The overall shape of a care network, not just its size, relates to mental health, they conclude, so assessments should map the whole configuration.
plos-pone-0357837:
Vasileia Karasavva and Amori Yee Mikami published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a systematic review of research on short-form social media videos about autism and ADHD. Most young adults now get mental health information from social media, and neurodiversity content is hugely popular, yet professionals worry about unvetted claims spreading as fact. No one has synthesized studies of these videos' accuracy or effects on viewers.

The review will search three major databases for peer-reviewed work in English, with paired reviewers screening independently. Three questions organize it. What does this content look like, and how popular is it? How closely does it follow clinical guidelines? And what does watching it do to stigma, to seeking diagnosis or treatment, and to how people read their own symptoms??? Descriptive and thematic analyses will combine findings. The registered protocol aims to give clinicians and platforms an evidence base.
plos-pone-0358137:
Fizza Ghulam Nabi leads a team of six studying how weather drains the power of industrial gas turbines in Pakistan, in PLOS ONE in 2026. At the Nandipur plant, three large turbines ran at full load for a year while the team logged output against temperature, humidity, and dew point. Hot air is thinner, so turbines swallow less of it, and operators need forecasts that price the weather in rather than discovering shortfalls at peak demand.

Ambient temperature dominated: as it climbed, output and efficiency fell in a strong, tight relationship. Humidity and dew point mattered too, but more weakly. The team built prediction models three ways, classical regression and two machine learning methods, and validated them on operating data. Their best models give plant managers a practical tool for scheduling generation and maintenance around Pakistan's summers, and for estimating the fuel and emissions cost of each hot day.
plos-pone-0358337:
Rebecca T Brown leads a team of eight tracking when everyday abilities start to fail in middle aged Americans, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Struggling to bathe, dress, shop, or cook is rising in this age group, yet the long view is missing. The team followed more than fourteen thousand Health and Retirement Study participants, all entering between ages fifty and fifty-six without difficulties. They fall into four birth cohorts spanning 1935 to 1959.

Group based models sorted the paths that difficulty counts followed before age sixty-five. Regression then tied cohort membership to those paths. Even the starting gate told a story: the share already impaired at entry ran near fourteen percent in the earliest cohort. It sat near ten percent in the middle cohorts and twelve percent in the youngest. Whether later generations are aging worse is a policy question this machinery was built to answer.
plos-pone-0358537:
Md Mamunur Rashid leads a team of eight mapping where rice neck blast disease strikes hardest in Cumilla District, Bangladesh, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The fungal disease can shrivel the rice neck just before harvest, and Cumilla is among the country's most intensive rice regions. Using field records from 2017 to 2025, the team hunted season specific hotspots separately for the rainfed and irrigated growing seasons, with clustering statistics and interpolation methods.

One subdistrict, Nangalkot, burned as a hotspot in both seasons. Rainfed season severity there averaged roughly half the crop's potential damage range, while irrigated season peaks in several subdistricts ran higher still. Weather trends around the rice's reproductive stage tracked the intensification. Probability mapping pinpointed zones likely to exceed a fifth severity, giving extension services a target list. The prescription is local: resistant varieties and forecasts tuned to each hotspot, not a blanket national spray calendar.
plos-pone-0358737: Wu and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a plant compound and wound healing in rats. The compound, ligustroside, was tested on open wounds cut into the skin. The title reports that it softened the scar-like remodeling that fibrosis brings and quieted fibrosis signals. Wounds that heal with less scarring stay more flexible, so such compounds interest skin researchers.
plos-pone-0358837:
Anneke Olson and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It tackles a methods problem in research on child maltreatment: contamination bias. The question is what happens to effect estimates when studies try to replicate how maltreatment affects children's behavior problems.

Contamination occurs when comparison groups are not as unexposed as researchers assume, quietly shrinking measured effects. If replication studies inherit that bias, real harms of maltreatment can look smaller than they are. Child welfare researchers and the policymakers who read their work are the audience for a warning about hidden bias in replication.
plos-pone-0359337: Barrio and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on deaths from heart and vessel disease in a Brazilian capital. The city lies in the Central-West region. They mapped where deaths cluster, how they changed over time, and what area traits link to them. Area-level maps can show city leaders which districts need clinics, prevention, and cleaner living conditions most.
plos-pone-0359437:
Laura Vancer and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It standardizes wrist X-rays by designing a positioning tool around the people who will use it, and then evaluating that tool. Where a patient's wrist sits during imaging changes what the radiograph shows, so inconsistent positioning undermines diagnosis.

Human-centered design builds the tool around the technologists and patients who will actually use it. A positioning aid that staff find awkward will be abandoned, however sound its geometry. Radiology departments and orthopedic teams reading wrist films are the readers for a tool meant to make every image comparable.
pmc-10158837:
The Gene Ontology Consortium's 2023 update describes the state of the Gene Ontology knowledgebase, a shared reference for what genes and their products do. The resource organises gene functions into a structured vocabulary used by labs worldwide. It links those terms to the evidence behind each assignment.

Updates reported for 2023 cover new terms, improved annotations and better tools for searching the base. Almost every large gene study leans on this vocabulary to make sense of gene lists. A careful annual update keeps that common language accurate as biology moves.  Users can browse it freely through the consortium's website.
pmc-10910037:
Guo, Jin, Chen, and co-authors review NF-kB, a protein system known to science for nearly forty years. When found, it was seen mainly as a switch for inflammation, the body's response to harm. Long study since then has widened that picture a great deal.

The review gathers fresh insight into the many roles this system plays across biology. It then turns to drugs that aim to block or tune it, and to what that could mean for patients. Because the system touches inflammation, immunity, and cancer, a clear summary helps both basic researchers and drug developers.
pmc-13202437:
A natural cyclic peptide is re-engineered for cancer in a 2026 study authored by Yujun Bao, which modifies Sansalvamide A by flipping one amino acid into its mirror-image form. The research article uses a light-driven cyclization method to build five analogs with a rigid isoindolinone unit built into the ring.

Cell tests showed the analogs inhibited tumor cell growth to varying degrees, with the multiply modified compound performing best among them. Target prediction and docking pointed to BCL2, a protein that helps cancer cells avoid death, as the key partner. Further cell assays showed the lead compound lowered mitochondrial membrane potential, consistent with triggering apoptosis, and predicted drug properties looked workable.
pmc-13240637:
Iwamoto and colleagues at Kyoto University asked how nurses decide which task comes first on a busy ward. Novice nurses find constant reprioritization especially hard. The team interviewed ten general-ward nurses about the factors behind their choices. The goal was to learn what a support system would need to know.

Nine categories grouped into three themes: judging medical condition, weighing patient-centered care, and handling work organization. Signs of sudden physical change anchored the medical side. Patient preferences and ward policies resist tidy quantification, the analysis found. The authors suggest language models may handle such fuzzy factors better than fixed rules.
pmc-13242437:
D. U. Junghaenel and colleagues tested whether very short health questionnaires can track well-being month after month in the general population. Their study appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. More than twelve thousand United States adults in the Understanding America Study completed three-item adaptive tests each month for thirteen months. The tests covered anger, meaning in life, and positive affect, with questions adjusting to each person's earlier answers.

Even at three items, the tests measured precisely and kept a steady ranking of people over time. Adults with more chronic conditions averaged poorer scores and swung more from month to month. Sudden health events moved anger and positive affect in the same month, while meaning in life reacted less, and most changes faded within a month or two. The authors say brief monthly testing can capture both steady levels and short-lived dips in population health.
pmc-13248837:
Apaapa-Timu and colleagues reviewed how research review processes serve Māori health, in a 2026 article from New Zealand. Ethics and locality approvals are meant to ensure hospital research advances Māori health equity. The authors gathered one hundred six sources published between 1980 and 2021, searching in both English and te reo Māori, and appraised each source twice.

Their reading surfaced both friction and promise in current review practice. Drawing on the story of Tāne gathering the baskets of knowledge, they propose a framework called Ngā kete o te Rangahau, the three baskets of research. It is meant to guide reviewers toward research that genuinely responds to Māori needs.
pmc-13249137:
Scharf and a Swiss team tested training that helps doctors offer a real choice in colon cancer screening, in a 2026 trial. Swiss family doctors usually prescribe colonoscopy directly, though a stool test is a valid alternative many patients prefer. Doctors in the intervention group received decision aids, an evidence summary, stool test kits, and feedback on their own habits.

Eighty-three doctors reported on more than three thousand patients. Trained doctors were far more likely to have at least one patient choose or complete the stool test. Looking at change over time weakened the contrast, and the authors concede self-selection may inflate the effect. Still, mailing simple tools appeared to widen the choice patients actually get.
pmc-13249637:
Bertazzo-Silva and a Brazilian team counted mushrooms fruiting in Antarctica, in a 2026 Current Microbiology study. In February 2023 they surveyed twenty sites on Byers Peninsula, Livingston Island, during the brief polar summer. Macroscopic fungi are barely documented on the continent, even as warming reshapes its land ecosystems faster than almost anywhere else.

They recorded more than twenty-five hundred fruiting bodies from eight kinds of gilled fungi in three genera. Omphalina species supplied over two thirds of all fruiting bodies, while one Arrhenia type appeared at nearly two thirds of sites. Abundance differed significantly between sites, though plant cover did not sort the communities. The authors set the survey as a baseline for tracking climate change, casting fungi as sensitive indicators.
pmc-13249937:
Duan and co-authors linked high blood sugar to shoulder pain in older Chinese adults, in a 2026 study. They used a national aging survey. One part compared more than thirteen thousand people aged forty-five and over at a single point in time. Another part followed about eighty-four hundred pain-free people from 2011 to 2015.

Shoulder pain affected thirteen percent of all adults. Among those with high blood glucose, the share was eighteen percent. The high-sugar group also developed new pain more often over the four years. Nearly a thousand fresh cases appeared during follow-up. The authors argue that sugar control may help prevent late-life shoulder pain, not only the classic harms of diabetes.
pmc-13250337:
Agus Santoso Budi and Kartika Ayu Pranindita report early cleft surgery through an outreach program in this 2026 case report. Their patient was a three-month-old boy with a complete cleft lip and palate on the left side, plus a small, under-formed left outer ear.

The family lived in a remote village with no local specialists, so a travelling cleft team handled the case. The baby had trouble feeding but no other defects. Surgeons repaired the lip early using a rotation-advancement method, a standard flap technique. The authors stress that community referral networks get such babies to surgery on time in poor, far-flung areas.
pmc-13251037:
Fiammetta Marini and colleagues study how recent faces sway snap judgements in this 2026 psychology paper. Whether a stranger looks trustworthy shapes choices from hiring to court cases, and these first impressions were long treated as fixed.

In a rating task, volunteers judged faces after seeing earlier ones. Long exposure to a first face pushed ratings away from it, while brief exposure pulled ratings toward it. Seeing a similar face strengthened the pull, while a different face caused pushback. Distance between faces changed the pull's strength but not the pushback. The team says basic timing, spacing, and likeness shape trust impressions, not just memory or choice habits.
pmc-13251137:
Brence and co-authors automate the counting of newborn synapses in living fruit fly larvae. Their 2026 BMC Bioinformatics paper tackles a bottleneck: watching early synapse seeds form at the nerve-muscle junction took slow manual scoring of microscope images. The seeds are transient protein clusters that either stabilize into synapses or vanish within about an hour.

Their semi-automatic three-dimensional pipeline finds faint and crowded seed sites more sensitively than the older two-dimensional manual method. A proofreading step lets users correct the machine's calls while adding only a tenth more time. Overall the workflow cut analysis time by about seventy percent. The authors expect the tool to speed studies of how circuits wire themselves during development.
pmc-13251437:
Abun Abun, Kiki Haetami, and Rahmad Ramdhan feed chickens a waste-based additive in this 2026 trial. The additive is made by fermenting catfish processing scraps and sealing them in tiny capsules, pitched as a way to replace antibiotic growth boosters in poultry feed.

Six diets were compared, from plain feed to feed with an antibiotic, plus four additive levels up to two percent. Energy use and nutrient digestion improved with the additive, peaking around the 1.5 percent level, where one harmful gut germ also fell by about a sixth. Other germs were unchanged. The authors back 1.5 percent as the sweet spot for a value-added use of fish waste.
pmc-13252037:
Cui and Huang review how gut and brain talk to each other when bowel inflammation arrives with anxiety or depression. Their 2026 International Journal of General Medicine paper covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which often travel with emotional disorders. The gut-brain axis, a two-way network of nerves, immune signals, hormones, and microbes, frames the story.

Four pathways form a self-reinforcing inflammatory cycle, the authors argue, letting gut inflammation disturb mood and stress worsen the gut. Open fights include which direction causality runs, which pathway dominates, and why microbe studies replicate poorly. Single-target anti-inflammatory drugs have performed unevenly in this comorbidity. The authors urge long-term cohorts, omics tools, and multi-target treatments that join gut and psychiatric care.
pmc-13252737:
Ali Alshhre and Miquel Vall-llosera Camps read Saudi proverbs about women through an ecological lens in this 2026 article. Proverbs still carry weight in daily Saudi life even as reforms expand women's public roles, and the authors ask how sayings tie womanhood to the home's material world.

Working with 60 proverbs from national encyclopedia archives, they trace how bread and heat stand for motherly care. Cooking pots stand for duty, and pests stand for moral taint, while kohl and henna police reputation. Praise for devotion often hides unequal labour, they argue, and warnings about scarcity discipline women's movement and freedom. The sayings act as tiny archives of household rule.
pmc-13252837:
Wafaa Mahmoud and colleagues survey how medical students in Jordan study in this 2026 paper. Medical school packs huge amounts of material into little time, and which study habits truly track with top grades was not well pinned down locally.

An anonymous online survey drew 556 students at one science and technology university. Just over half reported excellent performance. Use of evidence-based strategies, such as self-testing and spaced review, rose step by step with performance level and stayed linked to excellent grades after adjustments. Popular passive habits, like rereading, showed no such link. The authors call the results exploratory, not proof of cause, and back teaching proven strategies.
pmc-13252937:
Yang and co-authors are the subject of this 2026 Expression of Concern in the International Journal of Molecular Medicine, concerning their paper on hydrogen sulfide protecting heart cells. The original study claimed a heat-shock protein, HSP90, helped hydrogen sulfide shield rat cardiac myocytes from chemical low-oxygen injury. Editors now warn readers about the paper's figures.

A second reader reported that two panels in the key figure overlap, with one rotated and flipped to look different, matching an earlier concern about two other panels. The editorial office says it has asked the authors for an explanation twice and received no reply so far. This second notice keeps the warning in place while the investigation continues. Readers should treat the paper's image data with caution.
pmc-13253837:
Janna de Boer and co-authors compare mind and machine errors in a 2026 article. In mental health care, hallucinations mean sensing things that are not there, and confabulations mean filling memory gaps with made-up stories. Large language models and speech tools make strikingly alike errors, producing smooth but false output.

The authors sort out which machine error matches which human one, and why each arises. They argue both kinds of system predict and fill gaps, which creates the shared failure mode. That mirror could help psychiatry understand the mind, and help AI builders cut error rates, though false AI output stays a real risk.
pmc-13254137:
Brandt and a broad panel set rules for safely stopping long-term benzodiazepine receptor agonists. Their 2026 paper gathers thirty-five doctors and patients through three rounds of secret voting. These calming drugs are widely tapered in older patients because they are hard to stop and carry safety risks.

Strong backing supported consent before tapering, flexible gradual plans, and cuts that shrink in step as doses fall. Panels also backed raising the dose again when withdrawal bites, plus peer support and talk therapy. Support was weaker on switching to a longer-acting drug first and on skipping other add-on drugs. The ten rules aim to help more patients stop safely while sparing them withdrawal harm.
pmc-13254337:
Akgün and co-authors test whether DNA damage switches on the cell recycling system in human stem cells. Their 2026 Scientific Reports study uses induced pluripotent stem cells and the neural progenitors grown from them. Autophagy, the recycling of worn proteins and organelles, helps stem cells choose between rest, renewal, and specialization.

Starvation switched the recycling machinery on normally, proving it works in these cells. Two DNA-damaging chemicals at low doses raised clear damage markers and nudged repair proteins. Yet neither chemical triggered real recycling flow in stem cells or progenitors within the test window. Protein surveys changed little in stem cells and moderately in progenitors. The authors conclude that canonical autophagy stays inactive after this kind of damage here.
pmc-13254437:
Rutter-Locher and colleagues argue that pain in inflammatory arthritis needs personal treatment, not just inflammation control. Their 2026 Therapeutic Advances in Musculoskeletal Disease review notes that pain often persists when joint inflammation is treated. Sensory, psychological, and social factors all shape what patients feel.

The review gathers evidence on pain mechanisms in early and established disease, including nerve sensitization in the limbs and in the central nervous system. It also sorts out the shifting words used for pain types and what they mean for assessment and communication. Drug and non-drug strategies are matched to mechanism where possible. Barriers such as weak pain assessment and stretched services get frank discussion from the authors.
pmc-13261337:
Angelina Daher and co-authors argue that stopping cancer spread means cutting both its engine and its fuel. Metastasis demands energy and shape-shifting at once, supplied by mitochondria and Rho GTPase switches working as one system. Their 2026 review maps the two-way traffic between them.

Mitochondria hand ATP and reactive oxygen to Rho signaling, powering invasion machinery. In return, cytoskeletal remodeling drags mitochondria where energy is needed most, reinforcing the loop. Hitting either side alone invites the other to compensate, they contend. Their prescription pairs gene silencing of Rho switches with mitochondria-blocking repurposed antibiotics, aiming to collapse the partnership outright.
pmc-13261637:
Yu Chen and colleagues present a 2026 textual analysis of Chinese local tobacco control laws against the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. China ratified the treaty in 2005, but with no national smoke-free law, cities and provinces wrote their own rules unevenly. The team compared legal texts with the treaty's Article 8 on smoke-free environments.

They compiled 38 dedicated subnational regulations enacted or amended between 2006 and 2024, totaling 100,635 substantive Chinese characters. Only 10 regulations (26.3%) met the Article 8 compliance criteria, while 28 (73.7%) did not. Compliant texts were longer, with a median 3,249 versus 2,572 characters, and had more clauses. They more often banned e-cigarettes and required quitting services. The 10 compliant jurisdictions cover about 121.6 million residents, 8.6% of mainland China's 2020 population. The authors stress these are features of legal text, not proof of real-world enforcement.
pmc-13262937:
August Myers and colleagues follow one vaccinated monkey's B cells as they learn to neutralize an HIV vaccine construct. The BG505 SOSIP trimer mimics the virus's envelope spike, and protection in earlier work tracked with antibodies against a glycan hole. Their 2026 study sequences over four thousand seven hundred targeted B cells over time.

Three expanded families produced the neutralizing antibodies, all aiming at the same glycan hole. Structures show each family grabbing the hole differently, one even shoving a sugar aside to reach the CD4 docking loop. Some relatives bound the spot without neutralizing. Repeated vaccination drove the expansion and sharpening behind the strong serum response.
pmc-13263137:
Videha Sharma and colleagues build an open data model for gene-based prescribing in a 2026 journal article. Pharmacogenetics uses genetic tests to make drug choices safer and more effective, but results often arrive as documents that computer systems cannot easily share. The team drafted a standard format from literature and existing specifications, then refined it in expert workshops.

Twenty-four experts from ten countries reviewed the model in two rounds. The final version keeps test results separate from advice on treatment and uses standard medical and gene vocabularies. It is published on an open clinical knowledge platform. Tests of conversion to the FHIR health data standard showed information could flow both ways, with automated mapping making reuse easier at scale.

pmc-13263637:

pmc-13263737:

pmc-13263937:

pmc-13264637:

pmc-13269437:

pmc-13269837:

pmc-13270237:

pmc-13270337:

pmc-13273437:

pmc-13274037:

pmc-13275537:

pmc-13278237:

pmc-13289337:

pmc-13289537:

pmc-13289737:

pmc-13289937:

pmc-13290437:

pmc-13290637:

pmc-13290837:
