pmc-13292337:
Xiuhong Lyu narrates a 2026 case where a careful physical exam set off a diagnostic cascade in a 60-year-old man with hypertension. He had no heart failure symptoms, yet bedside findings prompted targeted testing that exposed severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction. The workup also uncovered critical carotid disease, as the title signals.

Aggressive guideline-directed drug therapy began at this silent, stage B phase of heart failure. Within four months his ejection fraction climbed from the 30 to 35 percent range up to 44 percent on repeat measurement. He stayed out of hospital for heart failure through follow-up. Lyu argues the case defends the humble physical exam, especially where advanced testing is scarce, because one routine visit rewrote the patient's trajectory.
pmc-13292937:
Yujun Guo and a large team report, in 2026, a catalyst that pairs methanol use with hydrogen making at factory scale. Splitting water wastes energy at the oxygen step, so swapping in methanol oxidation can cut power needs if the catalyst holds up.

The catalyst places ruthenium oxide particles on a molybdenum-based support, giving uneven ruthenium-oxygen sites that steady active states. It ran at very high current for over 300 hours in a two-electrode cell, a span the authors report, with high selectivity for the desired reaction. A membrane device also ran stably at high current. The design may suit joint output of hydrogen and useful chemicals.
pmc-13293737:
Heghine Papoyan and colleagues rank, in a 2026 study, foodborne parasitic diseases in Armenia by asking experts, since routine tracking data there are thin. A clear ranking can steer limited surveillance and control funds to the biggest threats first.

Experts from human health, animal health, food safety, and biology scored diseases on spread, illness, death, testing difficulty, and environmental detection. Ascariasis and echinococcosis topped the list by a clear margin, with giardiasis third. A middle group held three diseases, while three others ranked low. Job background and region barely swayed rankings, showing strong national agreement.
pmc-13294437:
Awad M. Almuklass and colleagues test whether wrist nerve speed tracks grades in a 2026 exploratory study. Fifty-four male medical students at King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences, mean age 21.26 years, gave ulnar nerve readings at wrist and elbow, a reaction time task, and four academic scores from high school through university.

Main analysis found no link between nerve speed and university grade average. Side analyses, uncorrected for many comparisons, hinted that slower wrist signals tied to lower high school grades and that grade average dipped slightly with age. The authors stress the work is preliminary and hypothesis-forming only, not evidence that nerve tests predict study success.
pmc-13294837:
Ruorui Yang and colleagues build a risk tool for anxiety and low mood after stroke in a 2026 study. They studied patients with acute ischaemic stroke treated at a hospital in Anhui between May 2023 and April 2025. Knowing who is most at risk could help staff act sooner.

Among 354 patients, 180 showed anxiety and depression symptoms while 174 did not. Age, several blood markers, one blood fat measure, and plaque stability separated the groups and entered a scoring chart model. The model sorted patients well in internal checks, suggesting it could flag high-risk patients for earlier support and closer follow-up.
pmc-13295837:
Samira D Rowland and colleagues explore oxygen teaching needs in scarred lung disease in a 2026 study. Long-term oxygen helps breathless patients with interstitial lung disease, yet teaching about its use is often thin. Most existing tools were built for a different lung condition, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Focus groups and interviews in Alberta, Canada, gathered patients with each disease plus experienced clinicians. Twenty professionals joined, alongside 13 patients with scarred lungs, one caregiver, and ten patients with the obstructive disease. Both patient groups wanted person-centred teaching, steady support, and confidence built through knowledge. Scarred lung patients additionally needed closer flow checks and higher flow emphasis.
pmc-13296037:
Francisco J. Corpas, Rosa M. Rivero and José M. Palma introduce, in 2026, a second special issue on reactive oxygen and nitrogen species in plants. These small molecules signal through germination, root growth, flowering and fruit ripening, and also help plants answer stress and attack.

Three research papers and two reviews extend that picture across plant organs and conditions. One study maps antioxidant genes in pepper fruit and how nitric oxide gas shifts their activity during ripening. Another tests salt priming in seeds. The editors present the set as fresh evidence on how plants use reactive chemistry to develop and defend themselves.
pmc-13296337:
Anja Heselich and co-authors propose, in 2026, judging jawbone preservation after tooth removal by where the implant finally sits. Scans before surgery only guess at bone quality, so the team grade the placed implant's position in three dimensions using data from a multi-centre trial.

Implants drifted most from the ideal spot when no preservation was done. Combining a bone substitute with platelet-rich fibrin most often allowed central placement in the old root's position. The authors argue final position is a practical, honest readout of whether preservation worked, capturing hidden bone problems that scans miss.
pmc-13297137:
Salah-Ud-Din Khan and co-authors review, in 2026, the three-way conversation between gut, brain and immune system in brain and metabolic diseases. Faulty gut microbes, leaky barriers and microbe-made chemicals feed harmful immune activity shared by Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, obesity and diabetes.

Layered tools, from gene reading to chemical profiling, plus computer analysis, now map the shared pathways. Those pathways include inflammasome firing and faltering cell powerhouses. Diets, live-culture foods and microbe-made chemical treatments look promising, the authors say, but still need large clinical proof before tailored clinical use in brain and metabolic care for patients worldwide.
pmc-13303037:
A sugar-burning enzyme in immune cells helps drive newborn brain injury, Yue Li and colleagues identify in a 2026 study of hypoxic-ischemic brain damage. Gene-network mining of public datasets singled out hexokinase 2 among glycolysis genes, and a mouse model confirmed the enzyme surging within a day of injury, mostly inside microglia. Blocking it early with the inhibitor 3-bromopyruvate tested causality.

Treated mice showed smaller infarcts, better neurological scores, less lactate buildup, and quieter inflammatory signals. A single early dose still protected brain tissue and behavior thirty days later. The authors nominate the hexokinase-glycolysis axis as an early-intervention target where cooling therapy often falls short.
pmc-13303137:
Squeezing a limb in cycles before heart catheterization shields the kidneys from contrast dye, Yanmin Wu and colleagues show in a 2026 randomized trial. Four hundred eighty-four coronary patients were assigned to remote ischemic preconditioning, brief cuff ischemia repeated over two days and again before the procedure, or to usual care. Kidney injury within the following week was the primary endpoint.

Injury struck 6.2 percent of the preconditioned group against 12.0 percent of controls, and the maneuver stood as an independent protective factor in adjusted analysis. Heart events over ninety days did not differ. The authors offer the cheap, drug-free routine as practical protection for patients facing contrast procedures.
pmc-13304437:
Andreea Georgiana Stoica and colleagues follow a rare lymphoma form in a 2026 single-center study. Small lymphocytic lymphoma grows in lymph nodes rather than blood, and its patients are often left out of trials for the related blood cancer.

Forty-six patients with node-only disease were watched for about five years on median. Stage, blood counts, and several lab and gene markers were tested against time until first treatment and time until worsening. Advanced stage, low hemoglobin, raised lab markers, a missing chromosome piece, and abnormal p53 staining all tied to sooner treatment and faster worsening. Simple checks may sort risk well.
pmc-13304837:
Liping Chen and colleagues speed up development of twin-screw wet granulation for a herbal capsule product in a 2026 methods study. Continuous granulation is flexible and fast, but material, machine, and settings interact in tangled ways.

A stand-in formula saved trial costs, and printed screw parts let the team vary kneading disc angle and thickness freely. Two rounds of planned experiments singled out those screw traits plus the liquid-to-solid ratio as the levers that matter. The best setup ran with low turning force, and granules flowed well with sizes matching factory batches.
pmc-13304937:
Federica Prinelli and Antonio Giampiero Russo follow an Italian cohort for 24 years to link protein source with death risk in a 2026 study. Whether animal or plant protein matters more for long life may depend on who is eating.

A total of 1,350 adults aged 40 to 74 enrolled in the early 1990s, and 405 deaths were recorded by 2015. A higher share of animal protein tied to higher death risk overall and in men. The link clustered among people who had ever smoked and among those of normal weight. Plant protein showed no overall link, though normal-weight women fared better with more of it.
pmc-13305937:
Jing Bi profiled nose and throat germs in kids with Mycoplasma lung infection in a 2026 study. Samples from 102 sick kids were set next to 104 kids with flu A and 103 healthy kids.

Gene tests showed less germ mix and more of some germ types in the sick group, such as Mycoplasma and Pseudomonas. The germ mix also split by illness form, with Mycoplasma more rich in one form than the other. A germ based test split sick kids from both other groups with high scores, near 0.978 in the reported curve check. Such a test may one day help doctors name this illness fast.
pmc-13306937:
Umar Iqbal surveyed self-driving systems through their sensors in a 2026 review. Cameras, LiDAR, radar and satellite plus motion units each fail in distinct ways, and drift in timing or alignment can make later decisions overconfident.

A sensor-centred frame links what each device truly measures to how doubt spreads through fusion, safety checks and risk-aware control. Uncertainty styles covered include probability, evidence and conformal methods, while fusion designs range from filters to transformer models. Aviation integrity ideas are reshaped for road use to force graceful failure. The frame ties each doubt source to a clear safety claim that teams can test.
pmc-13307037:
Xuan Wang catalogued sugar transporter genes in the endangered timber tree Phoebe bournei in a 2026 study. SWEET carriers move sugars for loading into veins and stress replies, yet this species had no family map before.

Twenty-one genes split into four subfamilies, with one branch expanding through tandem and segmental copying in reported analysis. All duplicate pairs showed ratios under one, signalling strong purifying selection on the family. Under hormone ABA stress, one gene spiked at once while another answered late, and sugar outweighed proline as a protective solute. Such gene maps may guide care of this rare tree in a warming world.
pmc-13307237:
Ngawang Norbu analysed niches and species links in white birch forests of Tibet's Niyang River Basin in a 2026 ecology study. Forty-eight plots recorded 71 woody species, mainly from rose, heather and honeysuckle families in the survey counts.

White birch plus three partners held the broadest niches, showing strong resource use and wide spatial fit in index results. Several niche and association measures, plus a stability method, tested how dominant trees share space and resources. Findings describe which species build the forest and how stable the whole community stands. The maps may guide tree care and grazing rules on the high plateau in years to come.
pmc-13308537:
Kirstin Gaffney, Megan E Bartlett, and Theresa Rueger test in 2026 whether anemonefish help their hosts to pay for a place to stay, apart from any kin benefit. In these fish, helpers are often unrelated to the breeders they aid, which makes them a clean test of the pay to stay idea.

The team blocked helping in three species, then watched for punishment from breeders or for extra effort from helpers to make amends. Both patterns showed up in all three species, with mix shifts tied to local and social limits on each reef. Help can thus grow from rent like pressure alone, and body size trades off with effort in that bargain.
pmc-13309137:
Sophie M Weiss and co-authors lay out in 2026 what lecanemab, an antibody drug for early Alzheimer disease, means for care in Canada, where it won approval in January 2026. The drug binds loose amyloid in the brain and helps clear it, which slows the disease at its root in the amyloid view.

Gains are modest, a slower slide in thinking that may not feel real to all who take the drug in clinic. Use is heavy work: proof of amyloid by spinal fluid or scan, shots each two weeks, and repeat brain scans for safety. Brain swelling or bleed marks are the main risk, though most stay silent. Two review bodies urged no public pay for it.
pmc-13309537:
Xing Tao and co-authors report a 2026 cell study on how HIV triggers a fiery form of cell death in macrophages, a type of immune cell. A chemical tag on RNA, called m6A, and a protein that reads it, TRA2A, were the focus. The protein was scarce in macrophages from people living with HIV.

Lowering TRA2A in lab cells boosted virus copying and switched on a death pathway that spills inflammatory signals. The protein normally grips tagged RNA for a partner protein and shortens its life, which keeps that pathway quiet. Raising TRA2A or blocking the partner reversed the effect. The authors name TRA2A as a brake that balances virus control against harmful swelling.
pmc-13309837:
Taslim UDDIN and co-authors describe daily-life limits after spinal cord injury in Bangladesh in a 2026 survey. Such injury reshapes movement, self-care, work, and social life, and surroundings can ease or worsen each limit. A shared world framework, the ICF, sorts those limits and their drivers.

Face-to-face interviews reached 789 people living in the community, as the Bangladesh arm of a world survey run in 2023 and 2024. Most respondents were men, over half were aged 18 to 40, and about a third lived with tetraplegia. People with higher injuries reported greater limits in every domain. Male sex, younger age, low schooling, rural home, and severe injury each tied to poorer outcomes.
pmc-13310237: A 2026 correction adds a section to the retraction notice for a study in Ibrain comparing two triple-therapy regimens for neuropathic pain. After the retraction appeared, co-author Vennila Jaganathan told the journal they had not known of the problems behind the decision. Their part was limited to data analysis. The retraction call, they said, was made solely by corresponding author Nithya Raju without proper notice to co-authors. The journal notes messages went to all listed contacts. The item adds no new data; it records that disagreement.
pmc-13310637:
Eugen Mengel and co-authors report a trial substudy of a drug for a rare lipid storage disease in infants in a 2026 article. Niemann-Pick disease type C harms the brain and organs from early life, and arimoclomol is approved in the United States from age two, paired with miglustat. Safety and handling in babies under two were untested.

Five infants aged 14 to 23 months at screening received arimoclomol beside standard care for up to 36 months, all also taking miglustat. Safety led the outcome list, with development scores, biomarkers, and drug levels behind. Most of the 108 reported side events were mild or moderate, though 15 serious events fell in two patients. Exposure ranged widely, from 72 to 1109 days across the small group.
pmc-13310737:
Jiaxi Yao presents a 2026 case of a rare kidney cancer type in a man aged 39 years from China. The cancer links to a fused gene that switches on growth signals. Fewer than many cases are known, so each well checked case adds useful detail for doctors and lab staff.

Surgeons removed part of the left kidney for a small tumor found on exam. Lab stains supported a kidney origin and ruled out close mimics. Gene testing found a fusion joining KIF5B with the ALK gene, which names this subtype. Care is hard due to few cases and few drug choices, though drugs aimed at ALK may help some patients.
pmc-13310837:
Amedeo Chiefa and co-authors build a math frame for how neural networks learn proton structure in a 2026 theory paper. Maps of quarks and gluons inside protons guide collider tests, and modern fits train neural networks on data to draw those maps. Knowing how training moves and how doubt spreads is vital as tests grow sharper.

Work uses the neural tangent kernel to write training steps in closed form under clear premises. The frame shows how network shape and data steer the fit, and how doubt flows from data to the final map. Tools can compare fit methods on equal ground. Results guide checks, not replace full fits.
pmc-13311137:
Modibo Diallo and colleagues prove a common gene variant harms pigment making in albinism in a 2026 study. Albinism stems from faults in melanin building genes, and most known faults are rare and sit in coding parts. A patient carried one rare coding fault plus a common intron variant in the OCA2 gene, whose role was doubted.

Blood RNA tests showed the intron variant made the gene skip two blocks, dropping 78 building units from the protein. Modeling showed the loss breaks a key fold and strips sugar tags, which likely traps the protein. The variant was classed as likely harmful. Common intron variants deserve functional tests.
pmc-13311637:
Jackie Zhanbiao Li and co-authors trace how hospital-centered management took root in China's health system in a 2026 history study. The pattern has aided control and growth but starved primary care of resources.

The authors follow seven phases from 1835 to today, from missionary hospitals through socialist planning to market reform and digital management. Four self-reinforcing forces kept hospitals on top: steering from above, growing roles, standard management, and market shifts. Sources span past studies, policy papers, and institutional records. The long view is offered as a guide for health reform debates beyond China.
pmc-13311937:
Elvan Wiyarta and co-authors present a 2025 network meta-analysis comparing first thrombectomy methods for major front-brain artery strokes. Aspiration, stent retrievers, their pairing, and balloon guide catheters are the contenders.

Nine databases yielded 44 studies with 19,268 patients. The paired method with a balloon guide ranked best for reopening the artery and for first-pass success, with odds ratios of 2.87 and 7.33 against rivals in this analysis. Outcomes also covered walking independence at 90 days, bleeding in the skull, and death. Rankings give stroke teams a map for choosing a first approach when seconds count.
pmc-13312337:
Yu Zhou and co-authors publish a 2026 protocol for a randomized, double-blind trial on the best dose of liposomal bupivacaine for nerve block pain control in shoulder arthroscopy. Shoulder surgery often causes severe pain that slows recovery. A superior trunk block numbs the area with less risk of diaphragm weakness than the classic block, but the right concentration of the long-acting drug is unknown.

The trial will enroll 282 adults having arthroscopic rotator cuff repair and assign them to 66, 44, or 33 milligrams of the drug, each diluted to 10 milliliters. Main outcomes are pain at rest 48 hours after surgery and total oral morphine use across the first 48 hours. The team will also track shoulder movement and recovery quality, aiming to pin down a dose that eases pain without holding back mobility.
pmc-13312537:
Michael S. Kim and co-authors track, in a 2026 study, how technology-assisted knee replacement spread across the United States from 2020 to 2024 and whether it outperformed manual surgery. Computer navigation and robotic help promise better implant alignment and soft tissue balance, but proof of clinical benefit has stayed mixed.

Drawing on the TriNetX network, the team identified 198,263 primary knee replacements and matched assisted and manual groups one to one on sex, body size, and health conditions. Assisted surgery's share climbed from 11.9 percent in 2020 to 27.0 percent in 2024. After matching, assisted cases carried lower risks of fracture around the implant, deep infection, revision surgery, and aseptic loosening across three years of follow-up, in every region studied. The authors back wider adoption while calling for long-term and cost studies.
pmc-13312837:
Nadeem Akhtar and fellow members of a United States Pharmacopeia expert committee report a 2026 safety review of turmeric and curcuminoid supplements after scattered reports of liver injury. The committee routinely watches the literature for ingredients in USP monographs and launched a full evaluation to decide whether turmeric products need a caution on their labels.

Animal studies showed liver harm only at high doses of powder or extract, and the many human trials of these supplements reported no organ toxicity or serious events. Published injury cases usually appeared after one to four months of use, often alongside other medicines, and they generally cleared once the supplement stopped. Rare liver failure has occurred, though. The committee recommends a cautionary label advising people with liver history to consult a practitioner and to stop and seek care if symptoms such as jaundice appear.
pmc-13314437:
Wenbo Bian, Qiaoran Liu, and Zhenyu Yao open a journal topic on the interplay of sugar and fat balance in an editorial published in 2026. Metabolic flexibility, the skill of switching between sugar and fat fuels as food and hormones change, sits at the core of metabolic health.

When that switching fails, extra fuel is shunted toward insulin resistance, fat stored in the wrong organs, faulty mitochondria, and lasting inflammation, the editors write. The frame helps explain obesity, diabetes, fatty liver disease, and kindred disorders. They note that big databases and multi-omics data now let risk be read as a whole pattern rather than lone markers, with combined indexes such as the triglyceride-glucose index in wide use. The topic gathers studies that use that joined view to judge and treat metabolic risk.
pmc-13314537:
Kirsty Hodgson and colleagues give an update on sugar coatings in prostate cancer in their 2026 review. Prostate cancer is common in men. Early detection and new drugs for advanced disease are urgent needs. Yet the sugar side of the disease has lagged behind gene and protein work.

Glycans, the sugar chains on proteins, feed into the classic marks of cancer and serve as signs for tests and as drug targets. In prostate cancer they shift in set ways. They grow more branched complex chains, changed sialic acid caps, and more fucose. Sugar on the PSA test protein also alters, and short truncated chains appear, as listed in the review. The authors trace how these sugars drive growth, spread, and escape from immune attack, and why they may sharpen both diagnosis and therapy.
pmc-13314737:
Jun Wang and colleagues use genetic tools to test whether kidney function and hearing loss cause each other, in work published in 2026. Hearing loss affects a share of 6.1 percent of the world population by the figure cited in the report, and kidney disease has long been suspected as a partner.

Their Mendelian randomization design uses gene variants as natural levers, testing both directions. One marker stood out: the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, a sign of kidney filter leak, acted as a risk factor that raised hearing loss odds when high. Three other kidney marks, two filtration estimates and urate, showed no causal tie to hearing loss, as the authors report. The result singles out early filter damage, rather than filtration rate, as the thread to watch in hearing care.
pmc-13315437:
Nena Hilmia and colleagues assembled the full mitochondrial genomes of two native Indonesian chickens in a 2026 study. Pelung, kept for ornamental traits, and Sentul, a dual-purpose bird, are named national genetic resources, but their mitochondrial makeup had not been fully described.

Using next-generation sequencing, the team found both genomes were 16,784 bases long with the usual set of 13 protein-coding genes, 22 transfer RNAs, two ribosomal RNAs, and a control region. They compared the pair with 35 other genomes drawn from Asia's domestic chickens and jungle fowls, and found five single-letter differences of interest. The data support conservation of local breeds.
pmc-13315537:
Amy Avakian and Muhammad Umair describe in 2026 how a dark-blood heart scan found a subtle scar missed by the standard scan. Their patient was a 67-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse and a 3-millimeter gap at the valve ring. She was sent for magnetic resonance imaging after a heart monitor showed frequent early beats and other rhythm faults.

Standard late-enhancement imaging was read as clear, with normal heart function. A matched blood-nulled sequence at the same slice positions showed a focal stripe of scar in the lower side wall, the classic site in this condition. Such scars can host dangerous rhythms, so sharper imaging may improve risk sorting.
pmc-13317537:
Huizi He and colleagues map, in a 2026 study, human papillomavirus infection across ethnic groups in China's Yili region, using records from 13,915 women screened between 2021 and 2023. Local patterns guide where cervical cancer prevention should aim first.

Overall, 22.0 percent of women carried the virus, and high-risk types made up 87.2 percent of infections in the tallied cases. Rates peaked under age 25, dipped in the late forties, and rose again near sixty. Kazakh women showed the highest raw rate, though the gap vanished after age adjustment. Among biopsied women, infection climbed with lesion severity, and type 16 dominated the worst grades. Hospital sampling limits reach, the authors note.
pmc-13318237: Rebecca Marie Ellul and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study of virulence factors in the fish bacterium Phocoenobacter atlanticus. The notice is a correction only: it fixes the data availability statement and a methods sentence, giving the correct genome accession JBTTGU000000000 in place of a project number. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13318937:
Sandra Igreja, Constança Paúl, and Soraia Teles present a 2026 mixed-methods study of craft skills passed down in families. The setting is a Portuguese UNESCO Creative City for crafts and folk art. Seventy professional artisans who inherited their practice took part. They walked researchers through their workshops and answered family questionnaires.

Participants ranged from 22 to 88 years old, with a median age of 63. Most were men, and all worked in one of eight craft sectors. Family functioning scores ran high, from 7 to 10 points on the scale used. Older artisans reported slightly better family functioning. Interviews traced eleven themes about how inheritance shapes family ties. Passing on a legacy strengthened solidarity and cohesion, artisans said, though tensions also surfaced.
pmc-13319637:
Annik Steimer and co-authors track how fast swollen joints settle under strong arthritis drugs in a 2026 Swiss registry study. Joint pain from this illness does not hit all joints in the same way, and whether some joints heal slower than others was unknown. Records followed people for two years after they started a new drug.

A first drug group held 598 people with at least one swollen joint, while a wider group held 1942 people across five drug types. Next to the wrist, nearly all joints settled faster, apart from two finger base joints and at times the knee. That slow set held across all drug types. Wrist and those finger joints may need a longer wait before care is judged.
pmc-13319937:
Yujie Liu and co-authors review brain chemicals and balance disorders in a 2026 article on the inner ear system. The balance system in the ear and brain stem keeps us upright and oriented, and its signals are tuned by chemical messengers. How one family of messengers, the monoamines, shapes recovery after balance loss on one side was the focus.

Four messengers are weighed in turn, covering their sites, roles, and drug links in balance care. Each one tracks with balance faults in past work, and drugs that tune them are already used for such ills. Early after injury, shifts in these messengers help the brain rebalance the two sides. Mapping their receptors more fully could point to sharper drugs with fewer side effects.
pmc-13320337:
Lorenzo Titone and co-authors track brain waves as adults learn a made up language in a 2026 study of rhythm and pattern. Speech carries sound rhythms that hint at word edges and count based patterns that do the same job in a hidden way. Past work could not pull the two apart cleanly, so a new stimulus build split them on purpose for this test.

Brain fields from 32 adults were logged while they heard steady syllable streams with both cues set at cross purposes. Distinct brain sources tracked sound, stress beat, and count patterns side by side. Later replies to three syllable chunks showed both pattern types were kept and used to learn new words. Behavior backed the joint need for both cues.
pmc-13320437:
Massimo Filippi and co-authors argue for a wider role for amyloid brain scans in governing new Alzheimer drug care in a 2026 viewpoint. Two lab made antibodies can now clear the sticky brain protein tied to the disease at group level. That shifts clinic work from naming the disease to steering long, costly, risky care for each person. Scans that count the protein could set a start line for that steering.

Repeat scans might guide calls to keep, switch, or stop a drug as care unfolds. Yet a falling scan count does not prove that one person feels or thinks better, and safety, burden, and clinic capacity all press on the plan. Lessons from a high volume European memory clinic ground the call for set care paths.
pmc-13320537:
Myeong Seong Bak and co-authors test gentle ear based nerve stimulation in a 2026 study of healthy adults. The method, called taVNS, sends mild pulses through the skin of the ear to the vagus nerve. The team asked whether it sharpens mental control and what brain wave changes go with any gain.

Twenty-three adults aged 19 to 40 did a Stroop word colour task across three sessions, with real or sham stimulation in between. The real group answered hard mismatched trials more accurately in the last session. Brain waves also differed, as a rise in high beta power seen in the sham group was softened by real stimulation, which hints at lower mental strain.
pmc-13321037:
Sharyu Ikhar, Yogesh Nagargoje, and Ruchita Shrivastava comment in a 2026 letter on a review of machine learning for grading mitral valve leakage. The review, by Eini and others, reported a pooled accuracy curve score of 0.97. The writers argue that the yardstick used to grade leakage in each study shapes that headline figure.

Some studies used measured Doppler methods under society criteria, while others used expert labels or text mined from reports, which carry observer noise. Models trained on soft labels inherit that noise, so pooling them with strict studies inflates apparent precision. The letter also questions frame level models, which sort single images rather than full clinical cases.
pmc-13321637:
Gaurav Sharma and a large team test biochar on wheat land in the Indo-Gangetic Plains in a 2026 field study. Burning crop waste each year fouls air and drains soil carbon and nitrogen. Turning waste into biochar may lock carbon away and enrich soil instead. A two year trial at a Punjab farm compared rice husk and rice straw biochar at several rates.

Biochar at 5 tons per hectare gave the strongest gains. Against non-biochar plots, plant height rose by 12.8 percent and grain yield by 32.8 percent at that rate in the trial, with more tillers, longer spikes, and heavier grains. The authors present that dose as a practical, lasting option for wheat growers.
pmc-13322137:
C. Dwan and colleagues study how pasture type and cow breed shape rumen germs tied to methane in a 2026 trial. Dairy cows grazed three sward systems: plain ryegrass with high nitrogen, ryegrass with white clover at half nitrogen, and a mixed species sward. Holstein-Friesian cows and Jersey crossbreds were compared, with rumen fluid sampled in August and October.

Sward type did not shift overall germ diversity, though several bacterial groups grew more common on clover and mixed swards. Total methane making archaea did not differ by sward, but their mix did, with Methanosphaera up and Methanobrevibacter down on diverse swards. Breed effects were minor. Diverse pasture alone looks unlikely to cut methane sharply.
pmc-13322837:
Elizabeth Beaulieu and co-authors review computer models of the lower spine in a 2026 article on biomechanical modelling. Such models estimate stress and load inside the spine for conditions from wear and deformity to weak bone and tumours, where direct measurement in living people is not possible.

Finite element models gave useful insight but took much labour, used simple loads and generic anatomy. Newer work uses automated image segmentation for patient-specific shapes, plus neural networks that respect physics and linked body models for more real loads. Uses include planning deformity surgery, judging fracture risk and improving implants. The authors stress weak outcome validation, uneven reporting and uncertain fit across varied patients.
pmc-13322937:
Rosa Di Micco leads a multicentre comparison of imaging after drug treatment for breast cancer, published in 2026, asking which scan best predicts full tumour clearance. The analysis held 143 patients, with 54 node-positive patients from San Raffaele Hospital in a prospective trial and 89 cases from Heidelberg Hospital records.

Ultrasound was judged against FDG PET/MRI, with complete response defined by no visible tumour on ultrasound and by absent tracer uptake plus no contrast enhancement on the combined scan. Accuracy was checked for PET alone, MRI alone, the pair read together and the pair read as agreeing. Subgroup work linked scan response with tumour features, aiming to guide surgery planning after systemic therapy.
pmc-13323737:
Liping Sun, Juan Lang and Zhongkui Xiong test paederoside as a shield for nerve cells in a Parkinson's model, in a 2026 cell study. Rotenone, which blocks mitochondrial complex I, damaged mouse Neuro-2A cells in a dose and time pattern used to mimic disease stress.

Pre-treatment with paederoside lifted complex I activity in damaged cells by over forty percent at one dose in their assay, and eased mitochondrial swelling across three doses. The highest dose also curbed caspase-3 activation, a step toward cell death. A co-culture with BV-2 cells let the team watch dopamine-marker cells under the same insult. The authors present paederoside as a candidate for protecting mitochondria in Parkinson's research.
pmc-13324437:
Xiao Wei and colleagues report a 2026 study of bone graft change after sinus lift surgery for dental implants. The team looked back at 80 patients who had a lateral window sinus lift with Bio-Oss graft particles and an implant placed at the same time.

Cone-beam CT scans taken before surgery, right after, and six months later measured graft shrinkage and sinus shape. Width loss and height loss were both recorded, and wider sinuses lost more graft material. A thicker sinus membrane was also linked to greater height loss. The findings can help dentists pick implant sites and judge how much graft material a wide sinus is likely to need.
pmc-13327537:
Brendan J Gibbs and co-authors follow red drum fish from lab tanks to a wild estuary in a 2026 study. They measured swimming costs in flowing water shaped by shapes mimicking mangrove roots and oyster mounds. Fish riding turbulent wakes used less oxygen and changed their tail beats, above all at high flow speeds.

Outdoor pool tests with motion sensors revealed eight distinct movement states, richer than lab views suggest. Tracking then followed wild fish along a 54 km estuary stretch for three years through 36 listening stations. Wild fish mostly chose slow water under 30 cm per second near complex habitat. Shelter, food, and staying put seem to matter more to the fish than saving energy in fast water.
pmc-13333437:
Juan Chen and colleagues tested whether advanced diffusion MRI can reveal a prostate cancer's TP53 mutation status without a biopsy of the gene, in a 2026 retrospective study. Tumors carrying the mutation resist hormone therapy and fare worse, so knowing the status before surgery could shape planning.

The study covered 84 men who had their prostates removed, comparing ordinary and advanced diffusion measures between mutated and normal-gene tumors. The mutated group showed lower water movement values across several measures and higher mean kurtosis, a sign of tissue complexity. In adjusted analysis only mean kurtosis stayed an independent predictor, with an odds ratio of 19.329. A model using kurtosis alone reached an AUC of 0.860, close to the best combined model at 0.889, and held up under internal re-checks at 0.858. The authors propose the kurtosis value as a practical noninvasive stand-in for mutation testing.
pmc-13336837:
Tarek Eid, Maryam Ebrahimiazar, Mohammad Zargartalebi, and David Sinton automate the mapping of how liquids mix in a 2026 methods study. Whether two liquids blend or split governs drug and product formulas, yet checking it by eye is slow and narrow. Their flow-through device senses phase borders by capacitance and reads cloudiness from several angles at once.

The platform sorted diverse liquid pairs, followed separation in real time, and caught partial mixing across recipes and temperatures. With active learning, it mapped three-part phase diagrams in about 2 h on its own, and extracted tie lines in about 5 min each in the reported runs. Self-running mapping could feed the data-hungry work of formula design.
pmc-13337437:
Yang Zhang and colleagues pool pacemaker rates after a demanding double-valve operation in a 2026 meta-analysis built on a systematic review. The Commando procedure rebuilds the tissue between the aortic and mitral valves, and its known hazard is heart block needing a permanent pacemaker. Estimates varied widely, so the team searched four databases through April 2, 2026.

Twelve studies covering 797 patients gave a pooled pacemaker rate of 22.3% after these operations in the random-effects model. One in five patients, roughly, needs a device. The Chimney modification looked safer at 6.3% against 28.3% for the traditional operation in subgroup results, though small-study effects urge caution. The numbers help surgeons counsel patients and weigh technique choices.
pmc-13337737:
Isaac S. Wheeler and co-authors build computer models of microwave-assisted freeze-drying in a 2026 study. Microwaves can speed drying of medicines in vials, yet weak models risk uneven heating and product damage. Good models are needed to make the process both fast and safe.

A two-dimensional level set model improves on simpler lumped models by using measured pore structure and allowing for poorly placed temperature probes. Results helped simplify the simpler model and set two values from electromagnetic simulation. Tests in microwave drying showed heating of the vial wall and heat flow into the frozen product cannot be ignored. Code is shared openly in Julia.
pmc-13339137:
Xin Yu and colleagues build a hydrogen-making enzyme with selenium swapped for sulfur in a 2026 study. The algal enzyme CrHydA1 uses an iron cluster to handle hydrogen. A selenium version tests how atom identity shapes that machinery.

A selenium-bearing iron complex matured the inactive enzyme into an active form. Spectroscopy showed the new complex takes a rare hydride form, unlike its sulfur twin. Formaldehyde, not serine, supplied a needed bridge piece as reported. Pure isotope versions confirmed the selenium enzyme keeps a similar shape and redox behavior to the natural one, with distinct fine details.
pmc-13341537:
Brain-computer interface training for stroke arm recovery is piloted by Wenjie Jin and collaborators in a 2026 randomized trial. Forty patients with first subcortical stroke in the subacute phase were split evenly between closed-loop interface training and an active control after two days of familiarization.

Both groups got standard care and matched motor imagery practice for 4 weeks; the interface group alone had glove feedback driven by their EEG signals. Arm function was scored with standard clinical scales, and brain rhythm measures were explored alongside. Small pilot trials like this test feasibility and safety before larger studies judge true benefit.
pmc-13341737:
Training quality for UK doctors varies more by site than by region, in a 2026 analysis by Arkadeep Dhali and colleagues of the 2025 General Medical Council National Training Survey. The dataset held 26,190 scored observations spanning 31 medical specialties, 16 deaneries, and 18 indicators.

Mean deanery gaps ran from +3.23 in the North East to −3.13 in the East of England; the North East beat the national average on 17 of 18 indicators, led by regional teaching at +7.34. Study leave in the East of England lagged by −10.17. Such decomposition tells regulators where problems live: whole regions versus single hospitals.
pmc-13341937:
A through-skin hearing implant proves cost-effective in Spain, in a 2026 economic analysis by Serafín Sánchez-Gómez and colleagues. A lifetime Markov model compared the transcutaneous Osia System against the through-skin Baha Connect for adults eligible for bone-conduction implants, from the Spanish health system's viewpoint.

Osia cost €24,555 per patient and yielded 15.94 quality-adjusted life years, versus €20,968 and 15.17 for the comparator, giving an incremental ratio of €4,651 per QALY. At a €30,000 threshold, probability of cost-effectiveness reached 62%. Utility values drove the model's sensitivity most, a caveat the authors disclose alongside the favorable headline.
pmc-13342037:
Climate change as a direct health threat is surveyed by Anna Apetrei-Pandrea and Stefan Dascalu in a 2026 narrative review. Global temperatures have risen about 1 °C since 1880, with warming since 2015 running above 0.35 °C per decade, roughly double the earlier pace.

Consequences span extreme weather, permafrost melt, and biodiversity loss, but the review centers on bodies: heat strain, oxidative stress, and weakened immunity raise infection susceptibility. Vector-borne diseases expand their ranges, while respiratory, cardiovascular, infectious, and psychiatric burdens all grow. Given modeling limits, the authors push proactive policy and adaptation over waiting for certainty.
pmc-13344237:
Boujenah Jeremy, Beddock Richard, and Patrick Rozenberg show that a small-but-normal first baby warns of a too-small second baby, in a 2026 matched case-control study. Subtle growth slowing in a first pregnancy may expose hidden placenta or mother vulnerability, so the team compared women whose second babies came out small against matched women with two normal births.

First babies of cases weighed about 300 grams less on average. A first birthweight below minus 0.5 standard deviations carried fivefold odds of a small second baby, and below minus 1 deviation the odds passed eightfold, a clear dose-response pattern confirmed in a second model. Even within the normal range, the authors argue, low weight deserves a flag for closer watching next time.
pmc-13344637:
Xiaoyun Li and co-authors describe the Big Data Science Center at the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility in 2026. Modern detectors pour out huge, fast datasets, and the center built one platform covering the whole life of the facility, from experiment setup through data archiving and sharing.

The superfacility follows findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable data principles while leaning on AI-enabled big data tools. Instead of wrestling complex operations, users get a single friendly surface that keeps the full data lifecycle compliant and traceable. The design favors the data-centric path over purely experiment-driven control, aiming to speed discovery and widen the facility's reach for outside researchers.
pmc-13346037:
Longyao Cao, Hui Lu, and Dongjie Zhang report a 2026 case of emergency spine bleeding treated through two small endoscope portals. A spontaneous epidural hematoma at the neck-chest junction, confirmed on MRI at levels C7 to T2, was squeezing the patient's spinal cord, a rare crisis usually handled with wide open surgery.

Working under general anesthesia, the surgeons cleared the clot in 90 minutes with about 50 milliliters of blood loss. The patient walked with a frame by day three, and at six months reached the top recovery grade with only slight extra leg stiffness left. The authors present the two-portal route as a gentler option that spares spinal stability and speeds recovery.
pmc-13347637:
XiHui Wang and colleagues engineer the yeast Yarrowia lipolytica to make a citrus flavonoid from waste cooking oil, in a study issued in 2026. The target, (2S)-hesperetin, serves drug, food, and cosmetic uses, so genes for its plant pathway were inserted, precursor paths for key building blocks were tuned. Fat-burning steps were adjusted to free more starting material.

Stepwise gains lifted output until a 5-litre fermenter reached 488.7 mg per litre in the reported run, a strong yield from a waste feed. Turning used frying oil into a high-value health compound at once cuts waste and avoids farming or chemical routes. The plan is offered as a template for other flavonoids.
pmc-13347737:
P. Kaviyarasan and co-authors pilot two hands-on treatments for painful trigger points between the shoulder blades, in a randomised study published in 2026. Fifty patients were split between myofascial release with active stretching and a hold-relax method with the same stretching, each given five times a week for four weeks. Pain and neck movement were scored before and after.

Release work cut pain from 7.28 to 5.28 on the reported scale, clearing the set bar for a meaningful change. While the rival method eased pain by a smaller step that missed that bar. Movement gains also favoured release work, so the pilot points that arm toward a full trial.
pmc-13349837:
ZiAng Wang and ZhengGang Luan reviewed the joint role of bacterial lipopolysaccharide and the protein HMGB1 in sepsis in 2026. Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to infection with high death rates worldwide.

Lipopolysaccharide from Gram-negative bacteria starts inflammation through surface and internal sensors. Outside cells it binds HMGB1, and the pair is pulled inside through another receptor to reach lysosomes, where the membrane leaks and the toxin triggers internal caspases. That cycle releases more HMGB1, driving inflammation, clotting, and organ failure. Blocking HMGB1 has helped in animal models but has not yet reached patient care. The review maps this loop as a target for future drugs.
pmc-13349937:
Yi Yao and co-authors measured tiny retinal blood vessels in people with chronic hepatitis B in a 2026 eye imaging study at Xiangya Hospital. Although the virus mainly attacks the liver, it can affect other organs, and eye vessel changes in patients without cirrhosis were unknown.

Scans of the macula in 24 patients and 24 matched healthy people measured vessel length and perfusion density across central, inner, outer, and full zones, plus the vessel-free centre. Results were compared against liver stiffness and virus markers. Finding vessel loss tied to liver measures could reveal silent circulation harm from long-term hepatitis B and suggest when eye checks are worthwhile.
pmc-13350437:
Stephanie J. Hachey and fellow editors introduced a 2026 collection on image processing for microphysiological systems, the organ-on-chip, organoid, and printed tissue models now used to mimic human biology. These systems copy tissue structure, chemical gradients, and sometimes flow, and can screen drugs at scales real tissue cannot.

Their data, though, are growing faster than the manual methods used to read them, which are slow and hard to reproduce. The collection gathers automated and AI-driven image analysis built for these platforms. Better measurement pipelines decide whether richer models actually yield trustworthy answers for drug testing and disease research.
pmc-13350537:
Lanxin Du and colleagues used contrast ultrasound in 2026 to study kidney size and damage risk in children whose urine flows backward from bladder to kidney. Records covered 261 children seen between 2022 and 2024, 119 with reflux and 142 without.

Kidney volume, calculated from ultrasound measurements, shrank as reflux grade rose. In a subgroup also given a radiation-based kidney scan, the team modelled which factors independently predicted one kidney doing less work and kidney scarring, including urine entering the kidney tissue itself. A radiation-free test that also flags damage risk could spare children repeated nuclear scans during years of follow-up.
pmc-13351937:
Hang Cao, Yang Zhang, Fangqiu Fu, and Haiquan Chen review over- and under-screening for lung cancer in 2026. Low-dose CT screening cuts lung cancer deaths, yet current rules miss much of its promise. The review compares screening results across regions and studies how tumours grow over time.

East Asian programmes find far more early disease, driven by ground-glass nodules in non-smokers. Slow nodules with long natural histories sit at one extreme, and fast cancers with narrow cure windows at the other. Smoking-centred rules mismatch both extremes, causing needless checks for some and missed chances for others. The authors argue for screening plans that adapt to risk and tumour behaviour.
pmc-13354337:
Bhawesh Bhattarai leads a 2026 case of an infected appendiceal mucocele blocked by a giant stone. Mucoceles are rare surgical emergencies, and stones over 2 cm count as giant with high rupture risk. A 25-year-old woman arrived with 12 hours of right lower belly pain, vomiting, and fever with chills.

Ultrasound showed the mucocele with its stone, and CT measured the dense stone at about 24 by 22 mm with appendix width of 22.6 mm. Open appendix removal was chosen to avoid rupture and mucus spread into the belly. Tissue study found no excess mucosal growth or tumour. Scan signs had raised cancer suspicion, but smooth walls argued against it.
pmc-13356637:
Sujan Ravendran and co-authors describe a 2026 platform to make gene therapy viruses in suspension cells, a more scalable route than flat cell layers. Their method grows cells in shaken flasks, adds DNA with a common carrier, and boosts output with sodium butyrate. Quality was checked by several distinct methods, from genome counts to single-particle mass measures.

Vectors made this way matched a commercial kit in genome soundness and gene delivery, in both dish cells and mouse liver and heart. One purification route gave more full virus shells and fewer cell impurities than another. The authors offer the workflow as a robust base for lab-scale virus production.
pmc-13356737:
Biao Yang and co-authors explored in 2026 how long non-coding RNAs tied to migrasomes, small structures shed by moving cells, relate to glioma brain tumors and their outlook. Using cancer atlas data for 674 patients, they screened linked RNAs and built an eight-RNA risk model, then checked it in outside cohorts where coverage allowed.

The risk score tracked survival closely in the main data, with strong accuracy. Partial scores in outside groups also tracked survival, led by one RNA called CRNDE. High-risk tumors showed more immune and stromal content and more of a certain immune cell type. The authors call the findings early leads that need full outside checks and lab work.
pmc-13357337:
Kaimei Zhou and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on lung squamous cell carcinoma, a harsh form of lung cancer. They studied a protein called CNTN-1 and its role in helping tumor cells grow and spread. Little was known about how this protein drives the cancer, so the team tested what happens when it is switched off.

In lab-grown cancer cells, turning CNTN-1 down slowed growth, spread, and invasion, and raised cell death. It also calmed stress inside the cells and a change that helps cancer cells move. Tests in mice backed up these effects. The findings mark CNTN-1 as a possible drug target for this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13358537:
Mengmeng Chen and co-authors map the research field on DNA methylation in lung cancer in a 2026 study. DNA methylation is a chemical tag that can switch genes off, and it plays a part in how non-small cell lung cancer starts. Instead of running lab tests, the team counted and charted the papers themselves.

They reviewed 573 papers from 2008 to 2025, written by thousands of researchers in 174 countries. China and the United States led the output, and seven main themes stood out, including genes being silenced by excess tags. Charts of who works with whom, and which topics are rising, help new researchers see where the field is heading.
pmc-13358737:
Michael Weis wrote a 2026 commentary on cholesterol care after heart transplant. A slow narrowing of the new heart's arteries, called cardiac allograft vasculopathy, is a top cause of late death in these patients. High cholesterol feeds the process, and standard statin drugs already help. Weis asks how far newer, stronger drugs should push cholesterol down.

The newer drugs block a protein called PCSK9 and can cut cholesterol far below what statins reach. The open question is whether that extra drop prevents the artery narrowing, and at what point low becomes too low. The piece weighs trial proof and safety to guide doctors treating transplant patients.
pmc-13358837:
Weibin Lv and co-authors present a 2026 study on a sugar-coated protein that fuels lung adenocarcinoma. The protein, MUC21, sits on cell surfaces. The team found it may drive tumor growth by quieting a receptor for retinoic acid, a vitamin A signal that normally restrains cell growth. They tested the link in patient tissue, lab cells, and mice.

Raising or lowering MUC21 in cancer cells changed how fast they grew, moved, and invaded. Tumors in mice followed the same pattern. Blocking the receptor undid some effects, backing the proposed chain. If the chain holds, MUC21 could serve as a drug target in a cancer that spreads early and often.
pmc-13360837:
Vasilios Pergialiotis led a 2026 study of how recovery pathways are put together in cancer surgery for women. Enhanced recovery programs bundle many steps, from feeding to pain control, to speed healing after surgery. The team asked whether these steps act as one linked system or as separate habits. They drew on the first 300 patients of a multi-center cohort treated at five major hospitals.

Only steps used in a fair share of cases entered the network model, which maps how steps connect to each other. The team measured which steps sit at the center of the web and hold the pattern together. Knowing the load-bearing steps helps hospitals that are just starting such programs. They can build the core first instead of chasing every item at once.
pmc-13360937:
Linfen Wu and co-authors studied licorice as a sweetener for spirits in a 2026 sensory paper. Licorice carries a potent natural sweetener, but its sweetness lingers too long in drinks, which has limited its use. Licorice extract is cheaper and easier to handle than the pure compound. The team measured how trained tasters sensed the extract in two base spirits of different strengths.

They set the levels at which tasters first notice the sweetness, name it, and still find it pleasant. A good dose came out at 30 milligrams per liter for the weaker spirit and 40 for the stronger one. They also tested puerarin, a plant compound, as a way to shorten the lingering sweet tail. The results give drink makers firm guidance for using this natural sweetener.
pmc-13361237:
Ovidiu Samoilă and co-authors review artificial intelligence for spotting a swelling eye condition in a 2026 paper. Papilledema is swelling of the optic disc caused by high pressure inside the skull. It can flag brain tumors, fluid buildup, or clots, so missing it is dangerous. The review covers AI tools that read photos of the back of the eye to find and grade this swelling.

Deep learning systems, above all the image networks called CNNs, matched or even beat expert eye doctors at the task in the studies covered. That level of skill opens doors for early spotting and quick sorting of urgent cases. The authors also see a role in telemedicine, where a photo taken far from a specialist can be read at once. The review weighs promise against the proof still needed.
pmc-13361337:
So Ra Kim and Byung-Wan Lee review a ketone body's double role in diabetes in a 2026 paper. The compound, beta-hydroxybutyrate, is best known as a backup fuel the body burns when sugar runs low. It also acts as a signal that steers stress defense, inflammation, and cell power plants. The authors ask whether its blood level is a helpful adaptation or a harmful load in diabetes.

Studies disagree. Some link higher levels to a healthier metabolic state or a useful compensation, while others tie them to worsening blood sugar control. The same split appears for diabetic heart muscle disease, where results point both ways. The review gathers the clash of evidence so clinicians can judge when ketone levels deserve worry, watching, or even welcome.
pmc-13362537:
Liang Hu and colleagues report a 2026 materials study on adding the rare earth metal cerium to an aluminum-silicon alloy used in cast parts. They tracked how cerium changed the alloy's inner structure, pull strength, and surface hardness. Cerium refined the chunky silicon crystals in the metal and created new cerium-bearing phases inside it.

The change brought an odd split: pull strength rose, reaching its best at a small cerium dose, while surface hardness fell. The team explains the split as a contest between tougher, softer phases and other strengthening effects. Breaks also turned from brittle snapping to a more ductile tearing. The findings help engineers tune cast alloys where strength matters more than surface hardness.
pmc-13364137:
Oluwatoyin Favour Olu-Olusegun and colleagues present a 2026 study on a film-forming antitranspirant, a spray that coats potato leaves and slows water loss, during tuber formation under moderate drought. Two pot trials, in a polytunnel and a glasshouse across seasons, compared drought alone against drought plus the spray, the product Vapor Gard. Leaf water state, stolon growth, and tuber count and size grades were measured.

Drought cut leaf water, stolons, and tuber set in both trials, confirming how touchy this growth stage is. The spray lifted leaf water clearly and more than doubled tuber number under drought in the first trial, with a similar gain in the second, and it shifted sizes toward market grades. Yields still trailed watered plants, so the authors call it a helper beside irrigation, not a swap.
pmc-13364737:
Abeer Omar and co-workers tell a 2026 case of a 45 year old woman whose heart stopped out of care and who woke to a hard heart call. Her heart's main pump showed the tip bulge and weak squeeze of stress heart ill, named Takotsubo. A tight bridge of heart muscle over an artery clouded the call.

Flow tests through the artery showed the bridge did not choke blood flow. Scans showed the weak squeeze heal fast, which fits stress heart ill, not a blocked artery. The case warns teams to weigh both calls when a heart stops.
pmc-13371237:
Amal Khalil Y Mohammed and co-authors describe lung disease care at El-Obeid Teaching Hospital in Sudan in a 2026 study. They tracked people with tuberculosis, a germ that harms the lungs, from April 2023 to April 2026. Those years fell in a time of armed war in the area.

The team counted 2,193 patients, most of them men, and split near half town and half country homes. Many started drugs late, by two to six months. War risk, lack of cash, and thin clinic stock were the main blocks. The work shows how war slows basic care and lets the disease spread.
pmc-13374537:
Souradeep Saha and co-authors probed the daily habits of med students in a 2026 study in India. The students live in hostels at their med school, with hard study loads and loose daily times. That mix can tilt food, sleep, and move habits in poor ways, though they learn health craft each day.

The survey scored food picks, first meal habits, sleep, screen time, and sport. It also asked how much they heed food tags and parts lists. A gap twixt what they know and what they do was the key ask. Schools can use such gaps to build real aids, like sound canteen food and sleep rules.
pmc-13377837:
Xiao Tang and co-authors mapped job-ready roots in Chinese students in a 2026 study. A stratified set of 1,279 students took scales on mind stock: trust in self, hope, bounce-back, and bright views. Job read was the end score in the math.

Each part of mind stock fed job read in a clear way. A skill to bend with career change sat in the chain and held the top direct tie. A felt crush of the job hunt weak­ened each tie. Schools that build mind stock and bend skill may lift job read more than drills that teach forms and talks alone.
pmc-13378037:
Anand Sekar G and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of systems-based care for adults who live with several long-term conditions at once. The conditions covered include high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease, high cholesterol, and obesity. Such patients often need care from many services that do not always work together.

From 252 records found, 11 studies met the rules for inclusion, and their results were combined in narrative form because the studies differed a lot. The clearest gains were in blood pressure and blood sugar control. Benefits were strongest when care included regular monitoring, careful adjustment of medicines, patient education, and support from pharmacists or nurses, including remote monitoring.
pmc-13382237:
Maurice van Steensel wrote a 2026 commentary titled From pixels to pimples, on screen time as a risk factor for acne. In a large genetic epidemiology study cohort spanning Singapore and Malaysia, the Chinese subgroup showed a clear link between screen time and developing acne. The author argues the link probably extends to other ethnic groups.

Screen time likely bundles several effects: light exposure and disturbed sleep unsettling the skin's daily rhythm, a sedentary lifestyle, and eating more high-energy food, which disturbs metabolism. The commentary suggests that people with moderate to severe acne should probably receive lifestyle advice alongside skin treatment. It frames acne partly as a modern lifestyle condition.
pmc-13383637:
Qiaolin Wang and colleagues measure whether gold can accept a hydrogen bond from a carbon-hydrogen group in 2026 work. The question matters for catalysis, where such weak contacts are often claimed but rarely measured well. The team used photoelectron imaging on gas-phase pairs of copper or gold ions with acetonitrile, backed by theory.

Bond strengths came out near 9.9 kilocalories per mole for copper and 11.8 for gold in the reported units. Charge-based attraction supplied about 60 percent of the total pull in both cases. The authors offer these values as benchmarks that settle the physical nature of this debated class of hydrogen bonds.
pmc-13385537:
Hang Wang and a large team build an AI system that drafts whole-body PET/CT reports for lung cancer staging in 2026 work. A single misplaced finding can shift a tumor stage and change treatment, yet drafting stays slow and error prone. Their two-stage system, RIDE, first writes structured stage-focused notes, then expands them organ by organ using retrieved examples.

The test cohort held 1,583 patients from three hospitals, with 520 held-out cases including many from outside sites. RIDE beat comparison systems on drafting quality and staging accuracy, and clinician ratings stayed high across sites. The authors frame the tool as decision support for human checking, not a replacement.
pmc-13386237:
Herrmann and co-authors test a thyroid hormone lookalike drug in mice in this 2026 study. The compound, called TRIAC, is a candidate treatment for conditions where thyroid hormone cannot reach tissues properly. Normal thyroid treatment risks racing hearts and overheating. The team gave TRIAC to healthy male mice for 14 days and checked body and organ responses.

The drug lowered circulating thyroxine and switched on classic thyroid responsive genes in the liver, showing real hormone like activity. Yet heart rate and blood pressure stayed normal, and the heart did not enlarge. Brown fat heat production and body temperature did not change either. Herrmann concludes TRIAC acts unevenly across tissues, sparing the heart and temperature control that standard therapy disturbs.
pmc-13386637:
Yuchan Kim, Kyung Hyun Cho, and colleagues build a self-adjusting control circuit for bacterial chemical production in 2026 work. Their E. coli strain makes 3-hydroxypropionic acid, a platform chemical needing both NADPH and malonyl-CoA in balance. Static settings cannot track shifting cell states, so the circuit senses the product itself.

Once product builds up, the circuit jointly tunes cofactor regeneration and precursor allocation without outside input. The final strain reached a titer near 3 grams per liter, about five times the unregulated control strain. Yield per glucose rose by a similar factor, which supports product-responsive control as a modular tool.
pmc-13387437:
Shinichi Yoshioka and colleagues fix a bowel blockage after hernia repair with an omental patch in a 2026 case report. The torn lining was too fragile to sew shut, so a flap of fatty omentum covered the defect, topped with an anti-adhesion sheet. Recovery ran smoothly, and a look inside four years later showed full lining regrowth without adhesions. The authors offer the patch as a simple, durable fallback.
pmc-13389437:
Fereshteh Shafiei, Zahra Jowkar, and Sepideh Eslamipanah compare, in 2026, final rinse fluids used during root canal treatment. The standard rinse removes the smeared layer left by filing but can weaken dentine and does not kill germs, so the team tested chitosan and benzalkonium chloride as alternatives, alone and combined.

Ninety-five extracted human premolars were prepared to a standard root length and file size. Seventy roots were filled and loaded until they broke to test strength, while fifty split specimens were checked for surface roughness. Dentists and materials researchers gain a direct comparison of cleaning benefit against root strength, helping them judge whether newer rinses protect treated teeth from later fracture.
pmc-13390737:
Ana Catarina Angelo and colleagues check, in 2026, whether magnetic resonance imaging reliably shows a newly recognised cause of outer elbow pain. Minor instability of the lateral elbow, from overuse rather than injury, was only recently described, and its imaging signs are still being defined.

Patients who had keyhole surgery between 2021 and 2024 for stubborn outer elbow pain without injury were reviewed. Several specialists scored set imaging features in confirmed cases to test how reproducible those features are between readers. Musculoskeletal radiologists gain a cross-specialty verdict on which scan signs can be trusted, since a feature that readers cannot agree on cannot guide surgery.
pmc-13391137:
Anton Alyakin and a large team test, in 2026, whether artificial intelligence can write neurosurgery board examination questions as well as human experts. Multiple-choice questions are the main format for board certification, but writing good ones consumes scarce expert time.

The team built an automated pipeline using the newest vision-language models to generate board-style self-assessment questions, then had them judged blind against authentic questions. Medical educators gain a quality comparison. It shows where machine drafting can safely save faculty time. It also shows where expert writing still wins. Every specialty that maintains large question banks faces this question.
pmc-13391437: Hulme Rios-Guerra and co-authors are the subject of a short correction notice only, issued in 2026 for their study of anticonvulsant aza-Biginelli compounds. The notice states a single fix: Maria Ines Nicolas-Vazquez should have been marked as a corresponding author, and the original article has been corrected to show this. No data, methods, or findings are changed.
pmc-13392637:
Li and co-authors present a 2026 feeding trial asking whether plant sterols, called phytosterols, can raise milk output while cutting methane intensity in dairy cows. Thirty-four mid-lactation Holstein cows were split into a control group and a group fed 15 grams per day of a phytosterol product over 50 days. Digestibility of organic matter, protein, fiber, and fat also improved. Blood glucose increased while total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol fell.
