pmc-13393237:
Dasha Shamarina, Lina María Cortes Rueda, David Alderson, and Anne T Collins gathered the worldwide evidence on what helps or hinders vaccination during pregnancy. Maternal shots protect newborns in their first vulnerable months, yet uptake lags in many countries. Searching seven databases produced a huge initial haul, and one hundred eighty-four studies from countries recommending whooping cough vaccination in pregnancy survived screening.

The commonest barriers sat with individuals and their circles: gaps in knowledge, pre-existing anti-vaccine beliefs, and worries about safety and effectiveness for the baby. The strongest enablers were direct recommendations from health professionals and health authorities, backed by trust in what those professionals said. The authors call hesitancy a layered problem and argue programmes must fix practical obstacles and perceptions together to lift coverage among pregnant people.
pmc-13393337:
Adrienn Molnár and co-authors profile horse blood plasma in seconds using a laser-based mass spectrometry method, aiming to check plasma quality before it is used as therapy. Plasma products are increasingly used to speed wound healing, but preparing them well is still an open problem. Their 2026 study pairs an automated sampling system with several established measurement methods.

The laser system vaporises tiny plasma samples and reads their lipid and metabolite fingerprints without extensive preparation. Certain phosphatidylcholines and fatty acids changed with centrifugation settings, marking them as candidate indicators of plasma stability and quality. Platelet and particle counts were measured by flow cytometry and light microscopy, and samples were imaged by electron microscopy. Lipid profiles correlated clearly with the density of platelet fragments, but not with vesicle counts, suggesting platelets drive much of plasma composition. The authors present the platform for high-throughput quality control and diagnostics.
pmc-13394037:
Ioanna Zimianiti and five colleagues asked whether a genetic variant tied to multiple sclerosis severity also touches cognition in the general population, using UK Biobank data. The variant, labelled rs10191329A, came out of a genome-wide study of MS disability and pointed toward brain resilience as a driver of outcome. If resilience is the mechanism, the variant might show its hand on thinking tests in healthy people and in other brain diseases too.

Reaction time, fluid intelligence, and prospective memory were the yardsticks. Associations in healthy controls were weak but consistently pointed toward poorer cognition in carriers. Similar trends appeared in MS, Parkinson's disease, and dementia groups without reaching significance. The authors read the pattern as support for their hypothesis: the variant may worsen MS outcomes by eroding general brain health rather than through anything specific to the disease.
pmc-13394837:
Damian M. Bailey leads a 2026 call for a new kind of training in space medicine, named SpaceMed. Crewed trips now aim past Earth orbit, toward the Moon and Mars. Space strains the body through radiation, isolation, odd gravity, and distance from help. No other setting taxes human health as broadly. The authors argue that future crews need doctors trained across many fields at once.

Their program would blend body science, clinic skills, and mission know-how in deep, hands-on study. Stressors in space act together, so training should treat the body as one system. The piece sets out why such training matters now. It frames space health as a core part of exploration, not an add-on.
pmc-13394937:
Faith C. Adams and co-authors test, in 2026, how two calming drugs affect talk between the brain's two halves. Magnetic pulses can probe how one motor area quiets the other across the corpus callosum. Twenty-four adults took baclofen, lorazepam, or a dummy pill on separate days, with no one knowing which. The team measured short and long forms of cross-brain quieting in a hand muscle.

Baclofen cut both forms of quieting, while lorazepam left them unchanged. The two drugs act on sister receivers of the same calming signal, GABA. Only the B-type receiver drug moved the needle. The authors say the split sharpens drug science for stroke and Parkinson's care.
pmc-13395437:
Pola Kuhn and co-authors show, in 2026, that one DNA tag site steers spore making in a gut germ. The germ, Clostridioides difficile, spreads in hospitals through hardy spores. An enzyme named CamA tags DNA and boosts spore output, but its key target was unknown. The team found one tag site in the control zone of a gene named spoIIE.

That single tag lifts the gene's output and wakes the spore program. Some cells woke the program early, before splitting, yet could call it off and grow again. Cells that woke it after splitting stayed committed. CamA also aided mouse infection beyond spore counts. The authors flag CamA as a drug target.
pmc-13395837:
Ramin Nashebi and co-authors build, in 2026, the first maths model of a mitochondrial carrier that matches how it truly works. The carrier, SLC25A10, swaps succinate, malate, and phosphate across the power plant wall. Old models assumed both cargoes bind at once, but structure shows a ping-pong swap at one site. The new model builds that swap in, with rivalry among cargoes and full reversibility.

Bayesian fitting tuned the model to lab uptake data with honest error bars. Runs showed a fast phosphate-driven uptake phase, then a slow reshuffle between the two main cargoes. Swollen power plants boosted early flow in the model. The authors offer the frame for cousin carriers too.
pmc-13396737:
Mahmoud S. Elkotamy built a computer pipeline to find new blockers of GSK-3β, an enzyme long targeted in Alzheimer's disease, and reports the screen in 2026. A useful blocker must be safe and able to cross into the brain, a combination that defeats most candidates.

The funnel started with shape models built from known blockers and from the enzyme itself, run against a public compound library. Survivors faced docking tests, filters for absorption and brain entry, and toxicity predictions. Two compounds passed every gate. Long simulations of 100 nanoseconds, with energy scoring, checked whether the final pair stayed locked onto the enzyme, marking them for lab testing.
pmc-13397137:
Farbod Ebrahimi and co-authors turned ordinary paper into an ultrasensitive chemical sensor by evaporating silver onto it in a single step, and report the method in 2026. The target technique, surface-enhanced Raman scattering, reads a molecule's fingerprint from laser light, but it needs metal nanostructures that focus light into hot spots.

Paper treated with a fluorine compound repels water so strongly that arriving silver atoms bead into separate islands rather than a film. The islands came out uniform, about 29 nanometers wide. The sheets amplified signals a millionfold and detected a test dye down to 2 picomolar, with readings steady within 10 percent across samples.
pmc-13398137:
Junzhi Wang and co-authors reveal the switchboard that lets barnyard grass shrug off herbicides. Their 2026 study targets cytochrome P450 detox enzymes, whose control wiring was unknown despite their central role in resistance. The weed, Echinochloa crus-galli, ranks among the world's worst and threatens rice and maize yields as resistance spreads.

A transcription factor named DOF2 directly switches on detox genes, including CYP81A21 in the weed and CYP81A6 in rice. Resistant grass carries extra DOF2 at rest and makes more when sprayed, while deleting the rice counterpart leaves plants tender. A growth hormone pathway, through the DELLA protein SLR1, normally holds DOF2 back, tying weed resistance to the plant's own growth controls.
pmc-13398837:
Ningning Zheng and co-authors report, in a 2026 paper in Portuguese, early heartbeats sparked from an unusual source: the inferior vena cava. Their case concerns a 78-year-old woman with nine months of palpitations, chest tightness and fatigue, episodes lasting 10 to 30 minutes five or six times a month. Premature atrial contractions usually arise from the pulmonary veins, and the great lower vein is normally electrically quiet.

Holter monitoring counted 15,838 premature beats in 24 hours, and tracings pointed below the heart rather than to the lung veins. Beta-blocker treatment had failed to ease her symptoms, so she chose an electrophysiology study with radiofrequency ablation. The case adds the vena cava to the map of treatable triggers doctors should check.
pmc-13400037:
Daniel Correia and colleagues compared round and anatomical breast implants for reconstruction after mastectomy, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Nine comparative studies met the inclusion criteria, together covering 2,535 patients, with 1,578 receiving round implants and 957 receiving shaped ones.

Pooling the studies with a random-effects model found no meaningful difference in overall problems: the odds ratio was 0.46 favoring round implants numerically, but the confidence interval was wide and the difference not significant at a p value of 0.19 in the analysis. The authors conclude that implant shape should not be chosen on expected safety or satisfaction grounds, because the evidence shows neither. Instead they recommend shared decision-making built around the patient's chest anatomy and preferences and the surgeon's experience with each device.
pmc-13400537:
Xianli Xu and co-authors study, in 2026, how castration changes meat quality in black Tibetan sheep raised on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Castration calms rams and eases herd management during grazing. Its effects on the meat itself, and on muscle chemistry, were unclear.

Using targeted and broad chemical profiling, the team compared meat from castrated and entire males. Castrated meat lost less drip but more water on cooking, and tested more elastic, chewy and cohesive. It also held more amino acids, including flavor-linked ones, and more fatty acids across all classes. Thirty-four differing compounds emerged, with several pathways tied to the quality shift. Castration, the authors conclude, measurably reshapes both texture and chemistry.
pmc-13400637:
Ivana Nanevski and a large German team release, in 2026, a synthetic health dataset for training artificial intelligence to assess fall risk in older people. Falls are a leading cause of accidental death in later life, yet real patient data cannot be shared freely. Fake but realistic data offer a way around the privacy barrier.

Their dataset, SynTabFall, holds over 745,000 records with 44 attributes spanning demographics, diseases, mobility and cognition. Models trained on the synthetic data matched the performance of models trained on real records for predicting fall risk. The team also describes the multi-year process, built with data protection officers and clinicians at a major hospital, plus the software used to generate and check the data.
pmc-13401137:
Demi Rianne Vintges, Marina Weerheim and Faiz Karim describe, in 2026, a man whose first clear sign of VEXAS syndrome, a recently recognized inflammatory disorder, was a fungal infection of the gullet. VEXAS arises from acquired mutations in blood-forming cells. It causes fierce, hard-to-treat inflammation with low blood counts. Its infection risks have had little attention.

The 62-year-old had recurrent fever, high inflammation markers, cartilage inflammation and skin features. His marrow showed changes too, and the causal mutation sat in most of his blood cells. Endoscopy confirmed Candida infection of the esophagus. An antifungal course treated it before the diagnosis was made. Steroids alone then failed to control VEXAS, while a weekly injected immune drug brought a good response.
pmc-13401637:
Namrata Singh, Jerry H Gurwitz, and Sarah B Lieber authored a 2026 narrative review of multiple chronic conditions in adults with autoimmune and inflammatory rheumatic diseases. Living with several long-term illnesses at once is the norm in these patients and tangles their care considerably.

The review summarises the epidemiology of multimorbidity across rheumatic diseases. Rates run higher than in age-matched general populations. They reach about 86 percent in rheumatoid arthritis and about 82 percent in lupus cohorts. Heart, lung, and mental health disorders recur often in the patterns. The burden tracks with higher death rates, worse function and quality of life, faster disability, and greater health service use and cost, driven by chronic inflammation, lifestyle, and treatment effects. The authors call for holistic, person-centred rheumatology care using multidisciplinary teams.
pmc-13401937:
Binayak Deb and a large trauma team report their experience with one-lung ventilation during surgery for chest trauma. Their 2026 look-back study comes from the apex trauma centre at AIIMS in New Delhi. Ventilating one lung while the other is operated on is harder in trauma than in planned surgery, because patients arrive short of oxygen, unstable, and inflamed.

Over six years, from January 2020 to December 2025, 117 trauma patients in a row needed one-lung ventilation. The team recorded how injuries happened and their patterns, pre-surgery body state, ventilation technique and settings, surgical approach, and results after surgery. Subgroup checks separated blunt from penetrating injuries. A central aim was finding what predicts acute respiratory distress syndrome, the severe lung failure that polytrauma patients are primed for. Data on technique choice in this group have been scarce, and the series is meant to guide practice.
pmc-13402237:
Sriram Nallamothu and co-authors recount a 40-year-old man whose mild sore throat turned into Lemierre syndrome, a dangerous spread of throat infection into the neck veins. Early signs looked like a viral cold, but within days he had fever, muscle aches, and pain on the right side of his face and neck. Local infections common in his setting could easily have masked the real problem.

Ultrasound and contrast CT, done within 48 hours of that turn, showed a clot in the internal jugular vein with septic emboli, infected fragments breaking off downstream. Treatment with intravenous antibiotics and blood thinners brought a full recovery. The authors press a simple point: a sore throat that worsens with one-sided neck pain and fever needs fast imaging, because early treatment is what keeps this rare syndrome from killing.
pmc-13402437:
Nitesh Sanghai and co-authors introduce borsantrazole, a boron-based pyrazole molecule built to fight oxidative stress on three fronts at once, tested in mice carrying the SOD1-G37R form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The compound showed brain-friendly chemistry, with low efflux ratios near 0.9 and 1.0 at the tested doses and fat solubility in a range suited to reaching the nervous system. No toxicity appeared, even over 120 days of chronic dosing.

Treated mice lived 15.1 days longer on average, with gains in both sexes, and lost far less weight, 18.3 percent against 27.1 percent in controls. Symptom onset slipped by about 24.9 days and disease onset by 25.5 days in the reported figures. Protein surveys found 51 proteins and 29 phosphorylation sites changed, including spots on neurofilament chains. The team calls the result proof of concept for a disease-modifying ALS drug, pending far more development.
pmc-13402837:
Massold and co-authors report, in 2026, the first neutral chiral tellurium catalysts that steer a reaction's handedness using only chalcogen bonding. That bond is a weak attraction between a tellurium atom's electron-poor patch and a substrate. Chalcogen bonding's directionality and the binding patches on one tellurium atom had blocked asymmetric catalysis with neutral donors. Their design pairs two triazole-telluride arms on a chiral cyclohexane backbone for two-point binding.

In the benchmark Reissert-type reaction of quinolines, the optimized catalyst reached enantiomeric ratios up to 11 to 89, strongly favoring one mirror-image product. Yields ran above 99 percent for the best substrate in their optimization. Early backbones gave over 99 percent yield but zero selectivity. The comparable hydrogen-bonding catalyst managed only 15 percent yield at a near-even 47 to 53 ratio, crediting the chalcogen bonds for the selectivity. Chloride binding studies and computation revealed the geometry behind the two-point grip.
pmc-13402937:
Victorine Mulur Ngachangong and colleagues examine what brings men into programs that prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV in the Bamenda Health District of Cameroon, and what keeps them away. Cameroon has cut HIV prevalence to 2.3 percent by 2024, yet prevention cover for infants lags. Only about a third of children under ten receive antiretroviral treatment, even as transmission to exposed infants at six to eight weeks fell to 1.78 percent.

Male partners shape testing, clinic attendance, and treatment decisions inside households, so their absence from antenatal HIV services weakens every link in the prevention chain. The study hunts the determinants of that involvement, social, economic, cultural, and service-side, in one district where progress has been slow. The authors aim the findings at program designers who need fathers present, not only mothers, to close the last gaps in infant protection.
pmc-13403037:
Shirley N Tang and colleagues use mice carrying the fat-1 gene, which converts omega-6 fats into omega-3 fats inside the body, to test whether fat balance shields spinal discs from obesity-driven decay. Low back pain, largely a disc degeneration story, is a leading cause of disability, and Western diets rich in omega-6 fats feed inflammation. Wildtype and gene-carrying mice ate control or omega-6 heavy high-fat diets.

At 16 weeks the high-fat diet raised body fat while gene carriers gained less weight; disc height ran lower in high-fat wildtypes and higher in carriers, with sex and spinal level differences. At 60 weeks, wildtype high-fat mice carried more inflammatory signals IL-6 and IL-17A in blood, and their discs showed fibrosis, cell loss, and matrix disorder, while carrier discs were protected. The authors pitch diet or gene-based fat rebalancing as therapy candidates.
pmc-13403437:
Li Qi and co-authors charted world research in 2026 on a brain stimulation method first put forward in 2017. Two high-rate signals cross in the head so that only deep spots feel a slow beat. The hope is to reach deep brain areas with no surgery at all.

Counting and mapping published studies showed a shift over time. Early work tested the basic physics in animals, while newer work builds head models tuned to each person. Current hot topics include dose, safety risks, and fair tests against older methods. The field still needs strong human trials before clinics can rely on the approach.
pmc-13403637:
Fernanda de Andrade Ribeiro Ferreira led a team that built a teaching game in 2026 for nursing students learning sterile supply work. Sterile supply units clean and prepare tools for surgery, following a strict flow. Ten expert judges and 38 students checked the game between April and August 2023.

The game, called Rota CME, copies the unit's layout so students can walk its steps in play. Judges gave its content a score near 98 percent for validity. One part, covering game build and display, scored lower and was reworked from feedback. The result is a workable classroom tool for a little-taught topic.
pmc-13403737:
Xiaohui Li led a 2026 materials study that pairs near-zero heat expansion with oxygen ion flow in one ceramic. Hot devices such as fuel cells fail when parts swell at unlike rates. Their test material is a lanthanum-doped crystal built from linked four-sided oxygen units.

Vibrations tilt those units together, which cancels most swelling across a wide heat range. The same tilts open paths for extra oxygen ions to hop between ring spaces. Bulk swelling ranked lowest among oxide ion conductors the team surveyed. The twin trick could ease strain in hot cells, sensors, and water-splitting gear.
pmc-13404037:
Benito D Isaac and colleagues asked health workers in 2026 how electronic medical records can survive in a fragile setting like Haiti. Records promise better care, yet power cuts, weak internet, and thin funding break many systems. The team spoke at length with doctors, nurses, and data staff chosen for their know-how.

Workers tied record survival to the health of the systems around it, from power supply to politics. Old paper habits and clashing software add strain. Their fixes include linking systems so data flows, adding backup routes, and growing local staff skill. Keeping some paper steps lean, they add, helps the shift stick.
pmc-13404637:
Rikke Løvendahl Eefsen and colleagues report the CheckPRO trial in 2026, testing immune drugs with or without focused radiation in advanced prostate cancer. The cancer had stopped responding to hormone treatment and had already passed at least two lines of therapy. Immune checkpoint drugs alone have shown limited effect in this disease.

Ninety-one patients were randomised evenly between two plans. Both used the immune drugs nivolumab and ipilimumab, and one plan added stereotactic body radiation, given in focused high doses. Eighty-one received treatment and could be assessed. Confirmed PSA response rates were close, at 21.6 percent with radiation and 20.5 percent without in the reported arms. Tumour shrinkage rates, survival and side effects complete the comparison the authors present.
pmc-13404937:
Eugen-Călin Secară, Nicolae-Adrian Opre and Tim Mackey run a 2026 online experiment on repeated health news and attitudes to dietary supplements. News feeds often show people similar stories again and again. Repetition can shift what feels true, yet few studies separate stated attitudes from automatic ones.

Over two weeks, 228 participants received one full-length article each day. Stories praised supplements, attacked them, mixed both views or stayed neutral, forming four groups. Attitudes were measured before, during and after exposure, in both explicit and implicit forms. The preregistered design also tests whether engagement with the stories carried the effect and whether starting attitudes changed the response.
pmc-13405837:
Bingxin Cai, Hengchang Huang and Xuhai Chen follow school emotions in 608 Chongqing teenagers across three years of high school, in a 2026 study. Average starting age was about fifteen and a half. Pressure in competitive classrooms builds over time, and coping style may decide who suffers most.

Negative school emotions rose steadily across the years, while positive emotions held roughly stable in growth models. Students who used shift-and-persist coping, reframing problems while staying optimistic, later showed better emotional balance. Emotions did not predict later coping, suggesting the strategy is a stable resource rather than a mood product. The authors extend control-value theory with this one-way pattern.
pmc-13407037:
Zikang Zeng and co-authors, in 2026, tested whether berberine, a plant compound, can shield mouse kidneys from cadmium poisoning. Cadmium builds up in kidneys and disrupts energy handling and oxidation balance, yet berberine's protective reach there had not been mapped well.

Male mice received cadmium daily for 30 days, with or without berberine at two doses. Cadmium raised injury markers, damaged kidney tissue, and weakened antioxidant defences, while berberine softened each change in line with dose. Chemical profiling showed cadmium suppressing energy-cycle intermediates and berberine restoring many of them. The compound also lowered a key glycolysis enzyme in tissue tests, and computer modelling suggested it binds that enzyme stably.
pmc-13407437:
Cosima C. Cosima C. Hoch and co-authors present a 2026 diagnostic case from Switzerland. A 39-year-old woman had a planned caesarean birth under spinal anaesthesia. Two days later she reported muffled hearing in both ears. She also had a rushing ear noise, heard her own voice loudly, and felt head pain and brief dizziness.

Ear examination and balance tests were largely normal, yet tone testing showed sensorineural hearing loss concentrated in low frequencies on both sides. The pattern, starting right after spinal anaesthesia, pointed to fluid leaking from around the spinal cord and lowering pressure in the skull. Rest, fluids, caffeine, and pain relief were chosen over an invasive blood patch. Headache and dizziness cleared within five days, hearing was normal again at one week, and only a faint ear noise remained, much reduced, at six weeks.
pmc-13408837:

Ocean heatwaves are lengthening under climate change and wrecking ecosystems and fisheries, yet their triggers are incompletely understood. Satellite records and atmospheric reanalysis covered the North Pacific and North Atlantic.

An atmospheric river overhead pulls the ocean surface in two directions at once. Its clouds shade the water and cool it, while its warm, humid air throttles the ocean's own heat loss and warms it. Which effect wins depends on season and region, so the same sky river can seed a heatwave in one place and smother it in another. The authors argue that forecasting ocean extremes now has to reckon with these compound air-sea events and how they shift as the climate warms.
pmc-13409037:
The European Food Safety Authority publishes in 2026 the first of its twice-yearly horizon scans of new research on organisms created with new genomic techniques. Those opinions compared these techniques with conventional breeding and established genetic methods.

The report explains the scanning method, describes how studies were screened for quality and relevance, and summarises what the literature search surfaced for this period. For regulators and developers, the value is procedural as much as scientific. A standing, transparent mechanism catches new findings early. It also tests standing opinions against them, rather than letting guidance quietly age.
pmc-13409337:
Swapnil Chandekar, Shishir Singh, Gaurav Kulkarni, Padmini Sekhar, and Hannah Wesley recount in 2026 how a front tooth with two strikes against it was saved and kept for four years. The upper right lateral incisor carried a developmental groove running down its palate side past the root's middle. That channel invites bacteria toward the pulp. Its root tip had never finished forming. Prognosis was poor by any textbook.

Care combined conventional root canal treatment from inside with a surgical approach from outside, sealing both the groove's pathway and the open apex. Four years of follow-up showed the bone around the root tip healed. The authors lay out their protocol step by step. Even grooved, open-apex incisors deserve an attempt at preservation before extraction is chosen. The groove's extent must be mapped honestly at the start.
pmc-13410137:
Kelly L'Engle and co-authors survey in 2026 how older teens in northern California feel about climate change. Hope, fear, and worry can push young people toward action or drag on their health. The team asked which feelings travel with climate anxiety, activism, and general well-being.

The survey reached 521 first- and second-year students at a city university, with an average age of 19. Feelings of drive and resolve lined up with taking action, while heavy worry lined up with poorer well-being. Climate messages worked best when they took mental health into account. The authors urge care in campaigns: strong calls to act should lift hope rather than pile on dread.
pmc-13410437:
Takuwa and co-authors pin down, in 2026, why sodium-ion battery cathodes resist the oxygen loss that triggers thermal runaway in lithium cells. The oxygen release energy measured about 1.7 electron volts for this sodium cathode, higher than the values for high-nickel lithium-ion cathodes in comparisons, quantifying the sodium material's lattice stability. Calculations showed the culprit: sodium deficiency creates high-valent nickel, which destabilizes lattice oxygen and greases the release pathway, while the sodium-stoichiometric material stays more stable. The authors conclude the work supplies a measurement method pairing experiment with theory and design rules for cathodes, supporting sodium-ion batteries' safety case for large-scale storage.
pmc-13411437:
Emma Jenkinson and co-authors lay out in 2026 a real-world study of digital mental health care for people with multiple sclerosis. Few MS clinics offer scalable routes to psychological help, which the pathway under study aims to fix.

Clinics will screen for distress with set cutoffs, then offer a twelve-week guided online therapy program tailored to life with MS, with up to six therapist sessions. Researchers will track how many patients get screened, qualify, join, and finish. Interviews with patients and staff will probe what helps or blocks rollout. Distress scores before and after will give an early read on benefit.
pmc-13412537:
Hedieh Alimi and co-authors explore in a 2026 pilot study whether a standard heart-attack risk score mirrors right-heart pumping strength. The GRACE score predicts in-hospital death after heart attacks, yet its link to right ventricular function was untested in inferior STEMI, where the right side often suffers. Forty stable patients at Qaem Hospital in Mashhad had three-dimensional ultrasound scans one to two days after artery-opening treatment.

Higher GRACE scores went with smaller right-heart filling volumes and lower stroke volumes in the scans performed. Heart rate also tied to several function measures on both sides of the heart. The authors frame the links as exploratory, since the group was small and no clinical outcomes were tracked. Larger prospective studies come next, they say.
pmc-13415537:
Lingfeng Liu and co-authors turn crystalline frameworks into pourable porous liquids to help pull lithium from salty brines, in 2026. The channels control how ions shed their water shells, favoring lithium strongly. Lithium passed at a high rate, with selectivity over magnesium above one hundred fifty. On simulated brine with forty times more magnesium, the output flipped to a lithium rich mix. The recipe offers a practical way to build precise ion filters at scale.
pmc-13415637:
Yang Wang and colleagues compare two brands of artificial neck disc in hybrid cervical surgery over at least seven years, in 2026. Seventy-eight patients had two level surgery mixing fusion with a Bryan or Mobi-C prosthesis between 2010 and 2018. Motion at the level above surgery was tracked by the path of its rotation center on bending X-rays.

Pain and function improved strongly in both groups, with no clear gap between brands. Range of motion stayed stable and similar. The rotation center drifted forward and down early in Mobi-C patients, a shift absent with Bryan. Later degeneration nearby appeared in about 13 percent of Mobi-C cases and about 24 percent of Bryan cases, a nonsignificant gap.
pmc-13416137:
Aya Osama Mohamed, Mai Ali Sayed Abdel Ghaney, and Yomna Ahmed Hosni test simple blood ratios as early warning tools in a pediatric intensive care unit, in 2026. Ninety-one critically ill children were followed prospectively over six months. Admission workups included full blood counts, inflammation markers, clotting, and liver and kidney tests, from which two cell ratios were computed.

Platelet count predicted death with moderate accuracy, using a cutoff near 245 in the reported units. The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio ran slightly higher in children who died, while the platelet to lymphocyte ratio ran higher in survivors, yet neither gap reached significance. The first ratio correlated with coma scores, age, and several lab values.
pmc-13416837:
Mengmeng Liu and co-authors characterise the first intron of a rice gene as a booster for gene expression, in a study published in 2027. Some introns raise output of the genes they sit in, an effect used in plant design. The intron, called OsNrx3i1, was tested in rice cells, whole rice plants, and a tobacco relative.

The intron worked best when placed early in the copied gene region, and it acted unlike a standard enhancer. Removing a small blocking segment inside it raised output further. Set into tiny synthetic promoters, it lifted activity up to 65 fold in rice cells. Performance varied by host, which the authors flag for designers.
pmc-13418537:
Osvaldo Rivera-Gonzalez and co-authors probe how a gut hormone's release is braked by Gi proteins in mice, in a 2026 study. Mutant mice let the team switch Gi signalling in K cells only, on or off, to see the effect in living animals.

Switching the brake on cut GIP release and worsened metabolic measures. Switching it off raised GIP and markedly improved glucose control in both lean and obese mice. A cyclic AMP activated exchange protein carried the braking signal. The pathway could inform diabetes drugs that raise natural GIP.
pmc-13419137:
Messaoud Bouragba and colleagues review ten years of hydatid cyst disease in farming and herding country, drawing on hospital records from Djelfa. The illness spreads from animals to people through a tapeworm cycle involving dogs and livestock, and it lingers where herding is a way of life. Their study covers 326 surgically confirmed cases treated at five hospitals between 2015 and 2024.

Rural living and close dog contact tracked together in the case data, and cyst site varied with age and exposure. Livestock surveys in the country have found very high infection in sheep and cattle, showing the animal side of the cycle stays active. The authors press for a joined One Health plan that treats human cases, dog control, and slaughter checks as one problem rather than three.
pmc-13419237:

A heart tracing is cheap and painless, yet reading it well takes training that many sites lack. Their system pairs a pattern-learning network with a frequency transform that exposes rhythm traits hidden in the raw line.

Tests used a large public set of tracings under the standard ten-fold checking routine, for both simple and five-way sorting tasks. The system's probability scores stayed well matched to real outcome rates, a trait doctors need before trusting risk numbers. Its small size suits clinics running on modest hardware. The work gives later teams a benchmark for automatic tracing analysis that stays honest about doubt.
pmc-13420137:
Natasha Noel-Barker and colleagues test a standing ultrasound method for measuring the height of the foot's inner arch, a posture marker tied to injury risk. Common ways to judge arch height rely on feel, rulers, or radiation images, each with limits. Their test-retest study ran two cohorts of physically active adults, one of 16 people in 2023 and one of 30 people in 2024.

A novel standing ultrasound platform scanned the arch bone position while weight rested on the foot. Palpation measures, foot length standards, joint motion, and a foot posture score were collected beside the scans. Repeat scans judged whether the method gives the same answer twice, the core promise in the title. A reliable bedside arch measure could sharpen rehab targets without imaging suites.
pmc-13420237:
Zhao and a large team examine in 2026 how nurses' shift work patterns relate to having anxiety and depression together. Rather than counting shifts alone, they looked for natural groupings in how nurses actually work.

Drawing on a Chinese occupational health cohort, the study grouped 2,791 shift-working nurses into three patterns using their survey answers and standard anxiety and depression questionnaires. The largest group worked fewer shifts but had long seniority; the smallest worked frequent shifts with long seniority. Compared with the low-frequency, low-seniority group, the low-frequency, high-seniority group faced clearly higher risks of anxiety, depression, and both together. The frequent-shift, high-seniority group carried the highest risk of all. Sleep quality did not change these links, so the authors suggest tailoring mental health support to each shift pattern.
pmc-13420337:
Matthew Wyke and colleagues describe a kidney transplant patient whose joint attacks turned out to be calcium crystal arthritis tied to his anti-rejection drug. Tacrolimus can drain magnesium from the body, a shift linked to crystal flares in other transplant groups. This patient suffered severe, repeated attacks across several joints while his transplanted kidney worked well.

X-rays of the shoulder, wrist, and both knees showed the chalky cartilage deposits typical of the condition. Joint fluid came back sterile with a white cell count of 33,300 in the reported measure and crystals visible inside it, settling the diagnosis. The authors call the link underrecognized, since joint pain in transplant patients is easily blamed on infection or gout. A crystal check could spare patients rounds of needless antibiotics.
pmc-13421237:
Anna-Lisa Cohen and Nicholas Buttrick ask, in a 2026 study, whether reading fiction in early adolescence shapes how vividly people later imagine their own future. Both story reading and future thinking rely on building imagined scenes, so the authors suspected a lasting link.

Participants pictured an average day ten years ahead, and the researchers measured their mental flexibility, their tendency to become absorbed in stories, and how much fiction they had read in middle school. Heavier adolescent fiction reading, especially stories opening onto unfamiliar worlds, predicted greater flexibility and absorption in adulthood. Both traits, in turn, were tied to future images that felt more vivid and more under personal control.
pmc-13421337:
Abraham and a large engineering team reported in 2026 a silicon quantum processing unit with digital control. Quantum computers need many qubits, the basic units of quantum information, that can be built at factory scale. Their unit joins a custom cryogenic chip that generates control signals, a dense superconducting ribbon cable, and a low-noise silicon qubit chip. The qubit chip holds a three-rail array of 54 quantum dots that can host up to eighteen exchange-only qubits.

Single-qubit and entangling operations on the system beat prior exchange-only results by about tenfold on key quality measures. The team also ran a distance-five repetition code and a distance-two error-detecting code, two schemes that catch quantum errors. The authors argue this split solves a wiring bottleneck for larger machines.
pmc-13421537:
Wenqiang Yan and seven colleagues tackle, in a 2026 paper, a practical barrier for brain-computer interfaces that read flicker responses from the back of the head. Such systems normally need electrodes over the visual cortex, which is impossible for some patients — for instance those lying flat or with head injuries — who may need communication most.

Their network, DSTF-Net, reconstructs the visual-area signal from forehead electrodes alone. A dynamic reconstruction scheme, three parallel frequency streams fused by attention, staged training and a neurophysiology-shaped penalty combine in the design. Trained on one healthy person's paired recordings, the model transferred to twenty new users, including eight brain-injured patients lying supine. The authors report accurate decoding from frontal signals only.
pmc-13421837:
Wirrell and Sullivan present a national expert consensus on handling drug mixes for Dravet syndrome in the United States, in this 2026 paper. The syndrome is a severe epilepsy starting in infancy. It typically starts between one and twenty months of age in previously healthy babies. Its seizures resist standard drugs. That forces clinicians into long-term polytherapy, several drugs at once.

Every added drug interacts with the others and with the child's development. So the consensus distills printed evidence and frontline know-how into practical principles. These cover choosing, sequencing, and pruning mixes. Its recurring theme is holistic balance. Seizure control must be weighed against sedation, behavior, appetite, and family burden. Chasing seizure counts alone is not enough. The document aims to standardize choices that currently vary widely between centers. It also gives general neurologists a specialist-informed framework for a rare, high-stakes condition.
pmc-13422637:
Yuma Inui leads a nine-author team reporting, in a 2026 case study, a four-year-old boy whose Kawasaki disease announced its persistence in an unusual place. Kawasaki disease inflames blood vessels in young children. It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease among them. Aneurysms form while inflammation burns, and doctors lack reliable signs that it is still active.

The boy improved on first treatment, then relapsed with fever and groin pain. A second round of immunoglobulin settled the fever, and that same day his right scrotum reddened and swelled — ultrasound showed fluid, with blood flow intact. Heart scans then revealed medium aneurysms in both coronary arteries. The scrotal signs cleared within a month. The authors propose them as a clue to ongoing activity.
pmc-13422937:
Nihaal Rahman leads a nine-author team examining, in a 2026 Japanese survey study, whether children of single mothers ate worse than classmates during the COVID-19 emergency. Parents of fifth and eighth graders in a nationwide sample from December 2020 recalled diet across three periods: before the April 2020 state of emergency, while it lasted, and once it ended.

Poor dietary quality meant missing at least one of four food groups — dairy, protein foods, vegetables, fruit — at the twice-daily bar. Among 1,534 parents, single-mother households showed a clearly higher risk of poor diet during and after the emergency, gaps of roughly thirteen and eight percentage points before adjustment. The difference survived adjustment for finances and cooking skill. The authors flag single-mother families for food support in crises.
pmc-13423437:
Fumihiko Nakamura and three colleagues report two cases where underwater endoscopic mucosal resection rescued an uncertain result after cold snare removal of early colorectal cancers. In both patients the removed tissue proved to be well-differentiated cancer, yet its side and deep margins could not be judged, leaving open whether cancer remained behind.

The first patient, a 70-year-old woman, had an 8 mm lesion in the descending colon; the second, a 60-year-old man, had a 6 mm rectal lesion. The team safely re-treated each scar with the underwater technique, which lifts tissue without injection. Pathology on the new specimens found no leftover cancer in either case, supporting the method as a salvage option.
pmc-13423937:
Mavrommatis and co-authors review where surgery stands for medial ulnar collateral ligament injuries, in this 2026 article. The ligament is the elbow band infamous among pitchers and other overhead throwers. Injuries have climbed over two decades, especially in adolescents. Technique has also evolved beyond the classic reconstruction called Tommy John surgery.

The review weighs four strategies. One is direct repair reinforced with an internal brace. A second is traditional reconstruction using a tendon graft. A third is reconstruction plus bracing. The fourth is revision surgery after a failed first surgery. Reconstruction remains the gold standard. But the authors find augmented repair and augmented reconstruction showing promising return-to-sport results. That holds in properly chosen patients. Their through-line is individualization. Keep native tissue when the tear pattern allows. Restore anatomy. Match the surgery to the athlete's age, tear location, and demands.
pmc-13424337: Correction: Sun and colleagues correct their 2015 paper on an FSP1-positive fibroblast group that supports the thymus gland's epithelial cells as they maintain and regrow the organ. In one figure panel, the fluorescent image showing FSP1 in a control mouse group was unintentionally duplicated from the untreated group. The notice supplies the corrected figure. It covers the thymus injury and recovery experiment, the recovery of thymus weight, and the return of epithelial cell subsets after treatment. No other part of the article changes.
pmc-13424537:
Éadaoin Whelan and six colleagues systematically review group-based treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder, asking not just whether it works but for whom. Groups are cheaper and easier to reach than one-to-one therapy. Shared membership and stigma might help or hinder, though. The review therefore set out to test trauma type and group fit as moderators.

Searches run in 2023 and refreshed in 2025 sifted 8,256 records down to forty studies, twenty-three of them randomised trials, covering group cognitive behavioural therapy, counselling, psychodynamic work, and more. Eligible groups needed at least three members and five sessions, with symptoms measured before and after. The synthesis also examined whether studies even reported the social identity factors their questions depend on.
pmc-13425937:
Akiko Eguchi and colleagues searched blood vesicle microRNAs for a test separating ME/CFS from look-alike fatigue conditions in a 2026 biomarker study. Myalgic encephalomyelitis and chronic fatigue syndrome overlap clinically with long COVID, idiopathic chronic fatigue, and depression, and no firm molecular marker exists. Vesicles from six patients with ME/CFS, six with idiopathic fatigue, and eight with depression underwent flow cytometry, particle tracking, and full microRNA profiling.

Comparing tiny groups is exploratory, yet distinct vesicle RNA patterns could point both to a diagnostic signature and to disease mechanisms. A validated blood test would spare patients years of exclusion-based diagnosis. Small group size is a clear limit here, and the team frames the work as a first step that needs a far larger test to stand firm.
pmc-13427137:
Liu and colleagues paired data mining with theory to design a better catalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction. That is the sluggish step that limits hydrogen production in acidic water electrolyzers. Mining 718 past catalysts showed multi-metal ruthenium oxides beating single-metal versions. Median overpotentials were 210 versus 283 millivolts in the dataset.

Modeling screened 20 options and singled out vanadium. So the team made vanadium-doped ruthenium oxide for testing. The compound reached an ultralow overpotential of 193 millivolts at the benchmark current density. It stayed stable for 3,000 hours of operation. In a real electrolyzer it delivered factory-scale current at only 1.725 volts. It also ran 140 hours at working load. Vanadium played a dual role. It created acid-like ruthenium sites that speed proton removal. It also shielded ruthenium against over-oxidation.
pmc-13427237:
Fernández‐Niño and colleagues presented in 2026 a design framework for synthetic biology that uses groups of microbes rather than a single engineered species. Such groups can split metabolic work, act in step, and stay more robust than one strain alone. The authors compare the task to conducting a symphony, where many parts must stay coordinated in time and space for the whole to work.

Fernández‐Niño sets out four layers of coordination: communication between species, timing control, ecological structure, and predictive modelling. The blueprint helps designers choose and combine these layers to fit a goal, drawing on signals between species, rhythmic control, and live monitoring. It also faces hard limits, such as drift in population shares, hard-to-move chemicals, and uncertain model values. The modular plan aims to guide stable consortia for industry, environmental cleanup, and therapy.
pmc-13427337: Lee and Jang published a correction in 2026 to their cross-sectional study of digital literacy, trust, and willingness to share patient-generated health data among Korean internet users. The notice fixes a single error: the corresponding author's affiliation. It should list the Department of Medical Device Engineering and Management at Yonsei University College of Medicine in Seoul as a second affiliation, replacing the Future Medicine Research Center address printed before. The corrected article has been resubmitted to the journal's repositories, and no findings were changed.
pmc-13427437:
Chiemela Ohanele and Jennifer Q. Kwong offer a 2026 plate reader protocol for measuring breathing of mitochondria in embryonic mouse hearts. Studying heart development is limited by tiny tissue amounts, and their fluorescence-based assay needs only one embryonic heart per measurement. Steps cover heart isolation, plate setup, signal acquisition, normalization, and conversion of readings into oxygen consumption rates.

Real-time respiration data from such small samples open metabolic study of congenital heart disease models at developmental stages previously too small to assay. The method adapts a commercial oxygen consumption kit for developmental biology laboratories. One small heart per well is all the test asks, which suits pups whose hearts are no bigger than a grain of rice at that age.
pmc-13428037:
Kou and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 66-year-old man who kept raising his own cholesterol drug dose. He took atorvastatin at eighty milligrams daily for two weeks, four times his prescribed dose, without medical advice. He arrived after fainting, and heart tracings showed sinus arrest, where the heart's natural pacemaker pauses, with only a backup rhythm keeping him alive.

Tests also showed acute liver and kidney dysfunction, disturbed salts, and clotting problems. Inflammation markers were high, while other common causes were not supported. Temporary pacing and supportive care restored his organs, but the sinus arrest persisted, so a permanent pacemaker was implanted. A year later his own rhythm had partly recovered, though the device still worked about a fifth of the time at gentler settings. The authors urge warning patients never to self-adjust statin doses.
pmc-13428737:
Camargo and colleagues test whether sensors worn in the ear can estimate energy expenditure, the calories burned, during outdoor walking. Wrist devices dominate the market, yet the ear sits near the body's core and barely moves. Their 2026 study fits twenty four adults with two in ear sensor models. The sensors record heart rate and motion. Participants walk on a treadmill and outdoors: uphill at ease, downhill, and uphill fast. A portable gas analyzer gives the energy cost.

Models trained on each person's lab data were applied to that person's outdoor walks, a person tuned approach. Both ear sensors showed promise for predicting outdoor energy use. The best model combined heart rate, motion, and biological sex, which suggests ear data carry more than step counts. The authors call it a feasibility step. Larger, less tuned tests must follow before earbuds can claim a place in energy tracking.
pmc-13429137:
Zhang and colleagues studied in 2026 brain activity changes in thyroid eye disease with restrictive myopathy, where swollen eye muscles trap the eye and limit its movement. Forty-five patients took part, 28 with the restrictive form and 17 without. The team measured resting brain signals and eye muscle sizes, then compared the groups and hunted for links between brain and eye measures.

Zhang found the restrictive group had higher eye pressure, thicker lower eye muscles, and worse scores on a disease-specific quality of life scale. One brain area, the left middle temporal gyrus, showed stronger resting activity. Its connections to a movement region at the back of the brain and to frontal areas on both sides were also stronger. These brain measures tracked eye deviation, bulging, and muscle size. The authors frame the pattern as the brain adapting to a trapped eye.
pmc-13430437:
Chengpeng Wang and colleagues reviewed what is known about fats from cell membranes and the signals they send during sepsis, a severe reaction to infection that can harm many organs. Their 2026 review pulls together work on how these signals shape swelling, immune action, and cell death. Sepsis still lacks drugs aimed at its root causes, so new targets draw strong interest.

The review traces three routes that break down the fat into many signal molecules. Some of these signals raise harm by widening leaks in blood vessels and adding stress inside tissues. Others seem to guard organs such as the heart, lungs, liver, and kidneys. Blocking the harmful routes or holding the helpful signals steady may guide future drugs and tests.
pmc-13430637:
Adolfsson and Seppälä report from the 2026 symposium of the Nordic Association for Clinical Physics, held in Gothenburg, Sweden. The meeting ran from March 24 to 26. Its theme was collaboration and future challenges. The triennial meeting drew medical physicists from four fields. These were radiotherapy, radiology, nuclear medicine, and magnetic resonance. Attendees surveyed emerging technology and its move into Nordic practice.

An opening on history traced the group from its 1962 founding. It covered a twelve-year dormancy and the 2004 revival. The opening also noted early Nordic work that fed into international dosimetry standards. Artificial intelligence led the forward-looking sessions, but with a changed tone. Earlier symposia debated methods. The 2026 meeting focused on implementation and rollout. Plenary talks covered the physicist's role beside AI. The report's recurring message casts the medical physicist as directly serving safe patient care. The role is not only a technical specialist.
pmc-13431437:
Han-Xing Li and co-authors ran a small crossover trial in 2026 of bright light care for sleep trouble in people with Parkinson's disease. Sleep faults strike most such patients, yet how light care may help the brain stayed unclear. Twenty-seven patients took both a month of strong light and a month of dim light, in mixed order, with a month of rest between rounds.

Strong light cut daytime sleepiness scores more than dim light did. It also lowered a sleep fault in which muscles stay tense during dream sleep. Brain scans at rest showed no clear shift in local activity or in links between watched areas after strong light. The authors read the sleep gains as real but early, with the brain path still unmapped, and they call for larger trials.
pmc-13431637:
Simon A Fromm and Simone Mattei presented a guided setup tool in 2026 for low-dose imaging on frozen-sample electron microscopes, built to work inside a widely used control program. Such microscopes now gather huge streams of sharp data for single-particle work and for views inside cells. Yet setting safe low-dose terms by hand stays a skilled, slow chore.

Beam strength, zoom, focus offset, and camera terms all shift with the machine and with the task at hand, from quick screening to full data runs. Shared labs add strain, since users arrive with wide gaps in skill. The guided flow walks each user through the same set steps, which speeds setup and keeps terms even across visits. The authors frame the tool as a way to make first-rate imaging more routine.
pmc-13432837:
López Ortíz and colleagues report a 2026 study of respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, in older adults in Mexico.  The team searched the national surveillance system for lab-confirmed cases from 2015 through 2023 and mapped patterns by age, illness, place, and time.

Of 7,958 confirmed cases at all ages, about one in eleven occurred in adults aged 50 or older. Six in ten of those patients were women, and over half had more than one long-term condition, most often high blood pressure and diabetes. About one in eight of the older patients died, a fatality share far above that in younger groups. Cases peaked in 2019. The numbers argue for RSV prevention aimed at older adults.
pmc-13434637:
Jiyao Han and coauthors forge crowded alcohol molecules with exact shape control in 2026. The targets carry three phenyl rings near one carbon, a layout prized in drug design. Crowding makes twin shape centers hard to set at once. A copper catalyst sorts a mixed starting pair as the reaction runs.

Both shape centers form with strong control across many variants. Later steps turn the products into a known anti tuberculosis drug and into shape twins of a second drug. Models show the catalyst coat plus weak contacts lower the energy hill. The route gives drug chemists a flexible path to dense targets.
pmc-13435637:
Masaru Usui and coauthors speed up drug resistance checks for a cattle germ in Japan in 2026. Mycoplasma bovis causes udder and lung disease, yet culture tests take about two weeks. Their nanopore method reads four genes tied to resistance in just six hours.

Gene codes from 329 isolates were matched to lab drug thresholds for seven drugs. Clear mutation patterns foretold which drugs would fail. Resistance linked mutations surged in recent isolates versus the 2013 to 2016 set. Macrolide linked changes jumped from 1.8 percent to 43.3 percent. Vets can now pick drugs by gene read the same day.
pmc-13436637:
Carmine Nasta and coauthors count surprise tumors found in an Italian emergency ward across 2023 in 2026. Among 35,081 visits, fifty three neoplastic incidentalomas surfaced on scans done for other complaints. That rate is 1.52 per thousand visits.

Most finds came in women and in patients over sixty five. Gut tumors led at thirty one percent, with lung finds next at twenty three percent. CT scans caught about half of the finds. All cases arrived triaged as non urgent, often for belly pain or anemia. Up to a fifth may lack clear follow up paths, the authors warn.
pmc-13439237:
Andrea Doddi and a large team pin down the fungal weapon that strips leaves from cotton and olive trees, in work published in 2026. Certain strains of the wilt fungus Verticillium dahliae cause heavy leaf drop and yield loss, while kin strains do not. Genome comparisons across strains located a DNA region found only in the leaf-stripping types. That region holds two copies of a gene for a secreted effector protein, a molecule the fungus sends into plants.

Deleting both copies at once stopped disease and leaf drop in cotton and olive. Adding the effector to mild strains made them strip cotton leaves, and purified protein alone caused wilting. The protein folds in a shape new to science, shared across two fungus families. Giant mobile DNA pieces called Starships appear to have carried the gene between lineages.
pmc-13440337:
Gao, Wang, and Xiao test vagus nerve stimulation against sepsis-related lung injury in this 2026 rat study. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, often damages the lungs and drives deaths in intensive care. Electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve is known to calm inflammation, but its downstream mechanism was unclear. The team induced sepsis by a standard abdominal procedure and examined a brain-related protein, proBDNF, in the lungs.

Stimulation significantly eased lung injury, cut inflammatory signals, reduced fluid swelling, and lowered protein leakage into the airways, while also restoring barrier-related genes. Sepsis had sharply raised lung proBDNF, and stimulation suppressed it; cutting the nerve raised it further, and blocking a cholinergic receptor weakened the benefit. Forcing proBDNF up in the lungs largely undid the protection, identifying it as a key effector.
pmc-13441237: Fan and Xie comment on a Global Burden of Disease analysis of reflux, peptic ulcer, and gastritis care quality from 1990 to 2021. They praise the scope. But they caution that the quality-of-care index is built from outcome ratios. It is not built from process measures, such as endoscopy access or Helicobacter pylori testing. So quality comparisons across health systems at different development stages may mislead. They also note that striking improvements in some low-income countries could reflect modeling and data changes, rather than real care gains.
pmc-13441337:
Pasche Koo and colleagues report a 31-year-old man who developed severe allergic contact dermatitis from wintergreen essential oil, Gaultheria procumbens, inside a compounded herbal ointment prescribed for a sprained ankle. Two days after starting it, an acute eczematous reaction erupted where the ointment touched, on the applying palm, and in both elbow and knee flexures.

Patch testing produced an extremely strong, triple-plus reaction to the ointment itself on days two and four of the readings. Ingredient-by-ingredient testing isolated the culprit: only the Gaultheria procumbens oil reacted, strongly even at 1 percent dilution, while five control patients showed no reaction to it. Tests on its component chemicals methyl salicylate, salicylaldehyde, and benzyl salicylate were all negative, pointing to another constituent of the whole oil. He also reacted to colophonium, balsam resin, fragrance mix, and lanolin, and a similar ointment had caused dermatitis three years earlier.
pmc-13442637:
Ekaterina Oleinik and colleagues test how pull patterns shape lab-grown tendon tissue in a 2026 study. Tendons heal poorly and lack good lab models, so the team grew 3D tendon tissue from tendon cells in a custom pull machine. One set of tissues sat under steady pull, while the twin set took pull in cycles.

Cycled pull raised three growth marks, Col1, Tnmd, and Sparc, past the levels in steady-pull tissue. Cells in cycled tissue also stretched long and lined up with the pull path. The authors read cycle pull as a push toward mature tendon form, closer to how real tendons work in the body. Their setup gives labs a shared bench for testing how dose and rhythm of pull steer tendon growth, a step toward better repair plans.
pmc-13442737:
Devaki Kalvapudi and colleagues describe sleep-drug care for a cesarean birth in a woman with Ellis-van Creveld syndrome in a 2026 case report. The rare gene state brings short stature, bone oddities, face and tooth traits, plus heart defects in many who carry it. The patient was 23 years old, pregnant, and set for a repeat cesarean.

Heart, airway, spine, and lung checks came first, since each one can sway the drug plan in this syndrome. The team chose a spinal block over a full sleep path, which kept her airway untouched and eased stress on her heart. A strong local drug gave full surgical numbness, and her blood flow stayed steady through birth and recovery. The authors urge case-by-case plans for rare bone states at birth.
pmc-13443037:
Benjamin Leahy and colleagues review water-pressure therapy for joint pain in a 2026 scoping paper. The method, hydrodissection, uses ultrasound-guided fluid to free stuck tissue near joints. Their search covered four databases and the past 15 years of work, with trials, group studies, and case sets all welcome.

From 138 finds, 21 studies passed the screens for close reading. Pain relief and function gains showed for frozen shoulder, outer hip pain, and knee arthritis in those studies. Harm rates stayed low across the set. Yet methods varied wildly, from fluid mixes to shot paths and outcome picks. The authors call the early signs bright but ask for large, strict trials with shared protocols before clinics adopt the method widely.
pmc-13443337:
Arnout Bruggeman and colleagues weigh stool transplants as care for Parkinson disease in a 2026 review. Gut signs often precede shakes by years, and clumped protein shows in gut nerves, which hints the illness may start low. Swapping gut microbes wholesale is the boldest way to reset that crew.

The review blames much of the clash on method drift: donor picks, prep steps, dose paths, and outcome sets vary trial to trial. Stool swaps also demand strict control at each step to stay safe. The authors sketch tighter trial designs and next-wave microbe goods. Their aim is a fair test of gut care for a brain illness.
pmc-13443937:
Zhenyu Wang and colleagues turn social media chatter into cues for 3D design in a 2026 paper. Posts brim with taste and style wishes, yet their loose, emotive shape reads as noise to design tools. Their frame, CoX-3D, inserts a mediation layer that turns social counts into rendering knobs with clear logic.

Tests drew on 60,500 real posts from social feeds. Stable taste patterns, once pulled out, cut shape rebuild error by more than 50 percent in their runs. Match to the target sense, read by CLIP scores, rose by 13.1 percent with those patterns in play. Factor maps split which cues steer shape and which steer style. The authors cast social text as a modelable design resource.
pmc-13445237:
Nathazsha Gande and colleagues track a gene switch during a rare cell change in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, where a glial cell turns into a neuron, published in 2026. The gene, cki-1, helps hold cells out of division, so its level may mark steps in the change. The authors map when the switch eases as the new neuron takes shape.

Working in the worm's tail sense organ, the team timed the change across late larval stages into adulthood. In males, cki-1 activity fell between forty and fifty hours after hatching as glial shape gave way to neuron traits. In hermaphrodites, the same cells kept strong cki-1 activity and stayed glial. The timeline gives later studies a firm frame for probing how one cell type becomes another.
pmc-13445837:
Songlang Liu and colleagues report a seventeen-year-old student whose ankle dislocated backward and inward during a basketball game, with no broken bone, published in 2026 with a review of past cases. Pure ankle dislocations of this kind are vanishingly rare, since the joint is built stable, and most stem from violent injury. A low-energy sports twist makes the case stand out.

Doctors reset the joint at once under local numbing and vein pain relief, then held it in a splint and later a walking boot. Scans confirmed a clean reset, no hidden fracture, and no vessel harm, and feeling and movement stayed intact. At one year he had full function back, with school and sport resumed without limits, which supports hands-on care over surgery here.
pmc-13446037:
Yupeng Qi and colleagues turn mung bean protein into thread-like fibrils and use them to build a calcium-set emulsion gel that works as ink for 3D food printing, in a 2026 study. Plant inks that flow under pressure yet snap back into shape are scarce. Plain mung bean protein gels too weakly for printing, so the fibril form was the bet.

Acid and heat drew the protein into worm-like fibrils, confirmed under the microscope. With calcium added and heat applied, the emulsion set into a self-standing gel that held more than ninety percent of its water. Flow tests showed the thinning under pressure and firm recovery that printing needs, and printed shapes held their form. The work opens a path to custom printed foods from plant protein.
pmc-13447237:
Kabirullah Lutfy and Marcelo López edit a 2026 collection on stress, brain peptides and alcohol use disorder. Few medicines exist for the disorder, and current ones curb drinking and relapse only modestly. One review covered here examines how two peptides interact in a thalamus hub and may drive stress-linked craving after long alcohol use. A mouse study tests whether a pain-related peptide in another brain hub fuels anxiety during early abstinence, using tools that switch specific cells on or off. Rat work shows blocking either of two peptide receptors blunted stress-triggered return to alcohol seeking. The editors present such circuits as promising ground for relapse prevention research.
pmc-13447737:
Dookhuu and colleagues charted in 2026 how the diets of South Korean primary school children changed between 2007 and 2022, using a long-running national health survey. Children's eating shapes lifelong health, and Korea's food culture has shifted fast. The analysis covered more than ten thousand children aged six to twelve, whose one-day food records were grouped into patterns.

Three patterns emerged: a rice-based pattern, a flour-based pattern of breads and noodles, and a varied, diversified pattern. Over the study years the rice pattern shrank from well over half of children to about a third, while the varied pattern grew to nearly half. Flour-pattern children were older, skipped breakfast more, and moved less. Rice-pattern children came more often from poorer homes, and the varied group had the most favorable home habits.
pmc-13448037:
Kotheeranurak and colleagues published a 2026 proposal for a registry built for keyhole spine surgery. Endoscopic spine surgery, done through tiny cuts, has spread fast worldwide. Standard spine registries miss the fine technique details this surgery creates. The team studied global registry models to design a better fit.

Extra modules cover imaging checks and surgeon learning curves under tight governance. Patient-reported outcomes, gathered on phones, track recovery from the first days onward. The authors offer the plan as an add-on to existing registries, not a rival. A shared dataset would let surgeons compare results fairly across countries.
pmc-13448237:
Min Hee Lee comments in 2026 on deep learning reconstruction for a special MRI method that pictures bone in spinal arthritis. Zero echo time MRI yields CT-like bone images without radiation, yet its low signal makes subtle joint damage hard to see. A study covered here tested whether artificial intelligence denoising could lift the method past standard MRI sequences for sacroiliac joint lesions.

Fifty-two joint scans from twenty-six patients were read by three readers against CT as the reference. Full-strength reconstruction gave the best image quality for two readers and the clearest lesion visibility for all. Best accuracy for bone hardening sat at mid-strength settings, while erosion detection peaked at full strength across readers. Tuning denoising strength to the lesion sought, and perhaps to body region, is the practical lesson Lee draws.
pmc-13448337:
Jain presents in 2026, as abstract MMDA-19, a national database study of breast cancer that has spread to the brain. It asks whether brain-only spread behaves differently from brain spread accompanied by metastases elsewhere, and whether the answer depends on the cancer's molecular subtype.

From the SEER registry's records of nearly thirty-seven thousand patients with newly metastatic breast cancer between 2010 and 2022, about twenty-seven hundred had brain metastases at diagnosis. Roughly eighteen percent of those had brain-only disease. Brain-only patients lived longer overall, a median of thirteen months against eleven. The gap was dramatic in one subtype: HER2-positive, hormone-negative patients with brain-only disease survived a median of twenty-nine months against eleven with wider spread. Triple negative brain-only patients also benefited modestly, while hormone-sensitive HER2-negative patients showed no difference. Surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy each added survival within the brain-only group.
pmc-13449337:

pmc-13456937:

pmc-13459537:

pmc-13469837:
