Factory reformers never forgave the claim, and the phrase last hour followed Senior for life. The letters made him the workers' enemy and the manufacturers' friend in the public mind. Historians still cite them as political economy's most notorious intervention in a live fight, a warning of what a neat theory can do in rough politics.
the-garden-of-allah-pg3637: Robert Hichens's The Garden of Allah blooms in the Sahara. A runaway monk and a lonely heiress find love in the desert. The exotic romance swept readers off their feet. Passion under the African sun.
the-merry-wives-of-windsor-pg2237: Falstaff gets his comeuppance in this Windsor edition: the Merry Wives lure the fat knight into the buck-basket, the fairy disguise, and Herne's Oak. Mistress Ford and Mistress Page teach the would-be seducer a lesson. Shakespeare's only purely English comedy, broad and joyful.
the-phrenological-journal-and-magazine-o: The Phrenological Journal and Magazine of Moral Science, 1837. The moral journal. This book preserves that periodical. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
tob-0037:
A requester report dated November 26, 2010 lists search results from the CIA's CHAOS database. Operation CHAOS was the agency's domestic spying program of the Vietnam era, run against American dissenters. The report is an inventory, in the agency's own fields: reference numbers, dates, page counts, and titles.

Entries name files such as briefing papers of the Special Operations Group and the Counterintelligence Staff, the units that ran the program. The list form is dry, but what it inventories is not: a secret index of surveillance at home. Released on request, the report lets researchers map the surviving CHAOS file and order the papers behind the lines.
tob-0137:
George Ripley, canon of Bridlington, stood at the head of English alchemy in the fifteenth century. Three of his chief works stand together here: the Compound of Alchymy, a poem of twelve gates; the Liber Secretissimus; and the Marrow of Alchemy. All rest on verified pre-1930 editions.

Ripley's verse walks the reader through calcination, solution, and the other stages of the Great Work, each guarded by a gate. Kings, serpents, and toads carry the chemical teaching in allegory. Later English alchemists, Ashmole among them, prized him above all native masters. The three works together give the richest surviving taste of medieval English alchemy.
tob-10337:
E. A. Wallis Budge translated the Egyptian Book of the Dead, the collection of spells ancient Egyptians placed in tombs. Its purpose was practical for the dead: guidance through the dangers of the underworld toward eternal life. Papyrus copies were buried with their owners as equipment for the journey.

Scenes include the deceased declaring innocence before forty-two judges while the heart is weighed against a feather. Spells address gods, gates, monsters, and transformations the soul might need. Budge's translation preserves the papyrus texts that made the afterlife seem navigable to Egyptians, and lets modern readers see their hopes and fears in concrete detail.
tob-11037:
Volume one of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, edited in English under A. Cleveland Coxe's direction, gathers the Apostolic Fathers: the earliest Christian writings after the New Testament. Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, and Polycarp appear, along with the Didache, an early church manual. These authors knew, or nearly knew, the apostles' generation.

Letters and treatises show the church of the martyrs thinking aloud about bishops, baptism, and the Eucharist while persecution remained a real prospect. Ignatius writes on his way to execution in Rome. Readers meet Christianity's first century of reflection in its own words, before creeds and councils settled the questions these writers argue fresh.
tob-13137:
Legge's Tao Teh Ching appears here in its plain Gutenberg dress: eighty-one chapters on the Way that cannot be spoken and the virtue that cannot be forced. Without heavy commentary surrounding it, the translation itself carries the reading. Lao Tzu's voice stays terse, paradoxical, and often funny at the expense of the powerful.

Read slowly, the catalog advises, since each verse is a riddle meant to undo the reader's certainties. Scholars cite Legge's version as a standard, but the plain text invites ordinary readers to wrestle directly. Advice on ruling, war, wealth, and contentment keeps turning common sense upside down.
tob-13537:
The Ars Notoria, the Notory Art, is a medieval book of prayers said to come from Solomon. It promises a strange gift: full knowledge of a subject, gained fast, through prayer and ritual. Students and clerks copied it for centuries despite church bans.

The user fasts, confesses, and recites long orations to the Holy Spirit while gazing at marked figures called notae. Done rightly, the art claims to pour grammar, rhetoric, and even theology into the mind. The book stands between prayer book and grimoire, and it shows how deep the hunger for quick learning ran in the Middle Ages.
tob-13837:
Nikola Tesla delivered his famed lectures on experiments with alternate currents of high potential and frequency in 1891 and 1892, before enthusiastic audiences in New York and London. Wireless lamps lit without connecting wires, early forms of the Tesla coil crackled, and demonstrations with his own body carrying high-frequency currents made him a scientific star.

Tesla also aired his dreams of sending power through the earth itself for the whole world's use. The lectures mix careful experimental reporting with showmanship he fully understood. Readers meet the inventor telling of his own magic at the height of his fame, in the years when alternating current was winning its future.
un-ga-res-237:
Israel took its seat at the United Nations under a vote the record files as Resolution 237. The Security Council had judged Israel a peace-loving state, fit and willing to keep the Charter's pledges, and had urged the Assembly to admit it. Israel had declared, without reserve, that it accepts the Charter and will honor it from the day it joins.

The Assembly recalls its own votes of 29 November 1947 and 11 December 1948, on partition and on the refugees. It notes the words of Israel's envoy to the ad hoc team on how those votes would be carried out. Acting under Article 4 of the Charter, the Assembly decides that Israel is a peace-loving state and admits it to membership. The vote passed in May 1949.
un-ga-res-a-69-37:
What nuclear arms do to people, not just to states, drives Resolution A/69/37, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the very first Assembly vote of 1946, and votes of 2012 and 2013 on the same theme. It states grave worry at the peril such arms pose to mankind, a worry that should shape all talks and acts on disarmament.

A shift in the world's grasp of the point is noted with pleasure. The 2010 review of the spread pact voiced deep worry at the ruinous human toll of any use of such arms. Talks at world meets in Norway in 2013 and Mexico in 2014 had dug into that toll. The case against the arms, in this text, is made in terms of flesh and towns, not flags.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 69/37 (2014), 'Towards a nuclear-weapon-free world,' presses for faster implementation of the nuclear disarmament commitments under the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It draws on the treaty's 2010 review conference and on the conferences on the humanitarian impact of nuclear weapons held in Norway and Mexico.

The Assembly insists every treaty article binds its parties at all times. It calls on the nuclear-weapon states to accelerate elimination of their arsenals, with transparency and verification. It urges the treaty's universality. It names India, Israel, and Pakistan as states that should join as non-nuclear-weapon states. It urges the Democratic People's Republic of Korea to abandon its nuclear weapons and programmes. It urges a return to the treaty and safeguards. The resolution voices disappointment at the lack of progress in the Conference on Disarmament. It builds the case, ahead of the 2015 review conference, that disarmament pledges were overdue.
un-sc-res-1037:
Croatia came before the Security Council in Resolution 1037, adopted on 15 January 1996. Croatia and the local Serb community had signed the Basic Agreement in November 1995. It covered Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium. Those lands were to return to Croatian rule in peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates a transitional administration, UNTAES, for twelve months. Up to 5,000 troops will oversee demilitarization within thirty days of full deployment. Civilian staff will build a temporary police force, run services, and organize elections. They will also watch rights, clear mines, and help refugees return. Member states may use close air support to defend the mission if asked.
un-sc-res-1337: Within the United Nations official record, Resolution 1337 is the Security Council text catalogued for 1973. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-137: Judge Sir Hersch Lauterpacht died in May 1960. His death left a vacancy on the International Court of Justice. On 31 May 1960 the Security Council set the election to fill the seat. The vote would take place during the General Assembly's fifteenth session. The decision was adopted without a vote. The short text follows the standard form under the court's statute. It performs that single scheduling act.
un-sc-res-1437:
The Prevlaka observer mission was given its last extension by the Security Council on 11 October 2002. The United Nations Mission of Observers in Prevlaka watched the demilitarized peninsula claimed by Croatia and Yugoslavia. The area had stayed stable and calm. Both sides were making progress in normalizing their relations, including talks on a transitional arrangement for the peninsula.

The Council authorized UNMOP to keep monitoring the demilitarization to 15 December 2002, calling it the last extension of the mandate. The Secretary-General was told to prepare the mission's end by drawing down its staff in stages. The parties had to respect the demilitarized regime and cooperate fully with the observers. The Council welcomed the warming ties between Zagreb and Belgrade. It kept open the option of ending the mission even sooner if the two governments settled the Prevlaka question themselves.
un-sc-res-1537: Resolution 1537, adopted in 2004, is part of the Security Council's continuous numbered record. The collection holds it as a Wikisource transcription of the official UN text. Its paragraphs move from the situation the Council faced to the steps it ordered, the standard path by which a debate in New York becomes action elsewhere.
un-sc-res-1637: Under number 1637, a formal decision of the Security Council is preserved in the record wording from English Wikisource. Resolutions bind together fifteen national positions into one voice, which is why their phrasing is so measured. The entry keeps that measured phrasing entire, letting readers hear the institution speak in its own register.
un-sc-res-1737:
The Security Council turned to Iran's nuclear program in Resolution 1737, adopted on 23 December 2006. United Nations inspectors still could not confirm that the program was purely peaceful. Iran had refused to halt uranium enrichment work as demanded that July. Gaps in knowledge about hidden material and past work stayed open.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council orders Iran to suspend enrichment, reprocessing, and heavy water projects at once. All states must block sales of goods that could feed those programs or missile work. Assets of listed people and firms tied to the program are frozen. A sanctions committee will track compliance. The vote was unanimous, the first sanctions round in a long standoff.
un-sc-res-1937: Security Council Resolution 1937 is held here as a transcription of the official record, sourced from English Wikisource. Its place in the numbered series is its identity in UN citation. The text at that place is complete: the members' stated grounds first, then the operative decisions through which the Council exercised its peace and security powers.
un-sc-res-2337:
Council members took up the Gambia and adopted Resolution 2337 on the Gambia on 19 January 2017. Adama Barrow had won the presidential election held on 1 December 2016. Yahya Jammeh first accepted the result, then rejected it days later. Soldiers seized the election office, and parliament tried to stretch Jammeh's term by three months.

The Council backs the African Union and the West African bloc, ECOWAS, in standing by the election result. It calls on Jammeh to hand power to Barrow by 19 January 2017, as the constitution requires. Gambian soldiers are told to stay calm and serve the elected government. The text matters because regional pressure, backed by the Council, forced a peaceful handover days later.
un-sc-res-237:
Days after the June 1967 war, the Council turned to the people caught in it. On 14 June 1967 it stressed the need to spare civilians and prisoners of war. It said basic human rights must hold even in war. It pointed to the Geneva Conventions of 1949. Those rules govern the treatment of prisoners and the protection of civilians.

The Council called on Israel to guard the safety of people in the areas it had taken. It asked Israel to help those who had fled to return home. It urged all governments in the conflict to respect the Geneva rules in full. The Secretary-General had to track compliance and report back.
un-sc-res-337:
Israeli jets forced down a civilian airliner over Lebanon in August 1973. The plane was Lebanese, leased to Iraqi Airways. Lebanon charged that the seizure broke its sovereignty and threatened civil aviation. On 15 August 1973 the Security Council condemned Israel's act. It found the diversion and seizure violated Lebanon's land and airspace. The act also broke the 1949 armistice and the aviation conventions, the Council said.

The world aviation body was told to weigh this ruling in its safety work. Israel had to stop all such acts at once. If they were repeated, the Council warned, it would consider fitting steps. The vote was unanimous. The incident remains a landmark case on the protection of civil aircraft.
un-sc-res-37: Rules for judging new members were written into the Security Council's own book by Resolution 37, passed on 9 December 1947. A state that seeks a UN seat must send its bid to the Secretary-General. The bid must hold a formal pledge that the state accepts the duties of the Charter. Rule 60 then states the Council's task: judge if the state is peace-loving, and fit and willing to keep those duties, and rule if its bid should be backed.
un-sc-res-837:
Attacks on United Nations troops in Mogadishu drew an armed response order on 6 June 1993. Forces of the United Somali Congress and Somali National Alliance had ambushed UNOSOM II staff on 5 June. Pakistani peacekeepers were among the dead. Radio broadcasts by the alliance had incited the attacks. The Council voiced outrage at the loss of life.

The Council strongly condemned the unprovoked attacks, which it saw as part of a planned drive against the operation. Condolences went to Pakistan and to the families of the fallen. Speed in disarming all Somali parties was again named crucial. The Council restated that the Secretary-General held authority under resolution 814 (1993) to take all necessary measures against those responsible. He was asked to inquire into the incident urgently, above all into the part played by the faction leaders involved. The full and rapid deployment of UNOSOM II's 18,000 troops was urged.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Eastern Slavonia is placed under UN administration by Resolution 1037, adopted on 15 January 1996. The Basic Agreement of 12 November 1995 between Croatia and the local Serb community provided for the region's peaceful reintegration into Croatia. The Secretary-General's December 1995 report set out the operation's design, and the Council stressed human rights for all residents.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council establishes the UN Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium, UNTAES, for an initial 12 months. A Transitional Administrator holds overall authority. The military component, up to 5,000 troops, supervises demilitarization, to be completed within 30 days once the force is ready, and monitors refugee returns. The civilian component builds a temporary police force, runs civil administration and public services, and organizes and certifies elections. Member states may provide close air support in UNTAES's defence.

Lebanon's long-running peacekeeping force, UNIFIL, comes up for renewal on 30 January 2001, at the Lebanese government's request. By then the Council accepted that Israel had pulled its forces out of Lebanon in line with resolution 425, the 1978 text that set the force's core task. What remained was keeping the south calm and helping Lebanon's own authority return.

UNIFIL's mandate was renewed for six months, until 31 July 2001, and its troop numbers were to return to the planned working level by that date. Lebanon was called on to send more of its own soldiers south. Both sides were told to respect the withdrawal line and avoid violence.

This file sits in the Year of Africa, yet its topic is a court seat. Judge Sir Hersch Lauterpacht died on 8 May 1960. He was a famed mind in world law, based in Britain. His death left a gap on the world court bench. Resolution 137 passed without a vote on 31 May 1960.

The Council set the cure for the fall. A ballot would be held at the Assembly's fifteenth session. Both big bodies vote on judges at the same time. The winner would serve just the rest of Lauterpacht's term. His books on law and human rights still shape the field. The text is a brief act of respect, mixed with the plain need to keep the court at full strength.

Resolution 1437 passed by a full vote on 11 October 2002. It winds down a small UN watch team on Croatia's Prevlaka cape. Watchers had kept an eye on this bare strip of land near Dubrovnik since the wars of the 1990s. A UN report that month called the area calm and still.

Croatia and Yugoslavia were mending ties, which the Council cheered. It stretched the team's term one last time, to mid-January 2003. The two states had pledged in 1992 to keep the cape free of troops. A 1996 pact then set their ties on a normal path. Prevlaka was a quiet win for the region, and this text closed the UN file.

Sierra Leone's mission, UNAMSIL, is extended until 30 September 2004 in this text of 30 March 2004. The mission had made good progress toward the benchmarks for winding down. Still, the gains were fragile, above all in the weak state of Sierra Leone's police and armed forces.

The government is urged to build an effective police force, army, prison system, and independent judiciary fast enough to take over law and order from the mission. Stronger control over diamond mining is also demanded. Donors and the mission are encouraged to keep helping, and the Mano River Union states are pressed to resume dialogue for regional peace.

The multinational force in Iraq and the oil-revenue arrangements that support the state are extended on 8 November 2005. Iraq was entering a new phase of its transition. Ahead lay the day Iraqi forces would take full charge of security, and the country's Transitional Government was committed, the text notes, to a federal and democratic country.

The force's mandate is extended, with a review at Iraq's request or by 15 June 2006 at the latest, and an earlier end if Iraq's government asked. The rules channelling oil income into the Development Fund for Iraq under world monitoring are extended until 31 December 2006. The United States is to keep reporting on the force's work on behalf of its member states.

Iran's nuclear programme draws its first Council sanctions in Resolution 1737, adopted on 23 December 2006. The IAEA could not confirm the absence of undeclared nuclear material or activities. Iran had ignored Resolution 1696 (2006). It refused to suspend enrichment-related and reprocessing work. It also refused to cooperate under the Additional Protocol. Six states and the EU were still pressing for a negotiated solution.

Acting under Article 41 of Chapter VII, the Council orders Iran to suspend all enrichment-related and reprocessing activities and heavy-water projects, verified by the IAEA. All states must block supplies of listed proliferation-sensitive items and nuclear-weapon delivery technology. They must stop related technical and financial assistance. They must freeze the assets of the persons and entities named in the resolution's annex. States must also notify a new sanctions Committee of listed persons' travel. The measures are framed to pressure compliance while leaving a diplomatic path open.

Lebanon asked for another year of the United Nations force in its south, and the Council agreed on 30 August 2010. Resolution 1937 concerns UNIFIL, the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon. UNIFIL patrols the area along the Blue Line, the marked border line with Israel. Lebanon's foreign minister had written to request the extension.

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2011, without changes. It voiced deep concern about breaches of the 2006 cease-fire terms. A serious clash along the Blue Line on 3 August 2010 was named in particular, and the Council awaited the force's report on it. All sides were pressed to respect the Blue Line. The text also backed the ban on arms outside state control, and it urged Lebanon's armed forces to take on more duties in the south.

The Gambia's election crisis is addressed by Resolution 2337, adopted on 19 January 2017, the day the term was to change hands. Adama Barrow won the 1 December 2016 election. The result was first accepted by the incumbent, Yahya Jammeh. He then rejected it, seized the electoral commission through the army, and declared a state of emergency. ECOWAS and the African Union stood by the result.

The Council urges all Gambian parties to respect the will of the people and endorses the ECOWAS and African Union decisions recognizing Barrow as President. It requests Jammeh to carry out a peaceful transition and transfer power to Barrow by 19 January 2017, as the constitution requires. It gives full support to ECOWAS action, by political means first. Gambian security forces are told to show maximum restraint and place themselves at the disposal of the elected authorities. An update is due within ten days.

Resolution 237 is a UN Security Council humanitarian appeal issued just after the Six-Day War, adopted unanimously on 14 June 1967. The Council cited the urgent need to spare civilians and prisoners of war further suffering and held that basic human rights must be respected even in war.

The resolution calls on Israel to keep the people of the fought-over areas safe, well, and secure, and to let those who fled return home. It recommends all governments concerned follow the Geneva Conventions on prisoners and civilians scrupulously, and asks the Secretary-General to track implementation. It became a reference point for later arguments over the occupied territories' population.

Israeli jets forced down a civil airliner in August 1973. The plane was Lebanese, leased to Iraqi Airways. It had just left Beirut's skies. Lebanon cried foul at once, in a note to the Council. Both sides were heard. Resolution 337 passed with no dissent on 15 August 1973.

Israel was damned by name for the act. The grab broke Lebanon's rule over its soil, the text says. It broke the 1949 armistice and the 1967 ceasefire texts. It broke the rules that guard civil flight as well. The world air body was asked to weigh the case. Israel got a grave charge: shun all such acts, or face steps to force the Council's word. Lives of crew and guests had been put at risk for a hunt that missed its quarry.

Rules for how states join the United Nations were written into the Council's rule book on 9 December 1947. Resolution 37 adds revised rules on admission of new members to the Council's rules of procedure. A state that wants to join applies to the Secretary-General, with a formal declaration that it accepts the obligations of the Charter. The Council then decides whether the applicant is a peace-loving state, able and willing to carry out those obligations. It forwards a recommendation, or a special report, to the General Assembly.

Uzbekistan's seat at the UN began with this line of 1992. On 29 January, the Council adopted Resolution 737 without a vote. The Republic of Uzbekistan had claimed freedom as the Soviet Union broke apart. That break came at the end of 1991. The new state now sought its own place in the world body.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Uzbekistan. The Assembly did so in March 1992. The bid was one of a swift series that winter and spring. Each former Soviet republic turned itself into a sovereign UN member state. The map of Central Asia took its modern shape in those months.

Resolution 837, adopted on 6 June 1993, answers the ambush that killed Pakistani peacekeepers in Mogadishu the day before. Forces linked to the United Somali Congress had launched premeditated attacks on UNOSOM II personnel. The Council expressed outrage at the loss of life and said such acts directly undermined the effort to restore peace and normal life in Somalia.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council reaffirmed that those responsible for the attacks would be held individually accountable. It authorized the UN operation to take all necessary measures against them, including arrest and detention for prosecution, and demanded that all Somali factions stop attacks on UN and relief personnel. The manhunt that followed reshaped the whole intervention.
wilkinson-manners-customs-ancient-egypti:
John Gardner Wilkinson built the first full English tale of old Egypt in Vol. 1 of Manners and Customs of the Ancient Egyptians, out in 1837. Wilkinson had lived in Egypt for years, drawn its walls, and read its script. Most books then gave kings and wars. He gives homes, dress, food, games, and work: life as it was lived each day.

His draws fill the tome with true scenes. The work taught a whole age how that lost world felt at close hand. All books of its kind since owe it a debt. This tome starts the set.

John Gardner Wilkinson turns to the state in Vol. 2 of Manners and Customs of the Ancient Egyptians, out in 1837. The first tome gave the home life of the land. Here come kings, courts, laws, troops, trade, and the work of priests and clerks. Wilkinson draws on walls he had drawn and texts he could read at first hand in Egypt.

His aim is a whole world, not just its kings. Farms, boats, and pay rolls sit by wars and crowns. The tome is the frame that holds the set's home scenes. It shows a state at work.

John Gardner Wilkinson ends his great survey with faith and art in Vol. 3 of Manners and Customs of the Ancient Egyptians, out in 1837. Gods, rites, death, and the tomb fill the first half. The next half turns to paint, carve work, build craft, and the tools of each trade in the land of the Nile in its prime.

Wilkinson writes as one who dwelt there and drew all he saw. The set as a whole founds the theme in English. No work of its age gives so full a world. This tome crowns it with the soul's side.
